With no contract signed, the owner should first weigh other options, such as an interpretable model or a service that explains each score. A vendor promise, option A, is the runner-up: it may help later, but a promised feature is not evidence the requirement will be met.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor could close the gap. But a promise of a future feature is not evidence the requirement will be met when vessels are prioritized.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because people can explain decisions. But reasons written afterwards may not reflect what drove the model's score, so vessel operators would get explanations that are not the model's.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it lets the project proceed. But requirements come before technology; dropping one to fit a preferred model reverses the order.

tips: Eliminate: D drops a requirement to fit the technology, and C has inspectors supply reasons that may not reflect what drove the model's score.
Final two: B beats A because sourcing must follow the requirement; a vendor's promise of future explanations is not evidence the chosen model can meet it.
Exam cue: when a preferred model cannot meet a stated requirement, revisit the sourcing choice; never bend the requirement to the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.5 (Explainable and Interpretable)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (sourcing follows the requirement: build, buy, fine-tune or hosted options are judged against stated needs before one is chosen). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Fine-tuning a language model
questions.question: A Ghanaian pharmacy regulator will fine-tune a language model once on its approved-medicines list, which changes weekly, to answer pharmacists' approval queries. Which concern should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Pharmacists may not be told a language model writes the answers
options.B: The model may invent medicine names that the list does not contain
options.C: Answers would reflect the list as it stood when fine-tuning ended
options.D: Fine-tuning and hosting may cost more than the business case assumed

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning fixes what a model knows at training time; a requirement for current answers needs a design that reads a maintained source.
questions.pre_read: Read the planned design and the content it covers before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning fixes what a model learned at training time; it does not look anything up later. A list that changes weekly would be out of date within days, so answers about newly approved or withdrawn medicines would be wrong while sounding certain. Invented medicine names, option B, is the runner-up: confabulation is a real risk, but the stem's deciding fact is a weekly-changing list learned once.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disclosure is good practice. But telling pharmacists that a model answers does not make its answers current or correct.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because language models can confabulate. But the stem's deciding fact is a list that changes weekly and is learned once, so stale answers are certain, not just possible.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI projects often overrun budgets. But cost does not affect whether pharmacists get correct answers about approved medicines.

tips: Eliminate: D is a budget question that does not affect answer quality, and A concerns disclosure to pharmacists, not whether the answers are correct.
Final two: C beats B because a list learned once goes out of date within a week; confabulation is real, but the stated fact points to stale knowledge.
Exam cue: fine-tuning bakes knowledge in at training time; content that changes often needs retrieval from a maintained source, not a one-time tune.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (the design must fit the requirement; fine-tuning fixes knowledge at training time, so content that changes often needs a maintained source). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Testing inventory completeness
questions.question: A Kuwaiti petrochemical company's AI inventory lists the AI products department heads said they bought, though its engineers also build their own models. Which source would BEST help the IS auditor find missing AI?

options.A: The IT asset register of approved hardware and software products
options.B: Department heads' signed statements that their survey answers are complete
options.C: The AI governance committee's minutes approving each model before use
options.D: Job logs from the cloud platform used for model training

questions.key_concept: AI inventories built from purchase surveys miss models built in-house; completeness is tested against sources such as training platform logs, not self-reports.
questions.pre_read: Ask how AI can enter the organization without anyone buying an AI product, then find a source that would show it.
questions.correct_explanation: A survey of purchases cannot see models that engineers build themselves, since nobody buys them as products. Job logs from the cloud platform used for training show which models were actually trained and run, an independent source for that blind spot. The IT asset register, option A, is the runner-up: it is independent of the survey, but it lists bought hardware and software, not models built in-house.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is an independent, complete list of software. But it records products the company acquired, not models its own engineers built and trained.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because signed confirmations add accountability. But the same department heads would confirm the same answers; they cannot report AI they do not know about.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because minutes are formal records. But they list only models that went through approval, so they cannot reveal models that bypassed it.

tips: Eliminate: B asks the same department heads to confirm their own answers, and C lists approved models, so it cannot reveal models that bypassed approval.
Final two: D beats A because in-house models are never bought; the asset register lists acquired products, while training job logs show what engineers actually built.
Exam cue: test AI inventory completeness against sources that show how AI really arrives, such as platform logs, vendor updates, network traffic and spending.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-8 (System Component Inventory)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (AI enters unseen through vendor updates and free tools, so inventory completeness is tested against independent sources, not self-reports). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Risk tiers and human approval
questions.question: An Ivorian cocoa trader's AI policy rates any use low risk if a person approves each output, including a model ranking warehouse staff for redundancy. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the low tier, since a person makes each final redundancy decision
options.B: Have the policy owner drop the rule that approval lowers the tier
options.C: Have managers record a reason for each ranking they approve
options.D: Have IT review the ranking model's access controls and hosting

questions.key_concept: Tier AI uses by inherent risk, before controls; a human approval step is a control to judge, not a reason to lower a tier.
questions.pre_read: Read the policy rule and the use it covers before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A person approving each output does not make a use low risk: a wrong ranking can still cost staff their jobs, and approvers may simply accept what the model shows. Tiers follow each use's inherent risk, before any approval step, so the policy owner should drop the rule that approval lowers a tier. Option C, recorded reasons, is the runner-up: it may help review this model, but the rule still under-rates every approved use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a person signs each decision. But approval does not reduce the harm of a wrong ranking, and approvers often accept what the model shows.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because written reasons discourage rubber-stamping. But it treats one model, while the policy rule keeps rating every use with an approval step as low risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff data needs protection. But access and hosting reviews are security checks; they do not correct a tier that ignores impact.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a person's approval lowers the impact of a wrong ranking, and D reviews security, which does not correct how the use was tiered.
Final two: B beats C because the tiering rule under-rates every use with an approval step; recorded reasons may help this model but leave the rule in place.
Exam cue: a human approval step does not make an AI use low risk; tier each use by inherent risk, then judge the approval as a control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.3 (Level of risk management activity set by risk tolerance); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (the AI policy sets risk tiers that scale approval steps to each use's impact; a human approval step does not lower impact). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Committee membership
questions.question: A Mozambican ministry's AI governance committee (two IT managers, one data science lead) approved a model ranking patients for scarce dialysis places; the lead, its builder, abstained. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: No one accountable for dialysis allocation took any part in approving it
options.B: The committee may meet too rarely to approve dialysis models quickly
options.C: The IT managers may lack training in machine-learning methods
options.D: No IS auditor sat on the committee as a voting member

questions.key_concept: High-impact AI uses need approval by people accountable for the decision and its legal duties, not only those who build and run the model.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the approval before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Ranking patients for scarce dialysis is a clinical, legal and ethical decision with direct harm to people, so the approving committee needs the clinical owner and the legal and ethics functions that answer for that harm. With the builder abstaining, only IT approved, and IT judges technical fitness, not whether delayed treatment is acceptable. Machine-learning training, option C, is the runner-up: it would sharpen technical review but add nobody accountable for allocation.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because slow approvals frustrate projects. But meeting more often would not give the committee the people who answer for dialysis allocation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI seems to need technical approvers. But more machine-learning skill would still leave nobody who answers for dialysis allocation approving the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit brings independence. But a voting IS auditor would be approving an AI use that audit must later assess; audit may advise, never approve.

tips: Eliminate: B is about meeting speed, which does not make approvals sound, and D would have the IS auditor approve an AI use that audit must later assess.
Final two: A beats C because technical training adds nobody who answers for dialysis allocation; the committee lacks the owners of the harm, not machine-learning skill.
Exam cue: AI risk is not an IT or data science matter alone; expect those who own the decision and its legal duties to approve high-impact uses.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.1 (Decisions informed by a diverse team); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (data scientists and IT do not own business decisions by default; high-impact uses need approval by those who answer for the decision). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Round 3 review: committee membership put in parentheses. Completeness fix, 4 Nov 2026: key reworded to end a length tie.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Agents across departments
questions.question: A Panamanian shipping agency's AI agent books port services, pays invoices and updates crew rosters in three departments' systems; its inventory entry names no owner. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent's language model may word supplier messages inconsistently
options.B: Each system may log the agent's actions in a different format
options.C: System owners may grant the agent more access than its tasks need
options.D: No one has authority to limit or stop the agent across systems

questions.key_concept: An AI agent acting across several systems needs one named owner with authority over its combined actions; each system owner sees only part.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the agent before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Each department owns one system, but the agent acts across all three, so its combined behavior, such as booking a service, paying for it and changing crews, belongs to no one. Without a named owner, nobody sets its limits, accepts its risks or can stop it. Excess access, option C, is the runner-up: least privilege matters, but each system owner sees only one slice, so no one judges the agent's total power.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because generated messages can vary. But inconsistent wording causes little harm compared with unowned payments and roster changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scattered logs slow investigations. But better logs record what the agent did; they give nobody authority to limit or stop it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because agents often hold excess access. But each system owner grants access for one slice; without an agent owner, nobody judges its total power.

tips: Eliminate: A is a wording issue with little harm, and B improves records of the agent's actions without giving anyone authority over them.
Final two: D beats C because access granted system by system leaves the agent's combined actions unowned; someone must answer for them and be able to stop it.
Exam cue: an AI agent that acts across systems needs its own named owner with authority to limit and stop it, beyond each system's owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (every model and AI-supported decision needs a named owner; an agent acting across systems needs one owner for its combined actions). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Program metrics for the board
questions.question: A Qatari investment group's board AI scorecard shows a model green if it passes most of ten equal checks; two high-impact models are green but overdue for validation. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add live monitoring accuracy for each model with overdue validation
options.B: Have owners of overdue high-impact models attest to their status
options.C: Show any high-impact model red once its validation is overdue
options.D: Have IS audit approve each scorecard before the board sees it

questions.key_concept: AI program metrics must show whether controls over high-impact models operate; equal checks can show a model green while its validation is overdue.
questions.pre_read: Read the scorecard rule and the two models' status before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: Ten equal checks let a high-impact model stay green with its validation overdue, though validation is the check that shows whether a model still performs as data and use change. Showing any high-impact model red once validation is overdue lets the board see whether governance keeps its riskiest AI under review. Live accuracy, option A, is the runner-up: it looks current, but one overall score skips the group-level errors and documented limits validation tests.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because live accuracy looks current. But it is one overall score, not the group-level errors and documented limits that validation tests, and the two models would still show green.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because attestation adds accountability. But owners would attest to the same equal-check status, which still shows the two overdue models green.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit adds independence. But approving management's scorecard would make IS audit part of a control it must later assess; audit recommends and reports, never approves.

tips: Eliminate: D has IS audit approve a report it must later assess, and B has owners attest to a status that still shows the overdue models green.
Final two: C beats A because live accuracy is one overall score that skips what validation tests; turning overdue models red shows whether controls over the riskiest AI operate.
Exam cue: when an AI scorecard weights every check or model equally, ask what it hides about high-impact models; their overdue reviews should show plainly.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.5 (Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (program metrics track whether governance works, such as overdue reviews, owners and incidents, not adoption or attendance). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Completeness fix, 4 Nov 2026: re-angled away from the notes 1B.3 example (an equal-check board scorecard that hides overdue validations of high-impact models). Round 2 fix, 4 Nov 2026: distractors share the stem's terms; runner-up is live accuracy used in place of validation. Round 3 fix, 4 Nov 2026: option A names the overdue validation so the key is not the only option echoing it.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. What program metrics count
questions.question: A Serbian gas utility reports 100% of its AI models validated; for 14 vendor models, validation meant reading each vendor's accuracy report on its own test data. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: The metric may not reflect accuracy on the utility's own data
options.B: The 14 vendor models may lack published model cards
options.C: The vendor reports may lack independent attestation
options.D: The metric may count models retrained since validation

questions.key_concept: A model's accuracy holds only for data like its test data; counting vendors' tests on their own data as validations overstates assurance.
questions.pre_read: Read what the reported figure counts as validation before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's accuracy holds only for data like the data it was tested on. Each vendor tested on its own data, not the utility's meters, customers or use, so counting those reports as validations overstates assurance for 14 models. Independent attestation, option C, is the runner-up: the reports are vendors' own claims, but an attested test on vendor data would still not show how the models perform at the utility.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model cards document a model's limits. But a card is the vendor's own description; publishing one would not show how the model performs on the utility's data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because self-reported tests lack independence. But an attested test run on the vendor's data still says nothing about accuracy on the utility's own data and use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a retrained model is a changed model that needs revalidation. But nothing shows any was retrained, while 14 vendor-data results are already counted.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on model cards, the vendors' own documents, and D assumes retraining that nothing in the facts shows.
Final two: A beats C because attesting a vendor's test does not change its data; accuracy shown on vendor data does not carry over to the utility's own use.
Exam cue: an AI model's accuracy belongs to the data it was tested on; a 'validated' figure needs testing on the organization's own data and use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (metrics must show whether the program works as intended; acceptance of AI output can reflect automation bias rather than quality). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Cross-domain gate fix, 31 Oct 2026: a program metric that counts vendors' own test reports as validations. Round 2 fix, 31 Oct 2026: AI-specific runner-up (retraining) and model-card distractor. Round 3 fix, 31 Oct 2026: AI-specific deciding fact (vendor accuracy measured on vendor data), attestation distractor as the CISA trap, key hedged to match.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Basis for accepting AI risk
questions.question: An Egyptian licensing board's exam face-verification model wrongly rejects candidates aged over 60 three times as often as others; the risk owner accepted it, citing 97% overall accuracy. What is the IS auditor's BEST action?

options.A: Reperform the 97% accuracy figure on recent check-in records
options.B: Report that the acceptance did not weigh harm to older candidates
options.C: Overturn the acceptance and suspend checks for older candidates
options.D: Leave the acceptance alone, since accepting risk is management's call

questions.key_concept: Risk owners choose the response, but an acceptance resting on overall accuracy that ignores harm to one group is uninformed and reportable.
questions.pre_read: Separate who decides the risk response from what the IS auditor checks about that decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk acceptance is the owner's call, but the IS auditor assesses whether it was informed. The 97% overall figure hides that candidates aged over 60 are wrongly turned away three times as often, a harm the acceptance never weighed, so the IS auditor reports it for the owner to reconsider. Reperforming the 97%, option A, is the runner-up: it checks the figure, but a correct overall figure would still hide the harm to older candidates.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reperformance is strong audit evidence. But a confirmed overall figure would still average away the higher error rate for candidates aged over 60.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the harm is clear. But overturning a risk acceptance or suspending the model is the owner's decision; the IS auditor reports and recommends.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because risk acceptance belongs to management. But the IS auditor still assesses whether the acceptance was informed and reports when it was not.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IS auditor overturning a decision that belongs to the owner, and D treats management's right to accept risk as putting its basis beyond audit.
Final two: B beats A because a correct overall figure would still hide the harm to older candidates; the gap is what the acceptance weighed, not the figure's accuracy.
Exam cue: an AI risk acceptance resting on one overall score is uninformed if one group bears more errors; report it and let the owner decide again.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.4 (Negative residual risks documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (the risk owner chooses the response; the auditor assesses whether the assessment weighed harm to the people and groups affected). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Benchmarks in risk ratings
questions.question: A Swiss canton's model translates flood warnings into eight languages; its risk register rates wrong warnings unlikely, citing the vendor's 99.5% benchmark on news articles. Which question should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Whether the translation vendor holds a current security certification
options.B: Whether the 99.5% was measured on the model version now in use
options.C: Whether residents are told that a model translated the warnings
options.D: Whether error rates were measured on warnings like those it sends

questions.key_concept: Likelihood in an AI risk rating needs evidence from the actual use; a vendor benchmark on other text can understate how often errors occur.
questions.pre_read: Read what the register's likelihood rests on before weighing each question.
questions.correct_explanation: A benchmark on news articles says little about flood warnings, which use specialized terms such as evacuation routes and water levels, in languages a news benchmark may barely cover. The likelihood in the register needs error rates measured on the canton's own warning texts. Whether the 99.5% reflects the model version in use, option B, is the runner-up: a current figure on news articles still misses this use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors handle the translations. But security certification says nothing about how often warnings are mistranslated.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a model update can change its accuracy. But a current figure measured on news articles still says little about flood warnings.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disclosure supports trust. But telling residents a model translated the warning does not show how often warnings are wrong.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the risk as a security question and C concerns disclosure; neither shows how often warnings are mistranslated.
Final two: D beats B because a current benchmark on news articles is still not evidence about warnings; the likelihood needs errors measured on this use.
Exam cue: a likelihood rating built on a vendor benchmark needs evidence from the actual use; measure errors on the organization's own texts and cases.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.2 (Treatment prioritized by impact, likelihood and resources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (AI risk is rated by likelihood and impact on people; a rare error can still be a high risk when its harm is severe). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Round 3 review: stem states the rating rests on likelihood alone. Cross-domain gate fix, 31 Oct 2026: likelihood evidence from a vendor benchmark on other text. Round 2 fix, 31 Oct 2026: key reworded to drop the stem echo.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Model confidence as an indicator
questions.question: A Tanzanian revenue authority's model holds suspected fraudulent VAT refunds; its early-warning key risk indicator, the model's average confidence, stayed above 90% after new tax rules reshaped claims. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: An average can hide low-confidence holds that need review
options.B: Confidence is a technical figure the board may not understand
options.C: The model can stay confident while more of its holds are wrong
options.D: Fraud losses prevented would show the model's value more clearly

questions.key_concept: A model's confidence scores are its own estimates and can stay high under drift, so they make a weak key risk indicator for its errors.
questions.pre_read: Read what the indicator measures and what changed before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's confidence is its own estimate, learned from its training data. After the new rules reshaped refund claims, it can keep scoring holds with high confidence while more of them are wrongful, so a steady figure cannot warn of a tolerance breach. Low-confidence holds hidden by the average, option A, is the runner-up: they matter for review, but each hold's confidence has the same blind spot.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because averages hide outliers. But each hold's own confidence is still the model judging itself; it can be high on holds that are wrong.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a KRI must be usable by decision makers. But plainer reporting would not make the figure warn of wrongful holds.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because value matters to management. But fraud prevented is a performance measure; it can rise while wrongful holds climb.

tips: Eliminate: B is about how the figure is presented, not what it measures, and D swaps the risk indicator for a performance measure.
Final two: C beats A because confidence, averaged or not, is the model rating itself; after the new rules it can stay high while holds go wrong.
Exam cue: a model's confidence is not an independent risk signal; prefer indicators drawn from data or outcomes the model does not control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (KRIs show when risk is climbing toward tolerance; when AI errors surface late, a leading indicator must warn first). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Cross-domain gate fix, 31 Oct 2026: model confidence as a weak key risk indicator. Round 2 fix, 31 Oct 2026: key sharpened after a blind ambiguity flag. Round 3 fix, 31 Oct 2026: stem adds the tax rule change that shifted claims, so the deciding fact is drift the confidence figure cannot show.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A claims model's error limit
questions.question: A Brazilian dental-plan provider's data scientists set the maximum wrongful-denial rate for its claims model at 6%, the best rate their models achieved. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have senior management set a tolerance within the risk appetite
options.B: Have the data scientists tighten the limit to 3% and retrain
options.C: Have the IS auditor set the limit from industry benchmarks
options.D: Have the model owner adopt 6% as the claims model's use-level limit

questions.key_concept: AI tolerances express acceptable harm, set by senior management within the board's risk appetite; they are never derived from what a model happens to achieve.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the 6% came from, and who should decide how many wrongful denials are acceptable.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance states how much harm the organization will accept, so senior management sets it within the risk appetite the board approved, instead of deriving it from what the model can do. Setting it at the best rate achieved turns the model's limits into the organization's appetite. Having the model owner adopt 6%, option D, is the runner-up: owners do set use-level limits, but inside a tolerance management has set, not from a capability figure.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a stricter limit sounds safer. But the builders would still be setting the limit; they measure against tolerances, they do not decide them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But setting the limit would mean deciding risk that management owns, which the IS auditor must later assess.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because model owners set use-level limits. But they set them inside a tolerance senior management has approved; adopting 6% still starts from what the model achieved.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the limit with the builders, who should measure against it, and C has the IS auditor setting a limit it must later assess.
Final two: A beats D because an owner's use-level limit must sit inside a tolerance senior management has set; adopting 6% still starts from capability.
Exam cue: a tolerance set to what the model achieves is backwards; tolerances come from appetite, and the model must meet them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (tolerances express acceptable harm, set by senior management within board appetite; they are not derived from what a model achieves). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Shared foundation models
questions.question: A Canadian workers' compensation board finds its claims-review, call-center and fraud-detection vendors, which its continuity plan treats as independent, all use a single hosted language model. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: The vendors' controls reports may not cover the shared model provider
options.B: One provider's outage or update could disrupt three services at once
options.C: Staff may need training on three different vendor interfaces
options.D: The three vendors may give different answers about the same claim

questions.key_concept: AI supply chains run below the direct vendor; several vendors built on one model concentrate failure and change risk in a single provider.
questions.pre_read: Look past the three vendor names and ask what they have in common.
questions.correct_explanation: Three vendors that the continuity plan treats as independent share one dependency. An outage, a withdrawn model version or a silent behavior change at the provider would hit claims review, the call center and fraud detection together, so a plan that assumes one vendor fails at a time would not hold. Controls-report coverage, option A, is the runner-up: it is a real assurance gap, but the concentration exists whatever the reports cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fourth parties often fall outside vendor reports. But better reports would not remove the single point of failure shared by all three services.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because three interfaces add effort. But training cost does not threaten the services the way a shared failure would.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because inconsistent answers confuse injured workers. But inconsistency is a quality issue; a shared provider failing would stop all three services at once.

tips: Eliminate: D is a consistency issue, not a threat to the services, and C is a training cost that does not threaten them either.
Final two: B beats A because a shared model is a single point of failure across three services; better assurance reports would not remove it.
Exam cue: map AI supply chains below the direct vendor; several vendors on one model concentrate risk that contracts with each vendor do not show.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.12 (Value Chain and Component Integration); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.2 (Contingency processes for failures in high-risk third-party data or AI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (AI supply chains run deep; several vendors built on one foundation model concentrate failure and change risk). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Monitoring a vendor's model
questions.question: A Turkish elevator-maintenance firm licenses a vendor's breakdown-prediction model; its only monitoring is a quarterly accuracy report the vendor itself computes, pooled across all clients. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner compare predictions with recorded breakdowns
options.B: Adopt the vendor's newest model version as soon as it ships
options.C: Have the vendor compute results for the firm's own elevators
options.D: Require the vendor to disclose the model's training data sources

questions.key_concept: Buying AI does not transfer accountability; the buyer monitors a vendor's model in its own setting, independently of vendor-produced reports.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced the monitoring evidence and whose elevators it describes.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor's report pools results across all clients, so it cannot show how the model performs on this firm's elevators, and the vendor chooses what to measure. Comparing predictions with technicians' recorded breakdowns gives the owner independent evidence from its own setting. A firm-specific vendor report, option C, is the runner-up: it removes the pooling, but the vendor still computes the measure, so the evidence is not independent.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because newer versions often perform better. But adopting versions untested in the firm's setting adds change risk and does nothing to monitor results.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because results for the firm's own elevators are more relevant. But the vendor still chooses the data and measures, so the evidence stays vendor-controlled.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training-data transparency helps judge a model. But a description of past data does not show how the model performs on this firm's elevators now.

tips: Eliminate: D describes the model's past training data, not its current results, and B adopts new versions without testing them in the firm's setting.
Final two: A beats C because the owner's own comparison is independent of the vendor; a tailored vendor report is more relevant but still the vendor's measure.
Exam cue: vendor reports on a model are inputs; expect the buyer to monitor the model's results in its own setting, independently of the vendor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (vendor reports give the vendor's view; ongoing monitoring adds independent checks of the model in the buyer's own setting). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Round 3 review: vendor computation made explicit in stem and option C.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Shared model features
questions.question: A Peruvian store group's marketing team redefined a shared 'loyal customer' feature for its model without telling anyone; the group's credit-limit and fraud models also use it. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have each model team keep its own private copy of the feature
options.B: Have the credit and fraud teams retrain on the new definition
options.C: Have IT limit who can read data in the shared feature store
options.D: Have a named owner approve changes to the shared feature

questions.key_concept: Shared features are data many models depend on; they need a named owner who approves changes and lineage showing which models use them.
questions.pre_read: Trace who else depends on the feature before judging how changes to it should be handled.
questions.correct_explanation: A feature shared by three models is data they all depend on. Redefining it for one model silently changed what the credit-limit and fraud models score, with nobody accountable for the change. A named owner who approves changes, with lineage showing which models use the feature, lets every affected owner assess a change first. Option A, private copies, is the runner-up: they isolate teams, but leave definitions drifting apart unowned.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because separate copies stop one team's change reaching others. But definitions then drift apart with no owner or lineage, and nobody knows which version each model scores.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the models should match the current definition. But that accepts a change nobody assessed for credit or fraud decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because access control protects data. But the problem is who may redefine the feature, not who may read it.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a change no one assessed for credit or fraud, and C limits who reads the data, not who may redefine it.
Final two: D beats A because an owner who approves changes, with lineage to every model using the feature, lets each model owner assess a change first; private copies drift apart unowned.
Exam cue: shared model inputs need a named owner and lineage to every model that uses them, so one team's change cannot silently alter another's model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (data that models depend on needs a named owner and lineage showing which models it feeds). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Round 3 review: stem states the change was made without telling the other teams.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Licensed training data
questions.question: A Dubai property portal's valuation model was trained on a licensed sales-transactions dataset, and the license ends next month. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important to confirm?

options.A: Whether valuations stay accurate once the dataset is deleted
options.B: Whether the license lets the portal keep its published valuations
options.C: Whether the license lets the portal keep using models trained on it
options.D: Whether the dataset was kept encrypted during the license term

questions.key_concept: A trained model keeps what it learned, so data licenses must permit continued use of models trained on the data, not only its storage.
questions.pre_read: Read what happens when the license ends before weighing each question.
questions.correct_explanation: A trained model carries what it learned from the data, so deleting the dataset does not end the portal's use of that data. Whether models trained on licensed data may stay in use after the license ends depends on the license terms; if they forbid it, the model must be retired or retrained. Keeping published valuations, option B, is the runner-up: it is a real license question, but the model keeps producing new valuations daily.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data loss can affect models. But a model that is already trained does not change when its source data is deleted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because published valuations were derived from the data. But they are past outputs; the larger exposure is the model, which keeps producing new valuations from what it learned.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because licensed data needs protection. But encryption during the term says nothing about whether use may continue after it ends.

tips: Eliminate: D concerns security during the license, not the right to keep using the data, and A assumes deleting the dataset changes a model already trained.
Final two: C beats B because the model keeps using what it learned to value new listings daily; published valuations are past outputs, a smaller exposure.
Exam cue: rights to use data for training must cover the trained model's life, not just how long the dataset is stored.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (rights to use come from contracts and licenses; a trained model keeps what it learned after the data is gone). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Synthetic data from real records
questions.question: A Greek cancer registry plans to share synthetic patient records, produced by a generative model trained on its real records, with outside researchers as non-personal data. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have researchers sign agreements to keep the synthetic records secure
options.B: Test the synthetic records for close matches to real patients
options.C: Encrypt the synthetic records before sending them to researchers
options.D: Strip names and ID numbers from the real records before generating

questions.key_concept: Synthetic data from a generative model trained on personal records can reproduce real people, so it is tested before being treated as non-personal.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the generative model learned from, and whether its output could still describe a real patient.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model trained on real records can memorize and reproduce them, especially rare cases, so synthetic output is not automatically non-personal. Testing the synthetic records for near copies of real patients shows whether sharing them could identify anyone. Stripping names first, option D, is the runner-up: it removes direct identifiers, but a rare diagnosis with an age and a town can still identify a patient.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because agreements bind researchers. But a contract does not settle whether the records identify patients; that needs testing first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because health data needs protection in transit. But encryption protects records on the way, not whether they describe real people.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removing direct identifiers is standard de-identification. But the records are already generated, and rare combinations of diagnosis, age and place remain for the model to reproduce.

tips: Eliminate: C protects records in transit, not whether they describe real people, and A binds researchers without settling whether the data is personal.
Final two: B beats D because removing names leaves rare combinations a model can reproduce; only testing the output shows whether real patients appear.
Exam cue: synthetic data from a model trained on personal data stays a privacy question until tests show it does not reproduce real people.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4 (Privacy Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (de-identified or derived data can still identify people; output from a model trained on personal data needs testing before sharing). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A ferry operator's pricing model
questions.question: A Polish ferry operator answers passengers' data-access requests with their bookings and contact details; its pricing model also scores each passenger's likely willingness to pay. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Passengers are not shown the scores the model infers about them
options.B: Some willingness-to-pay scores may be wrong for individual passengers
options.C: The booking site may not encrypt passengers' card payment details
options.D: Booking history may not be pseudonymized before the model scores it

questions.key_concept: Model inferences, such as scores and profiles, are personal data; privacy duties like access requests must cover them, not only collected records.
questions.pre_read: Read what the access responses contain and what the pricing model does before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: A score the model infers about a passenger is personal data, just like the bookings it was built from. Answering access requests with collected data alone hides the profile the model builds about each person. Pseudonymizing booking history, option D, is the runner-up: it is good privacy by design, but the model would still create a score about each identifiable passenger, and access responses would still leave it out.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wrong scores can mistreat passengers. But accuracy is a separate question; even a correct score is personal data that access responses should cover.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because payment data is sensitive. But card security is unrelated to what the model creates about each passenger.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pseudonymization is privacy by design. But the model would still create a score about each identifiable passenger, and access responses would still leave it out.

tips: Eliminate: C is a payment-security issue unrelated to the model, and B concerns whether scores are right, while even a correct score is personal data.
Final two: A beats D because pseudonymized inputs still yield a score about each passenger; inferred scores are personal data that access responses must include.
Exam cue: follow personal data out of the model as well as in; inferred scores and profiles are personal data, not just the records collected.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (personal data leaves a model through outputs and inferences, so privacy controls must cover what the model infers). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A staff assistant over expiring files
questions.question: An Albanian farm-subsidy agency deletes farmers' applications when their two-year appeal period ends, but its staff assistant answers from a search index built from those applications. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The assistant's answers may weaken once source applications are deleted
options.B: The two-year period may be too short for farmers' appeals
options.C: Indexed text from applications may outlive the deletion of the originals
options.D: Staff may search the index for farmers' details without a business need

questions.key_concept: Retrieval indexes and embeddings hold copies of source text, so deletion and retention schedules must cover them, not only the original records.
questions.pre_read: Read the deletion rule and how the assistant answers before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Deleting the applications removes the originals, but the search index holds chunks of their text, so farmers' personal details stay retrievable after the retention period ends, and the assistant can still quote them. Retention and deletion must reach every AI copy, including indexes and embeddings. Unneeded staff searches, option D, is the runner-up: access limits reduce misuse, but data that should be gone would still be kept.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deleting sources sounds like it would starve the assistant. But the index keeps its own copies, so answers continue, and that is the problem.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retention should match appeal periods. But the agency already keeps applications for the full appeal period; the gap is copies kept after it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because personal data needs access limits. But tighter access would still leave farmers' details stored past their deletion date.

tips: Eliminate: B questions an appeal period that retention already matches, and A expects answers to weaken, though the index keeps its own copies.
Final two: C beats D because access limits control who sees the data but not how long it is kept; the index holds farmers' details past their deletion date.
Exam cue: deleting source records does not delete their copies inside AI indexes, embeddings or caches; retention schedules must reach every copy.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (retention and deletion cover every copy an AI system holds, including retrieval indexes and embeddings, not only the source records). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Reusing fine-tuned models
questions.question: A Lebanese bank's marketing team wants to build its campaign-writing model on a retired chatbot that was fine-tuned on customer service chats. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Encrypt the retired model's files before marketing copies them
options.B: Confirm the chat training set was securely deleted from every system
options.C: Test the retired model's writing on sample marketing campaigns
options.D: Have the data owner decide whether the chats may serve marketing

questions.key_concept: A model can memorize its training data, so reusing a model trained on personal data for a new purpose needs a data owner's decision.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the retired chatbot before weighing each step.
questions.correct_explanation: A model fine-tuned on customer chats can memorize and reproduce them, so building on it carries the chats into a new purpose, marketing. Whether that reuse is allowed is the data owner's decision, with privacy advice, and it applies to the model as much as to the chats. Confirming the chat set was deleted, option B, is the runner-up: deletion removes the source, not what the model learned from it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model files deserve protection. But encryption controls who can read the files, not whether the chats inside the model may serve marketing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deleting source data is a sound retirement step. But the model still carries what it memorized, so the reuse question remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a new use needs a fitness check. But good campaign copy does not settle whether customers' chats may be reused for marketing.

tips: Eliminate: A protects the files without settling whether the reuse is allowed, and C tests writing quality, not whether customers' chats may serve marketing.
Final two: D beats B because the model keeps what it memorized after the chats are deleted; reusing it for marketing needs the data owner's decision.
Exam cue: a model trained on personal data carries that data's purpose limits; reusing the model needs the same decision as reusing the data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.3.2 (Information Extraction)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (models can memorize training examples, so retired models and their files are disposed of like the personal data they learned from). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Cross-domain gate fix, 31 Oct 2026: reusing a model fine-tuned on personal data for a new purpose.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Testing a fairness criterion
questions.question: A French broadband provider's fairness criterion covers ethnic groups, but privacy rules bar collecting ethnicity, so its purchased credit-check model has never been tested against it. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Treat the model as fair since ethnicity is not among its inputs
options.B: Have the owners agree a lawful way to test outcomes across groups
options.C: Rely on the vendor's fairness audit, which covered ethnic groups
options.D: Have the data team infer ethnicity from names to test fairness

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI characteristics can conflict; owners decide and document how to test fairness within privacy limits, since omitting an input does not prove fairness.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each option keeps both fairness and privacy in play, or gives one of them up.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness and privacy are both trustworthy-AI characteristics, and here they pull against each other. The model owners must decide, and record, how fairness will be tested within the privacy rules, for example through a lawful, protected study approved with the data protection officer. The vendor's fairness audit, option C, is the runner-up: it covered ethnic groups, but on the vendor's test data, not outcomes for this provider's customers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model cannot use what it never sees. But inputs such as postcode or employment history can act as proxies, so outcomes can still differ by group.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the audit covered ethnic groups. But it tested the vendor's data, not this provider's customers, and leaves the conflict between fairness and privacy unresolved here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it gives group labels to test with. But guessing ethnicity from names creates sensitive data the rules bar, and the guesses are often wrong.

tips: Eliminate: A treats leaving ethnicity out of the inputs as proof of fairness, though proxies remain, and D creates, by guessing, the sensitive data the privacy rules bar.
Final two: B beats C because a vendor's audit covers its own test data, not this provider's customers; the owners must still find a lawful way to test fairness here.
Exam cue: when two trustworthy-AI characteristics conflict, expect owners to decide and document the balance, not drop one of them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (characteristics trade off, so owners balance and document them for each use; leaving out a sensitive input does not make a model fair). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Round 3 review: key no longer echoes the stem; vendor audit made a stronger runner-up.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Criteria for a companion chatbot
questions.question: A Hong Kong charity's companion chatbot talks with older residents living alone, and some report feeling unwell; the owner's criteria cover accuracy and response time. Which added criterion should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Seeded distress messages reach a staff member within minutes
options.B: The chatbot is retested against the criteria after every model update
options.C: Residents are told plainly whenever they are talking to AI
options.D: Replies arrive within two seconds even at peak evening hours

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI criteria should cover the characteristic most at stake for the people affected; for vulnerable users, safety needs tested escalation.
questions.pre_read: Picture the worst message a resident living alone might send, and ask which criterion would catch it.
questions.correct_explanation: Some residents already report feeling unwell to the chatbot, and for people living alone a missed message about a fall or a crisis could cause serious harm. Safety means the system fails safely, and tests with seeded distress messages show whether a person is alerted in time. Telling residents plainly when they talk to AI, option C, is the runner-up: transparency matters, but a missed emergency would harm residents far more.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model updates can change behavior. But retesting only reruns the existing criteria, which contain no test of how emergencies are handled.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because older residents should know they are talking to AI. But transparency adds less protection than catching an emergency that a resident living alone reports.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because quick replies help residents. But response time is already among the owner's criteria, and speed alone does not get help to someone in crisis.

tips: Eliminate: D repeats response time, which the owner's criteria already cover, and B reruns those same criteria, which still contain no test for emergencies.
Final two: A beats C because a missed distress message could seriously harm someone living alone; transparency matters, but the safety gap carries the greater harm.
Exam cue: match criteria to the characteristic most at stake for the people affected; for vulnerable users, test how the system handles emergencies.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.2 (Trustworthy AI characteristics built into policies and processes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (each characteristic becomes a testable criterion for the specific use, weighted by what is most at stake for the people affected). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. New uses under AI laws
questions.question: A Spanish hotel chain's assistant, rated minimal risk under a risk-based AI law when it only summarized résumés, now ranks candidates for interviews. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Buy a compliance tool that checks the assistant against AI laws
options.B: Have legal counsel reassess its risk class for the new ranking use
options.C: Keep the earlier rating, since the underlying model has not changed
options.D: Have HR test the rankings for bias against groups of candidates

questions.key_concept: Risk-based AI laws classify systems by intended use, so a new use of an unchanged model can bring a higher risk class and new duties.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the assistant does now with what it did when it was classified.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based AI laws classify by intended use, not by technology. Ranking job candidates is a use such laws often treat as high risk, so the earlier minimal-risk rating may no longer hold, and duties such as oversight, documentation and logging could now apply. Counsel must reassess before controls are mapped. Bias testing, option D, is the runner-up: it is a sound control, but which obligations it must meet is not yet settled.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tools track many laws. But a tool cannot make the legal judgment on applicability; governance comes before tooling.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the technology is the same. But risk-based laws classify by use; ranking candidates is a different use from summarizing résumés.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ranking candidates raises fairness risk. But bias testing comes after counsel settles which duties apply, so the right controls can be mapped to them.

tips: Eliminate: C ties the risk class to the model, though such laws classify by use, and A buys a tool before anyone has decided which duties apply.
Final two: B beats D because the new use may carry new legal duties; bias testing is sound, but which obligations apply must be settled first.
Exam cue: under risk-based AI laws, a new use of the same model can change its risk class; reassess applicability before mapping controls.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.4 (Business value or context of use defined or re-evaluated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (risk-based laws set duties by the harm a use could cause, so applicability depends on purpose and is a legal judgment). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Evidence of AI compliance
questions.question: A Czech agricultural-drone maker's compliance tool has a language model read its policies and mark each applicable AI duty as met. Which evidence would BEST support the IS auditor's conclusion on compliance?

options.A: A board resolution adopting the tool as the compliance standard
options.B: A second language model confirming every duty marked met
options.C: Each duty traced to an owned control shown to be operating
options.D: The policy passages the model cited for each duty marked met

questions.key_concept: AI compliance is shown by mapping each applicable duty to an owned, operating control; a model's compliance marks, even with citations, are leads.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model looked at to mark each duty, and whether that shows a control operates.
questions.correct_explanation: A language model's 'met' marks are leads: it judged from policies, which show what is intended, not what operates. Compliance is shown only when each duty maps to a control with an owner and evidence that it operates, such as decision logs the drones keep or tested pilot overrides. The cited policy passages, option D, are the runner-up: they let the marks be checked, but only against documents, not operation.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because board adoption shows commitment. But a resolution adopting a tool shows no control operates for any duty.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a second source's agreement looks like corroboration. But a second model reads the same policies, so it confirms intent, not operation, and may share the first model's errors.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cited passages make the model's marks look grounded. But policies show what is intended; only owned controls with evidence show a duty is met.

tips: Eliminate: A adopts the tool by resolution, which shows no control works, and B has a second model re-read the same policies, which still shows only intent.
Final two: C beats D because the model judged from policies, which show intent; compliance is shown by owned controls with evidence that they operate.
Exam cue: an AI tool's compliance marks are leads; test the chain of duty, control, owner and operating evidence behind each one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (Legal, regulatory and contractual requirements understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (each applicable obligation maps to a control, a control owner and evidence that the control operates; tools only track laws). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Round 3 review: second-model check replaces the legal-opinion distractor.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Widening a summarizer's risk assessment
questions.question: A Norwegian patent office follows the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, yet its generative filing-summary assistant's risk assessment lists only accuracy and drift. Which source should the IS auditor recommend as BEST for widening it?

options.A: The vendor's model card listing the model's benchmark test results
options.B: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework used as the security baseline
options.C: The EU AI Act's list of banned AI practices
options.D: The twelve risks set out in NIST AI 600-1

questions.key_concept: The NIST Generative AI Profile extends the AI RMF to generative AI risks, such as confabulation and information integrity, that predictive-style assessments miss.
questions.pre_read: Read what the assessment lists and what the assistant does before weighing each source.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile applies the AI RMF to generative AI and describes risks a predictive-style assessment misses, such as confabulation, information integrity and intellectual property, all relevant to summaries of patent filings. The vendor's model card, option A, is the runner-up: its benchmark results are scores on tests the vendor chose, not a structured set of risks to check the assessment against.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model cards document a model's tested limits. But benchmark results are scores on tests the vendor chose, not a set of risks to widen the assessment against.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because NIST frameworks work together. But the Cybersecurity Framework organizes security outcomes, not risks such as invented facts in summaries.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI law sets firm limits. But banned practices mark uses that are prohibited outright; they do not list the risks of a lawful summarizing assistant.

tips: Eliminate: C lists banned practices, not the risks of a lawful assistant, and B organizes cybersecurity outcomes, not risks such as invented facts.
Final two: D beats A because the profile is a structured set of generative AI risks to check the assessment against; benchmark results are scores on tests the vendor chose.
Exam cue: for generative AI, widen risk work with the NIST Generative AI Profile; risks such as confabulation fall outside predictive-model checks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.8 (Information Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (a companion NIST profile applies the AI RMF to generative AI and describes risks such as confabulation). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. Round 3 review: key names the document, not its title, so it tests knowledge of AI 600-1. Final release fix, 18 Nov 2026: the stem now says the assistant is generative, the fact the Generative AI Profile key depends on. Final release fix 2, 18 Nov 2026: the runner-up now loses because benchmark scores are not a structured risk set, not because the model card is general, since the profile is general too. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Framework claims by vendors
questions.question: A Philippine university is choosing a vendor's model that flags essays as AI-written; the vendor says the model is 'NIST AI RMF certified' and unbiased. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Request bias test results for this model on similar essays
options.B: Have the vendor sign a formal statement that the model is unbiased
options.C: Ask which accredited body issued the vendor's NIST AI RMF certificate
options.D: Accept the claim, since NIST frameworks set recognized requirements

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance with no NIST certification; framework 'certified' claims are assertions, and model claims need model-level tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the framework named in the claim can certify anything at all.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, and NIST offers no certification against it, so 'NIST AI RMF certified' is the vendor's own description and says nothing about this model's fairness. Bias test results for this model, on essays like the university's, answer the claim. Asking which body issued the certificate, option C, is the runner-up: it is normal due diligence, but there is no recognized scheme to check.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it puts the vendor on record. But a signed statement is still the vendor's assertion, not evidence from testing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because checking a certificate's issuer is normal due diligence. But NIST offers no certification against the voluntary AI RMF, so any 'certificate' is a private opinion.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because NIST publications are respected. But the AI RMF is voluntary and use-case agnostic; it sets no pass mark a model can be certified against.

tips: Eliminate: D accepts a claim because NIST is respected, and B swaps evidence for the vendor's own signed assertion.
Final two: A beats C because NIST offers no certification against the AI RMF, so there is no issuer to check; only this model's test results answer the bias claim.
Exam cue: a voluntary framework guides risk work but certifies nothing; meet any 'certified' claim about a model with that model's own test results.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Executive Summary (Framework intended to be voluntary and use-case agnostic); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance that NIST does not certify against, so claims about a model need that model's own test results). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A claims-decision pilot
questions.question: A Chilean gadget insurer's pilot put each of 2,000 test claims once through a general-purpose generative model deciding coverage from the policy wording; it matched adjusters on 94%. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Adjusters' own decisions may be a flawed benchmark
options.B: The provider may have retrained the model during the pilot
options.C: The same claim could get opposite decisions on different runs
options.D: The insurer's claim history is too small to train the model well

questions.key_concept: Generative models sample their outputs, so the same input can get different answers; using one for yes-or-no decisions risks treating like cases differently.
questions.pre_read: Read how the pilot was run before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model builds each answer by sampling, so the same claim can come back covered on one run and not covered on the next. Running each claim once cannot show that, so the 94% says nothing about consistency, and customers with identical facts could be treated differently. Doubting the adjusters, option A, questions the benchmark, but even a perfect benchmark cannot reveal run-to-run variation; the risk comes from the kind of model chosen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because match rates depend on their benchmark. But even a perfect benchmark cannot show whether a sampling model decides the same claim the same way twice.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a third-party model can be updated silently. But generative output varies between runs even when the model is unchanged, so the bigger risk needs no provider change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because models learn from data. But a general-purpose model is prompted with the wording, not trained on the insurer's claims, so history size is not the issue.

tips: Eliminate: B needs a provider change, yet sampled output varies even when the model is unchanged, and D assumes the model was trained on claims when it is only prompted.
Final two: C beats A because even a perfect benchmark cannot show consistency when each claim ran once: a generative model samples its answers, so identical claims can be decided differently.
Exam cue: match the kind of AI to the decision; a generative model that samples its answers can treat like cases differently unless that variability is measured.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (generative models sample their outputs, so the same input can get different answers, which matters when they make decisions). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Classifying a vendor-supplied checker
questions.question: A Sri Lankan export bank's inventory lists its letter-of-credit checker as an AI model, matching the vendor's brochure; it applies a fixed decision table staff wrote. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner record it as rules-based software and test its rules
options.B: Drop it from IS audit coverage, since no AI is involved
options.C: Keep it listed as an AI model and schedule its model validation
options.D: Accept the vendor's product description as the basis for its risk rating

questions.key_concept: Rules engines run fixed, human-written logic and never learn from data; classify systems by how they work, not by marketing, to choose controls.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the checker before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: A fixed decision table written by staff is a rules engine: it learns nothing from data, so it has no training data or drift to review. Its risk sits in the rules, which are tested against the bank's trade-finance requirements like any software logic. Model validation, option C, is the runner-up: it looks cautious, but it follows the vendor's label and examines training data and drift this checker does not have.
