wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the system is not machine learning. But software that checks trade documents still needs its logic tested; the method changes, not the need for assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because validating anything labeled AI looks cautious. But model validation examines training data and drift; a fixed decision table has neither, so its rules need testing instead.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors know their products. But marketing labels are claims, not evidence; the classification should follow what the system actually does.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses a change of method with no need for assurance, and D lets a marketing claim set the rating instead of evidence of how it works.
Final two: A beats C because a fixed decision table learns nothing from data, so model validation has no training data or drift to examine; its rules are what must be tested.
Exam cue: classify a system by how it works, learned from data or written as rules, and choose the evidence to match.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (rules engines run fixed logic people wrote and do not learn from data; classify a system by how it works). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. Final release fix, 18 Nov 2026: the stem now says the AI label matches the vendor's brochure, so the explanations' references to the vendor's label rest on a stated fact. Final release fix 2, 18 Nov 2026: option C now keeps the AI label and sends the checker to model validation, a cautious step only the rules-engine fact defeats, replacing a request for training data that plainly cannot exist. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Near-perfect validation scores
questions.question: A Nicaraguan technical college's dropout-risk model, which flags students in each term's first week, scored 96% in validation on a year-end copy of student records. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner drop its strongest input and retrain the model
options.B: Add more students to the validation set to confirm the 96% score
options.C: Have the owner simplify the model, since 96% signals overfitting
options.D: Have the owner revalidate using only inputs known at prediction time

questions.key_concept: Target leakage: validating on records copied after the outcomes lets later events inflate scores; validate with only inputs known at prediction time.
questions.pre_read: Read the model's purpose and its validation setup before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: A year-end copy of student records includes what happened later in each term, such as withdrawals, unpaid fees or changed grades, so the 96% may partly come from reading the outcome. Revalidating with only the inputs known in each term's first week shows the model's real value for early support. Dropping the strongest input, option A, removes at most one leak; other fields updated later in the term could still inflate the score.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one input may carry a leak. But other fields updated later in the term could still inflate the score; only point-in-time validation removes them all.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because larger samples firm up results. But extra students' records would come from the same year-end copy, so the inflated score would simply repeat.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because very high scores invite suspicion. But overfitting shows as a gap between training and validation results; here the validation data itself reveals the outcome.

tips: Eliminate: B enlarges a validation set built the same leaking way, and C mistakes a high validation score for overfitting, which shows as a training-validation gap.
Final two: D beats A because point-in-time validation removes every input updated after the prediction date; dropping one input leaves the others.
Exam cue: a near-perfect score on records copied after the outcomes suggests leakage; validate with only what was known when each prediction would be made.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (data updated after the outcome leaks the answer and inflates validation; validate with inputs known at prediction time). Reworked so it does not mirror the AAIA notes 2A.3 example (an input filled in only after the outcome). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Targeting workplace inspections
questions.question: A South African labor inspectorate's model ranks workplaces for inspection; it is trained on past inspections, labeled by violations found, at sites inspectors chose to visit. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model on more years of the same past inspections
options.B: Have the owner add randomly chosen sites to each year's inspections
options.C: Rank sites by their past violation counts instead of using the model
options.D: Have inspectors record violations to one standard in every region

questions.key_concept: Labels that exist only for cases people chose to check teach a model their past choices; unselected cases must be checked to learn the rest.
questions.pre_read: Read how the training data was produced before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: The model only knows sites inspectors already chose to visit, so kinds of workplaces they rarely visited have no violation labels and stay ranked low, which keeps inspectors away from them. Inspecting some randomly chosen sites each year gives labels for parts of the population the old choices never reached. Standard recording of violations, option D, improves label quality, but only for sites that were visited.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more data often helps. But more years of the same choices repeat the same blind spot rather than filling it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems simpler and transparent. But past violation counts come from the same chosen visits, so the ranking inherits the same gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because inconsistent labels weaken a model. But better recording still covers only sites inspectors chose, so the unvisited kinds of workplace stay invisible.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more of the same chosen visits, repeating the blind spot, and C swaps the model for counts drawn from those same visits.
Final two: B beats D because only sites never chosen lack labels; better recording improves labels already collected but adds none for unvisited sites.
Exam cue: when labels exist only where people looked, the model learns where people looked; ask how the cases nobody checked get checked.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a model learns from its labels; labels that exist only where people chose to look teach it their past choices). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A ten-year advice chatbot
questions.question: A Cameroonian cocoa board's farmer-advice chatbot, required to run for ten years, uses a hosted model version its provider will retire in eighteen months. Which concern should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Its successor version may answer differently and need revalidation
options.B: Retirement will erase the chatbot's past conversation logs
options.C: The provider may raise usage prices once the successor version is live
options.D: Farmers' prompts may be used to train the successor version

questions.key_concept: Hosted model versions are retired on the provider's schedule; a long-lived system must plan to revalidate each successor version before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the chatbot and its model before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Hosted model versions are retired on the provider's schedule, and a successor can answer the same question differently, so a system required to run ten years will change its model several times. Each switch needs the board's own revalidation on farmers' questions before use. Higher prices for the successor, option C, belong in the business case, but a cost rise does not put wrong advice in front of farmers.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retirement sounds like deletion. But a model version does not hold the chatbot's conversation logs, so retiring it erases none of them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because successors can cost more. But price is a business-case matter; untested answers from a new version can give farmers wrong advice.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some providers train on customer prompts. But the stem gives no such terms, while the version's retirement is certain.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses retiring a model version with deleting conversation logs, which the version does not hold, and D raises prompt reuse that nothing in the stem points to.
Final two: A beats C because a successor version can change the advice farmers get; a price rise is a business-case detail.
Exam cue: a hosted model will be replaced during a long-lived system's life; plan revalidation for every version switch.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.2 (Pre-trained models monitored as part of regular maintenance); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (a hosted model version will be retired during a long-lived system's life; each successor must be revalidated). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Building a model in-house
questions.question: An Ecuadorian volcano observatory's business case funds a contract team to build an eruption-warning model over 18 months; it funds nothing after launch. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Newer modeling methods may make the model look dated within a year
options.B: The in-house model may prove less accurate than vendor products
options.C: Its accuracy could fade unnoticed as seismic patterns shift
options.D: Open-source modeling libraries may carry unmet license obligations

questions.key_concept: A model is not finished at launch: the data it meets keep changing, so building one needs funded owners who monitor, revalidate and retrain it.
questions.pre_read: Note what the business case pays for and what it does not, then rank each risk by realistic harm to the people relying on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Unlike fixed software, a model's accuracy depends on the data it meets, and a volcano's seismic patterns can shift over time. With nothing funded after launch, no one is paid to monitor or retrain the model, so accuracy could fade unnoticed in a life-safety system. Accuracy against vendor products, option B, matters at selection, but even the best model at launch needs upkeep.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI methods change fast. But looking dated is about novelty, not harm; the risk that matters is warnings degrading while nobody watches.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because build-or-buy choices weigh accuracy. But even a model that starts best can degrade; the business case leaves its upkeep unfunded.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because in-house builds often use open-source code. But license terms are a manageable legal check; they do not threaten whether eruption warnings stay reliable.

tips: Eliminate: D raises a manageable licensing check rather than a threat to the warnings, and A weighs novelty rather than harm.
Final two: C beats B because any model can degrade as conditions change; with no one watching, accuracy could fade unnoticed, whatever it starts at.
Exam cue: when building or buying AI, check the plan funds monitoring and retraining for the model's life, not just the build.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.2 (Mechanisms sustain the value of deployed AI); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (build, buy or tune decisions must cover what a model needs after launch: monitoring, revalidation and retraining by named people). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. AI strategy and other commitments
questions.question: A Finnish pulp-and-paper group's board pledged net-zero emissions by 2030; its draft AI strategy has a costed business case for training several large language models in-house. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have management compare in-house training costs with hosted licenses
options.B: Have management estimate the plan's energy use before approval
options.C: Have the strategy add explainability goals for in-house models
options.D: Have management buy carbon offsets once the models are trained

questions.key_concept: An AI strategy must fit enterprise objectives; training large models uses substantial energy, so its effect on climate commitments is estimated before approval.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the strategy and the board before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: Training large language models takes substantial computing power and energy, so the plan could add emissions just as the board has pledged to reach net zero, while its business case covers cost. Estimating its energy use lets management and the board judge whether the strategy fits enterprise objectives before approving it. Comparing costs with hosted licenses, option A, refines the business case but leaves the conflict with a board commitment unexamined.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because build-or-buy choices turn on cost. But the business case already covers cost; the unexamined conflict with a board pledge is the strategic gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because large models are hard to interpret. But the stem shows no explainability gap; the missing fact is the plan's energy use against the pledge.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because offsets address emissions. But buying them after training skips judging, before approval, whether the plan fits the board's pledge.

tips: Eliminate: C adds explainability goals the stem gives no reason for, and D offsets emissions after training instead of judging the plan before approval.
Final two: B beats A because training large models may undo a board commitment, a strategic conflict; comparing costs is a business-case detail.
Exam cue: test an AI strategy against the organization's other objectives, including sustainability, since training large models uses much energy.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.12 (Environmental impact assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.3 (Mission and goals for the AI technology documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (an AI strategy must fit the organization's objectives, including commitments such as emissions targets that AI's energy use can affect). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. Release audit fix, 18 Nov 2026: 'assessed on cost alone' replaced by a costed business case, so the stem no longer pairs the pledge with a cost-only cue. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Agents built by staff
questions.question: A Belgian chocolate maker's AI policy covers only models IT builds or buys; staff's agents, built in a no-code tool, send email and edit shared files. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Agent emails may vary in tone from those staff write
options.B: IT has set no write limits on the agents' file access
options.C: The tool's license may not cover every employee who builds
options.D: Agents act on company data with no owner or risk review

questions.key_concept: AI governance covers AI however it is made: agents staff build in everyday tools need the same policy, inventory and risk review as bought models.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the policy's scope matches every way AI now enters the organization, including tools staff configure themselves.
questions.correct_explanation: Agents that send email and edit shared files act on company data, yet a policy limited to IT-built or bought models leaves them uninventoried, unowned and unassessed, so nobody knows which exist or what they can do. Bringing them under policy and inventory comes first. Missing write limits, option B, is a real exposure, but limits can only be set well once each agent is known, owned and rated by risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because generated messages can sound off-brand. But tone is a quality issue; agents acting on data with no owner or review can do real harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because agents that edit files need limits. But limits are set well only once each agent is known, owned and rated; unknown agents stay unassessed whatever IT restricts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because license terms matter. But license coverage is a contract question; the larger risk is agents acting on company data unreviewed.

tips: Eliminate: A raises message tone, a quality issue, and C a license question; neither is the risk of agents acting unreviewed.
Final two: D beats B because governance comes first: missing write limits are one symptom, and limits can be set by risk only once each agent is inventoried and owned.
Exam cue: when AI enters through everyday tools, widen policy and inventory first; technical limits follow from knowing what exists.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-11 (User-Installed Software)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (AI policy and inventory must reach AI that staff build themselves in everyday tools, not only models IT builds or buys). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Requests for audit to approve
questions.question: A Slovenian car-leasing firm's credit model pauses itself when drift passes a limit; the firm wants internal audit, which audited the alert, to approve each restart. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner decide each restart against set criteria
options.B: Have the data scientists who built the model approve each restart
options.C: Let the model restart itself once its drift score returns to normal
options.D: Have internal audit approve each restart after reviewing retraining evidence

questions.key_concept: Deciding when a paused model returns belongs to its owner; internal audit assesses that control and never runs or approves it.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing who approves, ask whose decision a restart is and what internal audit would later have to assess.
questions.correct_explanation: Pausing and restarting a credit model are operating decisions with consequences for applicants and the firm, so they belong to the model owner, deciding against criteria set in advance. Internal audit can then assess whether the pause rule and restart decisions work. Internal audit approving restarts after reviewing retraining evidence, option D, sounds rigorous, but it makes internal audit part of the control it must later assess.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because builders know the model best. But builders approving their own model's return lacks independent challenge; the business owner answers for the decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes delay. But a drift score returning to normal does not show the model's errors were fixed, and no accountable person decides.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because internal audit knows the alert and would review evidence first. But approving restarts makes it part of the control it must assess, impairing its independence.

tips: Eliminate: C lets a drift score decide without an accountable person, and B has the builders approve their own model's return without independent challenge.
Final two: A beats D because restarts are the owner's operating decisions; internal audit approving them, however carefully, would mean auditing its own work.
Exam cue: when asked to approve, sign or run an AI control, the IS auditor recommends that the owner take it on and remains the assessor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1002 (Organizational Independence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (the model owner holds the authority to pause, override and restart a model; the IS auditor assesses those controls and never runs or approves them). Checked against KaiSip CISA d2_225 (audit's own check handed to the owner): this item keeps only the restart-approval angle. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Conditions on committee approvals
questions.question: At Morocco's postal service, the AI governance committee approved a chatbot if answers in Arabic, French and Amazigh are rechecked after each vendor update; nobody was assigned. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the IS auditor run the rechecks for the committee
options.B: Have the vendor certify each update's answers in every language
options.C: Have the committee name an owner for every approval condition
options.D: Have the data team recheck the three languages once now

questions.key_concept: Approval conditions on an AI use, such as rechecks after each model update, work only when each has a named owner reporting to the approver.
questions.pre_read: Ask who was supposed to make each condition happen, and how the committee would know it had not.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor update can change a chatbot's answers in one language while others stay sound, which is why the committee made rechecks a condition of approval. With no named owner, no one is told of updates or runs the checks, and other conditional approvals may share the gap. Naming an owner for each condition, who reports back, makes approvals enforceable. A one-off recheck now, option D, covers today's version only.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit is independent. But running a management control would make audit part of what it must assess; the committee needs an owner, not an auditor.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors test their updates. But the vendor's claim about its own update is not the postal service's check of answers its customers receive.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no recheck has run. But one run covers today's version; the next vendor update, and other approval conditions, would again go unchecked.

tips: Eliminate: A has the auditor operate a management control it must later assess, and B replaces the postal service's own check with the vendor's claim about its update.
Final two: C beats D because the cause is a condition with no owner; a one-off recheck misses the next vendor update and leaves other conditions to lapse.
Exam cue: an AI approval condition tied to model updates works only when a named owner is told of each update and reports the check.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (the AI governance committee's approvals carry conditions, such as rechecks after each vendor model update, and each condition needs a named owner who reports back). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Awareness content and policy duties
questions.question: A Vietnamese street-vendor licensing office's AI policy requires officers to verify every model-recommended permit refusal, but its awareness course says the model is right 95% of the time. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The 95% figure may no longer hold after the next retraining
options.B: Officers may approve the model's refusals without real checking
options.C: Verifying every refusal wastes officers' effort on a 95%-accurate model
options.D: Officers may override too many refusals and slow down permits

questions.key_concept: Training that stresses a model's accuracy can breed automation bias; awareness content must support the policy's human checks, not undercut them.
questions.pre_read: Read the training message from an officer's chair: what would it make you do with the next refusal?
questions.correct_explanation: Telling officers the model is right 95% of the time invites them to treat each recommended refusal as already correct, which is automation bias, so the policy's verification step could become a formality. Awareness content must reinforce the policy's duty, including what the model's errors look like. A figure that may change after retraining, option A, is a real accuracy issue, but the larger harm is officers who stop checking.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining changes performance. But the immediate problem is what the message does to officers' checking, whatever the current figure is.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 95% sounds high. But one refusal in twenty could be wrong, and street vendors bear that harm; the policy requires checking for that reason.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reviewers can overcorrect. But a message stressing the model's accuracy pushes officers toward accepting refusals, not overriding them.

tips: Eliminate: D reverses the effect, since praising accuracy pushes officers to accept refusals, and C treats 95% as enough when one refusal in twenty may be wrong.
Final two: B beats A because the message itself undercuts the policy's checks today; a figure that may change later is a smaller, separate problem.
Exam cue: check that AI training supports the policy's human checks; messages praising accuracy can quietly turn review into rubber-stamping.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.2 (AI risk management training for personnel and partners); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.4 (Operator and practitioner proficiency defined and assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (awareness and training must match the AI policy's duties; content that praises accuracy can breed automation bias). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Override rates and officer training
questions.question: A Nepali land-revenue office's AI program reports that all valuation officers finished training on questioning model output; officers overrode 3 of 40,000 model valuations last year. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team retest valuation accuracy each quarter
options.B: Repeat the training for the officers with the fewest overrides
options.C: Set a minimum number of overrides for every officer
options.D: Add a measure of whether officers catch seeded wrong valuations

questions.key_concept: Training completion shows activity, not oversight; measure whether reviewers actually catch the model's errors, for example with seeded test cases.
questions.pre_read: Read what the program reports and the override figure before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: Three overrides in 40,000 could mean an excellent model or officers accepting valuations without real review, and training completion cannot tell the two apart. Seeding known-wrong valuations and measuring how many officers catch them shows whether oversight works and where training is not taking hold. Repeating training for officers with the fewest overrides, option B, assumes both the problem and its location before anyone knows whether review fails.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model accuracy matters. But it measures the model, not the officers; the program's training claim needs a direct measure of whether officers catch wrong valuations.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training may not have stuck. But it treats few overrides as proof of weak review, which nobody has shown; the program first needs a measure of review quality.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because overrides seem healthy. But quotas push officers to disagree for the sake of it, producing worse decisions rather than real review.

tips: Eliminate: C sets a quota that forces disagreement rather than judgment, and A measures the model rather than whether officers catch its errors.
Final two: D beats B because seeded cases show whether officers catch errors; retraining low overriders assumes an answer the metrics cannot yet give.
Exam cue: program metrics should show whether human oversight catches AI errors, not just that people were trained.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (AI program metrics should show outcomes, such as whether reviewers catch the model's errors, not only training completion). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. Final release fix, 18 Nov 2026: option A's explanation and tip 1 now say it measures the model rather than the officers, instead of claiming it shows nothing. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Sources for identifying AI risk
questions.question: A Ugandan teachers' commission's model, trained on past transfers, ranks teachers for remote postings; its risk register holds only risks raised by IT, legal and data scientists. Which gap should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Harms seen by teachers and principals may be missing
options.B: Teachers' transfer risks may not be scored on one common scale
options.C: The register omits patch status for the model's servers
options.D: The register lacks the model vendor's accuracy benchmark

questions.key_concept: Identifying AI risk needs the people the model affects and those who work with it; internal technical teams alone miss harms only those people see.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would notice first if the ranking treated someone unfairly, and whether they were asked.
questions.correct_explanation: A model trained on past transfers can repeat whatever patterns shaped them, such as who was sent far from family, and apply them to every teacher at once. Those harms are visible to teachers and principals, not to IT, legal or data scientists, so a register built without them may miss the risks that matter most. Scoring on a common scale, option B, improves assessment, but it cannot rate risks nobody identified.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consistent scoring is good practice. But scoring works only on risks already identified; harms only teachers would raise are still missing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because server security matters. But treating AI risk as a security question misses the harm wrong rankings do to teachers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks inform likelihood. But a vendor benchmark is an input to assessment, not a source of the harms the register lacks.

tips: Eliminate: C treats AI risk as a server security matter, and D adds a vendor benchmark, which informs assessment but identifies no harms.
Final two: A beats B because a register can only score risks someone raised; without the people affected, the harms that matter may never appear.
Exam cue: AI risk identification draws on the people affected and the staff who use the system, not only technical and legal teams.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.2 (Regular engagement with relevant AI actors on impacts); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 5.1 (Feedback collected from those external to the team)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (identifying AI risk draws on the people affected and the staff who work with the system, not only technical teams). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Assessing an agent's tools
questions.question: A Polish cosmetics wholesaler's risk assessment rates its sales agent's three tools (reading the customer database, browsing the web and sending email) each low risk on its own. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Keep the low ratings, since each tool passed its own review
options.B: Have the owner reassess the agent's risks with its tools combined
options.C: Have the owner limit the agent's email to known customer addresses
options.D: Have each tool's supplier certify the tool as low risk

questions.key_concept: Agent risk comes from tool combinations: untrusted content, private data and a way out together let an outsider steer the agent to leak data.
questions.pre_read: Trace a path through the tools together: where could outside text enter, what could it reach, and how could it leave?
questions.correct_explanation: Rated one at a time, each tool looks harmless, but together they form a path: web pages can carry hidden instructions, the database supplies customer data, and email, or even the web requests themselves, can send it out. Reassessing the agent as one system finds that path and sets controls by the combined risk. Limiting email to known customers, option C, is sensible, but chosen first it closes one route and leaves others unassessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because each tool was reviewed. But the risk comes from the combination: outside text, private data and outbound channels in one agent.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it blocks the email route. But the agent could still leak data through the web requests it makes; only assessing the tools together shows every path.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because suppliers know their tools. But no supplier sees how this agent combines them; certifying each tool repeats the one-at-a-time mistake.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps ratings made one tool at a time, and D asks suppliers to certify tools they cannot see combined in this agent.
Final two: B beats C because the risk lies in the combination; blocking email first leaves other paths, such as web requests, unassessed.
Exam cue: assess an agent's tools together; outside input, private data and any outbound channel in one agent can form a leak path.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.4 (Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (AI risk is assessed for the system as a whole; an agent's tools can be low risk alone and high risk together). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Indicators for AI errors
questions.question: A Nigerian payment switch's monthly-average key risk indicator (KRI) for wrongly blocked payments stayed within tolerance, though a vendor model update tripled wrong blocks for four days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Count breaches when complaints pass the monthly limit
options.B: Have the vendor confirm each update stayed within tolerance
options.C: Track the indicator daily and by model version against tolerance
options.D: Lower the monthly threshold so smaller rises count as breaches

questions.key_concept: AI KRIs must be measured at a grain that shows harm after changes; averaging over a month can hide a model update's short, sharp spike.
questions.pre_read: Read how the indicator is calculated and what happened before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor update can change a model's behavior overnight, so harm arrives as spikes tied to versions, which a monthly average dilutes. Measuring daily and by model version shows each update's effect against tolerance and triggers escalation while customers are still affected. Lowering the monthly threshold, option D, makes the average more sensitive, but a short spike is still averaged away and still not tied to the update.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because complaints show customer harm. But complaints lag and undercount, so tying breaches to them hides harm the switch's own data already shows.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor made the update. But that replaces the switch's own measurement with the vendor's claim about its own update.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tighter thresholds catch smaller rises. But the window is the problem: a four-day spike is still diluted across the month, whatever the threshold.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor's claim about its own update, and A ties breaches to complaints, which lag and undercount the harm.
Final two: C beats D because the monthly window hides short spikes whatever the threshold; daily, versioned tracking ties harm to the update that caused it.
Exam cue: set AI KRIs at the grain where changes happen, such as each model version, so a bad update shows before the month ends.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (AI KRIs need thresholds and a measurement grain that show breaches of tolerance, including after each model change). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Several risk appetites
questions.question: A Scottish university's board has high appetite for technology risk and low appetite for harm to students; its register files its bursary-fraud model's risks under technology. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The appetites for students and for technology contradict each other
options.B: The AI governance committee, not the board, should set appetite levels
options.C: AI risks lack their own category in the university's risk register
options.D: Harm to students from wrong flags is judged at the higher appetite

questions.key_concept: AI risks belong under the appetite for the harm they cause; filing them under technology can judge harm to people against a looser appetite.
questions.pre_read: For each AI risk, ask whom it would hurt, then check which appetite the register applies.
questions.correct_explanation: A bursary-fraud model's main harm is wrongly accusing students, which falls under the board's low appetite for harm to students. Filing all its risks under technology judges that harm against the high appetite set for technology risk, so serious harms could look acceptable. A separate AI category, option C, might seem tidier, but a new category still needs mapping to the right appetite; the problem is which appetite applies, not the label.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because high and low appetites sound inconsistent. But boards set different appetites for different kinds of risk; the problem is filing AI harm under the wrong one.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the AI governance committee oversees AI. But the board approves risk appetite; the committee works within it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI risks are distinctive. But a separate category does not fix the problem unless it carries the low appetite for harm to students.

tips: Eliminate: A misreads different appetites for different risk types as a contradiction, and B moves approval of appetite from the board to a committee.
Final two: D beats C because the harm is judged against the wrong appetite; a new category without the right appetite changes only the label.
Exam cue: classify AI risks by the harm they cause, such as harm to people, not by the technology that causes it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Gaps in an AI vendor contract
questions.question: An Ontario school board's reading-support model contract makes the vendor report personal-data breaches; a faulty update mis-flagged another board's students for weeks before that board noticed. Which contract gap should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: No duty on the vendor to report model malfunctions promptly
options.B: No duty on the vendor to disclose its training data sources
options.C: No limit on how many model updates the vendor releases
options.D: No escrow of the trained model's source code if the vendor fails

questions.key_concept: AI vendor contracts need incident notice for model malfunctions, not just data breaches; a model can harm people for weeks while secure and available.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the school board would learn that the vendor's model had started making wrong decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: The other school board's experience shows the vendor's model can mis-flag students for weeks with no breach or outage, so a breach-only notice clause would leave this board unaware while students are wrongly placed. A duty to report model malfunctions promptly, with what changed, lets the owner suspend use and check its students. Disclosure of training data sources, option B, aids due diligence, but it would not reveal that a faulty update was mis-flagging students.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training data sources matter in due diligence. But knowing them would not have told the board that a faulty update was mis-flagging its students.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because frequent updates add change risk. But a cap on updates would not stop a faulty one, or tell the board when one starts mis-flagging students.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because escrow protects continuity. But source code alone cannot rebuild a trained model, and escrow does nothing to reveal wrong decisions.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on source code, which cannot rebuild a trained model or reveal errors, and C caps updates, which neither prevents a faulty one nor reveals it.
Final two: A beats B because the stem's failure was a malfunction nobody reported; knowing training data sources would not have revealed it.
Exam cue: AI contracts need notice of model incidents and changes, not just breaches and outages.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.2 (Contingency processes for failures in high-risk third-party data or AI); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (third-party AI contracts need notice of model malfunctions and changes, not only data breaches). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Rights in generated content
questions.question: A Colombian game studio plans to ship character art made with a vendor's image generator; the vendor will not disclose its training images or cover infringement claims. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Whether the generator outperforms rival tools in blind tests
options.B: Whether the studio carries liability if the art copies protected work
options.C: Whether the studio's prompts could train the vendor's image model
options.D: Whether the vendor's data centers hold a security certificate

questions.key_concept: Generative models can reproduce protected material from training data; with undisclosed training data and no indemnity, the user may carry the infringement risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to the studio if shipped art turns out to copy someone's work.
questions.correct_explanation: Image generators can reproduce elements of the works they were trained on, and this vendor will neither disclose its training images nor stand behind its outputs, so infringement claims over shipped games would fall on the studio. Settling who carries that liability, or choosing another vendor, comes before contracting. The studio's prompts training the model, option C, is a real confidentiality term, but the stem's facts point to intellectual property exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tool quality drives choice. But choosing on capability first skips the legal exposure the vendor's terms already reveal.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors may train on customer inputs. But the stem's facts concern undisclosed training images and no indemnity, so infringement exposure is the larger, stated gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because security certificates reassure buyers. But a data-center certificate says nothing about whether generated images copy protected work.

tips: Eliminate: D answers a security question the stem does not raise, and A chooses on capability before settling the legal exposure the terms reveal.
Final two: B beats C because the stated gaps, undisclosed training images and no indemnity, leave infringement liability with the studio; prompt confidentiality is a separate term.
Exam cue: for vendor generative AI, check who carries intellectual property risk in the outputs, especially when training data is undisclosed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.10 (Intellectual Property); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (third-party generative AI can carry intellectual property risk in its outputs; contracts must settle who bears it). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Correcting data for training
questions.question: Approved by the data owner, a Hungarian drug wholesaler's data scientists fixed miscoded categories in their training copy, logging fixes in a spreadsheet; the source system stays unchanged. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The fixes are logged in a spreadsheet, not a lineage tool
options.B: Correcting training data breaks the rule that training data stays unaltered
options.C: The live model will score records still carrying the old miscodes
options.D: The data owner lacked authority to approve the corrections

questions.key_concept: Training-serving skew: fixing data only for training leaves live inputs different from what the model learned, so data quality is fixed at the source.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the correction before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learns from corrected categories but, in use, reads the source system where the miscodes remain, so it meets inputs unlike its training data and can go wrong exactly where the miscodes sit. Data quality for AI is fixed at the source by the data owner. A spreadsheet log rather than a lineage tool, option A, is a record-keeping weakness, but it does not make live decisions wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because lineage tools tie data to model versions. But the fixes are recorded; the format is a record-keeping weakness, while the live model still meets the miscodes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data integrity matters. But correcting known errors with the owner's approval is normal data preparation, not a breach of integrity.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because approvals can be misplaced. But the data owner is exactly the person who should approve corrections to that data.

tips: Eliminate: B treats approved correction of known errors as an integrity breach, and D doubts the data owner, the right person to approve corrections.
Final two: C beats A because the miscodes stay where the live model reads them, skewing its decisions; a spreadsheet log is only a record-keeping weakness.
Exam cue: when data is fixed for training, check the same fix reaches the live inputs; otherwise the model meets data unlike what it learned.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (data quality for AI is owned and fixed at the source; corrections made only for training leave live inputs unlike the training data). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Controlling data used for training
questions.question: A New Zealand health insurer's data team may train models on any of 300 platform datasets it can access. Which control should the IS auditor consider BEST against training on data not cleared for it?

options.A: Owner-set tags of permitted uses, checked before each training run
options.B: Encryption of every dataset stored on the platform
options.C: Access rules limiting the data team to tables marked non-sensitive
options.D: Annual privacy and data-handling training for everyone on the data team

questions.key_concept: Rights to use data for training depend on purpose and terms, not sensitivity alone; owners record permitted uses so pipelines can check before training.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions: who may see a dataset, and what it may be used for.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether a dataset may train a model depends on its terms and purpose, such as consent, license or the reason it was collected, which its data owner decides. Tags recording each dataset's permitted uses, checked before training starts, turn those decisions into a preventive control. Limiting the team to non-sensitive tables, option C, controls who sees data, not what it may be used for: licensed or purpose-bound data can be non-sensitive.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects data. But the data team can still read and train on encrypted data it can access, so encryption does not limit use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because least privilege is a strong control. But sensitivity is not purpose; non-sensitive licensed or purpose-bound data may still be barred from training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training shapes behavior. But it relies on memory and cannot tell a data scientist which of 300 datasets are cleared for training.

tips: Eliminate: B protects data from outsiders but not from use by the team, and D relies on memory rather than a check of each dataset's terms.
Final two: A beats C because rights to use depend on purpose and terms, not sensitivity; access rules decide who sees data, not what trains models.
Exam cue: for training data, look for a control that records and checks each dataset's permitted uses before the model is built.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (rights to use data for training are decided by data owners and recorded, so pipelines can check them before training). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A false statement from an assistant
questions.question: A Canadian genealogy service's assistant told users a living member had a criminal record, which it invented; staff say no stored personal data exists to correct. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Close the complaint, as no stored personal data exists to correct
options.B: Delete the member's tree data so the claim cannot recur
options.C: Add a disclaimer that its answers about people may be wrong
options.D: Treat claims it generates about people as personal data to correct

questions.key_concept: Statements an AI generates about identifiable people are personal data, so accuracy and correction duties apply even when nothing is stored.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the false statement before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: Under many privacy laws, a generated statement about an identifiable person is personal data about that person, so a false criminal claim engages the duty of accuracy and the person's right to correction, stored or not. The owner needs routes to correct or block such outputs and stop the pattern recurring. A disclaimer, option C, warns users, but the false claim still reaches them and the person still has no remedy.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing is held in a database. But a generated statement about an identifiable person is personal data in itself, so the duties still apply.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the claim seems to come from somewhere. But the model invented it; deleting the member's own data does not stop generation and harms the member further.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it warns users about errors. But the false claim about a real person still spreads, and the person still has no way to have it corrected.

tips: Eliminate: B deletes data the model did not draw on, and A treats unstored output as outside privacy when statements about people are personal data.
Final two: D beats C because the person needs the false claim corrected; a disclaimer warns readers but leaves the claim and the harm in place.
Exam cue: AI outputs about identifiable people are personal data; accuracy and correction duties follow the output, not just stored records.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (AI outputs about identifiable people are personal data, so accuracy and correction duties apply to them). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Coded names in prompts
questions.question: A Peruvian addiction-support charity's caseworkers summarize case notes with a hosted language model after software replaces clients' names with codes, so staff call the prompts anonymous. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Coded notes will give caseworkers less accurate summaries
options.B: Details left in the notes may still identify clients
options.C: Caseworkers may struggle to link summaries back to clients
options.D: The hosted model will learn clients' details from each prompt

questions.key_concept: Replacing names in free text is pseudonymization, not anonymization: life details in notes can still identify people, so prompts remain personal data.
questions.pre_read: Read how the prompts are prepared before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Swapping names for codes is pseudonymization: free-text case notes about addiction usually mention family members, jobs, places and events that can identify a client, so the prompts sent to the hosted model remain sensitive personal data. Treating them as anonymous would skip the protections such data needs. A model learning from each prompt, option D, is a common belief, but answering a prompt leaves its weights unchanged; the notes identify clients regardless.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missing names might confuse a model. But summaries depend on the case content, not on names, so accuracy is not the main concern.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because codes add a step. But the charity holds the key to relink codes, so linking summaries back is an operational detail, not a privacy risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because models learn from data. But answering a prompt does not change a model's weights; prompts feed training only under provider terms the stem never mentions.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes names drive summary quality, and C raises a relinking step the charity's own key handles; neither is the privacy risk.
Final two: B beats D because the notes' details identify clients whatever the model does; answering a prompt does not change a model's weights.
Exam cue: removing names from free text is not anonymization; ask what the remaining details reveal before calling prompts anonymous.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Designing for deletion
questions.question: An Australian migration-advice agency must delete client files on request; its planned assistant could be fine-tuned on them or retrieve them at answer time. Which design should the IS auditor consider BEST for that duty?

options.A: Retrieve files when answering, dropping each from the index once deleted
options.B: Fine-tune afresh each quarter, leaving out files deleted since the last run
options.C: Retrieve files when answering, keeping answer logs with no time limit
options.D: Fine-tune once, then block answers naming any deleted client

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design: keeping personal data in a retrieval index, not in model weights, lets deletion requests be honored promptly and verifiably.
questions.pre_read: For each design, ask where a deleted client's information would still be the day after the request.
questions.correct_explanation: A fine-tuned model can memorize parts of its training files, and the only sure removal is retraining without them. Retrieval keeps client files outside the model, so removing a file from the index ends its use at once and can be checked. Fine-tuning afresh each quarter without deleted files, option B, does remove them eventually, but a deleted client's data stays in the model for up to three months after the request.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it does remove deleted files. But until the next fresh run, the model still holds what it learned from them, so deletion waits months.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retrieval keeps files out of the model. But answer logs quote client files, so keeping them with no time limit leaves deleted clients' data in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because blocked answers hide the client. But the data stays in the model and reworded questions can surface it; filtering is a fallback, not a design for deletion.

tips: Eliminate: D filters answers while the data stays in the model, and C keeps answer logs that still hold deleted clients' details.
Final two: A beats B because removing a file from the index ends its use at once; quarterly retraining leaves deleted clients' data in the model for months.
Exam cue: when data may need deleting, prefer designs that keep it outside model weights, such as retrieval from an index.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (privacy by design for deletion: keeping personal data in a retrieval index, not in model weights, lets requests be met promptly). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Fine-tuning at a provider
questions.question: A Kazakh airline fine-tuned a special-assistance planning model on passengers' request forms at its provider's tuning service; the IS auditor is testing whether forms are deleted when retention ends. Which evidence is BEST?

options.A: Logs showing the airline's own form copies deleted on schedule
options.B: The provider's terms barring use of the forms for other models
options.C: Provider deletion records for the uploaded files and the tuned model
options.D: Test results showing the tuned model does not repeat passengers' details

questions.key_concept: Retention and deletion must cover every copy an AI service creates: training files uploaded to a provider and the tuned model built from them.
questions.pre_read: List every place the forms went during tuning, then ask which evidence could show each was dealt with.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning at a provider's service uploads training files and creates a custom model from them there, both copies the retention rule must reach. Only the provider's records can show whether those copies were deleted when the forms expired. A memorization test, option D, is real evidence about leakage, but a model that repeats no passenger details still exists at the provider, built from them; it does not show deletion.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because they show the routine ran on time. But they cover only the airline's own copies; the uploads and the tuned model at the provider fall outside them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because providers may reuse customer data. But terms on reuse say nothing about whether the uploaded forms were deleted when their retention period ended.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because memorization tests are key evidence for trained models. But they show leakage, not deletion; a model that repeats nothing still sits at the provider, built from the forms.

tips: Eliminate: A covers only the airline's own copies, though the tuning service holds uploads and a tuned model, and B concerns reuse, not deletion.
Final two: C beats D because a memorization test shows leakage, not deletion; a model that repeats nothing still sits at the provider, built from the forms.
Exam cue: map every copy an AI service creates, including uploads and tuned models at the provider, before accepting that data was deleted.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Privacy protection and accuracy
questions.question: A Bolivian statistics office adds statistical noise to its school-funding model's training data to protect privacy; estimates for small rural districts become far less accurate. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Remove the noise for small districts so their accuracy is restored
options.B: Have the owner weigh the trade-off openly and record the reasons
options.C: Add more noise everywhere so every district is treated alike
options.D: Have the data scientists tune the noise level to balance both

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI characteristics can conflict; privacy protection can cost accuracy for small groups, so owners resolve the trade-off openly and justify it.
questions.pre_read: Notice when protecting one value harms another, and ask who must decide the balance.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI RMF notes that privacy-enhancing techniques can reduce accuracy where data is sparse, affecting fairness, and that such trade-offs should be resolved transparently and justifiably in context. Small rural districts could lose school funding through noisier estimates, so the owner must weigh options, decide and record why. Leaving data scientists to tune the noise level, option D, treats a judgment about who bears the loss as a technical setting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it fixes accuracy where it fell. But small districts are where people are easiest to identify, so dropping protection there removes it where it is most needed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it looks even-handed. But adding noise everywhere spreads accuracy loss to all districts without addressing the small districts' funding harm.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the noise level is a technical setting. But how much accuracy small districts lose for privacy is a value judgment; the owner decides it, advised by data scientists.

tips: Eliminate: C spreads the accuracy loss to every district, and A strips protection from small districts, where people are easiest to identify.
Final two: B beats D because how much accuracy small districts give up for privacy is a value judgment; the owner decides it openly, while data scientists advise.
Exam cue: when trustworthy-AI characteristics conflict, look for the owner weighing the trade-off in context and documenting the justification.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3 (AI Risks and Trustworthiness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Choosing a fairness measure
questions.question: A Taiwanese hospital's fairness criterion for its colon-cancer screening model requires every age group to be flagged at the same rate, though cancer rates rise with age. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Using age as an input makes the model unlawfully discriminatory
options.B: The criterion covers age groups but not sex or income groups
options.C: Equal flagging may raise the hospital's follow-up costs
options.D: Meeting it could mean more missed cancers among older patients

questions.key_concept: Fairness metrics must fit the use: where true rates differ by group, forcing equal flag rates can trade missed diagnoses for apparent equality.
questions.pre_read: Read the criterion and the screening facts before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: When cancer is more common in older patients, flagging every age group at the same rate pushes the model to under-flag older patients, over-flag younger ones, or both, so older patients' cancers can go unflagged. For screening, a criterion on error rates, such as equal miss rates across ages, fits the harm better. Extending the same rule to sex or income groups, option B, would spread the unfit measure rather than fix it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because age-based treatment can be unlawful. But age is a genuine medical risk factor in cancer screening, so using it is not discrimination by itself.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fairness checks often span several groups. But extending an equal-flag-rate rule to more groups spreads the same flaw; the measure does not fit screening.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because follow-ups cost money. But ranking the criterion's problems by hospital cost, not harm to patients, misses the missed cancers.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a genuine medical risk factor as discrimination, and C weighs hospital cost over harm to patients.
Final two: D beats B because forcing equal flag rates where cancer rates differ leads to missed cancers, the gravest harm; extending the rule to more groups spreads it.
Exam cue: check that a fairness criterion fits the use; where real rates differ by group, equal outcome rates can hide unequal errors.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Selling a retrained model
questions.question: A Swedish property-software firm retrained a purchased rent-arrears model and licenses it to landlords; its obligations register lists only duties for organizations using AI. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Duties that risk-based laws place on AI providers may be missing
options.B: Duties end once client landlords accept the model in their contracts
options.C: The original vendor keeps every duty for the retrained model
options.D: Duties in the landlords' own countries may be missing from the register

questions.key_concept: Risk-based AI laws assign duties by role; retraining a model and selling it can make an organization a provider with duties beyond a deployer's.
questions.pre_read: Ask what role the organization now plays for this model, not only what it does with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based AI laws, such as the EU AI Act, give different duties to those who supply AI systems and those who use them, and substantially modifying a model and placing it on the market can make the firm a provider. Provider duties, such as technical documentation for high-risk uses, are missing from a register built for users. Laws in the landlords' countries, option D, matter, but the stated gap is the changed role.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because contracts allocate responsibilities. But a contract with clients cannot remove duties the law places on the firm.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor built the original model. But retraining it and licensing it to others can make the firm a provider with its own duties.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because selling abroad adds laws. But the stem names no countries, while it does show the firm now supplies the model, a role the register ignores.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves every duty with the original vendor after the firm changed and resold the model, and B assumes contracts can remove legal duties.
Final two: A beats D because the stem shows the firm's role changed to supplier; other countries' laws are possible, but no fact points to them.
Exam cue: map AI obligations by role; building, changing or selling a model can bring provider duties beyond a deployer's.
