questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Documentation duties and retraining
questions.question: A Bulgarian grid operator must keep its load-shedding model's technical documentation for ten years; the model is retrained monthly and its model card is updated in place. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Monthly retraining is too frequent for a high-risk model
options.B: Ten years of documentation would breach data-minimization rules
options.C: Each retrained version's documentation will be overwritten by the next
options.D: The current card may not hold every item the law lists

questions.key_concept: Obligations attach to each model version; a control that updates documentation in place at every retrain cannot show what earlier versions were.
questions.pre_read: Read the documentation duty and how the card is kept before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Each monthly retrain creates a new model version with its own data, performance and limits, so the ten-year duty covers every version. Updating the card in place keeps only the latest, so if asked about a load-shedding decision from two years ago, the operator could not show the model behind it. Whether the current card holds every required item, option D, matters too, but even a complete card covers one version.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because frequent retraining raises change risk. But the duty does not limit frequency; it requires a record for each version, however often they change.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because minimization limits personal data. But technical documentation describes the model, not individual customers, and the law requires keeping it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a card must contain the required items. But even a complete card covers only the current version; every earlier version's record is gone.

tips: Eliminate: A objects to retraining frequency, which the duty does not limit, and B applies data minimization to documentation that describes the model, not customers.
Final two: C beats D because the duty covers every version; a complete card updated in place still erases each earlier version's record.
Exam cue: map AI obligations to each model version; retraining creates a new version that needs its own record.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (obligations are mapped to controls that work for each model version; retraining creates a new version that needs its own record). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Planning with the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: An Argentine provincial road-safety agency will use the NIST AI RMF to rank improvements across its twelve AI uses, seven of them generative. Which approach should the IS auditor consider BEST aligned with the framework?

options.A: Apply the Generative AI Profile's actions to the seven generative uses
options.B: Compare current and target profiles, then plan to close the gaps
options.C: Adopt the framework as mandatory regulation for its twelve AI uses
options.D: Plan improvements for the newest AI uses before older ones

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF uses profiles: comparing a current profile with a target profile shows gaps, and closing them is prioritized by risk.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the agency's plan before weighing each approach.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF describes current and target profiles: a current profile shows how AI risk is managed today, a target profile the outcomes needed, and comparing them reveals gaps for action plans prioritized by risk and resources. Applying the Generative AI Profile to the seven generative uses, option A, confuses NIST's cross-sectoral profile for generative AI with the current and target profiles that show this agency's own gaps.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because NIST AI 600-1 profiles generative AI. But it covers only seven uses and lists cross-sector actions; it shows neither where each use stands nor which gaps come first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because frameworks feel authoritative. But the NIST AI RMF is voluntary; the agency may adopt it, but that does not make it regulation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because new AI uses feel riskiest. But the framework orders gaps by risk and resources; novelty alone shows neither where harm is likely nor current gaps.

tips: Eliminate: D orders the work by novelty rather than risk, and C treats a voluntary framework as regulation.

Final two: B beats A because current and target profiles show this agency's own gaps to close by priority; the Generative AI Profile lists generative AI risks and suggested actions, not a gap analysis.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, current and target profiles turn the framework into a prioritized, risk-based plan.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 6 (AI RMF Profiles); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.2 (Treatment prioritized by impact, likelihood and resources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF uses current and target profiles to find gaps and plan improvements by priority). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. Release audit fix, 18 Nov 2026: the stem now asks how to rank improvements across all twelve uses, so applying the Generative AI Profile to seven of them is plainly partial. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. The Govern function
questions.question: A Japanese trading house finished its NIST AI RMF Govern work in 2024 and now applies only Map, Measure and Manage to each new model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have management treat Govern as complete, since policies were approved
options.B: Have the IS auditor refresh the AI policy every year
options.C: Have model owners update risk tolerances when mapping each model
options.D: Have senior management review Govern outcomes as AI uses change

questions.key_concept: In the NIST AI RMF, Govern is cross-cutting and ongoing: its policies, roles and tolerances need periodic review as AI uses change.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether governance set two years ago still fits the models adopted since.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF calls Govern cross-cutting, infused throughout the other functions, and calls attention to governance a continual requirement over an AI system's lifespan. Policies, roles and tolerances set in 2024 may not fit models adopted since, so senior management should review Govern outcomes as uses change. Having model owners update tolerances while mapping each model, option C, hands senior management's tolerances to owners and leaves the 2024 policies and roles unreviewed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the policies were approved. But Govern is cross-cutting and ongoing; policies set in 2024 need review as new AI uses arrive.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit sees where governance falls short. But writing policy is management's job; audit assesses the policy and would lose independence by maintaining it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the Map function documents risk tolerances. But senior management sets them; owners adjusting tolerances model by model leave the 2024 policies and roles unreviewed.

tips: Eliminate: A treats Govern as a one-time project, and B has the IS auditor maintain policy that audit must assess.
Final two: D beats C because Govern is ongoing and tolerances are senior management's; owners adjusting them model by model leave the 2024 policies and roles unreviewed.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, Govern is cross-cutting and continuing; look for periodic review of policies, roles and tolerances, not a finished project.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 5.1 (Govern is a cross-cutting function infused throughout the others); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.5 (Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (in the NIST AI RMF, Govern is cross-cutting and continual; its policies, roles and tolerances are reviewed as AI uses change). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Agents replacing scripted bots
questions.question: A Jordanian water utility's AI agent, planning its own steps, replaced a scripted billing-dispute bot and passed the bot's test scripts; system-enforced credit limits remain. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent's dispute decisions may be harder to explain than the bot's
options.B: No test shows the agent learned from the bot's past billing disputes
options.C: Passing the bot's tests cannot show how the agent will behave
options.D: The agent may grant credits above the system-enforced limits

questions.key_concept: A scripted bot follows fixed steps; an agent chooses its steps at run time, so passing the bot's scripts shows little about the agent.
questions.pre_read: Compare how the old and the new system decide a dispute before weighing each risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The bot's test scripts check fixed steps on fixed cases, which suited a bot that always followed them. An agent plans its steps at run time, so passing those scripts shows only how it handled those cases, not the paths it may choose on others; it must be tested as deployed. Harder-to-explain decisions, option A, are a real agent concern, but explainability is one property such testing would assess.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because agents are harder to trace than scripts. But that is one property to assess; the gap is that no test reflects how the agent now works.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models learn from data. But training on past disputes would not show how the agent behaves as deployed; only testing the agent itself does.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because agents can overreach. But limits enforced by the billing system hold whatever the agent plans, so they are not the main concern here.

tips: Eliminate: B treats training on past disputes as evidence of behavior, and D forgets that system-enforced limits bind whatever the agent plans.
Final two: C beats A because scripts with fixed steps cannot show the paths an agent chooses at run time; explainability is one property that testing the agent as deployed would assess.
Exam cue: when a scripted bot becomes an agent, passing the old scripts proves little; the agent must be tested as it now works.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (an agent plans its steps at run time, so evidence from testing a fixed script no longer covers what the system does). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Calculations by generative models
questions.question: A Ugandan vanilla growers' association has its clerk paste members' delivery records into a generative AI chatbot, which works out each member's season payout. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the process owner compute payouts with a spreadsheet formula
options.B: Fine-tune the chatbot on the association's past seasons' payout calculations
options.C: Have a clerk recheck a sample of the chatbot's payouts each season
options.D: Have the chatbot show its work beside each payout figure

questions.key_concept: A generative model predicts text; unless it calls a calculation tool, its figures are not computed, so fixed-rule work belongs in a formula or system.
questions.pre_read: Identify the kind of AI in use and the kind of task it has been given.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative chatbot produces the most likely next words, so unless it runs a calculation tool its payout figures can look exact without being calculated from the records. Payouts follow a fixed rule, so a formula in a spreadsheet or the accounts system computes them reliably and can be checked. Sampling the chatbot's figures, option C, catches some errors but keeps a method that cannot be relied on for arithmetic.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training improves models. But fine-tuning on past figures teaches the chatbot what payouts look like, not how to calculate them correctly.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because review catches errors. But a sample leaves most payouts unchecked, and the chatbot's errors follow no pattern a sample would reliably reveal.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because shown work looks like an audit trail. But the work shown is generated text too; it can look sound while not matching the figure.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes training teaches a generative model to calculate, and D treats the work shown as proof, though it is generated text like the answer.
Final two: A beats C because a fixed rule belongs in a formula that computes exactly; sampling the chatbot's figures checks a method that should not be doing arithmetic.
Exam cue: a chatbot's figures are predicted text unless a calculation tool produced them; when a task follows a fixed rule, a formula or rules engine beats checking AI output.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.1 (Resources and non-AI alternatives considered)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (generative models predict likely text rather than compute, so a task that follows a fixed rule belongs in a formula, not a chatbot). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Forecasting after a solar subsidy
questions.question: A Pakistani electricity distributor's demand model, which uses rooftop-solar share as an input, learned from years below 5%; a subsidy will lift it to 25% by June. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on forecasts that come with a high confidence score
options.B: Rely on the validation results, which covered several held-out years
options.C: Have the model owner retrain the model once June's demand is known
options.D: Have the model owner flag forecasts from out-of-range inputs

questions.key_concept: A model learns patterns only within the conditions in its training data; outside that range it extrapolates, often without signaling doubt.
questions.pre_read: Note what is new about this June before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A model learns patterns only across the conditions in its training data; at a 25% solar share it must extrapolate, yet it will still output a confident-looking number. Flagging forecasts made from out-of-range inputs lets planners treat them with caution and use other methods meanwhile. Retraining once June's demand is known, option C, helps later but leaves this June's grid planning resting on unflagged guesses.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because confidence sounds like reliability. But a model can stay confident outside the conditions it learned from; confidence does not mark the edge of its training data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because held-out testing is good practice. But the held-out years came from the same range, so validation says nothing about behavior at a 25% solar share.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because new data improves a model. But it arrives only after June has passed; this June's planning still relies on forecasts nobody has flagged.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes held-out data covers conditions it never contained, and A treats a model's confidence as proof it is inside its training range.
Final two: D beats C because it acts before June's decisions; retraining afterwards fixes a later model while this June's forecasts go unflagged.
Exam cue: models are reliable only inside the conditions they learned from; look for a control that flags inputs outside that range.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (models are reliable only inside the conditions they learned from; inputs outside that range need flagging, not trust). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Cutoff scores for public decisions
questions.question: A Montenegrin coastal authority closes beaches when its water-quality model scores over 0.3, which officials read as a 30% chance of unsafe water. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Officials rather than data scientists chose the closure cutoff
options.B: A 0.3 score may not mean a 30% chance of unsafe water
options.C: Rerunning the model may change a beach's chance of unsafe water
options.D: Closing at 0.3 may shut many beaches whose water is safe

questions.key_concept: Many models output scores between 0 and 1 that rank cases well but are not calibrated probabilities until checked against real outcome rates.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each party assumes about the model's output before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Many models output scores between 0 and 1 that rank cases well but are not calibrated probabilities. If 0.3 really corresponds to a 10% or a 60% rate of unsafe water, closures are set at a risk level nobody chose. Comparing scores with lab results shows what each score means. Needless closures, option D, are a cost, but judging them also depends on what the scores really mean.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data scientists know the model. But the closure cutoff is a risk decision for the accountable officials; the data team informs it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some AI varies run to run. But a trained scoring model returns the same score for the same inputs; variation is a generative-model trait.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because needless closures cost tourism. But whether 0.3 closes too many beaches depends on what a 0.3 score really means, which nobody has checked.

tips: Eliminate: A hands a risk decision to the data team, and C confuses a fixed scoring model with generative models that vary run to run.
Final two: B beats D because the officials' rule assumes the score is a probability; until scores are checked against lab results, nobody knows whether closures are too many or too few.
Exam cue: a score between 0 and 1 is not a probability unless shown to match real outcome rates; check what the score means before people act on it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a model score is not a probability unless it has been shown to match real outcome rates (calibration)). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Risk ratings for a planned model
questions.question: A Liechtenstein trust company's planned sanctions-screening model is rated medium risk because analysts will confirm each alert's pre-filled decision; it should raise 1,500 alerts daily for 10 analysts. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the model owner reassess the rating against review capacity
options.B: Have management hire more analysts to support the medium rating
options.C: Have the IS auditor review a sample of alerts each day
options.D: Let the model close low-score alerts without analyst review

questions.key_concept: Human review lowers AI risk only when reviewers can really check each output; a rating that assumes impossible review overstates the control.
questions.pre_read: Note what the medium rating rests on before choosing a step.
questions.correct_explanation: The medium rating assumes analysts really check each pre-filled decision, but 150 alerts per analyst a day leaves about three minutes each in an eight-hour day; under that pressure, people tend to accept the model's suggestion (automation bias). The owner should first reassess the rating against the review analysts can actually give, then choose a response. Hiring analysts, option B, may be part of that response, but deciding it first skips the risk judgment.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more reviewers fix the workload. But it jumps to one response before the owner reassesses a rating built on review that cannot happen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor tests alerts. But daily alert review is an operating control; performing it would impair the IS auditor's independence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it cuts the workload. But letting the model close alerts unreviewed removes the very oversight the rating relies on.

tips: Eliminate: D removes the human review the rating depends on, and C has the IS auditor run an operating control.
Final two: A beats B because FIRST asks for the risk judgment; hiring is one possible response, chosen after the owner reassesses a rating that assumed review the team cannot give.
Exam cue: human review lowers AI risk only if reviewers have the time and skill to check; test that the assumed oversight is feasible.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (human review lowers AI risk only if reviewers have the time to check, so review capacity is a requirement to confirm before relying on it). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Completeness fix, 12 Nov 2026: option B trimmed so the key is the single longest option (length-tell target). Re-audit fix, 12 Nov 2026: setting changed from a bank's anti-money-laundering model to a trust company's sanctions-screening model so it no longer repeats CISA d3_137.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Data a new model needs
questions.question: A Samoan mobile operator plans to build a model to approve handset installment plans it launched this year, so few plans have been repaid or defaulted. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Train the model on synthetic outcomes generated from current plans
options.B: License a vendor model trained on other lenders' installment plan outcomes
options.C: Have the owner confirm the outcome data can support training and testing
options.D: Pilot several algorithms and keep the most accurate one

questions.key_concept: A model learns from past cases with known outcomes; without enough of them, it can be neither trained nor validated for the people it serves.
questions.pre_read: Note what is new about the product and what that means for the data available.
questions.correct_explanation: A model learns to predict repayment from past plans whose outcome is known; with a product launched this year, few outcomes exist, so there is little to learn from and nothing to validate against. The owner should first establish whether the data can support a model at all, or whether rules suit the product until outcomes build up. A vendor model trained elsewhere, option B, still needs local outcomes to show it fits these customers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because synthetic data can fill gaps. But synthetic outcomes come from assumptions, not real repayments, so a model trained on them learns those assumptions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it skips the data gap. But other lenders' customers may differ, and with few local outcomes the operator cannot check whether the model fits its own customers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because comparing models is normal practice. But with few repaid or defaulted plans, every candidate's accuracy rests on too few outcomes to mean anything.

tips: Eliminate: D compares models before there are outcomes to judge them, and A trains on invented outcomes that only echo the assumptions used to make them.
Final two: C beats B because a model is only as good as its outcome data; a bought model also needs local outcomes to show it fits these customers.
Exam cue: before build or buy, confirm the labeled data needed to train and validate exists for the population served.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.1 (Resources and non-AI alternatives considered)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (before building or buying, confirm the outcome data needed to train and validate a model exists for the population it will serve). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Choosing which AI uses to fund
questions.question: A Senegalese port authority's AI strategy chooses which of 15 pilots, from tug scheduling to fee disputes, to fund by ranking the accuracy each vendor reports. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have management rank pilots by accuracy on the port's own data
options.B: Have management rank pilots by objectives served and risk to people
options.C: Have management fund the pilots with the largest projected savings
options.D: Have the IS auditor score each pilot's fit with the strategy

questions.key_concept: AI strategy links each use to business objectives and risk; accuracy scores from different tasks are not comparable and say nothing about value.
questions.pre_read: Note what the ranking figure compares across very different pilots, then ask what it can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: Accuracy figures from different tasks cannot be compared, and a high score says nothing about how much a pilot advances the port's objectives or what harm its errors could cause. A strategy should fund AI uses by business value and risk, including risk to the people affected. Ranking pilots by accuracy on the port's own data, option A, shows each model works there, not that the use is worth doing or safe enough.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendor-reported figures need checking on local data. But accuracy on different tasks still cannot be compared, and a model can be accurate on a use that adds little.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because savings serve a business objective. But ranking on savings leaves out what model errors could cost the people affected, which a strategy must weigh.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor can judge alignment. But scoring and choosing pilots are management decisions; the IS auditor assesses the method.

tips: Eliminate: C ranks pilots on savings, though a strategy must also weigh risk to people, and D has the IS auditor make management's funding choice.
Final two: B beats A because even locally measured accuracy shows a model works, not that its use serves the port's objectives within risk.
Exam cue: AI strategy links uses to business objectives and risk; accuracy shows a model works, not that the use is worth it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.3 (Mission and goals for the AI technology documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.4 (Business value or context of use defined or re-evaluated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (an AI strategy funds uses by the business objectives they serve and their risk; a model's accuracy shows it works, not that the use is worth it). Re-audit: the crane-maintenance pilot, which echoed a D2 notes example, became tug scheduling. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Approved tools on personal accounts
questions.question: A Ukrainian medical-device maker's AI assistant runs under enterprise terms barring training on company documents; a third of engineers use it via personal accounts on consumer terms. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Personal accounts may run an older model trained on less data
options.B: Personal accounts may bypass the firm's single sign-on controls
options.C: The firm pays for enterprise licenses that engineers leave unused
options.D: Engineers' inputs may be used to train the provider's models

questions.key_concept: With hosted AI, data protection often rests on contract terms; the same tool used through consumer accounts may allow the provider to train on inputs.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes the approved setup safe, and what changes when the same tool is used another way.
questions.correct_explanation: The protection the firm relied on is contractual: enterprise terms bar the provider from training on its documents. Consumer terms commonly allow it, so documents sent through personal accounts may become training data and could resurface in other users' outputs. Bypassed sign-on, option B, weakens access control, but the larger harm is the firm's documents leaving under terms it never approved.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because plans differ in features. But the model's version is not the risk; the terms covering the firm's documents are.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because identity controls matter. But sign-on governs who logs in, not what the provider may do with the documents sent under consumer terms.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because licenses cost money. But wasted spend is minor beside the firm's documents being used to train a provider's models.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about model quality, not data terms, and C ranks license cost above the exposure of the firm's documents.
Final two: D beats B because the approved tool's safeguard is its enterprise terms; sign-on controls who logs in, not whether the provider may train on what is sent.
Exam cue: with hosted AI, the same tool can carry different data terms by account type; check which terms govern what staff actually use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.10 (Intellectual Property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (the same hosted AI tool can carry different data terms by account type; acceptable use must cover which terms govern what staff actually use). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Models whose owner has left
questions.question: A Chadian cotton ginnery's lint-grading model, which sets the price paid to each farmer, has been retrained twice since its named owner left eight months ago. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Changed versions went live with no accountable owner accepting them
options.B: The retrained versions may grade lint differently from before
options.C: The retrains were not reviewed by the IS auditor before use
options.D: The AI inventory still lists a departed employee as the model's owner

questions.key_concept: A retrain changes a model's behavior, so each version needs acceptance by an owner with authority over the decisions it supports.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a retrain is, and who normally accepts one.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrain changes how the model behaves, so each new version needs acceptance by an owner with authority over the prices it sets. With the owner gone, two changed versions went live with nobody accountable accepting them, and nobody can decide to pause or override the grades. The stale inventory entry, option D, is a symptom; correcting the name without an owner exercising authority would leave the gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because changed grades can surprise farmers. But retraining is meant to change behavior; the concern is that no owner accepted the change, not that it happened.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor reviews changes. But approving releases is management's responsibility; the IS auditor assesses whether the owner accepted them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because records should be accurate. But fixing the name treats a symptom; the risk is that changed versions and their grades have had no one accountable for them.

tips: Eliminate: C makes the IS auditor an approver of releases, and B treats the expected effect of retraining as the problem.
Final two: A beats D because retrains are changes an accountable owner must accept; the stale record shows the gap but is not the harm.
Exam cue: when a model's owner leaves, check who has accepted its changes since; every retrain is a change that needs an accountable owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (each retrain is a change an accountable owner must accept; each retrain since the owner left went live with no owner accepting it). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A process-control model at a plant
questions.question: A Tunisian phosphate processor's flotation-control model, owned by the plant manager, raises recovery by adding reagent, which the environmental manager answers for under its discharge permit. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner fund extra treatment to stay within the permit
options.B: Make the environmental manager joint owner of the model
options.C: Have the owner set reagent limits with the environmental manager
options.D: Have the data science team add reagent use to the model's objective

questions.key_concept: A model trades off anything outside its target; its one named owner sets limits with the roles those side effects touch.
questions.pre_read: Read what the model does and who answers for each effect before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: The model pursues recovery, so it will keep adding reagent while recovery rises, putting the discharge permit at risk. The plant manager, its single owner, should set reagent limits with the environmental manager, who answers for the permit. Funding extra treatment, option A, leaves the model unbounded: treatment chases whatever reagent load the model creates.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner pays to protect the permit. But the model keeps adding reagent while recovery rises, so treatment chases a growing load while nothing limits the model.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it gives the environmental manager a say. But two owners blur who decides to pause or change the model; one owner should consult the other.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it changes the model directly. But how much recovery to trade for permit compliance is a business decision; the data team would make it for the owner.

tips: Eliminate: B splits ownership, so nobody clearly decides to pause or change the model, and D hands a business trade-off to the data science team.
Final two: C beats A because the model keeps adding reagent while recovery rises; its owner must limit it with the manager its side effects touch, not fund treatment to absorb them.
Exam cue: a model pursues the target it is given; its one owner limits its side effects with the people who answer for them, rather than leaving others to absorb them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (one named owner per model; the owner sets limits on the model's side effects with the roles accountable for them, without splitting ownership). Cross-domain gate fix, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled because the earlier version mirrored the notes 1C.2 example (problems handled by the data team never reaching the owner). Re-audit, 12 Nov 2026: option A replaced with a downstream-treatment runner-up so the AI fact (an optimizer keeps pushing an unbounded side effect) decides, not general single accountability; the side-effect lesson of aaia_d2_037 is no longer the runner-up. Round 3: option A now has the owner as actor (funding treatment), so the key is not the only option naming the owner and the unbounded-optimizer fact decides. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. What an AI incident metric counts
questions.question: A Grenadian insurer's AI program report tells the board of zero AI incidents; the count comes only from service-desk outage tickets for its pricing and claims models. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add each model's uptime and response time to the board report
options.B: Have model owners count harmful outputs found by sampling decisions
options.C: Have the service desk add a ticket category for AI incidents
options.D: Have the IS auditor confirm the incident count before each report

questions.key_concept: AI models can be wrong or unfair while running normally, so an AI incident metric must count harmful outputs found by checking decisions.
questions.pre_read: Read where the incident count comes from before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: A model can be wrong or unfair while running perfectly: a pricing model can overcharge one group of customers, or a claims model can misroute valid claims, and nothing breaks. Counting only outage tickets makes zero incidents a measure of uptime, not harm. The metric should count harmful outputs that model owners find by sampling decisions. A new ticket category, option C, only sorts tickets people raise; silent wrong outputs raise none.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because availability is easy to report. But uptime shares the outage tickets' blind spot: a model can run perfectly while its outputs harm customers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because clearer categories improve reporting. But a category only sorts tickets someone raises; wrong outputs break nothing, so they still raise no tickets.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor checks figures. But confirming each count makes the IS auditor part of the metric's operation, and a confirmed count still misses harmful outputs.

tips: Eliminate: A adds another measure of whether models run, not whether their outputs harm, and D has the IS auditor operate the reporting.
Final two: B beats C because wrong or unfair outputs break nothing and raise no tickets; sampling decisions finds them, while a new category just sorts the same outage tickets.
Exam cue: AI often fails silently; an incident metric fed only by outage tickets reports uptime, not whether models harm people.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 4.3 (Practices enable AI testing, incident identification and information sharing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (program metrics track whether governance works, such as AI incidents; an AI model can be wrong or unfair while running normally, so an incident count fed only by outage tickets misses harmful outputs). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Completeness fix, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled from board training on AI failure modes (the frame of aaia_d1_032) to an AI incident metric fed only by outage tickets; setting kept, key letter B and foundational difficulty kept. Re-audit fix, 12 Nov 2026: option B names the model owners as the ones who sample, so the IS auditor's role is not in doubt (blind-test note); key letter B kept.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Workforce changes after a model takes over
questions.question: A Salvadoran sugar mill's model, trained on inspectors' reports, flags burned fields from drone images; the workforce plan ends field inspections, keeping a crew on call for outages. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Drone flights may cost more than the field inspections did
options.B: Growers may object to flags made without anyone visiting
options.C: The on-call crew may be too small to cover a long outage
options.D: No ground truth will remain to check flags or label data

questions.key_concept: Models are checked and retrained against correct answers people supply; a workforce plan that removes those people leaves the model's accuracy unmeasured.
questions.pre_read: Read the model's history and the workforce plan before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learned from inspectors' reports, and those reports are also how anyone checks its flags and gathers labels to retrain it. Ending field inspections leaves no ground truth, so falling accuracy as fields, crops or cameras change would go unmeasured. The on-call crew's size, option C, matters in an outage, but the crew is called only once a failure is noticed, and a model that slowly grows less accurate causes no outage.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because running costs matter. But cost does not change the model's reliability; the loss that matters is the field truth it is checked against.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because growers deserve a fair process. But settling an objection needs facts; with no field reports, no one could show whether the flags are right.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because continuity capacity matters. But the crew is called only once a failure is noticed, and with no field reports nobody could measure the model's falling accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: A weighs drone costs, which do not affect the model's reliability, and B centers growers' objections rather than whether the flags are right.
Final two: D beats C because field reports are the ground truth that measures the model's accuracy and supplies labels for retraining; an on-call crew acts only after someone notices a failure.
Exam cue: when AI replaces the people whose judgments trained it, ask who will supply the correct answers needed to check and retrain it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 4.2 (Trustworthiness results validated with domain experts); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (assess AI's effect on the workforce: models need people who supply correct answers to check and retrain them). Cross-domain gate fix, 12 Nov 2026: re-angled because the earlier version restated the notes 2G.1 example and aaia_d2_088 (AI output problems with no place in IT incident categories). Release audit fix, 18 Nov 2026: an on-call crew added to the stem and option C changed to its size, so the manual-fallback runner-up no longer mirrors aaia_d1_031. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. Final release fix, 18 Nov 2026: explanation, key_concept and tip 2 now say accuracy goes unmeasured, not that drift goes undetected, since input drift can still be watched without labels (D2 notes). Final release fix 2, 18 Nov 2026: option D no longer echoes 'trained' or names the model, so matching stem words cannot find the key. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Impact ratings for a vendor credit score
questions.question: A Bosnian lender rates the impact of wrongful refusals by its vendor credit score as low, since refused applicants can borrow elsewhere; most local lenders share that score. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: A wrong score may shut applicants out at most lenders at once
options.B: The lender cannot see how the vendor calculates its score
options.C: Wrongly refused applicants may complain to the banking regulator
options.D: The vendor score may be less accurate than lenders' in-house models

questions.key_concept: When many organizations rely on one model, its errors repeat across all of them; impact on people is larger than any single use suggests.
questions.pre_read: Check each assumption behind the low rating against the stem's facts.
questions.correct_explanation: The rating assumes a wrongful refusal is a minor setback because applicants can go elsewhere. When most lenders use the same score, the same error follows an applicant everywhere, so one wrong score can shut a person out of credit across the market. That raises impact well above the rating. Score opacity, option B, is a real third-party concern, but it does not change the misjudged impact on applicants.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because opaque vendor scores are hard to assure. But the stem's flaw is the impact rating, which ignores that the same error repeats at most lenders.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complaints have costs. But it weighs the lender's exposure rather than the harm to applicants shut out across the market.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because in-house models can be tuned locally. But nothing shows an in-house model would be more accurate; the issue is errors shared across lenders.

tips: Eliminate: C weighs harm to the lender instead of applicants, and D assumes an in-house model is better with nothing to show it.
Final two: A beats B because the rating's reasoning fails when the same score is used everywhere; opacity is real but does not change how badly a shared error harms people.
Exam cue: when many organizations use the same AI model, its errors repeat across them; rate impact on people at that scale.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (when many organizations use the same model, its errors repeat across them, so impact on people must be rated at that scale (homogenization)). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Foreseeable misuse of generated output
questions.question: An Austrian teen-fashion retailer's styling chatbot, which teenage shoppers already trick past its rules, was risk-assessed for wrong answers, bias and privacy. Which missing risk should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Attackers stealing the chatbot's underlying model weights
options.B: Teenagers getting it to promise discounts the retailer refuses
options.C: Teenagers getting tips on starving themselves to lose weight fast
options.D: The provider updating the chatbot's model without notice

questions.key_concept: Generative AI can be steered into harmful content; risk identification covers foreseeable misuse, ranked by likelihood and the severity of harm to people.
questions.pre_read: Rate each option for likelihood and for severity of harm, using only facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative styling chatbot can be steered into harmful content, and teenagers already get it past its rules, so tips on starving themselves are a likely misuse as well as a severe one for shoppers who include minors. Foreseeable misuse belongs in the risk assessment beside accuracy and privacy. Tricked discount promises, option B, are likely too, but they cost the retailer money, far below harm to a teenager's health.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI security matters. But treating AI risk as theft of model files misses the harm the chatbot's own outputs can cause.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because tricked promises are likely and familiar. But their harm is a financial loss to the retailer, well below starvation advice reaching teenagers who already bypass the rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because silent vendor updates are a real AI risk. But an update changes how known risks behave; self-harm advice reaching minors is a missing harm far more severe.

tips: Eliminate: A treats AI risk as theft of model files, and D raises a change risk that leaves the most severe missing harm unassessed.
Final two: C beats B because teenagers already bypass the chatbot's rules, so harmful advice is likely, and harm to minors' health far exceeds a discount the retailer loses.
Exam cue: AI risk identification includes foreseeable misuse of generated output, ranked by likelihood and by harm to the people using or affected by it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.3 (Dangerous, Violent, or Hateful Content); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (AI risk identification includes foreseeable misuse of generated output, ranked by likelihood and harm to the people using or affected by it). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Completeness fix, 12 Nov 2026: setting changed from a tutoring firm's chatbot for secondary students to a chemistry-kit seller's chatbot used by teenage buyers, so it no longer repeats aaia_d3_028; runner-up is now tricked discount promises (business harm). Re-audit fix, 12 Nov 2026: setting changed from a chemistry-kit seller to a teen-fashion retailer's styling chatbot so it no longer repeats aaia_d2_209 (dangerous chemical instructions); pre_read made neutral; key letter C kept.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Tolerances for a benefits chatbot
questions.question: An Estonian unemployment fund's board has low appetite for claimants acting on wrong guidance; the tolerance for its benefits chatbot is average user satisfaction of 4 of 5. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: An average of 4 of 5 is too low a target
options.B: Claimants may rate fluent but incorrect answers highly
options.C: The board, not senior management, should set the tolerance
options.D: Satisfaction ratings come from a small share of claimants

questions.key_concept: A tolerance must measure the harm the appetite names; generative answers can satisfy users while being wrong, so satisfaction cannot stand in for accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the appetite names with what the tolerance measures.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance should measure the harm the appetite names: claimants acting on wrong guidance. Generative chatbots give fluent, confident answers, so users often rate wrong answers highly; satisfaction can stay high while errors rise. The tolerance needs a measure of answer accuracy, such as sampled answers checked against benefit rules. Few raters, option D, weakens the measure, but a full response rate would still measure the wrong thing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a higher bar sounds safer. But raising a satisfaction target still does not measure wrong guidance, the harm the board named.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the board owns appetite. But the board need not set tolerances itself; senior management often sets them within appetite, and who set this one is not the problem.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because low response rates bias surveys. But even if every claimant rated, satisfaction would not show whether the guidance was right.

tips: Eliminate: C treats who set the tolerance as the flaw, though senior management may set it within appetite, and A tightens a measure that cannot detect wrong guidance.
Final two: B beats D because the measure itself misses the named harm; fixing the survey's coverage would still measure satisfaction, not accuracy.
Exam cue: a tolerance must measure the harm the appetite names; user satisfaction does not show whether AI answers are correct.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (a tolerance must measure the harm the appetite names; user satisfaction does not show whether generated answers are correct). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Spending tolerances for an agent
questions.question: A Cambodian hotel chain's tolerance lets its ordering agent, told to keep kitchens stocked without delay, order up to $2,000 unapproved; an indicator counts larger orders. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent's model has not been trained to respect the limit
options.B: Requiring approval above $2,000 may slow the agent's ordering
options.C: The agent may obey a supplier email telling it to order more
options.D: Several purchases under $2,000 can add up to far more than $2,000

questions.key_concept: Agents pursue their task by whatever path their permissions allow; a per-action limit and indicator can miss exposure that builds up across actions.
questions.pre_read: Read the tolerance and the indicator literally, then ask what they would miss.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent pursues its goal through whatever its permissions allow; told to avoid delay, it needs no intent to meet a $3,000 need with two $1,500 orders, which pass the limit and never show in an indicator counting larger orders. The tolerance and indicator need a cumulative measure, such as spend per supplier per day. Injected email instructions, option C, are a real agent risk, but nothing in the stem points to them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because training shapes behavior. But limits belong in the ordering system, enforced outside the model; training cannot guarantee the agent respects them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the agent is told to avoid delay. But that goal is the risk's driver, not a cost to weigh; approval for large spending is the tolerance's purpose.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because agents that read messages can be steered by injected text. But nothing in the stem says this agent reads supplier email; the gap is the per-order measure.

tips: Eliminate: A puts a spending limit inside the model instead of the ordering system, and B weighs convenience against the tolerance's purpose.
Final two: D beats C because the tolerance and indicator count single orders, which an agent can stay under while spending more; injected instructions are a real risk the stem never raises.
Exam cue: when an agent acts within per-action limits, check cumulative exposure; a goal-seeking agent can meet a rule's letter and miss its purpose.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (an agent working toward a goal can stay under a per-action limit while exceeding its purpose, so tolerances and indicators must see cumulative exposure). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Completeness fix, 12 Nov 2026: option B trimmed so the key is the single longest option (length-tell target). Re-audit fix, 12 Nov 2026: stem no longer names order splitting; the agent's no-delay goal is now the deciding AI fact.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Exiting a vendor that tuned on your data
questions.question: A Georgian bank is leaving its document-extraction vendor next year; the vendor's model, also served to other clients, was fine-tuned on the bank's loan files. Which contract term should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Escrow of the tuned model's files and configuration for the bank
options.B: Service credits from the vendor if extraction accuracy falls
options.C: Limits on the vendor's use of models tuned on the bank's files
options.D: Deletion of the bank's loan files when the contract ends

questions.key_concept: When a vendor tunes a shared model on your data, deleting files at exit leaves what it learned; contracts must limit that model's use.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the bank needs from the vendor once the relationship ends.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning folds patterns, and possibly fragments, of the bank's loan files into the vendor's shared model, which other clients use. Unless the contract limits that use, the vendor may keep serving the model after the bank leaves, and confidential loan details could surface elsewhere. The bank is exiting, so escrow of the tuned model, option A, protects continuity it no longer needs and leaves its data inside the vendor's model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because escrow protects against vendor failure. But the bank is leaving by choice; keeping a copy does not stop the vendor using what it learned from the files.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy matters until exit. But service credits compensate for poor output; they do nothing about the bank's data inside the vendor's model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because deleting data at exit is standard. But a model tuned on the files keeps what it learned after the files are gone.

tips: Eliminate: D deletes the files but forgets the trained model, and B compensates for poor service rather than protecting the bank's data.
Final two: C beats A because an exiting bank needs its data out of the vendor's shared model; escrow keeps a copy for continuity the bank no longer needs.
Exam cue: a model tuned on your data carries that data; contracts must cover what happens to tuned models, not only the files.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (a model tuned on your data carries that data; contracts must cover what happens to tuned models, not only to the files). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. AI added by an outsourcing provider
questions.question: A Luxembourg fund administrator learns its outsourcing provider uses an AI tool of unknown design to choose which investor complaints reach it; its pre-AI contract grants audit rights. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the administrator assess the tool as a third-party AI risk
options.B: Leave the tool to the provider, which is accountable for it
options.C: Have the administrator amend the contract to cover the provider's AI use
options.D: Rely on the provider's annual assurance report on its controls

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing a process does not outsource accountability; AI a provider adds to it is third-party AI risk to identify and assess before choosing responses.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word, then ask who answers to investors for their complaints.
questions.correct_explanation: The provider's tool now decides which complaints the administrator ever sees, so an AI system outside its view shapes how investors are treated, while accountability stays with the administrator. It should first assess the tool as third-party AI risk, using its audit rights to learn how the tool decides and what missed complaints cost. Amending the contract, option C, may follow, but which terms are needed comes from that assessment.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the provider runs the tool. But outsourcing does not move accountability; the administrator still answers to investors for complaints.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because contract rights give leverage. But existing audit rights already allow an assessment, and terms chosen before it may miss what matters, such as how missed complaints are detected.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because assurance reports are standard for outsourcing. But a report on the provider's general controls does not show how its new AI decides which complaints matter.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on a general controls report for an AI tool's decisions, and B hands accountability to the provider.
Final two: A beats C because FIRST asks for the risk assessment; the right contract terms follow from knowing how the tool decides and what missed complaints would cost investors.
Exam cue: AI added inside an outsourced process is still your third-party AI risk; assess it first, then set contract terms.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (Supplier risks assessed and monitored over the relationship)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (AI added inside an outsourced process is still the organization's third-party AI risk; assess it first, then set contract terms). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Choosing training fields
questions.question: A Cypriot ship-management firm's data scientists trained a crew-retention model on all 600 HR fields, including marital status and religion, because more data usually helps. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Remove marital status and religion, then retrain the crew-retention model
options.B: Have the data owner approve each field against the model's purpose
options.C: Pseudonymize crew identifiers before the model retrains
options.D: Have the IS auditor choose which fields the model keeps

questions.key_concept: Training on every available field ignores purpose; data owners approve each field for the model's use, which also exposes proxies for sensitive data.
questions.pre_read: Ask on what basis data was chosen for this model, and who should decide that.
questions.correct_explanation: Training on every available field ignores purpose: each field used is a decision about personal data that the data owner should approve for this model. Removing the two sensitive fields, option A, treats the visible symptom; other fields can stand in for them, and the remaining hundreds were never justified for predicting crew retention. Purpose-based approval covers all fields, including proxies.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it removes the obvious sensitive data. But other fields can act as proxies for religion or marital status, and the rest still lack approval for this use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because pseudonymization protects identities. But fields keep their meaning without names, so the model still learns from data never approved for this purpose.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor can spot unjustified data. But choosing model inputs is for the data owner and model owner; the IS auditor assesses the approval.

tips: Eliminate: C treats pseudonymization as permission to use data, and D has the IS auditor make a choice that belongs to the data owner and model owner.
Final two: B beats A because purpose-based approval covers every field, including proxies; dropping two named fields leaves the other uses unjustified.
Exam cue: in data governance for AI, each training field needs an owner-approved purpose; "more data helps" is not a reason.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (each field used to train a model needs an owner-approved purpose; removing named sensitive fields leaves proxies and unjustified fields). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Reusing a marketing model's output
questions.question: An Albanian bank's marketing model estimates each customer's income; the estimates are written into the customer database's income field, which the credit team uses to set card limits. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Estimates may be less accurate for customers with irregular income
options.B: Customers are not told that the bank's model estimates their income
options.C: The marketing model has not been retrained since it was built
options.D: Inferred incomes are used as if customers had declared them

questions.key_concept: A model's output is an estimate with error; stored without a label, it loses its lineage and gets used as if it were verified fact.
questions.pre_read: Trace the income figure from where it was produced to the decision that now uses it.
questions.correct_explanation: Model output is an estimate with error, built for targeting offers. Written into the income field, it loses its lineage and is used as if customers had declared it, so card limits rest on estimates the credit process never validated. Inferred data needs its own label, owner and approved uses. Customers not being told, option B, is a real transparency issue, but the stem's harm is wrong credit decisions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because estimates vary in accuracy by group. But any estimate, however accurate on average, is not declared income, yet it now sets credit limits as if it were.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people should know what is inferred about them. But the stem's harm is credit limits built on unvalidated estimates, which telling customers would not fix.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because stale models drift. But a freshly retrained model still produces estimates; the gap is that its output is stored and used as declared fact.

tips: Eliminate: C refreshes the model while its output still stands in for declared income, and A questions accuracy when any estimate used as fact is the problem.
Final two: D beats B because model estimates stored as facts drive credit limits with no validation; disclosure matters but leaves the wrong limits in place.
Exam cue: model outputs are data with lineage; inferred values must stay labeled as inferred, with an owner and approved uses.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (model outputs are data with lineage; inferred values must stay labeled as inferred, with an owner and approved uses). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Privacy scope for an application agent
questions.question: A Mauritian study-abroad agency's application agent calls outside university, visa and housing services, passing whatever student details it judges useful; the privacy assessment covers only its case system. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Student data may go to outside services no assessment reaches
options.B: The agent's replies may differ for identical application requests
options.C: The privacy assessment may miss weak encryption to outside services
options.D: The visa service may return out-of-date entry rules to students

questions.key_concept: Agents choose at run time what data to pass to each tool; personal data can flow to services that no privacy assessment covers.
questions.pre_read: Follow the student data, step by step, through what the agent does.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent decides at run time which details to send to which service, so student data, possibly passport numbers, grades or health needs, can flow to outside services the privacy assessment never examined. The assessment must follow the data through the agent's tool calls. Out-of-date visa rules, option D, are a real accuracy risk, but the stem's gap is uncontrolled flows of personal data.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generative agents vary. But differing replies are a consistency issue, not the uncontrolled disclosure the stem describes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because data in transit needs protection. But encryption protects the channel, not whether student data should go to those services at all.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outside services can be wrong. But accuracy of returned data is a separate risk; the stem points to student data flowing where no assessment reaches.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a privacy question as one of encryption, and B raises a consistency issue the stem does not point to.
Final two: A beats D because the agent chooses what personal data to send, to services outside the assessment; wrong visa rules are a real but separate accuracy risk.
Exam cue: when an agent calls tools, personal data flows are decided at run time; privacy assessments must cover every tool the agent can reach.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Federated learning claims
questions.question: A Tanzanian keyboard app trains its Swahili word-prediction model by federated learning, which sends only model updates from phones, so management says no privacy assessment is needed. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Accept that no assessment is needed, since text stays on phones
options.B: Move training to central servers for simpler privacy oversight
options.C: Have the privacy officer assess what the updates could reveal
options.D: Have the model owner encrypt the model updates sent from phones

questions.key_concept: Federated learning keeps raw data on devices, but updates computed from it can reveal parts of it; this lowers privacy risk without removing it.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the design before weighing each step.
questions.correct_explanation: Federated learning keeps raw text on phones, but the updates sent back are computed from what users typed, and research shows updates can sometimes be used to reconstruct parts of it; the model can also memorize rare phrases. The privacy officer should assess these risks first. Encryption, option D, protects updates in transit, but the provider still receives and combines them, so it does not address what they reveal.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because raw text never leaves phones. But updates derived from that text can leak parts of it, so the design lowers privacy risk without removing it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because central data is easier to oversee. But collecting raw typed text increases exposure; it trades a smaller risk for a larger one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption is a standard safeguard. But it protects updates on the way; the provider still receives them, and what they reveal goes unassessed.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts that local training removes privacy risk, and B would collect the raw text the design avoids.
Final two: C beats D because the risk lies in what updates reveal, which encryption in transit does not touch; assessing that comes first.
Exam cue: privacy-enhancing designs reduce risk without removing it; assess what the remaining data flows, such as model updates, can reveal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-8 (Privacy Impact Assessments)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (privacy-enhancing designs such as federated learning reduce risk without removing it; what model updates reveal still needs assessing). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Data kept for a market-stall allocation model
questions.question: A Zimbabwean city council's retention rule deletes each model's training data after training, for data minimization; its new model will rank market-stall applicants for five years. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on the kept model, whose weights preserve what the data showed
options.B: Keep training data, access-limited, while the model is in use
options.C: Keep training data indefinitely so any complaint can be checked
options.D: Rebuild training data from the council's records when needed

questions.key_concept: Investigating or revalidating a model needs the exact data it learned from, so retention covers training sets at least while the model is in use.
questions.pre_read: Ask what reviewing the model's rankings over five years would need.
questions.correct_explanation: Over five years, applicants may challenge the model's rankings and it should be revalidated; both need the exact data it learned from, to check whether some groups were under-represented. A set rebuilt from the council's records, option D, cannot be shown to match it: records may have been amended since, and no copy remains for comparison. Minimization limits retention; it does not bar keeping training data, access-limited, at least while the model is in use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models encode patterns from their data. But weights cannot show which applicants were in the data or how they were labeled, so causes stay hidden.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because challenges may come at any time. But data kept with no end date breaks minimization; the end should follow the model's use and any review of its choices.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because source records still exist. But they may have been amended since extraction, and with no copy kept, nobody can show a rebuilt set matches what the model learned.

tips: Eliminate: A expects model weights to show what the training data held, and C keeps data with no end date, which minimization does not allow.
Final two: B beats D because only the kept training data shows what the model learned from; with no copy, nobody can show a set rebuilt from the council's records matches it.
Exam cue: retention for AI covers training sets; keep the exact data a model learned from, access-limited, at least while the model is in use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (retention schedules cover training sets: the exact data a model learned from is kept, access-limited, while the model is in use, since a rebuilt set will not match). Round 1 review: reworked to a new angle and setting, as the appeals-retention frame repeated aaia_d2_116. Cross-domain gate fix, 12 Nov 2026: 'while in use' stated as a floor, in line with aaia_d2_006, d2_116 and d2_146. Re-audit, 12 Nov 2026: setting moved from a tax authority's inspection-selection model, which repeated the principles.json reproducible-ai-evidence example and aaia_d3_012; a city council's market-stall allocation model is unused elsewhere. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure requests and quarterly retrains
questions.question: A Finnish e-scooter app erases riders' trip histories on request and retrained its pricing model once to remove them; quarterly retraining still uses a snapshot taken last year. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Retraining each quarter is too seldom for a scooter rental app
options.B: The snapshot may be too old to reflect current riders' trips
options.C: Erasing trip histories may lower the model's pricing accuracy
options.D: Trips riders asked to erase may train each new pricing model version

questions.key_concept: A training snapshot is a frozen copy; cleaning the live model does not touch it, so each retrain from it brings erased data back.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about erasure and retraining before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: The one-off retrain removed erased trips from today's model, but the snapshot is a frozen copy that still holds them, so each quarterly retrain teaches the next model from trips riders asked to have erased, undoing the erasure. Erasure handling must reach training copies. A stale snapshot, option B, may hurt pricing quality, but that is a performance issue, not a violation of riders' rights.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fresher retraining tracks change. But retraining more often from the same snapshot would reuse the erased data even more often.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because old data can hurt performance. But staleness is a quality concern; retraining on data riders asked to have erased violates their rights each quarter.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because less data can weaken a model. But a possible accuracy dip is no reason to keep data riders asked to have erased.

tips: Eliminate: C puts model accuracy ahead of riders' erasure rights, and A changes how often the model retrains without touching the snapshot.
Final two: D beats B because the snapshot brings erased data back at every retrain, violating riders' erasure rights; staleness affects only pricing quality.
Exam cue: erasure must reach every copy a model learns from, including frozen training snapshots, or each retrain undoes it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (erasure must reach every copy a model learns from, including frozen training snapshots, or each retrain undoes it).
