questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Reliability criteria for a shortlisting model
questions.question: Using the NIST AI RMF, a Rwandan urban-resettlement agency judges its household-shortlisting model reliable by one criterion: 99.95% monthly uptime of its hosting platform. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner add a disaster-recovery test to the criterion
options.B: Have the model owner raise the uptime target to 99.99% monthly
options.C: Have the model owner add a criterion on correct outputs over time
options.D: Have the model owner add an ongoing criterion on group fairness parity

questions.key_concept: In the NIST AI RMF, reliable means performing as required, without failure, over time and in use; platform uptime does not measure it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the current criterion actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: In the NIST AI RMF, reliable means the system performs as required, without failure, over time and under its conditions of use. Uptime shows that the platform answers, not that its shortlists are right. Fairness parity, option D, is a separate RMF characteristic: groups can be treated alike while shortlists are wrong for all of them, so the criterion must measure correct shortlists over time.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recovery tests strengthen resilience. But they still measure the platform, not whether households are shortlisted correctly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a higher target sounds more reliable. But any uptime figure shows the platform answers, not that its shortlists are right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it tracks the model's outputs over time. But fairness is a separate RMF characteristic; parity across groups can hold while shortlists are wrong for every group.

tips: Eliminate: B and A both measure the hosting platform, which says nothing about whether households are shortlisted correctly.
Final two: C beats D because the RMF's reliable means performing as required over time; fairness is a separate characteristic, and parity can hold while every shortlist is wrong.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, reliable means performing as required over time in real use; uptime and other characteristics, such as fairness, do not show it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.1 (Valid and Reliable); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (each characteristic becomes a measurable criterion; in the NIST AI RMF, reliable means performing as required over time in use, which platform uptime does not measure). Round 1 review: reworked to a new angle, as the fairness-after-human-changes frame repeated aaia_d2_204. Re-audit, 12 Nov 2026: option D changed from launch accuracy to ongoing fairness parity, so only the RMF meaning of reliable, not an ongoing-versus-one-off cue, separates the final two. Round 3: key reworded to 'correct outputs' so no stem word is echoed only in the key; principle tag removed, as the RMF meaning of reliable versus fair (knowledge) decides, like aaia_d1_046. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Showing reasons for automated rejections
questions.question: A Kuwaiti ad platform's explainability criterion requires showing advertisers each rejected ad's top three factors; advertisers already share rewordings that slip banned health claims past the model. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The factors shown may teach advertisers which edits avoid rejection
options.B: Three factors may not fully explain each rejection to advertisers
options.C: Server tests may not cover the new explanation feature
options.D: Explaining each rejection may require a simpler screening model

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy characteristics trade off: explanations that show which inputs drive a result can help people game the model, so explainability criteria must weigh security.
questions.pre_read: Read what advertisers already do, then ask how each option's risk would play out.
questions.correct_explanation: Trustworthy characteristics can trade off. Advertisers already share rewordings that slip banned health claims past the model, so showing the top factors behind each rejection tells them which edits to try next, weakening the model's security and resilience. The criterion should weigh that risk, for example by testing manipulated ads before release. Partial explanations, option B, are a real explainability limit, but they do not give an active evasion practice a guide.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because top factors are only a summary. But a partial explanation is a known limit; the larger risk is guiding advertisers who already evade the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because new features need security testing. But server tests check the hosting, not how the model responds to crafted ads, which is where advertisers act.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because complex models are harder to explain. But established methods explain individual results of complex models, so replacing the model is not required.

tips: Eliminate: C treats AI security as server testing, though advertisers act through inputs, and D assumes complex models cannot explain individual rejections.
Final two: A beats B because advertisers already evade the model, so factor lists can guide their next edits; a partial explanation is a lesser, known limit.
Exam cue: trustworthy characteristics trade off; explanations showing which inputs drive a score can help people game it, so weigh security too.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.3 (Secure and Resilient); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.2 (Evasion Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (characteristics trade off; explanations that show which inputs drive a result can help people game the model). Round 2 review: reworked to a new angle, as the criterion-measured-by-infrastructure frame repeated aaia_d1_135. Re-audit: setting moved from a motor insurer's broker-facing pricing model, which repeated crisc_d2_025 and sat beside aaia_d2_205, to an ad platform's ad-screening model. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Emotion scoring under a new law
questions.question: Counsel confirms that a law now in force where a Turkish parcel firm runs warehouses bans emotion recognition at work; cameras there score workers' emotions for engagement. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner add human review before scores are used
options.B: Have management stop the emotion scoring where the law applies
options.C: Have the owner collect workers' consent to emotion scoring
options.D: Have counsel and the owner map the law's duties to controls

questions.key_concept: Risk-based AI laws place some practices in a prohibited tier; no consent, review or other control makes a banned use lawful there.
questions.pre_read: Note what kind of rule counsel found before choosing a response.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based AI laws reserve a top tier for practices they prohibit outright; no control, review or consent makes a banned use lawful there. Once counsel confirms the ban is in force, management should stop the scoring first. Mapping duties to controls, option D, is the usual first step for high-risk obligations, but a prohibition has one response, ceasing the use, and mapping first keeps the banned practice running.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because oversight reduces AI risk. But human review manages risk in permitted uses; it cannot make a prohibited practice lawful.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because consent often permits processing. But consent does not lift a prohibition, and workers' consent to an employer is rarely freely given.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because mapping obligations is normally first. But a ban has one response, ceasing the use; mapping while the cameras keep scoring prolongs the violation.

tips: Eliminate: C and A both try to manage a practice the law prohibits, which no consent or review can make lawful.
Final two: B beats D because a prohibited use has only one compliant response; mapping suits duties you can meet, not a practice you must stop.
Exam cue: risk-based AI laws ban some uses outright; when counsel confirms a ban applies, stopping comes before control design.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.3 (Responses to high-priority risks planned: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (risk-based AI laws ban some uses outright; when counsel confirms a ban applies, stopping comes before control design). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Counsel's view on legal duties
questions.question: Counsel at a bank in Botswana says its loan-pricing model carries no legal obligations because the country has no AI-specific law. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Treat the NIST AI RMF as the bank's legal obligations
options.B: Accept counsel's view, since applicability is counsel's decision
options.C: Have counsel monitor upcoming AI bills and map them to the model
options.D: Have counsel map current lending and data laws to the model

questions.key_concept: Laws on lending, consumer protection, discrimination and data apply to decisions however they are made; an AI-specific law is not the only source of duties.
questions.pre_read: Ask where legal duties for loan pricing come from.
questions.correct_explanation: Laws on lending, consumer protection, discrimination and data protection apply to decisions however they are made, including by a model. An AI-specific law is not the only source of obligations, so counsel should check existing laws against the pricing model now. Tracking AI bills, option C, prepares for future duties but leaves today's obligations unmapped.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the NIST AI RMF is a respected framework. But it is voluntary guidance; adopting it does not create or discharge legal obligations.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because counsel decides which laws apply. But the stated basis is flawed, so the IS auditor reports it and recommends reconsideration rather than accepting it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because new AI laws are coming. But waiting for them leaves current lending and data obligations unmapped while the model prices loans today.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a voluntary framework as law, and B accepts a conclusion whose basis, the lack of an AI-specific law, is flawed.
Final two: D beats C because existing lending and data laws already apply to model decisions; tracking new bills addresses tomorrow's duties, not today's.
Exam cue: no AI-specific law does not mean no obligations; existing laws apply to decisions whether a person or a model makes them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (Legal, regulatory and contractual requirements understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (no AI-specific law does not mean no obligations; existing lending, consumer and data laws apply to decisions a model makes). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Gaps in a trustworthiness assessment
questions.question: An Ethiopian research institute's assessment rates its crop-yield model fair, explainable and privacy-enhanced, though its predictions were never checked against harvests. Under the NIST AI RMF, which gap should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Secure and resilient, which the assessment does not mention
options.B: Accountable and transparent, as the code is unpublished
options.C: Valid and reliable, which the assessment does not rate
options.D: Safe, the characteristic the others rest on

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF shows valid and reliable as the base for the other trustworthy characteristics; an unvalidated model cannot meaningfully be called fair.
questions.pre_read: Recall how the AI RMF arranges its trustworthy characteristics.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF shows valid and reliable as the base for the other trustworthy characteristics: a model not shown to work cannot meaningfully be called fair, explainable or privacy-enhanced. Without validation, the yield predictions may simply be wrong. Secure and resilient, option A, is also unassessed and matters, but protecting a model nobody has shown to work protects possibly wrong outputs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because security is a trustworthy characteristic too. But the RMF treats validity as the base; securing an unvalidated model protects outputs that may be wrong.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because openness sounds transparent. But in the RMF, transparency concerns information about the system and its outputs, not published code, and nothing shows that information is missing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because safety sounds most basic. But the RMF shows valid and reliable as the base the others rest on, and the stem points to no safety gap.

tips: Eliminate: D gives safety the base role the RMF gives to valid and reliable, and B equates accountability and transparency with published code.
Final two: C beats A because the RMF treats valid and reliable as the base of the other characteristics; an unvalidated model's other ratings mean little.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, valid and reliable is the base characteristic; check validity before trusting claims of fairness or explainability.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3 (AI Risks and Trustworthiness); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.1 (Valid and Reliable)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (in the NIST AI RMF, valid and reliable is the base characteristic the others depend on). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Risks without a metric
questions.question: A Canadian public broadcaster using the NIST AI RMF removed the risk that its recommender narrows audiences' news exposure from its register, as no metric exists. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner track it qualitatively on the register
options.B: Keep it off the register, since unmeasured risks cannot be managed
options.C: Have the model owner formally accept the risk until a metric exists
options.D: Replace it with click-through rate, which can be measured

questions.key_concept: The AI RMF expects risks that current techniques cannot measure to stay tracked; being hard to measure does not make a risk high or low.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the AI RMF expects when a known risk has no ready metric.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF expects risks that are hard to measure to stay tracked with qualitative or expert methods, and notes that being hard to measure does not make a risk high or low. Removing it hides a known harm to audiences, so the owner should return it to the register and track it qualitatively. Formal acceptance, option C, keeps a record but decides the response before anyone has judged how large the risk is.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because measurement drives management. But unmeasured risks still exist; dropping them leaves known harms unmanaged.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because acceptance is a documented response. But accepting a risk nobody has sized is not an informed decision; tracking it first lets the owner judge it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it gives a number. But click-through measures engagement, which can rise as exposure narrows; it hides the risk it replaces.

tips: Eliminate: D swaps the risk for an easy metric that can move the wrong way, and B treats hard to measure as not worth managing.
Final two: A beats C because a risk nobody has sized cannot be accepted on an informed basis; tracking it qualitatively keeps it visible until it can be judged.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, risks that are hard to measure stay tracked with qualitative methods; no metric is no reason to drop them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.2 (Risk tracking where measurement is difficult); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.1 (Existing, unanticipated and emergent risks tracked)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Search tools that rank by meaning
questions.question: A Lithuanian tax tribunal's clerks find past rulings with an AI search tool that ranks published rulings by similarity of meaning and writes no text. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Clerks cannot see why one ruling ranks above another
options.B: The tool may invent rulings that do not exist
options.C: Relevant rulings may rank too low for clerks to see them
options.D: Rulings issued after the model's training cutoff cannot be found

questions.key_concept: Search that ranks stored documents by meaning writes no text, so its main risk is missing or misranking relevant documents, not inventing them.
questions.pre_read: Classify the AI from the stem's facts before weighing each risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool returns real, published rulings ranked by similarity of meaning, so clerks can read in full whatever it shows them; the risk lies in what it fails to show. A relevant ruling ranked on page five is effectively missing, and nobody notices an absence. Not knowing why one ruling outranks another, option A, limits trust, but clerks still read and judge each returned ruling themselves.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because explainability matters in AI. But clerks read every returned ruling themselves; the harm comes from rulings the ranking never shows them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generative AI can invent sources. But this tool only ranks stored rulings and writes no text, so it cannot create one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because language models have training cutoffs. But search covers whatever is in the index; new rulings are found once added, without retraining.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a search tool as generative, though it writes no text, and D confuses a model's training cutoff with what its index holds.
Final two: C beats A because clerks can read and judge every ruling shown, but cannot judge a ruling the ranking buried.
Exam cue: classify the AI first; retrieval tools fail by omission and ranking, generative tools by invention.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (a search tool that ranks stored documents by meaning writes nothing, so its main risk is what it leaves out or ranks low, not invention). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Acting on a model's predictors
questions.question: A Croatian coworking chain's renewal model ranks booking desks in its app as the strongest predictor of renewal; managers plan to require app booking to lift renewals. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team improve accuracy until the ranking is reliable
options.B: Have managers pilot compulsory booking at some sites before adopting it
options.C: Have an independent team validate the model's ranking before acting
options.D: Have managers adopt compulsory booking and then watch renewal rates closely

questions.key_concept: A predictive model finds patterns that go with an outcome; its strongest predictors are associations, so using one as a lever needs evidence of cause.
questions.pre_read: Note what kind of model this is before judging how its output is used.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learned that members who book through the app tend to renew; it did not learn why. Engaged members may simply prefer the app, so forcing everyone onto it may not lift renewals. A pilot at some sites, compared with the rest, tests the cause before the chain commits. Independent validation, option C, would confirm the ranking predicts well, but not that booking causes renewal.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accuracy builds trust. But even a perfectly accurate model shows which members renew, not what makes them renew.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because independent checks strengthen evidence. But validation shows the ranking predicts renewal; it cannot show that changing the input will change the outcome.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because monitoring follows most changes. But with every site changed at once, renewal shifts cannot be told apart from other causes such as prices or season.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes enough accuracy turns a predictor into a cause, and D changes every site at once, leaving nothing to compare renewals against.
Final two: B beats C because validation confirms the model predicts well, while only a pilot shows whether compulsory booking changes renewals.
Exam cue: a model's strongest predictor is a correlation; before it becomes a business lever, expect a test of cause.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a predictive model's strongest predictor shows association, not cause, so using it as a business lever needs a test of cause first). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Answers that must show their source
questions.question: A Kyrgyz hydropower operator's assistant for dam-safety engineers must cite the operating-manual clause behind each answer; its developers will fine-tune a model on the manual. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Engineers' questions may retrain the model away from the manual
options.B: Engineers may stop reading the clauses the answers cite
options.C: Too few answers may be checked against the manual's text before launch
options.D: Clauses the model cites may not be what drove its answers

questions.key_concept: Retrieval logs the passages each answer was given, so citations can be checked; a fine-tuned model blends its sources, so its citations are generated text.
questions.pre_read: Start from what the system is required to do, then weigh each risk against it.
questions.correct_explanation: The requirement is traceability: each answer must rest on a clause an engineer can check. Fine-tuning blends the manual into the model's weights, so any clause it cites is generated text that may not match what produced the answer; retrieval logs the passages each answer was given, so citations can be checked. Checking more answers before launch, option C, catches some wrong citations, but cannot make later ones traceable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people think chatting teaches a model. But a deployed model does not retrain on users' questions unless someone builds that in.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people over-trust cited answers. But even an engineer who reads every cited clause cannot tell whether it produced the answer; the design fails before anyone reads.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing catches errors. But answers that pass before launch cannot make later citations traceable; a tuned model's citations stay generated text.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a deployed model retrains itself on users' questions, and B blames engineers' reading habits for a gap the design itself creates.
Final two: D beats C because testing samples answers, while the traceability requirement fails by design on every answer a tuned model gives.
Exam cue: when answers must show their source, prefer retrieval at answer time; a tuned model's citations are generated, not traced.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (when a requirement says each answer must show its source, fine-tuning cannot meet it, because a tuned model's citations are generated rather than traced).
