questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. What inventory entries record
questions.question: A language-model provider reported a flaw in one model version; an Icelandic fishing company's AI inventory records each AI tool's vendor product, owner and risk tier. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the AI program owner record each use's underlying model and version
options.B: Have IT block the flawed version until the provider releases a fix
options.C: Have each vendor formally accept accountability for flaws in its products
options.D: Have the AI program owner record each vendor product's AI features

questions.key_concept: An AI inventory should record each use's underlying model and version, since vendor products often run on another firm's model and can switch it silently.
questions.pre_read: Read what the inventory records and what the provider reported before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Vendor products often run on another firm's language model, and vendors can switch the model or version underneath without the product name changing. Recording each use's underlying model and version lets the company find every exposed use whenever a provider reports a flaw. Listing AI features, option D, brings embedded AI into view, but features show what a product does, not which model runs it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because blocking stops exposure. But many uses reach the model through vendors' products, and the company cannot yet say which, so a block misses them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors built the products. But accountability for each use stays with the company; contracts can add duties, not take ownership away.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because embedded AI belongs in the inventory. But features describe what a product does, not which model runs it, so a flawed version still cannot be traced.

tips: Eliminate: B cannot reach uses that run the model inside vendors' products, and C tries to move accountability that stays with the organization using the AI.
Final two: A beats D because a flaw sits in a model version, and only a record of what runs underneath each product shows which uses carry it.
Exam cue: an AI inventory should show what runs underneath each use, not just the product name on the invoice.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (vendor products often run on another firm's model, which can change under the same product name, so the inventory records each use's underlying model and version). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. The committee's role after launch
questions.question: An Uzbek fertilizer producer's AI governance committee approves high-impact models before launch; afterwards, only the data team reads the models' monitoring reports. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the committee re-approve each model when a change is submitted
options.B: Have the data team retrain any model whose reports show drift
options.C: Have model owners get monitoring results and escalate breaches
options.D: Have internal audit review every model's monitoring reports monthly

questions.key_concept: Approval at launch is not lifelong oversight; monitoring results should reach each model's accountable owner, who escalates breaches to the committee.
questions.pre_read: Follow the model's life after approval before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's behavior can shift in any week as its data drifts, with no change anyone submits for approval, so oversight after launch has to run on monitoring. Sending results to each accountable owner, with breaches escalated to the committee, puts decisions with people who can act. Re-approval when a change is submitted, option A, covers retrains and updates, but drift submits nothing, so it would pass unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because changes need approval. But drift can push a model past its limits with no change submitted, so change-triggered review leaves owners blind in between.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining treats drift. But the data team would change high-impact models with no owner deciding, which is the gap, not the remedy.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit is independent. But reviewing monitoring is management's oversight duty; audit doing it monthly would take over a control it must later assess.

tips: Eliminate: D gives internal audit a management monitoring duty it must stay independent of, and B lets builders change models with no accountable owner deciding.
Final two: C beats A because drift can arrive any week without a submitted change, so owners need monitoring results, not only change-triggered re-approval.
Exam cue: approval at launch is not oversight for life; look for monitoring results that reach an owner who can act and escalate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (a model's behavior can shift in any week without a submitted change, so oversight after launch runs on monitoring results that reach an accountable owner). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Usage figures offered as proof
questions.question: A Mongolian legal-aid office's AI program reports 92% of AI-drafted client letters sent unedited, above its 90% target, as proof its drafting model is reliable. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The share should be benchmarked against other legal-aid offices' rates
options.B: The share backs the reliability claim once system-logged, not self-reported
options.C: The share may prove reliability once held above target for a year
options.D: The share can rise with lawyers' trust, even if accuracy falls

questions.key_concept: An unedited-output share measures reviewers' acceptance, not accuracy; as automation bias grows, the share rises even when errors get through.
questions.pre_read: Read the program's claim and what its figure counts before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: An unedited letter shows that a lawyer accepted the draft, not that it was right. Lawyers who see drafts pass often trust the model and check less, and a target for unedited letters adds pressure not to edit, so the share can climb while errors reach clients. Logging the share in the system, option B, makes the count accurate, but an accurate count of acceptance cannot show the letters were correct.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because benchmarks give context. But other offices' unedited shares measure acceptance too, so a comparison cannot show whether these letters were correct.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a metric is only as good as its data. But a system-logged share still counts acceptance, which can rise with trust whether or not the letters are right.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a steady result looks dependable. But a share held for a year can reflect settled trust in the model, not letters that were correct.

tips: Eliminate: A compares one acceptance rate with others, and C treats a lasting share as accuracy; neither shows whether any letter was correct.
Final two: D beats B because better logging only counts acceptance more accurately; the share can rise as trusting lawyers check less, whatever the letters' accuracy.
Exam cue: an unedited or acceptance rate measures reviewers' trust, not model accuracy; reliability needs errors found when outputs are rechecked.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (an unedited-draft share measures reviewers' acceptance, which automation bias inflates, not the drafts' accuracy). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Mitigations a risk assessment relies on
questions.question: A Kosovo payment provider's risk assessment lists one mitigation for wrongful refusals by its merchant-scoring model, retrained yearly: refused businesses may resubmit the same application next month. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Businesses may not know a model refused them or why
options.B: The same application would be scored and refused again
options.C: The same application may score differently each time, as outputs vary
options.D: The mitigation was chosen by the risk owner, not the data scientists

questions.key_concept: Between retrains, a scoring model returns the same output for the same input, so resubmitting an unchanged application repeats its error.
questions.pre_read: Check each assumption behind the assessment against the facts given.
questions.correct_explanation: Between retrains, a scoring model gives the same output for the same input, so a resubmitted application reproduces the same wrongful refusal every month until the yearly retrain. The assessment relies on a mitigation that cannot work, so the risk to wrongly refused businesses stays untreated. Telling businesses a model refused them, option A, would help them challenge errors, but it does not make the listed mitigation work.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people cannot challenge what they cannot see. But the assessment's flaw is its mitigation: resubmitting cannot change a scoring model's answer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because generative AI varies run to run. But a scoring model unchanged since its yearly retrain returns the same score for the same application.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because builders know the model. But choosing a risk response is the risk owner's call; data scientists supply facts about the model, not the response.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a scoring model as if its output varied like generated text, and D hands the choice of risk response to the model's builders.
Final two: B beats A because the assessment's only mitigation is resubmission, and a scoring model repeats the same refusal until it is retrained.
Exam cue: when the remedy for an AI error is 'try again', ask whether the model will answer any differently.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (a scoring model gives the same output for the same input, so 'apply again' cannot undo its error and a mitigation resting on it is empty). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. What a KRI is compared with
questions.question: A Moldovan concert-ticketing site's tolerance for its bot-detection model wrongly canceling orders is 3%; its risk indicator alerts at 0.5 points above the last monthly retraining's rate. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the data team retrain the model whenever the indicator alerts
options.B: Have the owner report every indicator alert to senior management
options.C: Have the owner set a fixed alert level below the 3% tolerance
options.D: Have internal audit recheck the rate against the 3% tolerance monthly

questions.key_concept: A KRI should alert at a fixed level below tolerance; a trigger set from the last retraining's rate moves with each retrain, missing slow creep.
questions.pre_read: Test each option against the facts in the stem before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Because the comparison point resets at every monthly retraining, the rate can rise just under half a point a month without a single alert and still pass 3%. A fixed alert level set below the tolerance warns before a breach, however the rise is spread. Reporting every alert to senior management, option B, sets up escalation, but an indicator that never fires gives it nothing to escalate.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining treats rising errors. But automatic retraining skips the owner's decision and change approval, and each retrain resets the indicator's own baseline.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because breaches must reach senior management. But a trigger measured from the last retraining may never fire, so nothing reaches anyone while the rate creeps past 3%.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit tests indicators. But checking the rate each month is management's monitoring job; audit tests the KRI's design and does not operate it.

tips: Eliminate: A lets builders retrain without the owner and resets the baseline again, and D has audit operating a management indicator it should assess.
Final two: C beats B because escalation helps only if the indicator fires, and a trigger measured from each retraining can miss slow creep entirely.
Exam cue: set a KRI's alert level against the approved tolerance, not against a baseline that retraining keeps resetting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (a KRI measured from the rate at the last retraining resets with every retrain, so slow creep passes tolerance unseen; read the KRI against the tolerance itself). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Vendor service terms
questions.question: A Honduran civil registry tested its vendor's face-matching model for ID-card renewals; the contract lets the vendor switch to a smaller backup model at peak load. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Applicants' peak-hour photos may retrain the backup model
options.B: The vendor may answer for peak-hour rejections, not the registry
options.C: The vendor's uptime commitment may not hold at peak load
options.D: Peak-hour decisions may come from a model the registry never checked

questions.key_concept: Testing covers only the model tested; vendor terms that let a backup model decide at run time leave those decisions untested.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Testing covers only the model tested. A scheduled update arrives as a release that notice-and-test terms can catch; a run-time switch puts the backup model into service with no release to test, so peak-hour renewals may be decided by a smaller model that could reject genuine applicants more often. The uptime commitment, option C, matters, but switching models is how the vendor keeps service up.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people think use teaches a model. But matching photos does not retrain a model unless someone builds that in; the risk is which model decides.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor runs the model. But the registry answers to applicants for its renewal decisions; a contract cannot move that accountability to the vendor.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because peak load threatens availability. But switching to a backup model is how the vendor keeps service up; the gap is decisions from a model nobody tested.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes matching photos retrains a model, and B tries to move accountability for applicants' renewal decisions to the vendor.
Final two: D beats C because the backup keeps service up; unlike a scheduled update, which notice-and-test terms can catch, a run-time switch puts an untested model in charge.
Exam cue: read AI vendor terms for any right to substitute the model at run time; evidence covers only the model that was tested.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.2 (Contingency processes for failures in high-risk third-party data or AI); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (testing covers only the model tested, so contract terms that let a vendor decide with a substitute model leave those decisions untested). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Training data from outside contributors
questions.question: An Indonesian legal publisher will retrain its case-summary model on summaries by freelancers paid per summary, whose output tripled this year under contracts silent on drafting method. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data owner require freelancers to declare model-written summaries
options.B: Have the data team train the model on the corpus's newest summaries
options.C: Have the publisher stop using freelancers' summaries for training
options.D: Have staff editors sample-check summaries for errors before training

questions.key_concept: Lineage should show which training records a model wrote, since heavy training on generated text can narrow a model; the data owner sets their use.
questions.pre_read: Read the retraining setup closely before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Output that tripled under pay per summary suggests freelancers may now draft with a language model. Model-written summaries can be accurate, yet heavy training on them pulls a model toward another model's habits, which NIST links to model collapse. Unless freelancers declare which summaries a model wrote, the data owner cannot limit their share. Staff editors' error sampling, option D, finds wrong summaries, but cannot show which accurate ones a model wrote.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because new summaries reflect current law. But the newest summaries are the likeliest to be model-written, which deepens the problem.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes the uncertain source. But freelancers' summaries can be used once their origin is known; the gap is lineage, not the source.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because review catches errors. But accurate model-written summaries still carry a model's habits, and checking for errors cannot show which summaries a model wrote.

tips: Eliminate: B picks the period most likely to hold model-written text, and C drops the freelancers' work instead of controlling what enters training.
Final two: A beats D because error sampling cannot tell accurate model-written summaries from human ones, while declaring them lets the owner limit their share.
Exam cue: know which training records a model wrote; even accurate generated text can narrow a model trained on it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SR-4 (Provenance); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.6 (Harmful Bias and Homogenization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (training data from outside contributors may hold model-written text, which can narrow a model trained heavily on it, so lineage must mark model-written records and the data owner controls their use). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Assistants that search staff files
questions.question: A Romanian city hall's AI assistant for staff answers from any file the asking employee can open, including loosely shared folders holding colleagues' medical notes. Which privacy risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Prompts and answers naming colleagues may be kept in logs
options.B: Any colleague can now pull up those medical notes with one question
options.C: People outside the city hall can now query the medical notes
options.D: The assistant may learn the medical notes and repeat them to anyone

questions.key_concept: An assistant that searches everything a user can open makes old oversharing easy to find, so file permissions should be corrected before it goes live.
questions.pre_read: Consider who uses the assistant and what it can reach for each of them.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant respects each employee's existing access, but much of that access was never meant to be used: medical notes sat in loosely shared folders few knew to look in. By finding and summarizing content on request, the assistant turns forgotten oversharing into answers any colleague can get by asking. Logged prompts and answers, option A, also hold personal data, but they are a smaller store that can be limited and secured.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs often hold personal data. But logs can be limited and secured; the larger harm is every employee now reaching colleagues' health records by asking.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because exposure sounds external. But the assistant answers employees using their own access, so the risk is inside the city hall, not outside it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because people think AI absorbs what it reads. But retrieving a file to answer does not train the model; exposure follows the asker's file access.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes reading a file to answer trains the model, and C assumes outsiders gain access, though answers follow each employee's own permissions.
Final two: B beats A because the assistant makes long-hidden overshared records easy for every employee to find, a wider exposure than its logs.
Exam cue: before an assistant searches everything a user can open, fix who can open what; AI turns old oversharing into easy answers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (an assistant that answers from every file a user can open turns long-forgotten oversharing of personal data into answers anyone can get by asking). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Evidence that erased data is gone
questions.question: A Slovak debt-advice charity's vendor 'unlearned' a former client's letters from the charity's fine-tuned drafting model after an erasure request; the vendor's extraction tests no longer reproduce them. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: No erasure step was needed, as trained models hold no personal data
options.B: The tests cannot be relied on, as the vendor ran them
options.C: The tests show no leakage was found, not that data was removed
options.D: The erasure is complete, as the letters can no longer be extracted

questions.key_concept: Memorization tests show leakage, not deletion; only retraining without the data reliably removes its influence, otherwise the owner documents the remaining risk.
questions.pre_read: Read each conclusion for what it claims about the letters and the model.
questions.correct_explanation: Unlearning may retrain the model without the data or only adjust its weights, and an extraction test probes only the prompts testers thought of. A pass shows leakage was not found, not that the letters' influence is gone; only retraining without them reliably removes it, otherwise the model owner documents the remaining risk, with the privacy officer confirming. Vendor-run tests, option B, weaken the evidence, but an independent pass would prove no more.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models are not databases. But fine-tuned models can memorize training text, so erasure must consider them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor checked its own work. But independence would not fix the gap: no extraction test, whoever runs it, proves data was removed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because nothing leaked. But memorization tests show only that probes failed to extract the letters; their influence can remain in the weights.

tips: Eliminate: D treats a failed extraction as proof of deletion, and A forgets that fine-tuned models can memorize and reproduce training text.
Final two: C beats B because the limit is in what extraction tests can show, which an independent tester would face too.
Exam cue: memorization tests show leakage, not deletion; only retraining without the data reliably removes it, and anything less is an owned, documented risk decision.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (an extraction test that no longer reproduces erased data shows no leakage was found, not that the data's influence was removed, whoever runs the test). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Safety criteria for autonomous machines
questions.question: A Djiboutian container terminal's only safety criterion for its self-driving straddle carriers is 99.9% pedestrian detection. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner raise the detection target to 99.99% before launch
options.B: Have the vendor certify the carriers as safe for the yard
options.C: Have internal audit retest the detection rate in the yard
options.D: Have the owner add safeguards for when detection misses someone

questions.key_concept: Safe AI fails safely: safety criteria cover what the system does when the model misses or is unsure, not only how often it succeeds.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the stated criterion before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Even 99.9% detection misses about one pedestrian in a thousand, and over thousands of encounters a miss will happen. A safe system is judged by what happens when the model fails as well as how often it succeeds, so the criteria need safeguards for misses, such as speed limits near walkways, stopping on uncertain detections or separate sensors. A higher target, option A, narrows misses but never removes them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a stricter target sounds safer. But no detection rate reaches zero misses; safety also depends on safeguards that protect pedestrians the model misses.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification sounds like assurance. But a vendor certificate does not set the terminal's own criteria or test the carriers in its yard.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors reperform tests. But a retest could only confirm the 99.9% rate; it sets no safeguard for the misses that will still occur.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on a vendor certificate instead of the terminal's own criteria, and C retests the same detection rate, which sets nothing for the misses that remain.
Final two: D beats A because no detection rate eliminates misses, so safety needs safeguards for the misses that will still occur.
Exam cue: for safety-critical AI, look for criteria on failing safely, not just a higher accuracy target.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (no detection rate removes every miss, so a safety criterion must also set how the system behaves when the model fails). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Controls mapped to explanation duties
questions.question: An AI law gives jobseekers profiled by a Portuguese employment service's model a right to an explanation; its obligations register maps that duty to the vendor's model card. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The card explains the model overall, not any one jobseeker's result
options.B: The duty falls on the model's vendor, not the employment service
options.C: The card is written for data specialists, not for jobseekers
options.D: Caseworkers make final decisions, so jobseekers need no explanation

questions.key_concept: An explanation duty is met per decision; a model card describes the model in general, so it cannot explain any one person's result.
questions.pre_read: Read the duty and the mapped control side by side.
questions.correct_explanation: A right to an explanation concerns each person's decision: which factors drove that jobseeker's profile. A model card describes the model in general, such as its purpose, data, overall performance and main factors on average, so the mapped control cannot meet the duty for anyone. A plain-language card, option C, would be easier to read, but it would still explain no single profile.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors build the model. But risk-based laws give organizations using high-risk AI their own duties toward the people affected.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because explanations must be understandable. But even a plain-language card describes the model in general; it never explains why a given jobseeker got their profile.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a person decides. But a caseworker's final say does not remove the duty, and the model's output still shapes each decision.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes only the vendor has duties, though users of high-risk AI have their own, and D assumes a person's final say removes the duty to explain.
Final two: A beats C because a model card explains the model in general, however plainly written, while the duty asks why each jobseeker got their result.
Exam cue: when mapping a duty to a control, check the control delivers what the duty asks, at the level it asks: one person's decision, not the model overall.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.9 (Model explained, validated and documented, output interpreted in context); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.8 (Transparency and accountability risks examined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (a duty to explain each affected person's decision is not met by a model card, which describes the model in general). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Cybersecurity frameworks and AI risk
questions.question: An Omani driving-test center is told its NIST CSF 2.0 profile, at Tier 3, covers the risks of its model scoring candidates' driving tests. Which gap should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Tier 3 is below the Tier 4 that regulators require
options.B: The profile addresses cybersecurity, not the outputs' validity or bias
options.C: CSF 2.0 profiles must be certified before test centers rely on them
options.D: Tier 3 describes how practices are managed, not whether controls operate

questions.key_concept: Cybersecurity frameworks cover security outcomes; an AI model's validity, harmful bias and explainability need AI-specific criteria such as the NIST AI RMF.
questions.pre_read: Read the claim made in the stem and decide what evidence it would need.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 covers security outcomes such as protecting, detecting and recovering. A scoring model's main risks lie elsewhere: whether its scores are valid, whether it treats candidates fairly and whether people can explain and challenge it, which the NIST AI RMF addresses. A Tier 3 rating, option D, describes how rigorously practices are managed, but even a strong security profile leaves those AI risks unassessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tiers sound like grades. But tiers describe how rigorously risk is managed; the framework does not set a tier that regulators require.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because certificates reassure test centers. But CSF 2.0 is voluntary guidance with no certification scheme; organizations rely on assessed outcomes, not certificates.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tiers do not prove controls work. But even proven security controls would leave the model's validity and fairness unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a voluntary framework as needing certification, and A reads tiers as required grades, which the framework does not set.
Final two: B beats D because a perfectly operating security profile still leaves validity and fairness untested, while tier rigor is a lesser question.
Exam cue: match the framework to the risk; cybersecurity frameworks cover security, while AI risks such as bias need AI-specific criteria.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.1 (Valid and Reliable); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (a cybersecurity framework profile covers security outcomes, not an AI model's validity or harmful bias, which need AI-specific criteria such as the NIST AI RMF). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 9, 18 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Speech transcription tools
questions.question: A Belizean police department transcribes suspect interviews with a speech-to-text tool built on a generative language model; officers check only passages the tool marks low-confidence. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Officers may not record which marked passages they checked
options.B: Each interview may retrain the model and surface in later transcripts
options.C: Fluent words nobody said may appear and carry no warning
options.D: Accented speech may be misheard and marked for review more often

questions.key_concept: Speech-to-text built on a generative model can insert fluent words never spoken, and its confidence marks may not flag them.
questions.pre_read: Picture the tool in daily use before ranking the risks.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model writes the most plausible text, so in pauses or crosstalk it can insert fluent words nobody spoke, often with high confidence. Checking only marked passages then misses the errors that matter most in a suspect's statement. Recording which marked passages officers checked, option A, improves evidence of review, but the review itself still never looks where invented text hides.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because review evidence matters in audits. But a perfect record of checking marked passages still leaves unmarked, invented text unchecked.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data reuse is a real privacy worry. But producing a transcript does not by itself retrain the model, and nothing in the stem suggests training on interviews.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because accents do cause recognition errors. But errors the tool marks are the ones officers already check; unmarked errors are the gap.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes using a model retrains it, and D describes errors the tool marks, which officers already check.
Final two: C beats A because recording the checks of marked passages cannot catch invented text the tool never marks.
Exam cue: when a tool is built on a generative model, expect fluent, confident errors, and test outputs its own flags do not cover.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (speech-to-text built on a generative model can insert fluent words nobody said, often without a low-confidence mark). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Agents that work through screens
questions.question: A Lithuanian patent-attorney firm's AI agent files trademark applications by operating staff's browser sessions, under logins that can also withdraw applications and pay fees. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Page layout changes may make it fail to finish filings
options.B: Its actions will be logged as if staff had taken them
options.C: Accountability for its filings passes to the agent's vendor
options.D: Nothing limits the agent to the steps that filing needs

questions.key_concept: An agent working through a user's screens holds every right that login has, and chooses its own steps, so limits must sit outside it.
questions.pre_read: List what the system touches and how, before ranking the concerns.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent plans its own steps, and content on the pages it reads can steer it. Working under staff logins that can withdraw applications and pay fees, it is bounded only by what those logins allow, not by the filing task it was given. Logging its actions as staff actions, option B, weakens the audit trail, but better logs would only show the harm after an unintended withdrawal or payment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because screen-driven automation breaks when pages change. But a failed filing is visible and can be redone; it is far less serious than unbounded actions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit trails must show who acted. But clearer logs reveal misuse after the fact; the larger gap is that the agent can withdraw and pay at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the agent seems to act on its own. But accountability stays with the firm and a named owner; neither the agent nor its vendor takes it over.

tips: Eliminate: C moves accountability to the vendor, though the firm keeps it, and A names a visible failure that staff would notice and redo.
Final two: D beats B because the agent chooses its own steps under logins that can withdraw and pay, and better logs only reveal that harm later.
Exam cue: for agents, judge risk by the access they inherit, not by the task they were given.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (an agent that operates staff's browser sessions inherits everything their logins allow and chooses its own steps, so only access limits outside it bound what it does). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Retraining on unchanged data
questions.question: An Argentine university retrained its math-placement model on unchanged data with a new random starting point; accuracy held at 88%, so the model owner treats it as unchanged. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Many students could be placed differently despite equal accuracy
options.B: A random start makes the model's placements impossible to explain
options.C: Accuracy did not improve, so the retraining added no value
options.D: The 88% may have been measured by the team that retrained it

questions.key_concept: Two models with equal accuracy can disagree on many individual cases, so a retrained model is a new model for the people it scores.
questions.pre_read: Note what the owner's claim rests on before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Training involves random choices, so two runs on the same data can reach the same accuracy while placing many individual students differently. A student near a boundary could move course purely because of the rerun, so the new version needs review as a change. Independent measurement, option D, would confirm the 88%, but the same figure can still hide those changed individual placements.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because randomness sounds opaque. But a random starting point affects which model results, not whether its placements can be explained.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining usually aims to improve. But this rerun was not meant to raise accuracy; the risk lies in changed individual placements, not lost value.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because builders' own figures need independent checking. But even a confirmed 88% says nothing about which students' placements moved.

tips: Eliminate: C judges the rerun by whether accuracy rose, and B confuses random training choices with lost explainability.
Final two: A beats D because a verified 88% can still hide many students whose placements changed.
Exam cue: equal accuracy does not mean equal decisions; treat any retrained model as a change for the people it scores.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 100-1 Appendix B (How AI Risks Differ from Traditional Software Risks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (two training runs on the same data can match accuracy yet score many individuals differently, so a rerun is a change for the people it scores). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Classifiers in changing conditions
questions.question: A Norwegian bakery chain's self-checkout camera model, trained on its 40 regular pastries, prices every item scanned; a seasonal pastry goes on sale next week. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: It will learn the seasonal pastry from items as they are scanned
options.B: It can assign only one of the 40 pastries it learned
options.C: Its confidence will drop and flag the seasonal pastry for staff
options.D: Its accuracy on the 40 regular pastries may have drifted

questions.key_concept: A standard classifier picks only from the classes it learned, so a case unlike any of them still gets one of those labels, often confidently.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the stem states from what it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: A model trained on 40 pastries has only those 40 answers. Every seasonal pastry will be priced as one of them, often with high confidence, so customers are charged wrongly and sales of the new item go unrecorded. Drift on the regular pastries, option D, is possible over time, but the seasonal pastry is a certain failure from launch that the model cannot even report.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models seem to improve with use. But a deployed classifier does not add new classes on its own; that needs labeled images and retraining.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because low confidence often marks doubtful cases. But models are often confident on unfamiliar inputs, so confidence will not reliably flag the new pastry.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because drift erodes accuracy over time. But nothing in the stem points to drift, while the seasonal pastry is certain to be misnamed from launch.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes the model learns new classes in use, and C trusts confidence to flag inputs unlike anything it learned.
Final two: B beats D because mispricing the seasonal pastry is certain from launch, while drift on the regular 40 is only possible.
Exam cue: a classifier can only answer with the classes it learned; ask what happens to cases outside them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a classifier can answer only with the classes it learned, so a case it never saw gets one of those labels, often confidently). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Acceptance testing scope
questions.question: An Armenian department-store chain's staffing model passed acceptance on manual shopper counts; live, it will use counts from a camera model its vendor rates 96% accurate. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner estimate chain accuracy from the two models' figures
options.B: Have an independent team revalidate the staffing model's test results
options.C: Have the owner test the two models together on real footage
options.D: Have the owner raise the staffing model's accuracy target

questions.key_concept: When one model feeds another, the first model's errors become the second's inputs and often cluster, so acceptance testing covers the chain on real inputs.
questions.pre_read: Decide what the question asks before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Camera models miss more shoppers in crowded scenes, so their errors cluster in the peak hours when staffing matters most, and the staffing model never saw them in testing. Testing the two models together on real footage shows how the chain performs as used. Estimating chain accuracy from the two figures, option A, assumes the errors are random and evenly spread, which camera miscounts rarely are.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because combining known accuracy figures looks like careful analysis. But camera miscounts cluster when stores are crowded, so arithmetic on two averages cannot show their effect on rosters.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because independence strengthens evidence. But it would confirm results from clean manual counts, leaving the camera model's miscounts untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a higher target sounds safer. But a stricter target on manual counts still says nothing about counts taken from video.

tips: Eliminate: D tightens a target measured on the wrong inputs, and B independently confirms results from clean manual counts.
Final two: C beats A because camera miscounts cluster in crowded hours, so arithmetic on two accuracy figures cannot show their effect on rosters.
Exam cue: when models are chained, acceptance tests cover the whole chain on the inputs it will really receive.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.2 (Internal risk controls for components identified)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (when one model feeds another, the first model's errors become the second's inputs, so acceptance testing covers the chain on real inputs). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Models that run without a connection
questions.question: A Malian agricultural extension service plans a crop-disease model that diagnoses from photos offline on farmers' phones, which sync only at twice-yearly village visits. Which concern should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: The model cannot keep learning from farmers while offline
options.B: Lost phones could expose farmers' photos and diagnoses
options.C: A model small enough for phones cannot be accurate enough
options.D: Wrong diagnoses could go unnoticed for months at a time

questions.key_concept: A deployed model needs a route for monitoring results and pushing fixes; an architecture that cuts it off leaves drift and errors unseen.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem once for facts and once for the question.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's accuracy can fall as seasons, crop varieties or diseases change, and only results flowing back to the owner reveal it. With phones syncing twice a year, wrong diagnoses could guide spraying and replanting for months before anyone sees a pattern or can push a corrected model. Lost phones, option B, expose some photos and diagnoses, a narrower harm that device controls can limit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models seem to improve with use. But deployed models need not learn in the field; updates come from controlled retraining.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because lost devices are a familiar risk. But crop photos and diagnoses are limited data that device controls can protect; unseen wrong diagnoses affect every farm using the app.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because smaller models can be less capable. But accuracy is tested before launch; size alone does not make a model unfit.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes size alone decides accuracy, which testing shows, and A assumes a deployed model should learn as it goes.
Final two: D beats B because months without results or updates let errors spread to every farm, while lost phones expose limited data.
Exam cue: in architecture reviews, ask how the owner will see live results and update the model; no route back means unmonitored AI.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.2 (Mechanisms sustain the value of deployed AI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (a deployed model needs a route for its results to reach the owner and for fixes to reach users; an offline design that cuts it leaves errors and drift unseen). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Policy rules for integrated assistants
questions.question: A Slovak health insurer's AI policy bars typing members' health details into the hosted AI assistant in its email client, which answers questions about whichever thread is open. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Staff may not know the rule unless training covers it
options.B: The assistant's drafts may state members' health details wrongly
options.C: A rule is weaker than banning the assistant outright
options.D: Health details staff never typed still reach the model

questions.key_concept: Integrated assistants send context such as open documents or threads automatically, so a rule on what staff type does not control what the model receives.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: To answer questions about the open thread, the assistant must send that thread to the hosted model, so members' health details already in those emails reach it no matter what staff type. A typing rule covers little of what leaves; the control has to address what the tool sends. Training staff on the rule, option A, helps them follow it, but full compliance still leaves email contents flowing to the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because policy duties need training. But perfect compliance with a typing rule still sends every thread's health details to the hosted model.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generated drafts can contain errors. But the policy aims to keep health details from the hosted model, and that fails whatever the drafts say.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a ban sounds safest. But bans push use out of sight; the gap is a rule that misses how the tool sends data.

tips: Eliminate: B raises draft accuracy, which the policy does not address, and C treats a ban as stronger, though bans drive use out of sight.
Final two: D beats A because training improves compliance with a rule that, even fully followed, misses the emails the tool sends.
Exam cue: test AI policy rules against how the tool works; integrated assistants send context the user never typed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.4 (Risk management process established through transparent policies and controls); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (integrated assistants send open threads or files as context, so a policy rule on what staff type does not control what the model receives). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Smart devices and AI governance
questions.question: A Czech smart-thermostat maker's AI inventory lists its heating model's data as readings from 200 test homes; once installed, each thermostat's copy keeps adapting to its home's habits. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Each copy learns from customers' homes, which the record omits
options.B: The 200 test homes stand in for every customer's real home
options.C: Firmware updates may erase what each copy has learned
options.D: Each home's adapted copy may need its own named owner

questions.key_concept: A model that keeps learning in use trains on the data where it runs, so the AI inventory must record that data.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Each thermostat's copy keeps learning from its home's habits, so customers' household data is training data, not only the 200 test homes. With the inventory silent on it, privacy reviews and risk tiers that rely on the record can miss that use. Unrepresentative test homes, option B, could weaken the shipped model, but each copy adapts to its own home; the unrecorded use of customers' data is the larger gap.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training data should fit where a model runs. But each copy adapts to its home; the larger gap is customers' data training it with no record.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because lost learning annoys customers. But that is a product quality issue; customers' data training the model with no record is the governance gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because every model needs an owner. But one owner answers for the model across all copies; what the record lacks is the customer data each copy learns from.

tips: Eliminate: C is a product quality issue, and D asks for an owner per copy, though one model owner answers for every copy.
Final two: A beats B because each copy keeps learning in customers' homes, so their data trains it unrecorded; test-home coverage matters less once each copy adapts.
Exam cue: a model that keeps learning in use trains on the data where it runs; the inventory, privacy review and risk tier must show that data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)

Round 1 fix, 19 Nov 2026: re-angled from bringing product AI into the program's scope, which reused the frame of aaia_d1_088, to what the inventory must record for a model that keeps learning in customers' homes. Round 2 fix, 19 Nov 2026: option B restated as a fact the stem gives, so the key is no longer the only plain statement among hedged options. Round 3 fix, 19 Nov 2026: option A no longer echoes the stem's 'data', and the principle tag is dropped because test-home coverage, the runner-up, is not a tooling move, so online-learning knowledge decides. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Reading a model registry's owner field
questions.question: A Nigerian bank's AI inventory takes each model's owner from its registry, which names whoever registered the latest version, usually the data scientist running the monthly retrain. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have each model's training-data owner recorded as its owner
options.B: Have senior management name a business owner for each model
options.C: Have the registry block any model registered without an owner
options.D: Have the registry keep the first registrant as owner across versions

questions.key_concept: In a model registry each retrain is registered as a new version, so a registrant field tracks builders, not the business owner accountable across versions.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem for who does what.
questions.correct_explanation: The registry names whoever registered the latest version, so 'ownership' passes to whichever builder ran the latest retrain, and the field never names someone who answers for the model's decisions across versions. Senior management naming a business owner for each model fixes accountability. Keeping the first registrant across versions, option D, gives continuity, but still names a builder, not someone answerable for how the model's outputs are used.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data owners are accountable for their data. But one dataset can feed many models; its owner does not answer for each model's use and decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because system rules enforce completeness. But any registrant's name would satisfy the rule; a tool cannot decide who is accountable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it stops the owner changing each month. But it fixes one builder's name in the field; continuity without business accountability leaves decisions unowned.

tips: Eliminate: A names a data owner, who answers for data rather than decisions, and C lets a system rule settle ownership.
Final two: B beats D because each retrain re-registers the model; holding one builder's name steady still leaves no business owner to answer for decisions.
Exam cue: when a tool fills an ownership field, check whether it records accountability or just activity.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Accountability for confirmed outputs
questions.question: An Indonesian home-services app makes each staff member confirming a model-flagged cleaner suspension accountable for it, treating that as covering the model, retrained monthly. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data scientists who retrain the model own its errors
options.B: Have IS audit review each suspension before it takes effect
options.C: Have senior management assign an owner able to pause the model
options.D: Have support staff trained to question each flag they confirm

questions.key_concept: People confirming single outputs cannot see or fix a model's error patterns; a named owner answers for its results across all cases.
questions.pre_read: List who does what in the stem before choosing a fix.
questions.correct_explanation: A model retrained monthly can shift or skew all its flags at once, for example against cleaners in one district. Staff who confirm one case at a time cannot see those patterns, accept the model's risk, pause it or approve its retraining; only a named model owner can. Training staff to question flags, option D, improves each review, but leaves nobody able to pause the model or answer for its overall results.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because they know the model best. But builders do not own the business decision to suspend cleaners or accept that risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review adds assurance. But reviewing each case would make the auditor part of the control, impairing the independence the audit needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reviewers need skills to challenge AI. But better case reviews still leave no one to pause, retrain or answer for the model's overall error patterns.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the business risk to the model's builders, and B puts the auditor inside the process it must later audit.
Final two: C beats D because better case reviews cannot fix error patterns across all flags, which only a model owner can act on.
Exam cue: accountability for single AI outputs does not replace an owner for the model; look for both.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (people who confirm single outputs cannot see or fix a model's error patterns, so a named model owner must answer for its results across all cases). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Awareness content on approved templates
questions.question: A Chilean fruit exporter's awareness course says outputs from an approved prompt template need no checking; its template for certificates of origin was approved after ten good outputs. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Ten outputs are too few to justify approving the template
options.B: Staff may edit the template's wording after it was approved
options.C: The ten approval outputs may have been checked by the template's author
options.D: Drafts made after approval may contain errors the ten lacked

questions.key_concept: A generative model produces each output fresh, so checking sample outputs approves a template, not the outputs it will draft later.
questions.pre_read: Read every option before settling on one.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model samples each output anew, so the same template and similar inputs can yield a wrong origin or a missing clause on a later run. Ten good drafts approve the template's wording, not every certificate it will produce, and the course tells staff to skip the only check that would catch a bad one. A bigger approval sample, option A, still cannot cover outputs not yet generated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because ten is a small sample. But even a thousand good drafts would not cover outputs the model has not yet generated.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because templates should be change-controlled. But nothing in the stem suggests edits; even an unchanged template yields new, unchecked outputs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because builders' own checks are not independent. But an independent check of the same ten drafts would still not cover drafts not yet generated.

tips: Eliminate: C questions who checked the ten drafts, which changes nothing about later drafts, and B raises template edits the stem never suggests.
Final two: D beats A because no sample, however large, covers drafts the model has not yet generated.
Exam cue: approving a prompt or template is not approving its outputs; generative output varies from run to run.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. After a drafting model is replaced
questions.question: A Bolivian ministry's mining-permit reviewers learned to catch its drafting assistant's invented regulation numbers; its new model passed its acceptance tests but errs mainly by omitting conditions. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner update reviewers' training for this version's errors
options.B: Have IS audit check each permit draft before it is issued
options.C: Have the owner rerun acceptance tests on a fresh set of permits
options.D: Have reviewers double their checks of regulation numbers

questions.key_concept: Different model versions fail in different ways, so reviewers' training must change when the model does, even after acceptance tests pass.
questions.pre_read: Note what changed in the stem and what stayed the same.
questions.correct_explanation: Reviewers are the control on each draft, and they learned to catch the old model's typical error, invented numbers. The new model errs differently, by leaving out conditions, which reviewers hunting for wrong numbers can easily miss. Updating their training to the new error pattern keeps oversight effective. Rerunning acceptance tests, option C, repeats checks the model already passed and leaves reviewers looking for the wrong errors.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because extra review sounds safe. But checking each draft would make the auditor part of the control, impairing independence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retesting is a careful step. But the model has already passed; another test leaves reviewers hunting for the old model's errors.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because invented numbers were the known problem. But that was the old model's habit; more checking of numbers will not catch omitted conditions.

tips: Eliminate: D aims more checking at the old model's errors, and B makes the auditor part of the review it must later assess.
Final two: A beats C because the model already passed its tests, while reviewers still hunt for errors it no longer makes.
Exam cue: when an AI model changes, update the human checks built around it, not only the model's tests.
