questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. When a model replaces staff
questions.question: A Costa Rican transport ministry kept the risk rating for taxi-permit renewals when a model replaced clerks, since both wrongly refuse about 2% of renewals. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Drivers may not be told that a model decided their renewal
options.B: The model's errors may hit the same kind of driver every time
options.C: Drivers refused by the model may have no way to appeal
options.D: The rating should now be owned by the data science team

questions.key_concept: A model repeats the same errors for similar people, while staff errors usually scatter more; equal error rates can hide concentrated harm.
questions.pre_read: Read the reason given for the rating before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Clerks' mistakes tend to scatter across drivers, but a model applies the same learned pattern to everyone, so its errors can recur for one kind of driver, renewal after renewal. Equal 2% rates can therefore hide harm concentrated on some people's livelihoods, which the kept rating never weighed. Not telling drivers a model decided, option A, matters for transparency, but it is narrower than repeated wrongful refusals.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people should know when AI decides. But telling them would not stop the model wrongly refusing the same kind of driver again and again.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because people affected by AI need a way to challenge it. But the stem never suggests appeals are missing; repeated refusals of one kind of driver harm more.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data scientists understand the model. But the risk rating belongs to the business risk owner, who answers for harm to drivers.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes an appeal route is missing, which the stem never says, and D gives the business risk rating to the builders.
Final two: B beats A because concentrated, repeated wrongful refusals cause more harm than a lack of notice that a model decided.
Exam cue: equal error rates are not equal risk; ask whether AI errors repeat for the same people.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (a model's errors repeat for similar people while staff errors scatter, so an equal error rate can hide harm concentrated on one group). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Reassessing a long-running model
questions.question: A Philippine electric cooperative reassesses AI risk yearly and after code, data-source or use changes; its crew-dispatch model, accuracy tracked monthly, is unchanged since 2022. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner retrain the model, as it is four years old
options.B: Move high-impact models to quarterly reassessment
options.C: Add shifts in the model's monitored results as a trigger
options.D: Have internal audit reassess the model each storm season

questions.key_concept: A model's risk can rise with no change to the model, as the world it scores shifts, so reassessment triggers include monitored performance shifts.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: Storm patterns, the grid and repair practices change, so a model untouched since 2022 can dispatch crews less well without any change to its code, data sources or use. A trigger tied to monitored results catches that drift when it happens. Quarterly reassessment, option B, shortens the wait but stays tied to the calendar, so degraded dispatch could still run for months before the next scheduled review.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because older models often drift. But retraining without evidence of a problem is a technical fix ahead of the risk process, and it needs its own approval.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more frequent reviews sound safer. But drift does not follow the calendar; dispatch could degrade for months between quarterly reviews.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor sees the gap. But reassessing is the risk owner's job; internal audit assesses whether the process works.

tips: Eliminate: A jumps to a technical fix without evidence, and D has the auditor do the owner's reassessment.
Final two: C beats B because drift can start any day, and only a trigger tied to monitored results catches it when it does.
Exam cue: AI risk can change with no change to the system; look for triggers tied to monitored performance, not only to changes or dates.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.1 (Existing, unanticipated and emergent risks tracked); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.5 (Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (a model's risk can rise with no change to the model as the conditions it scores shift, so reassessment triggers include monitored performance, not only changes or dates). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A tolerance for a penalty-review model
questions.question: A Lao railway caps honest passengers its fare-evasion model wrongly picks for penalty review; a lower score cutoff was approved as low risk since AUC was unchanged. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have senior management raise the cap to fit the lower cutoff
options.B: Have the change board require AUC retests for every cutoff change
options.C: Have IT restrict who can edit the cutoff setting
options.D: Have the owner test the new cutoff's false positives against the cap

questions.key_concept: Moving a model's cutoff can raise wrongful flags while its AUC stays the same, so the owner rechecks harm at the new cutoff against tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Read what changed, then ask what each option would show about it.
questions.correct_explanation: AUC, the area under the curve, measures how well the model ranks evaders above honest passengers across every possible cutoff, so moving the cutoff never changes it. A lower cutoff sends more passengers to penalty review, honest ones among them. The owner sets the cutoff inside the cap, so false positives, the wrongful picks, at the new cutoff must be measured against it. AUC retests, option B, would pass whatever cutoff runs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tolerances can be revised. But the cap follows the risk appetite; loosening it to fit a cutoff whose effect on passengers is unknown reverses that order.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because changes need testing. But AUC covers every cutoff at once, so it is the same whatever cutoff runs and never shows how many honest passengers are picked.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because settings need access control. But this cutoff change was approved; restricting edits does not show whether the new cutoff keeps wrongful picks within the cap.

tips: Eliminate: A loosens the cap to fit a change whose effect is unknown, though tolerances follow appetite, and C controls who edits the cutoff, not whether the approved one stays within the cap.
Final two: D beats B because AUC is the same at every cutoff; only wrongful picks measured at the new cutoff show whether the cap still holds.
Exam cue: a cutoff change can raise wrongful flags while the model and its AUC stay the same; recheck the harm at the new cutoff against the tolerance.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.1 (Methods and metrics selected starting with the most significant risks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (moving a model's cutoff can raise wrongful flags while its AUC stays the same, so the owner rechecks harm at the new cutoff against tolerance). Round 1 fix, 19 Nov 2026: re-angled from a tolerance stated as AUC, which reused the frame of aaia_d1_125, to checking an approved cutoff change against the tolerance. Round 2 fix, 19 Nov 2026: key D says 'wrongful flags' so it no longer echoes the stem's 'picks', B names every cutoff change, and the explanation no longer names travel cards the stem never gives. Round 3 fix, 19 Nov 2026: key D says 'false positives' so it no longer echoes the stem's 'wrongly'. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Reading a fall in refusals
questions.question: An Azerbaijani tax service reports as a performance gain that its taxpayer chatbot's 'cannot answer' rate fell from 12% to 2% the week after a vendor model update. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The fall may mean more wrong answers, not more right ones
options.B: The fall shows the updated chatbot now answers more accurately
options.C: The fall is a KPI, so it belongs outside risk reporting
options.D: The fall may reflect easier questions rather than the update

questions.key_concept: An assistant that declines less may be guessing more, so a falling 'cannot answer' rate needs an accuracy check before it counts as a gain.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else could make the reported figure move.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model that declines less fills more gaps with plausible guesses, so an update that cuts 'cannot answer' replies from 12% to 2% may have turned honest refusals into confident wrong tax guidance. Only sampled answers checked for accuracy show which happened. Easier questions, option D, could also move the figure, but a drop the week after the update points first to the model's new behavior.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fewer refusals look like progress. But a 'cannot answer' rate measures willingness to answer, not whether the answers are right.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because KPIs track value. But a value figure can signal rising risk, and this one needs reading against accuracy, not filing away.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a change in questions can move any rate. But the fall came the week after the model update, so the model's new behavior is the first suspect.

tips: Eliminate: B reads willingness to answer as accuracy, and C treats a KPI as irrelevant to risk, though it can signal it.
Final two: A beats D because the drop arrived with the update, so a model that now guesses is the first explanation to test.
Exam cue: when a generative model refuses less, check whether its answers got better or it simply started guessing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 4.3 (Performance improvements or declines identified and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (an assistant that declines less after an update may be guessing more, so a falling 'cannot answer' rate needs an accuracy check before it counts as a gain). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Safeguards supplied by a model provider
questions.question: A Slovenian foraging app's chatbot tells users which wild mushrooms are safe to eat; it relies only on its model provider's built-in safety filters for harmful content. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The provider may change its filters without telling the app
options.B: Unsafe mushroom advice may pass filters made for general use
options.C: Filters may block too many harmless questions about mushrooms
options.D: The provider is liable for harmful advice its filters let through

questions.key_concept: Provider filters target general harms; harms specific to one use, such as unsafe foraging advice, need the deployer's own controls and tests.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: A provider's built-in filters are designed for harms common to all customers, such as violence or hate speech. Advice calling a poisonous mushroom edible reads as ordinary text and passes them easily, so the app needs its own use-specific controls and testing. Silent filter changes, option A, are a real third-party risk, but even unchanged filters were never built to catch unsafe foraging advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because providers do change hosted components quietly. But even unchanged filters were built for general harms and would still pass unsafe foraging advice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because over-blocking frustrates users. But blocked questions are visible and inconvenient, while unsafe advice that passes can poison users unseen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider supplies the filters. But the app chose to advise on wild mushrooms and stays accountable for it; a contract cannot shift that.

tips: Eliminate: D shifts accountability to the provider, which the app keeps, and C weighs inconvenience above the risk of poisoning users.
Final two: B beats A because even unchanged general-purpose filters would pass advice that is harmful only in this use.
Exam cue: a provider's safeguards cover general risks; the organization deploying the model owns the risks of its own use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.2 (Internal risk controls for components identified)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (a model provider's built-in filters target general harms, so harms specific to one use, such as unsafe foraging advice, need the deployer's own controls and tests). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Change-notice terms in a supply chain
questions.question: A Dominican utility's vendor drafts replies to outage-compensation claims using a foundation model whose provider updates it unannounced; the vendor must give 30 days' notice of model changes. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Provider updates usually improve replies, so notice matters little
options.B: Thirty days' notice may be too short to retest changes
options.C: The vendor cannot pass on updates it never hears about
options.D: Accountability for the replies now rests with the vendor

questions.key_concept: A notice clause binds only the vendor; if its own provider updates silently, the clause fails without matching upstream terms or pinned versions.
questions.pre_read: Note each party in the stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The 30-day clause binds the vendor, but the replies come from a foundation model whose provider changes it without telling anyone, the vendor included. Replies could then shift with no notice ever reaching the utility, so the clause protects nothing unless the vendor pins model versions or holds matching terms upstream. A short notice period, option B, matters only once notice actually arrives.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because updates often aim to improve models. But any update can change replies in ways nobody tested, which is why notice matters.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retesting needs time. But the period only matters if notice arrives, and the provider's silent updates mean it may never come.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor drafts the replies. But accountability for replies to customers stays with the utility; contracts add duties, not a transfer of accountability.

tips: Eliminate: D moves accountability to the vendor, though it stays with the utility, and A assumes updates only improve a model.
Final two: C beats B because the notice period is irrelevant if the vendor itself never learns of the provider's changes.
Exam cue: follow AI contract terms down the supply chain; a duty binds only the party that signed it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.12 (Value Chain and Component Integration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (a change-notice clause binds only the vendor, so it fails when the vendor's own model provider updates silently unless versions are pinned or matching terms run upstream). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Documents an assistant retrieves
questions.question: A Guatemalan hospital group's AI assistant for nurses, used via each hospital's sign-in, searches one index of its four hospitals' current care protocols, which differ on some doses. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Answers may quote dose tables that have since been replaced
options.B: Nurses may trust the assistant's drug answers over the protocols
options.C: The index may show one hospital's protocols to other hospitals' staff
options.D: Nurses may be given another hospital's dose for the same drug

questions.key_concept: Retrieval matches passages by similarity, not by where they apply, so documents pooled from several sites need owner-set records of where each applies.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: A hospital sign-in controls who uses the assistant, not which passages it retrieves, unless each protocol records where it applies and retrieval filters on it. Four hospitals' protocols for one drug match a question almost equally well, so a nurse can get another site's dose with no sign it is wrong. Staff seeing other sites' protocols, option C, stems from the same gap, but only a wrong dose harms a patient.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because outdated documents are a common retrieval risk. But the index pools current protocols; the stated difference is between hospitals, not versions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because over-reliance is a real oversight concern. But the facts give no sign of it, and the harm here comes from which protocol is retrieved.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one index behind separate sign-ins looks like an access-control gap. But staff seeing a sister hospital's protocol matters far less than a wrong dose reaching a patient.

tips: Eliminate: A raises replaced dose tables when the index holds current protocols, and B assumes over-reliance the facts never give.
Final two: D beats C because both follow from a sign-in that does not scope similarity search, but only a wrong dose can harm a patient.
Exam cue: when one assistant searches documents from several owners or sites, ask whether each document records where it applies.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (retrieval matches by similarity, not by where a document applies, so pooled documents need owner-set records of their scope). Re-angled in batch 10 review from document currency, which 2A.1 already teaches, to where each document applies. Revised in batch 10 round 2 to add the per-hospital sign-in, which does not scope retrieval. Final fix round: runner-up named as C (cross-site visibility), which loses on harm to patients. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Openly published training data
questions.question: An Indian test-prep firm will train the question generator it sells on textbook passages a volunteer group scraped from publishers' sites and shared under a permissive license. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Whether the group that compiled the data held rights to it
options.B: Whether the dataset is large enough to train the model well
options.C: Whether the passages are accurate and match current syllabuses
options.D: Whether the group's license allows training a model for sale

questions.key_concept: A dataset's license passes on only rights its grantor held; scraped content can carry a permissive license yet give no right to train on it.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the stem states from what it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: A license can pass on only the rights its grantor holds. Volunteers who scraped passages from publishers' sites gained no copyright by doing so, so unless the publishers granted them rights, the group's permissive license cannot authorize training a commercial generator, and a trained model is hard to unwind later. Checking that the license allows training for sale, option D, reads the grant's terms, but even generous terms grant nothing the group never owned.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because data volume affects model quality. But size is a technical question; whether the firm may use the data at all comes first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because practice questions must be correct. But accurate passages still may not be used if no one with the rights allowed it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because license terms decide permitted uses. But the group could license only rights it held, and scraping textbooks gave it none to pass on.

tips: Eliminate: B asks a technical sizing question before rights, and C checks quality when the question is whether the firm may use the data.
Final two: A beats D because a license cannot grant rights the group never held, however permissive its terms.
Exam cue: for open training data, trace the rights back to their source; a license is only as good as its grantor's rights.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.10 (Intellectual Property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (a dataset's license passes on only the rights its grantor held, so scraped content shared under a permissive license may carry no right to train a model that is sold). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Voice analysis of recorded calls
questions.question: A Moroccan intercity bus company will build voiceprints from booking-call recordings to spot repeat card fraudsters; its privacy assessment treats them like the recordings, as ordinary customer data. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner update the privacy notice after launch
options.B: Have the privacy officer reassess voiceprints as biometric data
options.C: Have the owner delete recordings once voiceprints are built
options.D: Have the owner test how often voiceprints match the wrong caller

questions.key_concept: A speaker model turns ordinary recordings into voiceprints that identify people, a new purpose and often biometric data, so privacy assessment comes before building them.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem for each use of the recordings.
questions.correct_explanation: A speaker-recognition model turns recordings into voiceprints that identify individual callers, which many privacy laws treat as biometric data needing a specific lawful basis, notice and stronger safeguards. An assessment that files them as ordinary customer data has not asked those questions, so the privacy officer must reassess before anything is built. Testing false matches, option D, matters once the use is lawful, but accuracy cannot settle whether it is.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because notice is part of the fix. But updating it after launch leaves voiceprints built without a basis; assessment comes first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deleting source data minimizes it. But the voiceprints themselves identify callers, so deleting recordings leaves the biometric processing unassessed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because false matches would wrong innocent callers. But accuracy comes after deciding the processing is permitted; a precise voiceprint can still be unlawful.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes recordings while the voiceprints still identify callers, and A tells callers only after voiceprints exist.
Final two: B beats D because whether the processing is permitted comes before how accurately it works.
Exam cue: when AI turns ordinary data into identifiers or inferences, treat it as new personal data processing and assess it first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-8 (Privacy Impact Assessments)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (a speaker model turns ordinary call recordings into voiceprints that identify people, a new purpose and often biometric data, so privacy assessment comes before building them). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Hosted models and patient messages
questions.question: A Uruguayan mental-health clinic's privacy assessment finds no risk in sending patients' messages to a hosted model, because the provider's terms bar training on them. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the clinic encrypt messages before the model reads them
options.B: Have IT anonymize messages by removing patients' names
options.C: Have the privacy officer assess the provider's storage and access
options.D: Have the privacy officer confirm the provider's no-training term

questions.key_concept: Terms barring training do not settle privacy: prompts still travel to the provider, where logs, retention, staff access and location all need assessment.
questions.pre_read: Check what the assessment's conclusion rests on.
questions.correct_explanation: A ban on training addresses only one use of the messages. Each message still travels to the provider, which may log it for abuse monitoring, keep it for a period, let staff review it or process it in another country. The assessment must cover each of these uses of sensitive mental-health details. Confirming the provider's no-training term, option D, verifies the one safeguard the assessment already relies on, leaving the rest unexamined.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects data. But the model must read messages as plaintext to work on them, so encryption cannot apply at that point.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because names identify people. But mental-health messages carry dates, symptoms and life events that can identify patients without names.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because claims should be checked against evidence. But confirming the no-training term proves only that one safeguard, not how messages are stored, accessed or moved.

tips: Eliminate: A encrypts data the model must read as plaintext, and B treats removing names as making free text anonymous.
Final two: C beats D because confirming the no-training term verifies one safeguard, while storage, access and location stay unassessed.
Exam cue: 'the provider won't train on it' is one privacy safeguard, not a privacy assessment.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (terms barring training on prompts are one safeguard, not a privacy assessment; prompts still travel to the provider, whose storage, access and location need assessing). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Support emails as tuning data
questions.question: A Latvian car-parts retailer will fine-tune a reply-drafting model on support emails that quote one customer's dispute letters 300 times. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST to protect that customer?

options.A: Filter drafts for that customer's name and account number
options.B: Delete the source emails once fine-tuning is complete
options.C: Encrypt the support emails used for fine-tuning
options.D: Remove duplicate passages from the tuning data

questions.key_concept: Models memorize repeated text more readily, so removing duplicates before training cuts the chance that one person's details are reproduced.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each control by what it would actually stop.
questions.correct_explanation: Text repeated hundreds of times in training is far more likely to be memorized and reproduced word for word, so the customer's dispute letters could surface in drafts sent to other customers. Removing the repeats before fine-tuning cuts much of that memorization at its source. Filtering drafts for the customer's name and account number, option A, catches only those exact details, while reproduced letters can carry other identifying details.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because output filters catch leaks. But they match only listed details, while reproduced letters can carry others; prevention at the source is stronger.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deleting sources sounds thorough. But what the model memorized stays in it after the source emails are gone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption protects stored emails. But training uses the decrypted text, so the model can still memorize it.

tips: Eliminate: C protects stored data the model trains on anyway, and B deletes sources while the model keeps what it memorized.
Final two: D beats A because removing repeats cuts memorization at its source, while a filter catches only the exact details it lists.
Exam cue: heavily repeated records are the ones a model memorizes; deduplicate before training rather than filter after.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.10-003 (Verify deduplication of GAI training data samples)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (models memorize text they see many times, so removing duplicates before training cuts the chance that one person's details are reproduced). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Rolling back after an erasure retrain
questions.question: A Singapore insurer retrained its claims-letter model without letters customers asked to erase; it now fails, so the owner plans to restore the earlier version, trained on them. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner and privacy officer rule on the old version
options.B: Have the owner test the old version on current claim inputs
options.C: Have IT delete the erased letters from the old version's files
options.D: Have the data team fix the new version before any rollback

questions.key_concept: A rollback can restore a version trained on data since erased, so the owner and privacy officer must approve its return first.
questions.pre_read: Read the whole stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The earlier version was trained on the letters customers asked to erase, so it may still reproduce them, and a rollback would put it back into service. The owner, with the privacy officer confirming, must decide whether it may return or another option is needed. Testing it on current claims, option B, shows whether it works, but a version that works well can still reproduce what customers asked to erase.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rollback targets should be tested. But a version that handles current claims well still holds what it learned from the erased letters.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deletion sounds direct. But a model holds what it learned in its weights, not as stored letters, so there is nothing to delete file by file.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fixing forward avoids old versions. But choosing between rollback and a fix is the owner's call, and the erasure question still needs an answer.

tips: Eliminate: C treats learned data as files that can be deleted, and D lets the data team choose a response the owner decides.
Final two: A beats B because a version that passes tests on current claims can still reproduce letters customers asked to erase.
Exam cue: before restoring any earlier model version, ask what data it was trained on and whether that data may still be used.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (a rollback restores a model version trained before erasures, so it still holds what it learned from erased data and must be cleared before it returns). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A fairness criterion for cadet selection
questions.question: A Seychellois airline's cadet-pilot selection model must keep women's selection rate at least 0.8 of men's; nine women and 140 men apply each year. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner replace the ratio with error-rate parity for each sex
options.B: Have the owner define how the criterion is judged for small groups
options.C: Have the owner drop the sex criterion until more women apply
options.D: Have the owner raise the ratio threshold to 1.0

questions.key_concept: A fairness criterion needs a rule for judging small groups, since one decision can swing a measure on a handful of people.
questions.pre_read: Restate the requirement in your own words before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: With nine women a year, one more or one fewer selection moves their rate by about 11 points, so the 0.8 ratio can pass or fail by chance. A testable criterion must say how small groups are judged, for example by pooling several years' intakes or stating the uncertainty. Error-rate parity, option A, measures a different harm, but it splits the nine women further and swings even more.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because selection rates can hide unequal errors. But with nine women any group measure, error rates included, swings with a single decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small groups seem to matter less. But the fewer women apply, the more each wrongful rejection matters; small numbers call for a better method, not none.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because perfect parity sounds fairest. But a stricter threshold leaves the swing untouched; on nine applicants a single decision still decides pass or fail.

tips: Eliminate: C drops the criterion because the group is small, and D tightens a ratio that one decision can already swing.
Final two: B beats A because nine applicants make any group measure, error rates included, unstable unless the criterion says how small groups are judged.
Exam cue: a testable fairness criterion states the measure, the threshold and how it applies when a group is small.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (a fairness criterion must say how small groups are judged, for example pooled intakes or stated uncertainty, since a measure on a handful of people swings with one decision). Re-angled in batch 10 review from reading a test result, which 2E.2 already teaches, to designing the criterion. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Criteria for generated images
questions.question: A Kenyan children's-book publisher uses an image generator to illustrate careers in primary-school readers; its owner's criteria cover image quality, copyright and age-appropriate content. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Images may copy protected photos from the training data
options.B: Pupils may not be told the career pictures were made by AI
options.C: Images may tie each job to one sex or skin color
options.D: Different runs may draw the same career differently

questions.key_concept: Image generators reproduce stereotypes in their training data, so fairness criteria for generated content cover how people are portrayed, not just quality.
questions.pre_read: Read the criteria list before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Image generators learn from huge collections of pictures and tend to repeat their stereotypes, such as drawing nurses as women and engineers as men, or favoring lighter skin. In readers that shape how children see careers, that is a harmful-bias risk the criteria never test. Not telling pupils the images are AI-made, option B, raises a transparency point, but disclosure would not undo a stereotyped picture of who does which job.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because generators can copy training images. But the owner's criteria already cover copyright; the untested risk is how people are portrayed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because transparency is a trustworthy-AI characteristic. But a label saying AI made a picture would not stop it teaching children a stereotype.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generative output varies from run to run. But different drawings of a career are harmless here; the risk is what they consistently teach.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats a risk the criteria already cover, and D treats harmless variation between drawings as the problem.
Final two: C beats B because disclosure would not undo stereotyped pictures teaching children who does which job.
Exam cue: for generated content about people, the NIST characteristic 'fair, with harmful bias managed' includes how groups are portrayed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.6 (Harmful Bias and Homogenization); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (image generators reproduce stereotypes in their training data, so fairness criteria for generated content cover how people are portrayed). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Counsel's view of a foreign AI law
questions.question: Counsel says an EU AI law cannot apply to a South African firm's staff-rating model, as the firm operates only from Johannesburg; two clients use it in Ireland. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have internal audit decide whether the law applies to the firm
options.B: Have clients take on every duty the law gives the model's users
options.C: Have counsel confirm the clients, not the firm, deploy it in Ireland
options.D: Have counsel reassess the law's reach where clients use the model

questions.key_concept: Risk-based AI laws can reach providers abroad whose systems are sold or used in their market, so applicability depends on where the AI is used.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based AI laws such as the EU AI Act can apply to providers based elsewhere when their systems are placed on that market or their outputs are used there. With clients rating staff in Ireland, the firm's location does not settle the question, so counsel should reassess on where the model is used. Confirming that the clients deploy it, option C, is relevant, but their duties sit beside the firm's own duties as provider.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the auditor spotted the issue. But applicability is a legal judgment for counsel; the auditor tests the mapping and the evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the clients run the model. But laws can place duties on providers that users cannot take over, and the firm is the provider.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deployers carry their own duties. But the firm still places the model on that market as its provider, so neither location nor the clients' role ends its duties.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes users can take on a provider's duties, and A has the auditor make counsel's legal judgment.
Final two: D beats C because the clients' deployer duties sit beside the firm's own duties as provider in a market where the model is used.
Exam cue: AI-law applicability turns on where the system is sold or used and the role played, not only where the firm sits.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (risk-based AI laws can reach providers abroad whose systems are used in their market, so applicability turns on where the AI is used, not where the firm sits). questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. AI inside regulated products
questions.question: An Israeli firm's ECG-reading model is a regulated medical device; each monthly retrain changes no code, is independently validated and is released through its billing software's change process. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The change process may not ask if a version needs clearance
options.B: Monthly retraining is too frequent for a medical model
options.C: Patients may not be told an AI model reads their ECG
options.D: The change process may not record each version's training data

questions.key_concept: In a regulated product, sector law can treat a retrained model as a change needing regulator review, so obligation mapping must reach retraining.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Medical-device rules generally require significant changes to a regulated product to be assessed, and sometimes reviewed by the regulator, before release, unless an agreed change plan covers them. A retrained diagnostic model can be such a change even with no code change, yet a process built for billing software is unlikely to ask that question. Recording each version's training data, option D, supports review, but it does not meet the regulator's requirement.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because frequent change adds risk. But frequency itself is not the problem; how each version is controlled and cleared is.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because people should know when AI shapes their care. But telling patients, however fair, does nothing to clear each retrained version for use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because each version should trace to its data. But lineage records support review; they do not decide whether a version needs the regulator's review before release.

tips: Eliminate: B objects to frequency rather than control of each change, and C raises patient notice, which does not clear a changed device.
Final two: A beats D because lineage records, however complete, do not decide whether a retrained version needs the regulator's review before release.
Exam cue: when AI sits inside a regulated product, map the sector's change rules to retraining, not only to code releases.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (when AI sits in a regulated product, sector law can treat a retrained model as a change needing regulator review, so obligation mapping must reach retraining). Final review: option A reworded to name the change-process gap the stem implies, not assert it. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. What the NIST AI RMF sets
questions.question: A Swiss reinsurer adopting the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) asks the IS auditor which false-alarm tolerance the framework sets for its claims-fraud model. What is the IS auditor's BEST answer?

options.A: Its sector regulator's limit, which the framework adopts by reference
options.B: The rate at which the framework says use must stop
options.C: None; senior management must set one for this use
options.D: The rate its Measure work shows the model can achieve

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF helps prioritize AI risk but does not prescribe risk tolerance; the organization sets it, using any sector rules that apply.
questions.pre_read: Recall what kind of document the framework is.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF states that it can help prioritize risk but does not prescribe risk tolerance. Tolerance depends on context, so the reinsurer's senior management must set it for this use within the board's appetite, drawing on any sector rules that apply. A sector regulator's limit, option A, can shape that choice where one exists, but the framework neither adopts nor sets it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the framework tells organizations to follow sector rules. But it adopts no regulator's limit; the organization still sets its own tolerance.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the framework says development and deployment should cease when risk is unacceptable. But it leaves the organization to decide where that line sits; it sets no rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Measure produces the metrics. But a tolerance set at what the model achieves describes the model, not how much harm is acceptable; the framework sets no number.

tips: Eliminate: D sets tolerance at what the model achieves, which describes the model, not acceptable harm, and B reads the framework's stop rule as a numeric limit.
Final two: C beats A because the framework leaves tolerance to the organization; sector rules inform that choice but are not adopted by it.
Exam cue: frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF structure risk work; the organization still sets appetite and tolerances.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 1.2.2 (Risk Tolerance); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF helps prioritize AI risk but does not prescribe risk tolerance; the organization sets it, informed by any sector rules). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 10, 19 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Using the Generative AI Profile
questions.question: A Sri Lankan tea broker that only deploys a vendor's generative assistant treats every NIST AI 600-1 suggested action as a mandatory control and reports 40% compliance. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Drop the profile, as it is written for model developers
options.B: Select the actions that fit its role and its own risks
options.C: Assign each action an owner and a completion date
options.D: Seek certification against the profile to show compliance

questions.key_concept: NIST AI 600-1 lists suggested actions, not requirements; each organization selects those that fit its role, such as deployer, and its uses.
questions.pre_read: Picture the broker acting on each option before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST AI 600-1 presents suggested actions and says not every action applies to every AI actor; applicability depends on the organization's role and its own uses. A broker that only deploys an assistant should select the actions that fit, so developer-only actions stop distorting the 40% figure. Assigning every action an owner and date, option C, looks disciplined, but it commits effort to actions that do not apply.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because many actions target developers. But the profile also covers deployers, and the actions written for them still fit the broker's assistant.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because owners and dates drive completion. But it treats suggestions written partly for developers as duties the broker must meet.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because certificates reassure boards. But the profile is voluntary guidance with no certification scheme.

tips: Eliminate: D seeks a certification the profile does not offer, and A drops guidance that also covers organizations deploying generative AI.
Final two: B beats C because owners and dates for every action enforce suggestions that do not fit a deployer.
Exam cue: framework profiles offer actions to select by role and use; treat them as a menu matched to risk, not a checklist.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 3 (Suggested Actions to Manage GAI Risks); NIST AI 100-1 Section 6 (AI RMF Profiles)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (NIST AI 600-1 lists suggested actions, not requirements; each organization selects those that fit its role, such as deployer, and its uses). questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Routing complaints with a generative model
questions.question: A Malawian water board's general-purpose generative model sorts each complaint into one of 12 category names; a routing rule sends each exact name to one team. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: It may put complaints under names that staff would not choose
options.B: It may need thousands of labeled complaints before it can sort
options.C: It may return text that matches no allowed label
options.D: Its sorting rules may need staff to update them by hand

questions.key_concept: A generative model asked to classify writes free text, so it can return labels outside the allowed list unless its output is constrained and checked.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model writes text rather than picking from a fixed set, so even given the 12 names it can return a variant, a merged label or a sentence. A routing rule keyed to exact names then has no team for that complaint, and nobody may notice. Choosing a name staff would not, option A, is the usual classifier risk, but a misrouted complaint still reaches a team, which may pass it on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because misclassification is the usual model risk. But a wrongly chosen name still reaches a team, which may pass the complaint on; a label matching no name reaches nobody.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because classic classifiers learn from labeled examples. But a general-purpose generative model can sort from instructions alone; its risk here is free-text output.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because routing tools often run on fixed rules. But a generative model follows its prompt and learned patterns, not rules that staff maintain.

tips: Eliminate: B expects a general-purpose generative model to need a large labeled set before it can sort, and D treats it as a rules engine that people maintain.
Final two: C beats A because a wrong but valid name still reaches a team, which may reroute it; a generative model's free-text label can match no name and reach nobody.
Exam cue: when a generative model fills a field that only accepts fixed values, ask what happens to output that fits none of them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (a generative model asked to classify writes free text, so it can return labels outside the allowed list, which a routing step keyed to exact names cannot place). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A chatbot with a lookup tool
questions.question: A South African self-storage chain's chatbot for customers can query the live unit-rent list through a tool, but the model decides itself when to use it. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The chatbot may need retraining whenever the chain's unit rents change
options.B: Tool outages may go unnoticed by the chain's IT staff
options.C: Customers may not be told where the rent figures come from
options.D: It may answer from outdated learned figures instead of the tool

questions.key_concept: A tool-using model chooses when to call its tools; it can skip the lookup and answer fluently from older training data.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how likely each is and how much harm it would do.
questions.correct_explanation: When a model decides for itself whether to use a tool, it can skip the lookup and answer from figures learned in training, which may be out of date, and the reply reads just as confident. Wrong rents quoted to customers then go unchecked. Unnoticed tool outages, option B, are a real operations gap, but even with the tool working, the model may never call it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models hold what they learned in training. But a live lookup reads the current rent list, so changes need no retraining; the gap is whether it looks.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because monitoring outages is sound practice. But a working tool helps only when the model chooses to use it, which the stem leaves to the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because users should know a figure's source. But disclosure does not make a rent figure correct; wrong quotes are the larger harm here.

tips: Eliminate: A thinks a live lookup tool needs retraining when rents change, and C is a disclosure gap that leaves every quoted figure as right or wrong as before.
Final two: D beats B because the model, not a rule, decides whether to look up the rent list; a working tool it never calls protects nobody.
Exam cue: when an AI may choose whether to use a tool, ask what it does when it does not; access to a source is not use of it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An assistant for kitchen managers
questions.question: A Uruguayan restaurant chain's kitchen managers ask its generative assistant, which searches current food-hygiene rules, to confirm storage practices they already plan to use. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Answers may lean toward whatever each question seems to expect
options.B: Its answers may be identical each time, hiding any error
options.C: Each confirmation may teach the assistant to approve more practices
options.D: Answers may rest on hygiene rules changed after its training cutoff

questions.key_concept: Models tuned on human approval can favor answers users seem to want, so leading questions draw agreement rather than an independent check.
questions.pre_read: Note which facts in the stem each option depends on before ranking them.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative models are tuned partly on human ratings, which tend to reward agreeable answers, so a request to confirm a planned practice can draw a yes that the rules do not support. Managers then get their own view back as advice. A training cutoff, option D, could date answers, but this assistant searches current rules; questions built to invite agreement are the gap the stem describes.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because uniform answers could hide a fault. But generative answers usually vary between runs, and nothing in the stem suggests identical replies.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI seems to learn from use. But answering a prompt does not retrain the model, so confirmations do not shift later answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because models do miss rules made after their training. But this assistant searches current rules, while questions built to invite a yes can still draw one.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes each answer retrains the model, and B expects identical replies from a model whose answers usually vary between runs.
Final two: A beats D because the assistant searches current rules, yet questions framed to invite a yes still draw one from models tuned on human approval.
Exam cue: when users ask an AI to confirm their own view, expect agreement, not a check; neutral questions and source checks are the control.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Forecasts behind work stoppages
questions.question: A Greek labor inspectorate halts outdoor building work only when its model's forecast afternoon temperature exceeds 40°C; tomorrow's forecast is 38.5°C. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Work may be halted more often than it is needed
options.B: The single figure may hide a real chance of passing 40°C
options.C: Updated forecasts may differ from the one issued today
options.D: The forecast model may not have been tested on recent heatwaves

questions.key_concept: A model's forecast is an estimate with a spread; deciding on its single figure ignores the chance that the true value crosses the limit.
questions.pre_read: Restate the decision rule in your own words before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Forecasts are estimates: a central value of 38.5°C can still leave a sizable chance that the afternoon passes 40°C, yet the rule treats it as no risk at all. Decisions where the harm is heatstroke need the forecast's range or its probability of crossing the limit. Testing on recent heatwaves, option D, would refine the estimate, but even a well-validated forecast is a range, not a promise.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because needless stoppages carry costs. But this rule halts work only above 40°C, so missed dangerous heat, not excess stoppages, is its weak side.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because changing forecasts look unreliable. But updating as new weather data arrive is normal and useful, not a flaw.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because validation on recent seasons is good practice. But a well-tested model still gives an estimate with a spread, and the rule ignores that spread.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about too many stoppages under a rule that triggers only above the limit, and C treats normal forecast updates as a defect.
Final two: B beats D because even a validated forecast is an estimate with a spread; deciding on its single figure ignores the chance of passing 40°C.
Exam cue: when a decision compares a model's single figure with a hard limit, ask for the chance of crossing the limit, not just the central estimate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Reusing a no-show model
questions.question: A Fijian hospital's no-show model, validated at 88% accuracy only for reminder calls, may now be used to remove priority booking from patients it scores as likely no-shows. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Its 88% accuracy may not hold for this year's patients
options.B: Managers, not data scientists, would set the score cutoff
options.C: Its scores were never assessed for deciding access to care
options.D: Scoring more patients may wear down the model's accuracy

questions.key_concept: Requirements bind a model to its stated purpose; a new use with different error costs needs its own requirements and testing before reliance.
questions.pre_read: Note who is affected at each step before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: The model was specified and judged only for reminder calls, where a wrong score costs a phone call. Using it to withdraw priority booking turns the same errors into delayed care, and no requirement, acceptance criterion or test covers that use. Rechecking the 88% on this year's patients, option A, would confirm fitness for reminders, but accuracy fit for a phone call says nothing about errors that delay care.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accuracy can fade as patients change. But even a fresh 88% would show fitness for reminder calls; nobody judged its errors for withholding priority care.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because cutoffs look technical. But business managers setting the cutoff is how ownership should work; it is not the gap here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because heavy use sounds like wear. But scoring more cases does not make a model less accurate; changes in data or purpose do.

tips: Eliminate: D treats extra use as wearing a model out, and B objects to business managers setting a cutoff, which is their role.
Final two: C beats A because 88% was judged for reminder calls, where errors are cheap; withholding priority care needs its own requirements and tests.
Exam cue: when a model's output is put to a new decision, check that requirements and tests cover that decision, not only the original one.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Buying a payment-risk model
questions.question: A Tanzanian microlender wants to spot borrowers likely to miss their next weekly payment; its preferred vendor model predicts default, defined as 90 days unpaid. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the IS auditor validate the model before officers rely on it
options.B: Have the owner test the vendor model's accuracy on its own loans
options.C: Have the vendor retrain its model on the lender's borrowers
options.D: Have the owner compare the vendor's outcome with the need

questions.key_concept: A model predicts the outcome it was trained on; check that outcome matches the business need before testing how accurately it predicts it.
questions.pre_read: Read the whole stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A model is only as useful as the outcome it was trained to predict. This one predicts 90-day default, while the lender needs early warning of a missed weekly payment, a different and much earlier event. Testing accuracy on the lender's loans, option B, would measure how well it predicts default, so a high score could hide a poor fit. The outcome comparison comes first.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the IS auditor knows validation. But validation belongs to a function independent of the builders, and approval to management; the IS auditor assesses and recommends.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because testing on your own data is sound. But it would measure how well the model predicts 90-day default, not the earlier event the lender needs flagged.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because local data helps. But retraining is a sourcing step that comes after the owner confirms which outcome the model must predict.

tips: Eliminate: A has the IS auditor validate the model, a job for independent validators, and C jumps to retraining before the requirement fit is known.
Final two: D beats B because an accuracy test would score the model on 90-day default; only comparing outcomes shows whether it predicts what the lender needs.
Exam cue: before testing a bought model's accuracy, check what outcome it predicts; a model can be accurate at the wrong thing.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Applying the AI policy to a monitor's alerts
questions.question: A South Korean baby-monitor maker's AI policy requires a person to check AI output before use; its monitors' breathing-alert model warns parents directly, within seconds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the policy owner add controls suited to real-time product AI
options.B: Have the policy owner require staff checks before alerts are sent
options.C: Have the IS auditor exempt the monitors from the policy
options.D: Have the app tell parents that an AI model raises alerts

questions.key_concept: AI policies written for staff tools may not fit AI built into products; real-time product AI needs controls such as validation, monitoring and fail-safes.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy's rule assumes a person can check output before it is used, which fits staff tools but not a safety alert that must reach parents within seconds. The policy owner needs controls for product AI, such as release validation, monitoring of missed alerts and fail-safe design. Staff checks before each alert, option B, satisfy the rule's wording, but the delay could cost a baby's life.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because human review is the policy's control. But holding a breathing alert for a staff check delays the warning when seconds matter.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rule does not fit. But exempting systems from policy is management's decision; the IS auditor assesses and recommends.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because people should know when AI is involved. But disclosure leaves the alert model without controls suited to how it runs.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IS auditor grant a policy exemption, which management decides, and D offers disclosure where the gap is control design.
Final two: A beats B because a breathing alert cannot wait for a staff check; product AI that acts in real time needs validation, monitoring and fail-safes instead.
Exam cue: when a policy's human-review rule meets AI that acts in real time, look for controls that fit the speed, not a literal review step.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Inventory entries for agents
questions.question: A Swedish municipality's AI inventory tiers each of its 40 agents by its own tools; letter-drafting agents, tiered low, can hand tasks to the payments agent. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT bar agents from payments until internal audit approves
options.B: Have the program owner rate agents by every action they can reach
options.C: Have the program owner record which staff can use each agent
options.D: Have the program owner rate the 40 agents as high risk

questions.key_concept: Agents that can call other agents reach those agents' actions, so risk tiers follow every action an agent can reach.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent that can hand tasks to another can trigger whatever that agent may do, so a letter-drafting agent tiered low can still cause payments. Tiers must follow every action an agent can reach, directly or through other agents. Recording which staff can use each agent, option C, helps access reviews, but the agents' links, not their users, decide what they can do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because payments are high risk. But approving high-impact agent uses is the AI governance committee's decision; internal audit assesses and recommends, and never approves use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because access reviews start with users. But links between agents, not their users, decide what a low-tier agent can trigger.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because caution feels safe. But rating every agent high hides real differences in impact and spreads review effort thin.

tips: Eliminate: A has internal audit approve agents, which the AI governance committee decides for high-impact uses, and D gives every agent one tier regardless of impact.
Final two: B beats C because a low-tier agent that can hand tasks to the payments agent can cause payments; users show who asks, not what the chain can do.
Exam cue: tier an agent by every action it can reach, including through other agents it can call.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-8 (System Component Inventory)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A model tuned for another team
questions.question: A Saudi telecom's legal team fine-tuned the HR department's policy-answering model to draft supplier contracts; the AI inventory lists the HR director as owner of both models. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the AI governance committee own both models jointly
options.B: Have the data team own both models, since it maintains them
options.C: Have the HR director extend validation to drafting contracts
options.D: Have the leader who answers for contracts own the tuned copy

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning creates a new model for a new use; ownership follows the use, so the leader answering for that work owns the tuned model.
questions.pre_read: Separate what changed in the system from what stayed the same.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning made a new model with new behavior for a new use, drafting supplier contracts, which the HR director neither answers for nor is placed to judge. Ownership follows the use, so the leader who answers for contract work should own the tuned model and accept it. Extending validation, option C, is needed, but run by the HR director it leaves contract risk owned by someone who answers only for HR policy.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because committees oversee AI. But a committee sets standards and approves uses; each model needs one named owner who answers for it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the data team knows the models best. But building and maintaining a model does not make anyone accountable for its business decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tuned model does need validating. But under the HR director, contract-drafting risk stays owned by someone who answers only for HR policy.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the builders owners, and A gives ownership to a committee; each model needs one named business owner.
Final two: D beats C because the tuned model serves contract drafting, so its owner is the leader who answers for that work, not the owner of the model it came from.
Exam cue: when a model is copied, tuned or reused for a new purpose, look for an owner tied to the new use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.1 (Decide whether the system meets its purpose and should proceed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (fine-tuning a model for a new use creates a new model; ownership follows the use, so the leader answering for that work owns the tuned model). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Clerks approving AI-drafted summaries
questions.question: A Croatian county court's clerks check every name, date and amount in each AI-drafted case summary against the file; judges read only the summary before short hearings. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the IS auditor review a sample of case summaries monthly
options.B: Have judges stop using summaries until the model is retrained
options.C: Have the owner make clerks look for facts summaries omit
options.D: Have the clerks sign and date each summary they approve

questions.key_concept: Generated summaries can be accurate in every stated detail yet omit material facts, so reviewers must check the source for omissions too.
questions.pre_read: Note who does what in the stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative summaries can leave out facts that matter while every stated name, date and amount is right. Judges here read only the summary, and checking what it says cannot find what it omits, so clerks must also read the file for facts that should appear. Signatures, option D, add accountability for each approval, but a signed check of stated details still misses omissions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit sampling finds errors. But routine monthly checks would make the IS auditor part of a control they must later assess.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a model fix sounds thorough. But retraining does not change what clerks check, and any model's summaries can still omit facts.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because signatures create evidence and accountability. But a signed check of stated details still cannot find facts the summary left out.

tips: Eliminate: A puts the IS auditor inside the control, and B treats a review gap as a model defect that retraining would fix.
Final two: C beats D because a generated summary can be right in every detail it states yet omit what matters; only reading the file finds omissions, and a signature does not.
Exam cue: checking AI output against the source catches errors in what it says; finding what it left out needs a check from the source to the output.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (generated summaries can read well yet omit or invent facts, so a reviewer's role must require checking them against the source, not reading for clarity). questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. AI-filled fields in a case system
questions.question: A Portuguese social-security office's AI policy requires officers to check AI output; a new case-system feature fills household fields from scanned letters, shown exactly like typed fields. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner mark AI-filled values on the case screen
options.B: Have the owner check a monthly sample of AI-filled fields
options.C: Have the vendor certify the feature's accuracy before further use
options.D: Have officers retype each household field from the letters

questions.key_concept: A rule to check AI output works only if staff can tell which output is AI's, so AI-filled values must be marked on screen.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: Officers can only follow the checking rule if they can see which values the AI wrote, and the screen shows them like a colleague's entries. Marking AI-filled fields makes the policy duty workable at the point of use. Monthly sampling, option B, would measure the error rate, but officers would still decide cases on unmarked AI values every day.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sampling measures how often the feature errs. But it finds errors after decisions are made, while officers still cannot tell which values to check.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendor evidence feels reassuring. But a certificate is an input, not assurance, and officers still could not see which values the AI wrote.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retyping removes AI errors. But it discards the feature instead of making the checking duty workable, and retyping adds its own errors.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a vendor certificate, which is an input, not assurance, and D drops the feature rather than making the policy's check workable.
Final two: A beats B because officers can apply a checking duty only to output they can recognize; sampling measures errors after unmarked values have shaped decisions.
Exam cue: a rule to check AI output works only if people can tell which output is AI's.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.2 (AI risk management training for personnel and partners); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Replacing payables clerks with an agent
questions.question: A Slovak shared-service center's AI agent now posts the invoices 12 clerks once handled; two staff check its postings, and their corrections go straight into its monthly retraining. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent's supplier may not answer for wrong payments
options.B: A mistaken fix may be repeated across later invoices
options.C: The clerks' know-how may be lost if the agent fails
options.D: Each invoice it posts may retrain the agent at once

questions.key_concept: When an AI is retrained on a few people's corrections, one wrong correction becomes training data and can repeat across later outputs.
questions.pre_read: Note each party in the stem before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Each month the agent is retrained on the two staff's corrections with no further check, so one mistaken correction, or one person's habit, becomes training data and is repeated on every similar invoice instead of staying a single slip. Lost know-how, option C, matters only if the agent fails, and the two staff who check postings still hold the skill, while their corrections shape every posting each month.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because supplier liability is a familiar third-party risk. But accountability for payments stays with the center, whatever any contract says, so recovering losses is secondary.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because skills fade once a task is automated. But the two staff who check postings keep the skill, while their corrections retrain the agent every month.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI seems to learn from use. But posting invoices does not retrain the agent; only the monthly retraining on the staff's corrections does.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes each posting retrains the agent, though only the monthly retrain does, and A treats supplier liability as the issue, though accountability for payments stays with the center.

Final two: B beats C because retraining on two people's corrections turns one mistaken fix into an error repeated monthly; lost know-how matters only if the agent fails, and the two checkers still hold it.
Exam cue: when an AI learns from a few people's corrections, their mistakes become its behavior; ask who checks the corrections before retraining.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)
