questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Likelihood ratings for a multi-step agent
questions.question: A Paraguayan property manager rates its tenant-onboarding agent's error likelihood low, citing 95% accuracy on single steps tested alone with correct inputs; each onboarding takes about ten steps. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The 95% figure needs retesting by a team independent of builders
options.B: The rating holds, since about 95% of onboardings will be error-free
options.C: The rating holds once the agent learns from each onboarding error
options.D: The rating understates how often whole onboardings go wrong

questions.key_concept: Errors compound across an agent's steps: ten independent steps at 95% each leave about 60% of tasks fully right, so judge likelihood per task.
questions.pre_read: Restate the rating's claim in your own words before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Errors compound across an agent's steps: if each of ten steps were right 95% of the time and errors were independent, only about 60% of onboardings would come out fully right. Steps tested alone with correct inputs also never show one step's error feeding the next. The rating uses the wrong unit, a step instead of a task. An independent retest, option A, would only confirm the step figure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because independence improves evidence. But an independent retest would confirm the per-step figure, which still compounds to frequent errors across ten steps.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because 95% sounds like the task's success rate. But it is per step; across ten steps the chance of an error-free onboarding falls to about 60%.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI is assumed to learn as it works. But completing onboardings does not retrain the agent, and learning would not fix the rating's unit error.

tips: Eliminate: B reads a per-step rate as a per-onboarding rate, and C assumes the agent improves by working, which does not retrain it.
Final two: D beats A because step accuracy compounds across ten steps, to about 60% error-free if errors are independent; independent testing would confirm the step rate, not undo the compounding.
Exam cue: for multi-step agents, judge likelihood per completed task; step accuracy compounds across the chain.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (an agent's step accuracy compounds across a task: ten steps at 95% leave about 60% of tasks error-free, so likelihood is judged per task). questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Rating fraud risk for photo refunds
questions.question: A Turkish grocery app's model approves refunds from photos of damaged items; its 2022 risk rating called fake photos unlikely, since few were found. Which question should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Whether a higher accuracy score would rule out fake photos
options.B: Whether refund fraud found since 2022 is still rare
options.C: Whether image generators now make convincing forgeries easy
options.D: Whether stored photos are encrypted once refunds are approved

questions.key_concept: Generative tools make convincing fake images cheap, so likelihood ratings built on past incident counts need reassessing.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The 2022 rating rests on history: few fakes had been found. Image generators now let anyone produce a convincing photo of a damaged item in seconds, so the past rate says little about likelihood today. Rechecking fraud found since 2022, option B, seems careful, but fakes that fool the model are paid and never found.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accurate models seem harder to fool. But accuracy on ordinary photos says nothing about convincing forgeries made to pass as genuine.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fresh loss data is sound evidence. But convincing fakes pass as genuine, so a low count of fakes found may show what the model misses, not what happens.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because stored photos need protection. But encryption answers a security question, not whether fake photos fool the model into paying out.

tips: Eliminate: A treats accuracy on ordinary photos as protection against forgeries, and D treats an AI fraud risk as a storage-security question.
Final two: C beats B because cheap image generators changed the threat; fakes that fool the model are never counted, so recent fraud counts cannot show likelihood.
Exam cue: when generative AI makes an attack cheap, likelihood ratings based on past incident counts need reassessing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.8 (Information Integrity)

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Alert levels for a drift indicator
questions.question: A Malaysian travel insurer's tolerance caps claims its model wrongly delays at 4%, found only through appeals months later; its drift alert uses its monitoring tool's default. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have internal audit set the alert level for the owner
options.B: Have the owner base alert levels on drift's link to delays
options.C: Have the owner replace the drift score with model confidence
options.D: Have the owner set the drift alert at the 4% delay tolerance

questions.key_concept: A drift score measures input change, not harm; when harm surfaces late, set drift alert levels from how drift predicts it against the tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Restate the insurer's monitoring setup before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Wrongful delays come to light only through appeals months later, so the owner needs an early warning. Input drift can give one, but only at a level set from how drift relates to delays against the 4% tolerance; the tool's default is linked to nothing. Setting the drift alert at 4%, option D, copies a limit on wrongful delays onto a score that measures input change.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because internal audit understands indicators. But setting alert levels is management's job; the IS auditor assesses whether they fit the tolerance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because confidence is easy to track. But a model can stay confident while its errors rise, so confidence is a poor risk indicator.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because alert levels should come from the tolerance. But 4% limits wrongful delays, while a drift score measures input change; the same number means something else.

tips: Eliminate: C uses the model's own confidence, which can stay high as errors rise, and A has internal audit set a management control.
Final two: B beats D because a drift score measures input change, not delays; its alert level must come from how drift tracks delays, not from the 4% figure itself.
Exam cue: when AI outcomes arrive late, a leading indicator such as drift needs alert levels calibrated to the tolerance it protects.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A tolerance for shrimp-lot testing
questions.question: A Taiwanese food-safety agency's model picks shrimp lots to test; the only tolerance caps clean lots held at 2%, so the owner raised the cutoff to meet it. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Missed contaminated lots can rise with nothing to flag it
options.B: A higher cutoff may hold more clean lots than before
options.C: The model's AUC may fall when the cutoff is raised
options.D: The cutoff change may not have gone through change control

questions.key_concept: A cutoff trades one error for the other; a tolerance on only one kind lets the other grow unchecked as owners tune to meet it.
questions.pre_read: Restate what the owner changed and why before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Raising a cutoff trades one error for the other: fewer clean lots are held, but more contaminated lots pass. With a tolerance only on wrongful holds, each move to meet it can push misses up with nothing to flag them. Change control for the cutoff, option D, is sound, but an approved change that meets the only tolerance would still let missed contaminated lots grow unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because cutoffs and holds are linked. But raising the cutoff flags fewer lots, so clean lots held fall; misses are what rise.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cutoffs and performance seem linked. But AUC summarizes ranking across all cutoffs, so moving the cutoff leaves it unchanged; it shifts which errors happen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a cutoff change alters outcomes and needs approval. But approval tests against the only tolerance set, which says nothing about contaminated lots missed.

tips: Eliminate: B gets the cutoff's direction backward, and C expects AUC to change with the cutoff, though AUC covers every cutoff.
Final two: A beats D because a cutoff trades wrongful holds for missed contaminated lots; even an approved change that meets the only tolerance leaves misses unchecked.
Exam cue: when a tolerance caps only one kind of error, ask what happens to the other kind as owners tune to meet it.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A vendor model's training data
questions.question: A Kazakh fintech's loan approvals rely on a vendor's statement-reading model that passed the fintech's tests; due diligence found it learned from statements a broker sold without consent. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The model may misread some applicants' bank statements
options.B: The fintech may need consent from every person in the data
options.C: A regulator may order the model deleted, halting all lending
options.D: Accountability for wrongful refusals may pass to the vendor

questions.key_concept: A vendor's rights to its training data are a continuity risk for the buyer: a model trained on unlawfully collected data can be ordered destroyed.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by how likely each is and how much harm it would do.
questions.correct_explanation: Regulators have ordered companies to delete models trained on data collected without consent, not only the data itself. If that happens here, the fintech's loan approvals stop with the model, whatever the contract says. Misread statements, option A, remain possible, but the model passed the fintech's tests, while the due-diligence finding could remove the model entirely.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because any reading model can err. But this one passed the fintech's accuracy tests; the due-diligence finding threatens the model's very existence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consent was missing. But the vendor bought the statements; the fintech's exposure is losing a model it relies on, not consenting each person.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the model. But the fintech still answers for its loan decisions; buying a model never moves that accountability.

tips: Eliminate: D moves accountability for decisions to the vendor, and B gives the fintech the vendor's consent duty for data it never collected.
Final two: C beats A because a model trained on unlawfully obtained data can be ordered destroyed, stopping loan approvals outright; the model already passed accuracy tests.
Exam cue: a vendor's rights to its training data are a continuity risk for the buyer, since the model itself may have to go.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A vendor that reads sick notes
questions.question: A Danish payroll bureau's vendor model reads employees' scanned sick notes; the vendor's terms mention 'quality review' of low-confidence readings, and due diligence covered only its data center. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Low-confidence readings may fall outside the bureau's accountability
options.B: The model may misread handwriting on some notes
options.C: The model may retrain on every sick note it reads
options.D: Health details may reach readers no one has assessed

questions.key_concept: AI services often pass items the model is unsure of to human workers; due diligence must reach those people when items hold sensitive data.
questions.pre_read: Restate the stem's facts in your own words before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: In AI services, quality review of low-confidence readings often means people read the items, and here those items are employees' sick notes, which hold health data. Due diligence looked only at the data center, so the bureau has not assessed who these reviewers are, where they work or what they keep. Misread handwriting, option B, is a real accuracy risk, but it does not expose health details.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people, not the model, may read uncertain notes. But the bureau answers for every note processed for it, whoever or whatever reads it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because handwriting does trip up reading models. But misreads can be caught and fixed; health details shown to unassessed people cannot be recalled.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI is assumed to learn from every input. But reading a note does not retrain the model, and the terms describe quality review, not training.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes reading a note retrains the model, and A limits the bureau's accountability to part of the processing.
Final two: D beats B because quality review of low-confidence readings often means people read the notes, and due diligence never reached them; exposed health data cannot be recalled.
Exam cue: when an AI service mentions review of uncertain items, ask who the reviewers are and whether due diligence reached them.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Errors found in shared data
questions.question: A Bulgarian furniture retailer logged dispatch dates as delivery dates for eight months; the data owner has validated the corrected order dataset several teams' models trained on. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT reconcile the corrected dates with signed delivery notes
options.B: Have each model owner retest their model on the corrected dates
options.C: Have the data owner reapprove the corrected order dataset for model training
options.D: Have IT log every correction made to the shared order dataset

questions.key_concept: Correcting source data does not change models already trained on it; each model should be retested on the corrected data before it is relied on.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Any model that used these dates learned that deliveries arrive sooner than they do, and correcting the dataset does not change what it learned; it keeps predicting from the errors until retrained. Retesting each model on the corrected dates shows whether and how far its predictions are off, so its owner can decide on retraining. Reconciling the dates with delivery notes, option A, rechecks a fix the data owner already validated, not the models.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reperformance confirms a fix. But the data owner has already validated it, and correct data now does not change what models learned from eight months of wrong dates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because training use needs the data owner's approval. But the dataset's permitted use has not changed; the gap is the models trained on the wrong dates.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because changes to data should be recorded. But a log records the data fix; it does not show how far each trained model's predictions are now off.

tips: Eliminate: D records the data fix without testing the models that learned from the errors, and C reapproves a use that has not changed.
Final two: B beats A because the data fix is already validated, yet models trained on the wrong dates keep what they learned; only retesting them shows the damage.
Exam cue: when source data is corrected, ask which trained models learned from the errors; fixing data does not fix a trained model.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A quality assistant's document store
questions.question: A Swiss watchmaker's assistant searches a drive that must keep every procedure version; a register, updated each release and tested last month, marks each current or replaced. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The assistant may rank replaced steps above current ones
options.B: The register may mark some replaced versions as current
options.C: Keeping every version may breach data minimization rules
options.D: The assistant may need retraining each time a procedure changes

questions.key_concept: Similarity search ignores status labels unless it filters on them, so an accurate version register alone keeps no replaced step out of answers.
questions.pre_read: Read each option as a risk and ask what would cause it.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant finds passages by how closely they match a question, ignoring status marks unless set to filter on them. So an old step that matches well can outrank the current one even though the register labels it replaced. A wrongly labeled version, option B, is less likely in a register updated each release and recently tested, and even a perfect register keeps nothing out of answers unless the search uses it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because document control rests on an accurate register. But this one is updated each release and tested last month, and the search ignores its labels unless filtered.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because keeping data longer than needed is a privacy fault. But assembly procedures are not personal data, and the watchmaker must keep every version.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI seems to need retraining to learn new facts. But a retrieval assistant reads the drive at answer time, so a changed procedure needs no retraining.

tips: Eliminate: D retrains an assistant that reads the drive at answer time, and C applies data minimization to procedures that hold no personal data.
Final two: A beats B because similarity search ignores status labels unless it filters on them; a register updated each release, however accurate, keeps no replaced step out of answers.
Exam cue: for retrieval assistants, ask whether the search itself uses a document's status; a well-kept register controls nothing until the search does.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.2 (Internal risk controls for components identified)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (similarity retrieval ignores currency unless filtered, so an accurate version register reaches answers only if the search uses it). Final round: the stem now says the drive must retain every version, so plain document control (remove obsolete versions) no longer settles it and only the retrieval fact beats recency weighting. Re-audit: re-angled because the key and runner-up (an owner keeps replaced versions out of the index, beating a tool-side preference for newer files) repeated aaia_d2_051; it now asks whether an accurate version register reaches similarity search. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Street photos as training data
questions.question: An Australian city council blurs faces and car plates in 2 million street-level photos with a detection model, then trains a tree-health model on them. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the data team delete the photos once the model is trained
options.B: Have IT encrypt the blurred photo store before training
options.C: Have the privacy officer record the blurred photos as anonymous
options.D: Have the owner measure how often the blurring model misses

questions.key_concept: Automated blurring or redaction is itself a model with misses; measure its miss rate before treating the output as anonymous.
questions.pre_read: Follow the data from collection to output before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The blurring is done by a detection model, and detection models miss some faces and plates, at angles, in shadow or far away. Across 2 million photos even a small miss rate leaves many people identifiable in the training set, so the miss rate must be measured on samples first. Recording the photos as anonymous, option C, would rest on the untested assumption that blurring caught everything.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because keeping less data is privacy by design. But deleting after training is too late to keep missed faces out of training, and may remove records needed later.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because stored photos need protection. But encryption limits who opens the store, not whether the photos still show identifiable people.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the privacy officer decides how data is classed. But calling the set anonymous rests on blurring nobody has measured, and detection models miss some faces.

tips: Eliminate: B answers an identifiability question with encryption, and A deletes photos only after training, too late to keep missed faces out.
Final two: D beats C because a detection model blurs only what it detects; until its misses are measured, nobody can call the photos anonymous.
Exam cue: when one AI model cleans data for another, ask for the cleaning model's error rate before trusting the cleaned set.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-8 (Privacy Impact Assessments); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (automated blurring or redaction is itself a model with misses, so its miss rate is measured before its output is treated as anonymous). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Publishing estimates from loyalty data
questions.question: A Rwandan fuel retailer retrains its town-demand model weekly on loyalty-card data with differential privacy, privacy-loss setting 1 per run, and publishes the estimates for planners. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Published estimates may need encrypting to protect customers
options.B: A setting as low as 1 may protect customers too weakly
options.C: Repeated releases may add up to weak protection
options.D: Weekly estimates for small towns may be too noisy to use

questions.key_concept: Differential privacy's loss adds up across repeated releases about the same people, so a strict per-release setting can still add up to weak protection.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each number in the stem controls before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Differential privacy's loss adds up across releases about the same people: each weekly run at a setting of 1 spends more of a regular customer's privacy, so after a year the worst-case total can reach about 52 unless the design caps an overall budget. Noisy small-town figures, option D, are a real usefulness cost, but noise protects people; the accumulating loss is what weakens protection.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because published data needs protection. But these estimates are meant to be read; encryption would hide them from planners without changing what they reveal.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because privacy settings can be weak. But a lower privacy-loss setting means more noise and stronger protection; 1 is strict for a single release.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because noise can swamp small-town figures. But that is a usefulness cost; protection weakens through repeated releases, not through noise.

tips: Eliminate: A encrypts estimates meant for publication, and B reads a low privacy-loss setting as weak, when lower means stronger protection.
Final two: C beats D because each weekly run spends more of the same customers' privacy; noisy small-town figures cost usefulness, not protection.
Exam cue: for differential privacy, ask about the total privacy loss across all releases, not just the setting for one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.6 (Privacy-Enhanced); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (differential privacy's loss adds up across repeated releases about the same people, so a strict per-release setting can still add up to weak protection). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Examples inside a prompt template
questions.question: A Montenegrin music school's reply-assistant prompt template, sent with every request, holds three real student complaint emails as style examples; student emails are deleted after two years. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner add the template to the retention schedule
options.B: Have the owner swap in invented examples for the current ones
options.C: Have IT encrypt the template wherever it is stored
options.D: Have the owner retrain the model to drop the examples

questions.key_concept: Prompt examples that only show a format need not be real: invented ones carry no personal data, so data minimization favors them.
questions.pre_read: Restate how the assistant is set up before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The examples only show the model a style to copy, so invented complaints work as well as real ones, and data minimization means using no more personal data than the purpose needs. Swapping them removes the students' data from every request. Adding the template to the retention schedule, option A, keeps real emails going out with each request until they expire, then needs newer real ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the template holds personal data under the two-year rule. But real emails still go out with every request until replaced by newer ones; invented examples need none.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because templates holding personal data need protection. But encryption still sends real emails with every request; invented examples remove them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removing data from a model sounds like retraining. But the examples sit in the prompt, not the model's training, so retraining changes nothing.

tips: Eliminate: D retrains a model to fix data that sits in the prompt, and C encrypts emails that invented examples would remove.
Final two: B beats A because the examples only show a style, so data minimization favors invented ones; a retention rule only rotates real emails through every request.
Exam cue: when personal data sits in a prompt only to show a format, ask whether invented data would serve.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (examples in a prompt template only show a format, so invented examples serve as well as real personal data and remove its retention and exposure duties). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Tuning a coding assistant
questions.question: A Romanian software firm will fine-tune a coding assistant it sells on its repository history; earlier commits hold passwords and keys removed from current code but never changed. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The assistant may suggest those credentials to its users
options.B: Suggestions may follow coding styles the firm has since dropped
options.C: Suggestions may include code with known security flaws
options.D: Training may alter the passwords and keys in earlier commits

questions.key_concept: Secrets removed from current code but never changed stay live in history a model trains on, and models can memorize rare strings such as keys.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the stem states from what it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: Training on full history feeds the model every commit, including passwords and keys removed from current code but never changed, so they still work. Models can memorize rare strings like these and reproduce them when a prompt resembles their context, so customers' developers who never had repository access could be shown them. Flawed suggestions, option C, are a real risk, but the stem's stated fact is live secrets in the history.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because history holds practices the firm has dropped. But dated style is a quality nuisance; live credentials shown to outsiders are a security breach.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because coding assistants can suggest flawed code. But the stem points to unchanged secrets in commit history, which the model can memorize and hand out.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training touches the repository. But fine-tuning reads the history; it does not change commits or what they contain.

tips: Eliminate: D thinks training alters the repository, and B weighs dated coding style, a nuisance beside live credentials.
Final two: A beats C because keys removed but never changed still work, and a model trained on the history can memorize and repeat such rare strings.
Exam cue: secrets removed from code but never changed stay live in history; ask whether a model will train on that history.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.9 (Information Security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (secrets removed from current code but never changed stay live in the history a model may train on, and models can memorize rare strings such as keys). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Safety criteria for a health chatbot
questions.question: A Tunisian health hotline's chatbot, tuned until red-team tests found zero unsafe medical answers, now refuses 40% of routine clinic-hours questions. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The chatbot meets its safety goal, as tests found no unsafe answers
options.B: The vendor should retune the chatbot and approve the result
options.C: Refusals are a usability issue outside the safety review
options.D: Needless refusals are themselves a risk to callers

questions.key_concept: Refusing safe, needed answers is a harm too; tuning a model hard toward one trustworthy-AI characteristic can cost the others.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Tuning only against unsafe answers can teach a model to refuse anything health-related, and a red-team score counts that as success. But a caller refused clinic hours may not get care, so the refusals are a harm that zero unsafe answers never measures. Treating the test result as meeting the safety goal, option A, counts only one side of the harm the tuning created.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because zero unsafe answers is strong test evidence. But it measures only one side; refusing routine questions harms callers the tests never counted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor can retune the model. But approving the result is the owner's decision, and the vendor would be approving its own work.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because refusals look like a convenience problem. But a caller refused clinic hours may not get care; harm from refusing belongs in the safety review.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the vendor approve its own fix, and C files refusals under usability, though refusing needed answers can harm callers.
Final two: D beats A because zero unsafe answers measures only one side of safety; refusing routine questions harms callers the tests never counted.
Exam cue: when an AI is tuned to one trustworthy-AI characteristic, ask what the tuning costs the others, including harm from refusing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3 (AI Risks and Trustworthiness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (refusing safe, needed answers is a harm too, so tuning hard toward one trustworthy-AI characteristic can cost the others). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Explaining refusals with similar cases
questions.question: A Slovenian town's kindergarten-admission model explains each refusal by showing three similar accepted families' anonymized profiles: street, household size and parents' jobs. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Similar-case explanations may expose the model's exact formula
options.B: Refused families may use the profiles to game reapplications
options.C: Neighbors could recognize the families in the profiles shown
options.D: Showing families as examples may make decisions less accurate

questions.key_concept: Explanations that show similar real cases trade explainability against privacy, since the cases shown can identify other people.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Example-based explanations show real people. In one town, a street, household size and parents' jobs are often enough for neighbors to recognize a family, so each refusal letter can expose three other households' details. Explainability here trades against privacy. Gaming reapplications, option B, is a known risk of explanations, but these fields are hard to change honestly, while the exposure harms families outside the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because explanations reveal something about a model. But example-based explanations show past cases, not the model's internal formula.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because explanations can teach people to game a model. But street, household size and parents' jobs are hard to change honestly; exposing other families is the graver harm.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because extra features can seem costly. But showing examples leaves the model's decisions unchanged; it affects what is disclosed, not accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: A thinks showing similar cases discloses the model's formula, and D links showing examples to accuracy, which they do not change.
Final two: C beats B because the shown fields identify real neighbors in a small town; gaming needs features families can change, and these are hard to change honestly.
Exam cue: explanations that show similar real cases trade explainability against privacy; check what the examples reveal about others.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.5 (Explainable and Interpretable); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.6 (Privacy-Enhanced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (explanations that show similar real cases trade explainability against privacy, since the cases shown can identify other people). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 11, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. AI-law duties that start later
questions.question: A Maltese ed-tech firm is training an exam-grading model to sell once an AI law's high-risk duties start next year; compliance work is scheduled to begin at launch. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The firm may have to stop training until the duties apply
options.B: Training records the later duties need may not be kept
options.C: Duties not yet in force cannot be used as audit criteria
options.D: Counsel may not track changes to the duties' start dates

questions.key_concept: High-risk AI duties often need records of how a model was built; map later duties now if their evidence is created during development.
questions.pre_read: Restate the firm's plan and timeline before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: High-risk duties typically require documentation of how the model was built: training data sources, data governance and design choices. That record has to be made while the model is trained now; it cannot be rebuilt reliably once sales start. Compliance work that starts at launch misses this. Tracking start dates, option D, is useful, but knowing the date precisely does not recover records that were never kept.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it avoids building ahead of the rules. But nothing bars training now; the gap is failing to keep the records the later duties need.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because future duties are not yet binding. But the IS auditor may select any suitable criteria, and a dated, known duty can be one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because start dates do shift. But knowing the exact date does not recover development records that were never kept while the model was trained.

tips: Eliminate: C limits audit criteria to duties in force, and A halts training that no rule forbids.
Final two: B beats D because high-risk duties need records of how the model was built, which must be kept during training; the start date matters less than the evidence.
Exam cue: when AI duties phase in, map them now if the evidence they need is created now, during development.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A human step in automated denials
questions.question: A Lithuanian rent-to-own retailer says data-protection rules on solely automated decisions do not reach its contract-refusal model, since a clerk approves each refusal; none has ever been changed. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The rules may bar rent-to-own retailers from using any AI model
options.B: The model's supplier, not the retailer, may answer for refusals
options.C: Clerks may not record a reason when they make no change
options.D: Sign-offs that never change outcomes may not count as human review

questions.key_concept: Rules on solely automated decisions look at substance; a human approval that never changes outcomes may not take a decision outside them.
questions.pre_read: Restate the stem's claim in your own words before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules on solely automated decisions look at substance: a person must have the authority, competence and information to weigh and change each outcome. Sign-offs that have never changed an outcome may count as no human review at all, so the retailer may owe applicants rights it believes do not apply. Recording reasons, option C, improves evidence, but reasons on rubber-stamped approvals do not make the review meaningful.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI laws can restrict uses. But such rules set conditions and rights for automated decisions; they do not ban rent-to-own retailers from using models.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models often come from suppliers. But the retailer makes the refusals and answers for them, whoever built the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recorded reasons are good evidence. But reasons written for approvals that never change anything do not make the human role meaningful.

tips: Eliminate: A reads rules on automated decisions as a ban on models, and B moves accountability for refusals to a supplier.
Final two: D beats C because a review that never changes outcomes may not count as human involvement at all; recorded reasons only document a rubber stamp.
Exam cue: when an organization relies on a human step to avoid automated-decision rules, test whether that person really weighs and changes outcomes.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Mapping one framework to another
questions.question: A Malaysian chip-packaging firm claims its AI governance conforms to ISO/IEC 42001:2023, citing a consultant's crosswalk from its NIST AI RMF practices to the standard's clauses. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: The consultant who drew the crosswalk may not be independent
options.B: ISO/IEC 42001 conformance would prove each model is fair
options.C: A crosswalk shows overlap, not that each clause is met
options.D: NIST AI RMF practices meet ISO/IEC 42001 clauses by design

questions.key_concept: A crosswalk between frameworks shows where they overlap, not that either one's requirements are met; conformance needs testing against each requirement.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of document each source is before weighing the claim.
questions.correct_explanation: A crosswalk maps where two frameworks address similar topics; it does not test whether the firm meets each requirement of the standard. ISO/IEC 42001 has its own required elements, such as a defined scope, AI objectives, internal audit and management review, which NIST AI RMF practices may only partly cover. The consultant's independence, option A, matters for any assessment, but even an independent crosswalk shows overlap, not conformance.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because independence affects how far work can be relied on. But an independent crosswalk would still show only where frameworks overlap, not conformance.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because conformance sounds like proof. But a management-system standard covers how AI governance runs, not whether any model is fair.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the frameworks cover similar ground. But NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, and following it does not meet another standard's requirements by design.

tips: Eliminate: D treats a voluntary framework as automatically meeting another standard, and B reads management-system conformance as proof that a model is fair.
Final two: C beats A because a crosswalk, however independent, maps overlapping topics; only testing each requirement shows conformance.
Exam cue: a mapping between frameworks shows where they overlap; it is not evidence that either one's requirements are met.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Threat models built on MITRE ATLAS
questions.question: A Peruvian bank's threat model for its fraud models covers every MITRE ATLAS technique, so its owner records the threat model as complete. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: New techniques outside the catalog may go unassessed
options.B: The bank may need certification against the ATLAS standard
options.C: Listed techniques may be rated without the bank's own likelihood
options.D: ATLAS coverage may count as compliance with the NIST AI RMF

questions.key_concept: MITRE ATLAS is a growing knowledge base of observed attacks on AI, with mitigations; it guides threat modeling and testing but is never complete.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: MITRE ATLAS is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI, built from real attacks and research, and it grows as new ones appear. Recording the threat model as complete on that basis leaves the bank blind to attacks that are new or not yet cataloged. Rating listed techniques by the bank's own likelihood, option C, sharpens the model but cannot reach attacks the catalog does not yet hold.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because ATLAS is widely cited. But it is a voluntary knowledge base, not a standard anyone certifies against.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because likelihood should reflect the bank's own setting. But better ratings of listed techniques still leave out every attack the catalog does not yet hold.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both concern AI risk. But ATLAS is an attack knowledge base and the NIST AI RMF a risk framework; using one does not show compliance with the other.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a voluntary knowledge base as a certifiable standard, and D treats ATLAS coverage as compliance with a different framework.
Final two: A beats C because ATLAS records known attacks and grows as new ones appear; rating listed techniques better cannot cover attacks the catalog does not yet hold.
Exam cue: an attack catalog is a starting point for threat modeling, not a complete list; ask what covers attacks it does not yet hold.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Escalating answers from a generative assistant
questions.question: A Mauritian pharmaceutical importer's generative assistant writes a confidence percentage into each answer on whether permit conditions are met; staff propose checking only answers below 80%. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner test its percentages against checked results
options.B: Have the owner approve 80% as the check level
options.C: Ask the provider how the assistant computes its percentages
options.D: Have the owner raise the check level to 95%

questions.key_concept: A generative model's stated confidence is text it generates; test it against checked results before it decides which answers get checked.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each part of the process relies on before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative assistant that writes its own confidence figure produces plausible text, not a measured chance of being right, so nobody knows whether 80% means anything. Before any check level is set, the percentages must be compared with how often answers prove right on checked permits. Owner approval of 80%, option B, settles who decides, but approves a level on a number nobody has tested.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because check levels need an accountable owner. But approving a level does not show the percentages measure anything; that needs testing first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because providers document their products. But a percentage the assistant writes into its answer is generated text; only checked results show what it means.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a higher level checks more answers. But it still trusts untested percentages; confident wrong answers above 95% would pass unseen.

tips: Eliminate: D still trusts untested percentages, and C asks the provider about figures only checked results can explain.
Final two: A beats B because a generative model's percentage is text it writes; only testing it against checked answers shows whether any level means something.
Exam cue: a percentage a generative model writes about its own answer is generated text; test it against checked results before it decides which answers skip review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (a generative model's stated confidence is text it generates, so it is tested against checked results before it decides which answers get checked). Review round 1: key and runner-up rebuilt after a frame clash with aaia_d3_038 (confidence cutoff for checking). Review round 2: stem says the assistant writes the percentage, so the explanation's 'generated text' fact is given. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A spreadsheet model outside the inventory
questions.question: A Belgian railway ranks level crossings for upgrades with a regression fitted to past incidents in a spreadsheet; IT omits it from the AI inventory as plain statistics. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: It may invent crossings that appear in no railway record
options.B: Its learned weights may go unvalidated and drift unseen
options.C: Its spreadsheet formulas may be changed without review or a log
options.D: It may keep adjusting itself after each new incident

questions.key_concept: A regression fitted to past data learns its weights from it, so it needs validation and drift monitoring, whatever it is called.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option assumes about the system before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Whatever it is called, a regression fitted to past incidents learns its weights from data, so it brings machine learning risks: the data may not reflect today's crossings, its rankings may never have been validated, and nothing may watch for drift. Off the inventory, it escapes that review. Uncontrolled spreadsheet changes, option C, are a real end-user computing gap, but locking the file would not test whether its learned rankings are sound.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because some AI invents content. But a regression is predictive: it scores the crossings it is given rather than generating new records.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because end-user spreadsheets often lack change control. But a locked file still holds weights nobody has validated or monitored.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some models update themselves. But nothing in the stem says new incidents feed it; however it is refitted, the gap is weights that escape validation and monitoring.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a predictive regression a generative model's failure, and D assumes it keeps updating itself, which the stem never says.
Final two: B beats C because the weights were learned from data, which brings validation and drift into scope; change control on the file cannot show the rankings are sound.
Exam cue: if a system's logic was fitted to past data, give it model-risk review, validation and drift monitoring, whatever its label or tool.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST AI 100-1 Appendix B (How AI Risks Differ from Traditional Software Risks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (a regression fitted to past data learns its weights from that data, so it is machine learning and needs validation and drift monitoring whatever it is called). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Correcting an assistant in chat
questions.question: A Portuguese shoe manufacturer's HR staff correct its hosted assistant's wrong answers about leave rules in chat, believing it learns; the provider's terms bar training on chats. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The corrected answers may spread to the provider's other clients
options.B: Each correction may teach the assistant new wrong answers
options.C: Later questions may get the same wrong answers again
options.D: Corrections typed in chat may pass staff details to the provider

questions.key_concept: A hosted model learns only when its provider trains it; chat corrections do not retrain it, so other conversations get the same answers.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each party believes about the system, and test it against the facts given.
questions.correct_explanation: A hosted model learns only when its provider trains it, and these terms rule out training on chats. Each correction therefore changes nothing beyond that conversation, so the next employee who asks gets the same wrong leave answer while HR believes the problem is fixed. Corrections carrying staff details, option D, are a privacy question, but they do not explain or end the wrong answers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because provider training can spread data. But the terms bar training on chats, so corrections do not reach other clients' answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people assume chat corrections retrain AI. But a hosted model is not trained by chatting, so corrections teach it nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because chats do send content to the provider. But that is a separate privacy question; the stated fault is that wrong answers keep coming.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes chatting retrains the model, and A falls to the stated terms that bar training on chats.
Final two: C beats D because a model changes only when trained, so the wrong answers persist; the privacy point does not touch the stated problem.
Exam cue: a correction typed in chat does not fix a hosted model for other users; wrong answers are fixed at their source, such as documents, prompt or training.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a hosted model learns only when its provider trains it, so corrections typed in chat leave its later answers unchanged). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A generative model sorting claims
questions.question: A Thai university's finance office sorts expense claims into 'approve' or 'query' with a generative model whose prompt shows six example claims, five labeled 'approve'. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The model may retrain itself on each claim it sorts
options.B: A provider update may change how it sorts the same claims
options.C: Six examples may not cover every kind of expense
options.D: The examples' mix may tilt its answers toward one outcome

questions.key_concept: Generative models learn from examples placed in their prompt and tend to copy their mix, so lopsided examples tilt outputs toward the common label.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative models pick up patterns from the examples in their prompt, and with five of six marked 'approve', they tend to favor that label, so claims that deserve a query can be waved through. Thin coverage of claim types, option C, is a fair worry for any example set, but even a full range of types would still carry the same lopsided label mix.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI seems to learn from use. But sorting claims does not retrain the model; only its prompt and its training shape its answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hosted models change with provider updates. But nothing in the stem points to an update, while the five-to-one example mix tilts answers now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a few examples rarely cover every case. But the stated fact is the five-to-one label mix, which tilts answers whatever types are shown.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes each use retrains the model, and B rests on an update the stem never mentions.
Final two: D beats C because models copy the label mix of prompt examples; better coverage of claim types would keep the five-to-one tilt.
Exam cue: examples inside a prompt teach a generative model; check what they show, including the balance of their answers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (generative models learn from examples placed in their prompt and tend to copy their label mix, so lopsided examples tilt outputs). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A pool-supplies assistant's design
questions.question: A Croatian pool-supplies retailer requires a chemist to approve every AI-drafted answer on mixing chemicals; for speed, its design streams each answer to customers as it is generated. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner hold each answer until a chemist clears it
options.B: Have a chemist watch answers stream and stop unsafe ones
options.C: Have the vendor confirm its model gives safe advice
options.D: Show customers a notice that each answer is AI-generated

questions.key_concept: Generative output streamed to users as it is produced cannot be reviewed first; where requirements demand prior human approval, the design must hold output.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against every fact in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Streaming shows customers each answer word by word as the model generates it, so no chemist can approve it first and the requirement fails by design. A wrong mixing instruction can release toxic gas. The owner should hold each answer until it is approved, even if replies slow down. Watching answers stream, option B, lets a chemist stop one, but customers have already read whatever streamed first.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a chemist can stop an unsafe answer mid-stream. But each word reaches the customer's screen as generated, so unsafe text is read before it is stopped.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But a vendor's assurance is a claim, not a control, and the requirement calls for a chemist's approval of each answer.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because telling customers about AI is good practice. But a notice stops no wrong instruction; customers still act on unapproved answers.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on the vendor's own claim about its model, and D adds a notice that stops no wrong answer reaching customers.
Final two: A beats B because streamed text is on the customer's screen as it is generated; a chemist who stops an answer mid-stream acts after part of it is read.
Exam cue: when a requirement puts a person between AI output and the people it affects, check the design gives that person the chance to act.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (requirements set human checks the design must allow; streamed generative answers reach users before anyone can review them). Batch 12 re-audit: runner-up B changed from a daily sample (the key/runner-up pair of aaia_d2_034) to approval after streaming, so the streaming fact, not the word 'every', decides. Batch 12 round 3: runner-up B changed from approval after streaming (which audit sense alone drops as detective) to live oversight that only the streaming fact defeats; key A says 'clears' so the stem's 'approve' is not echoed only in the key. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An agent that merges records
questions.question: A Zambian health insurer plans an AI agent that merges 30,000 pairs of duplicate member records and permanently deletes the extras; it merged 99% of test pairs correctly. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent may invent members found in no source record
options.B: Some 300 wrong merges could mix two members' medical histories
options.C: The 99% may not hold on live records unlike the test pairs
options.D: The agent may retrain itself on each pair it merges

questions.key_concept: Even a highly accurate agent makes many errors at scale; when its actions delete data, the design must let each action be checked or undone.
questions.pre_read: Read each option against every fact in the stem before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Even if the 99% holds, about 300 of 30,000 merges would be wrong, each joining two people's medical histories, and deleting the extras may leave no clean copy to separate them. The design needs a way to review or undo merges before anything is deleted. Whether 99% holds on live records, option C, is worth testing, but a perfect retest would still predict hundreds of hard-to-reverse errors.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because generative AI can invent content. But this agent joins and deletes existing records; the stated risk is wrong joins, not new records.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because test results may not transfer. But even if 99% holds exactly, hundreds of wrong merges remain, and deletion makes them hard to reverse.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because agents seem to learn as they act. But merging records does not retrain the agent's model unless someone retrains it.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes acting retrains the agent, and A gives a record-merging agent a content-inventing failure.
Final two: B beats C because 1% of 30,000 is about 300 wrong merges even if the test rate holds, and deletion makes them hard to undo.
Exam cue: multiply an AI's error rate by its volume; when its actions delete or move data, ask how errors get reversed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.2 (Potential costs of AI errors examined against risk tolerance); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (even a highly accurate agent makes many errors at volume, so a design whose actions delete data needs a way to review or undo them). Review round 2: 'for good' removed from the key (it echoed 'permanently deletes'). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Tier rules in an AI policy
questions.question: A Polish health inspectorate's AI policy tiers each model once, at approval; inspectors now prompt its low-tier report summarizer to draft pharmacy-suspension recommendations. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT put every change to the summarizer through change control
options.B: Have IT block summarizer prompts that mention suspensions
options.C: Have management tier each use and re-tier new uses
options.D: Have the IS auditor re-tier the summarizer for suspension work

questions.key_concept: A general-purpose model can gain new uses through prompts alone, with no system change, so risk tiers must attach to uses, not models.
questions.pre_read: Read each option for who acts and what it would change.
questions.correct_explanation: A general-purpose generative model takes on a new use whenever users ask it for something new, with no build, purchase or release. Tiering once at approval left a summary tool's light review on suspension advice that can close pharmacies. The policy should tier each use and require re-tiering before a new one. Change control, option A, governs changes to the system, but here nothing in the system changed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because system changes need control. But the summarizer itself never changed; inspectors simply asked it for something new, which no change ticket records.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it stops the riskier use at once. But keyword blocks are easy to word around, and the policy would still miss the next new use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor has spotted the gap. But tiering is management's job under the policy; the auditor recommends and reports, never rates on management's behalf.

tips: Eliminate: B blocks one wording of one use and leaves the policy gap, and D has the auditor set a tier that management must own.
Final two: C beats A because a generative model takes on new uses through prompts alone, so change control has nothing to catch; tiers must follow the use.
Exam cue: with general-purpose AI, risk follows the use, and a new use can arrive by prompt with no system change.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.3 (Level of risk management activity set by risk tolerance); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (risk tiers attach to each use and are revisited when a use changes, as a general-purpose model can gain a use through prompts alone). Review round 1: setting moved from an insurer's claim-denial model (shared with a CISA AI item) to a health inspectorate's pharmacy-suspension model. Completeness round 1: re-angled from tiering by accuracy (its key and runner-up repeated aaia_d1_012 and aaia_d1_058) to a policy that tiers once at approval while prompts alone add a new use; runner-up is change control, which a prompt-only use change never triggers. Review round 3: key reworded to name management as the actor, removing a stem word echoed only in the key. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Model experiments under an AI policy
questions.question: A Brazilian hospital group's AI policy exempts experiments from approval; as a test, a new model now assigns admitted patients to beds on one ward in ten. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Its bed choices may differ from the current model's
options.B: Results may not be logged by model version for later review
options.C: Ward staff may not trust beds chosen by a test model
options.D: Those wards' live bed choices have no owner's sign-off

questions.key_concept: A model tested on live cases is making real decisions, so it needs the same approval and controls as any model in production.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Calling it a test does not change what happens: on one ward in ten, a model no owner has approved places real patients, and a wrong placement can harm them now. The policy gap lets live decisions skip governance. Logging results by version, option B, helps compare the two models later, but it records unapproved decisions rather than preventing them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because differences between models need explaining. But differing from the current model is the point of a test; the gap is that its choices take effect.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because version logs make decisions traceable. But tracing decisions does not make the model fit to make them; approval must come before live use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because staff acceptance matters to any change. But trust is a rollout question; patients are exposed whether or not staff trust the choices.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the expected difference between models as the risk, and C is a rollout question that leaves patients exposed.
Final two: D beats B because a live test is a live decision; logging by version records unapproved bed choices but does not stop them.
Exam cue: when a model decides for real people, it is in production, whatever the policy calls it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.4 (Risk management process established through transparent policies and controls); COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (a model tested on live cases is making real decisions, so it needs the same approval as any model in production, whatever the policy calls it). Review round 1: setting moved from an online lender's live credit test (near aaia_d2_027) to hospital nurse staffing, and two distractors replaced. Re-audit: AI use moved from nurse staffing (an AAIA d2 notes example) to bed assignment, and 'unapproved' removed from the stem. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A cutoff tuned by a service provider
questions.question: A Japanese ski-lift operator's managed-service vendor raises its pass-sharing model's blocking cutoff weekly to cut complaints, each move passing IT change control; the owner sees monthly summaries. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have internal audit approve each weekly cutoff change
options.B: Have the owner set limits on how far the cutoff moves
options.C: Have the vendor, not the owner, answer for lost lift revenue
options.D: Have IT test each cutoff move before release

questions.key_concept: A cutoff decides which skiers are stopped and how much pass sharing slips through; the owner sets limits it moves within, whoever runs it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the roles in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Each cutoff move trades wrongly stopped skiers against shared passes let through, a risk choice the operator's model owner answers for, whoever runs the model. IT change control checks that a change is made properly, not whether its trade-off is acceptable, so the owner should set limits within which the vendor may tune, with breaches escalated. Testing each move before release, option D, shows it works as made but leaves the trade-off with the vendor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit is independent. But approving changes would make internal audit part of the control it audits.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor runs the model day to day. But accountability for the operator's decisions cannot pass to a supplier; the operator answers to its skiers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cutoff changes should be tested. But testing shows a change works as made; it cannot decide how much pass sharing the owner will accept.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the operator's accountability to a supplier, and A has internal audit approve changes it must later audit.
Final two: B beats D because a cutoff is a risk trade-off the owner answers for; testing each move shows it works, not that the trade-off is acceptable.
Exam cue: whoever operates an AI model, the owner sets the limits on settings that decide who is harmed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (a cutoff decides who is blocked and how much harm slips through, so the model owner sets the limits it moves within, whoever operates the model). Completeness round 1: setting moved from a bank's fraud model (it repeated the principles.json check scenario for ai-changes-are-changes) to a ski-lift operator's pass-sharing model. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A refusal across chained agents
questions.question: A Peruvian refinery routes contractor-access requests through three AI agents, for documents, safety and badges; after a wrong refusal, each owner blamed another agent, citing passing tests. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have each agent's model vendor certify the whole chain
options.B: Have IS audit approve each change to the chain's agents
options.C: Have the three owners test each agent on the others' real outputs
options.D: Have senior management name an owner for the chain's outcome

questions.key_concept: When AI agents act on each other's outputs, errors can pass along the chain; one named owner answers for the combined outcome.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Each agent acts on what the one before it produced, so a misread document can pass into safety and badge decisions that no single agent's tests cover. With each owner blaming another agent, nobody answers for the access decision the chain makes. Senior management should name one owner, who then sets end-to-end criteria and testing. Testing on the others' outputs, option C, closes one gap, but nobody would own the combined result.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors know their models. But each vendor knows only its own agent, not this refinery's chain, and accountability for its access decisions stays with the refinery.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit is independent. But approving changes would make IS audit part of the control it must later audit.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because agents should be tested on real handoffs. But better tests still leave no one accountable for the chain's combined decisions or able to set their criteria.

tips: Eliminate: A hands the refinery's accountability to vendors, and B has IS audit approve changes it must later audit.
Final two: D beats C because agents act on each other's outputs, so the chain's decisions need one accountable owner; more tests do not supply one.
Exam cue: when AI agents hand work to each other, look for an owner of the end result, not only of each agent.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.1 (Existing, unanticipated and emergent risks tracked)
