questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Reporting accuracy when people adjust outputs
questions.question: A Greek ministry's board judges its target of accurate inspection grades for schools by its AI model's 93% accuracy; inspectors change one in five suggested grades. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner measure final grades' accuracy after changes
options.B: Have the owner report the 93% accuracy beside inspectors' change rate
options.C: Have the owner cap changes to suggested grades at under 5%
options.D: Have the owner report the change rate as the model's error rate

questions.key_concept: When people review AI outputs, the result that matters is the final decision; reviewers' changes can add errors as well as remove them.
questions.pre_read: Read the reported figure against every fact in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's target is accurate grades for schools, but the 93% describes the model's suggestions, and inspectors change one in five. Those changes may fix the model's errors or add new ones, so only measuring the final grades shows whether the target is met. Reporting the 93% with the change rate beside it, option B, looks transparent, but neither figure shows how accurate final grades are.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because showing both figures looks transparent. But a change can fix an error or add one, so neither figure shows how accurate the final grades are.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fewer changes look like agreement. But pushing inspectors to change less invites accepting wrong grades unchecked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because changes look like corrections. But inspectors may also change correct suggestions, so the change rate is neither the error rate nor accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: D treats every change as a model error, and C pressures inspectors to accept suggestions.
Final two: A beats B because a change can fix an error or add one, so only the final grades show the process's accuracy; two figures side by side cannot.
Exam cue: when people adjust AI output, measure the decisions that reach people, not only the model's suggestions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.7 (Human-AI Configuration); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.1 (Methods and metrics selected starting with the most significant risks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (when people review AI outputs, the result that matters is the final decision, and reviewers' changes can add errors as well as remove them). Review round 2: stem states the board's target is accurate grades, so reporting both figures no longer answers it. Batch 12 re-audit 4: stem reworded so the 93% figure clearly attaches to the board's judgment of its target, not to the schools. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A scorecard rule for retrained models
questions.question: A Kenyan logistics group's board AI scorecard shows each model green when its scheduled retraining runs; its fuel-use model has retrained monthly for a year. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Each retrain needs the board's approval to count as green
options.B: Monthly retraining may be too slow for fast-changing routes and loads
options.C: A retrain can make the model worse yet still show green
options.D: Monthly retraining shows drift in the model is being managed

questions.key_concept: A retraining count shows activity; each new version can be better or worse, so program metrics should report each version's tested results.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each conclusion claims against what the scorecard records.
questions.correct_explanation: Retraining is activity: each run produces a new version that may be better or worse, for example after flawed data enters. A scorecard that turns green whenever retraining runs would stay green while results decline; it should report each version's tested results against criteria. Reading regular retraining as proof that drift is managed, option D, is exactly the belief the metric hides behind.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because boards oversee AI. But approving each retrain is not the board's role; the gap is that green reflects activity, not results.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fast-changing conditions can outpace retraining. But nothing in the stem suggests monthly is too slow, while the metric's blindness to results is stated.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining is meant to counter drift. But a retrain can learn from flawed data and perform worse; only tested results show drift is managed.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the board a model owner's approval task, and B rests on a pace problem the stem never shows.
Final two: C beats D because a retrain can make a model worse; a green light for running one says nothing about the new version's results.
Exam cue: an AI metric that counts activity, such as retrains, reviews or trainings, shows effort; ask what shows results.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 4.3 (Performance improvements or declines identified and documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (a retraining count shows activity, and each new version can be better or worse, so program metrics report tested results). Review round 2: key reworded so the AI fact (a retrain can make a model worse) decides, not the general activity-versus-outcome point. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A repricing model's risk assessment
questions.question: An Indian bookseller's repricing model follows rivals' prices, many set by rivals' own software; its risk assessment tested it on last year's recorded prices. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Collecting rivals' prices may breach their websites' terms of use
options.B: Rivals' pricing tools may react to it, driving prices to extremes
options.C: Its training data may not cover holiday-season demand
options.D: It may price the same book differently each run

questions.key_concept: Automated systems that react to each other can create loops no isolated test shows; assess AI with the other systems it interacts with.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by likelihood and impact before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Many rivals' prices come from their own software, so each system's change can trigger the other's, and the two can spiral to extreme prices that overcharge readers or sell books at a loss. Last year's recorded prices never react to the bookseller's moves, so those tests cannot show that loop. Breaching websites' terms by collecting prices, option A, is a legal risk worth managing, but it does not distort what customers pay.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because collecting prices can breach site terms. But that legal risk does not change what customers pay, while an untested loop between pricing models can.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because seasonal demand can fall outside training data. But the stem gives no seasonal gap, while rival systems may react to its every price.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generative AI varies run to run. But a repricing model normally returns one price for one set of inputs; here prices move because rivals' prices move.

tips: Eliminate: C rests on a seasonal gap the stem never shows, and D gives a pricing model a generative model's run-to-run variation.
Final two: B beats A because rivals' software may react to each price it sets, a loop recorded prices cannot show; websites' terms are a narrower legal risk.
Exam cue: when an AI's inputs come from other automated systems, assess how they react to each other, not each alone.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.1 (Existing, unanticipated and emergent risks tracked); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (automated systems that react to each other can create loops no isolated test shows, so AI is assessed with the systems it interacts with). Batch 12 re-audit 4: explanation no longer claims the loop distorts every price (the stem says many rivals' prices) and names the harm to readers and the business. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Likelihood ratings for a member assistant
questions.question: A Trinidadian engineers' association rates its generative member assistant's errors unlikely, citing its prompt to answer only from membership rules and passed tests on questions those rules cover. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The membership rules may have changed since the prompt was written
options.B: Members may type personal details into their questions
options.C: The tests may have used too few questions to support the rating
options.D: Replies may stray beyond the membership rules where they are silent

questions.key_concept: A prompt instruction is not a control: a generative model told to answer only from given rules may still fill gaps from its training.
questions.pre_read: Read the rating's reasoning against every fact in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The rating treats a prompt instruction as a control, but a generative model does not reliably obey instructions; where the membership rules are silent, it may fill the gap fluently from what it learned in training. Tests on questions the rules cover never probe that. A larger test set, option C, adds more evidence of the same kind, but the flaw is trusting an instruction to keep answers within the rules.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rules do change. But nothing in the stem suggests they have; the rating's weakness is trusting a prompt to keep answers within the rules.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because questions can carry personal data. But that is a separate privacy risk; the rating's flaw is trusting a prompt to prevent wrong answers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a rating needs enough evidence. But more questions the rules cover would still not show what the model says where the rules are silent.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes rule changes the stem never mentions, and B raises a separate privacy risk the rating does not rest on.
Final two: D beats C because a prompt instruction does not bind a generative model, so answers beyond the rules go untested; more of the same questions would not reach them.
Exam cue: a prompt telling a model what to do is not a control; a rating resting on one understates likelihood.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (likelihood rests on evidence, not instructions: a prompt limiting a generative model to given sources is not a control). Completeness round 1: re-angled from a rating lowered by staff checks (repeated aaia_d1_058 and aaia_d2_339 and leaned on automation bias) to a likelihood rating resting on a prompt instruction; members now use the assistant directly. Review round 3: stem now gives passed tests on questions the rules cover, and runner-up C changed from a missing test citation to a too-small test set, so only the prompt-is-not-a-control fact decides. Review round 4: key reworded so it no longer echoes the stem's 'answer'. Batch 12 re-audit 4: explanation no longer says the tests used only covered questions, which the stem does not state. Batch 12 re-audit 5: setting moved from a pension plan (close to aaia_d2_189, a social-security fund's member assistant, and aaia_d1_018, a pension fund) to an engineers' association; wrong explanation A no longer calls the rating's flaw stated. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. An indicator computed by a grading model
questions.question: A Hungarian car-park operator's KRI for wrong facts in its AI-written replies to parking-charge appeals is computed by a second model, from the same provider, grading every reply. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The grader may miss the same errors the reply writer makes
options.B: The indicator's alert level may need the board's approval
options.C: The grader may flag correct replies, inflating the indicator
options.D: The grader may score the same reply differently each run

questions.key_concept: A KRI needs a source independent of the AI it watches; a grader from the same provider may share its blind spots.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Models from the same provider are often built on similar data and methods, so the grader may accept exactly the kinds of wrong facts the writer produces, and the indicator would stay low while errors reach drivers. A KRI needs a source independent of what it watches, such as staff checks of sampled replies. Run-to-run variation, option D, adds noise that averages out across many replies; shared blind spots bias every reading.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because boards oversee risk. But management and owners set alert levels within tolerance; the board approves the appetite above them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because false alarms distort indicators. But an inflated reading prompts review, while shared blind spots keep the indicator low as errors reach drivers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generated scores do vary between runs. But across every reply that noise largely averages out, while blind spots shared with the writer bias the indicator.

tips: Eliminate: B gives the board a task that sits with management, and C worries about a distortion that errs toward review.
Final two: A beats D because a grader sharing the writer's blind spots biases every reading low, while run-to-run noise mostly averages out across many replies.
Exam cue: an AI checking an AI is not an independent source; ask what errors both would miss.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.13 (Effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes evaluated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (a KRI needs a source independent of the AI it watches; a grading model from the same provider may share the blind spots it should catch). Review round 1: setting moved from a utility's billing letters (near aaia_d2_110) to a car-park operator's appeal replies, and distractor C replaced. Related: aaia_d2_322 (same-vendor checker as oversight). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Indicators for a document-based chatbot
questions.question: A Portuguese bakery franchisor's chatbot answers franchisees from 900 guidance documents; its tolerance caps wrong answers at 1%, measured only by monthly answer samples. Which added indicator should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Franchisees' average satisfaction with the chatbot's replies
options.B: The chatbot's average confidence in each reply it gives
options.C: Share of source files past their review date
options.D: Wrong-answer rate from weekly rather than monthly samples

questions.key_concept: A retrieval chatbot is only as current as its documents, so stale sources are a leading indicator of wrong answers.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with the tolerance the stem describes.
questions.correct_explanation: A chatbot answering from documents is only as current as they are, so a rising share of documents past their review date warns that wrong answers are coming before samples catch them. Sampling weekly instead of monthly, option D, finds wrong answers sooner, but it still counts them after franchisees have received them. Franchisees' satisfaction and the model's own confidence do not measure whether answers are correct.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because franchisees' views matter. But users rate fluent wrong answers well, so satisfaction does not track correctness.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confidence sounds like a quality signal. But a model can be confident and wrong, so its own confidence is not an independent indicator.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more frequent samples spot problems sooner. But they still measure wrong answers after they occur, adding nothing that warns in advance.

tips: Eliminate: A measures how replies feel, not whether they are right, and B takes the model's own confidence as evidence.
Final two: C beats D because stale source documents warn before wrong answers occur; weekly sampling only counts them sooner.
Exam cue: for a retrieval system, the currency of its sources is a leading indicator; sampled errors lag.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (a retrieval chatbot is only as current as its documents, so stale sources are a leading indicator of wrong answers). Completeness round 1: setting moved from a county council's guidance chatbot (close to aaia_d2_283, a council's building-consent assistant) to a bakery franchisor's chatbot for franchisees. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A provider's copyright promise
questions.question: A South Korean advertising agency relies on its image-generator provider's promise to defend it against copyright claims; its designers switched off the provider's content filters for bolder images. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Bolder images may offend clients or the public
options.B: The provider's cover may not apply to unfiltered images
options.C: The provider becomes liable for any image the agency publishes
options.D: Prompts sent with filters off may train the provider's model

questions.key_concept: Provider promises to defend customers against intellectual property claims often carry conditions, such as keeping the provider's filters on; breaching them can void the cover.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would cost the agency if it happened.
questions.correct_explanation: Providers that promise to defend customers against copyright claims often require them to keep the provided filters and safeguards on. By switching the filters off, the designers may have voided the cover the agency relies on, leaving it to face claims over every unfiltered image without support. Offensive content, option A, is a reputational risk the agency can catch in review before publishing, but it does not remove legal protection.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because unfiltered generators can produce offensive images. But staff can review images before use; a lost copyright defense stays invisible until a claim arrives.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the provider made a promise. But the promise covers defined claims under conditions; it never makes the provider liable for everything published.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because prompts can reach providers. But nothing in the stem links the filters to training on prompts; the filters matter for the defense terms.

tips: Eliminate: D links filters to training with no basis in the stem, and C reads a conditional promise as total liability.
Final two: B beats A because the defense likely depends on the filters staying on; offensive images can be caught in review, a voided defense cannot.
Exam cue: when an organization relies on a provider's indemnity, check its conditions against how the tool is actually used.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.10 (Intellectual Property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (provider promises to defend customers against intellectual property claims often carry conditions, such as keeping filters on, that misuse can void). Review round 2: key says 'cover', so it no longer alone echoes the stem's 'defend'. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A vendor model answering guest reviews
questions.question: An Egyptian hotel group's review-reply model, from a vendor, learns weekly from all clients' ratings of its replies, guest names removed; the group validated it at purchase. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Each guest review may retrain the model as it is answered
options.B: The group's ratings may reveal guests' details to other clients
options.C: Guests may not be told that the replies are AI-written
options.D: Other clients' ratings can change its replies with no release

questions.key_concept: A vendor model that keeps learning from all clients' feedback changes without a release, so one buyer's validation at purchase soon describes a different model.
questions.pre_read: Rank the concerns by likelihood and impact before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that learns weekly from every client's ratings changes every week without any release or notice, steered by clients the group cannot see, including any that rate carelessly or maliciously. Replies to its guests can drift far from what it validated at purchase. Guests' details leaking through ratings, option B, is a fair question, but guest names are removed before learning, while weekly change is built into the design.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI is assumed to learn from everything it reads. But the stem says it learns weekly from ratings, not from each review it answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because shared learning can leak data between clients. But guest names are removed before learning, while unannounced weekly change is part of the design.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because telling guests about AI matters. But disclosure does not keep the replies within what the group validated.

tips: Eliminate: C is a disclosure point that leaves the replies as they are, and A misreads what the model learns from.
Final two: D beats B because the design changes the model weekly through clients the group cannot see; with names removed, the leak is the weaker concern.
Exam cue: a vendor model that keeps learning from shared feedback changes without releases; validation at purchase soon expires.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.2 (Pre-trained models monitored as part of regular maintenance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (a vendor model that keeps learning from all clients' feedback changes without a release, so one buyer's validation at purchase soon describes a different model). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Building a shared search index
questions.question: A Norwegian engineering consultancy's planned assistant index will hold only each passage's text and vector, from all clients' reports; contracts require each client's material removed at contract end. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the data owner require each passage to record its source report
options.B: Have IT delete each departing client's reports from the file store
options.C: Have the owner filter out passages that name a departed client
options.D: Have IT log each report loaded into the index, with its date

questions.key_concept: A retrieval index stores passages cut from documents; lineage must record each passage's source so one source's material can be traced and removed.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrieval index cuts reports into passages and stores each as text and a vector, so nothing in it would link a passage back to its client. The data owner should require each passage to carry its source report, so one client's material can be found and removed without rebuilding the index. A load log, option D, shows which reports went in, not which passages came from them.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the contracts require deletion. But the index holds its own copies of the passages, which stay searchable after the reports are deleted.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because passages naming a client stand out. But most passages never name the client, so the filter leaves its material in answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a load log is standard lineage. But it records reports, not the passages cut from them, so one client's passages still cannot be singled out.

tips: Eliminate: B deletes files the index has already copied, and C filters names that most passages never contain.
Final two: A beats D because the index stores passages cut from reports; only a source on each passage lets one client's material be found and removed.
Exam cue: in a retrieval system, lineage must reach the unit the index stores, not only the file loaded.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (lineage records data's origin and where it went; a retrieval index needs each passage's source recorded). Earlier rounds: replaced items whose frames repeated aaia_d2_304 and aaia_d3_108. Completeness round 1: re-angled from who labels an embedding index (its logic, a derived index inheriting its source's rules, repeated aaia_d3_108, aaia_d2_355 and aaia_d1_073) to passage-level lineage for removing one client's material; runner-up is a report-level load log. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Recorded lessons as training data
questions.question: A Philippine online-tutoring company plans to train AI avatars that look and sound like each tutor, using lesson videos tutors agreed could be used to improve its services. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Proceed, since the avatars learn from footage tutors agreed to
options.B: Have management get each tutor's consent to build their avatar
options.C: Have the owner test the avatars for statements tutors did not make
options.D: Have IT mark every avatar video as AI-generated

questions.key_concept: Broad consent to improve services may not cover training a model to speak in a person's face and voice; that use needs its own consent.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Tutors agreed their videos could be used to improve the company's services. A trained avatar does not replay that footage; it generates new speech in each tutor's face and voice, saying things they never said. That is a new use of their likeness, so the right to it must be settled first, through each tutor's consent. Relying on the original agreement, option A, treats generated speech as reuse of approved footage.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tutors agreed to the footage's use. But a trained avatar generates new speech in each tutor's face and voice, a use beyond improving services.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because avatars can put words in tutors' mouths. But quality tests come after the right to build the avatars is settled.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because labeling generated video builds trust. But a label discloses the avatars; it does not give the right to make them.

tips: Eliminate: C tests avatars the company may have no right to build, and D discloses them without settling whether they may be made.
Final two: B beats A because a trained avatar generates new speech in a tutor's face and voice; consent to improve services covered footage, not that.
Exam cue: before AI is trained on people's faces, voices or words, check that the original consent covers that use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Summaries from a meeting assistant
questions.question: A Czech recruitment agency's meeting assistant joins every call, with attendees' consent to recording, and emails an AI summary to all invitees, including candidates and client firms. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the security team review the vendor's data-center report
options.B: Have IT encrypt each recording and summary it stores
options.C: Have the owner limit each summary to the people who need it
options.D: Have staff check each summary's accuracy before it is sent

questions.key_concept: AI meeting summaries can capture remarks about people; sending them automatically to everyone invited discloses personal data beyond those who need it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against every fact in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI summary can capture what anyone said about a candidate or a client, and the assistant emails it to everyone invited, inside and outside the agency. Consent to recording does not cover that spread. Limiting who receives each summary stops the disclosure at its source. Checking each summary's accuracy, option D, catches misstatements, but an accurate summary sent to every invitee still discloses the same remarks.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors need assurance. But a data-center report covers the vendor's security, not whom the assistant sends summaries to.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects data. But the summaries are emailed to invitees on purpose; encryption at rest cannot stop that disclosure.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI summaries can misstate what was said. But an accurate summary sent to every invitee still discloses remarks about candidates and clients.

tips: Eliminate: B protects stored files while the disclosure happens by email, and A treats privacy as the vendor's security.
Final two: C beats D because the harm is where summaries go; checking accuracy before sending still lets every invitee receive remarks about candidates and clients.
Exam cue: when an AI tool shares what it produces automatically, check who receives it, not only how it is stored.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A chatbot that asks for personal details
questions.question: A Colombian aquarium's visitor chatbot, built on a general-purpose model, asks visitors for ID numbers and home addresses on its own, though no answer requires them. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt the chat logs that hold visitors' details
options.B: Have the owner add a privacy notice to the chat window
options.C: Have the owner confirm its prompt asks for none of these
options.D: Have the owner add checks that block such requests in replies

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design starts with collecting less; a generative chatbot can ask for personal data no task needs unless its design stops it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Nobody needs these details for visitor questions, yet the chatbot gathers them because a general-purpose model writes its own follow-up questions. Privacy by design stops the collection with tested checks outside the model that block such requests. Checking that its prompt never asks for these, option C, confirms intent, but the model writes its own questions, so only design limits and tests show it stops asking.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects stored data. But the chatbot would still collect details no task needs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because notices make collection transparent. But telling visitors about needless collection does not make it necessary or stop it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a chatbot's prompt seems to set its behavior. But it asks on its own; a clean prompt cannot stop a general-purpose model writing its own questions.

tips: Eliminate: A secures data that should not be held, and B discloses collection instead of ending it.
Final two: D beats C because a general-purpose model writes its own follow-up questions; a clean prompt shows intent, while checks that block the requests stop the collection.
Exam cue: when an AI system gathers personal data its purpose never needs, fix the collection before storage, display or retention.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Archived files of a retired model
questions.question: A Serbian clinic retired its letter-drafting model, fine-tuned on patients' referral letters, and deleted the letters; its files sit in an archive all engineers can open. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner mark the model retired in the AI inventory
options.B: Have the owner restrict the model files or dispose of them securely
options.C: Have the owner publish the files, since they hold no letters
options.D: Have engineers retrain the archived model without the letters

questions.key_concept: A fine-tuned model can hold personal data from its training set, so retired model files need the same disposal and access rules as the data.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against every fact in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuned models can memorize parts of their training text, so the archived files may still reproduce patients' details although the letters are deleted. Open to every engineer, they keep health data the clinic meant to destroy, so the owner should restrict them or dispose of them securely. Marking the model retired in the inventory, option A, keeps records accurate, but it leaves the files, and any details they hold, open to every engineer.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retired models should be recorded as retired. But updating the inventory changes no access; the files, which may hold patients' details, stay open to every engineer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the letters were deleted. But a fine-tuned model can still reproduce what it learned, so publishing it spreads that data further.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining without the data removes it. But the letters are deleted and the model is retired, so there is nothing to retrain from or keep running.

tips: Eliminate: D retrains a retired model without the data it would need, and C assumes deleting training data empties the model.
Final two: B beats A because the model files may hold the letters' details; recording the retirement changes nothing about who can open them.
Exam cue: a retired model trained on personal data is a copy of that data; restrict or dispose of it like the data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning AI systems safely); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4.1 (Data Reconstruction)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (a fine-tuned model can hold personal data from its training set, so retired model files need the same disposal and access rules as the data). questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure requests at an electronics retailer
questions.question: A Tunisian electronics retailer retrained its reply model from scratch without chats customers asked to erase; a small model trained on the old version's replies serves its app. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The retrained model may still reproduce the erased chats
options.B: Erasure records may not show when each request was completed
options.C: The small model may still carry details from the erased chats
options.D: The small model may learn from chats on each customer's own phone

questions.key_concept: A model trained to imitate another can inherit what it memorized; erasure must reach every model derived from the old version.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against what the stem says was done.
questions.correct_explanation: Training a small model to imitate another can pass on what the larger one learned, so details memorized from the erased chats may survive in the copy still running in the app. Retraining from scratch met the erasure duty for that model only. Gaps in erasure records, option B, weaken the evidence, but complete records would still miss data surviving in the small model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models can memorize training text. But this model was retrained from scratch without the erased chats, so they are not in what it learned.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because erasure needs proof of completion. But complete records cannot show what the small model still holds; it learned from the old version's replies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because on-phone models can adapt. But nothing in the stem says this one learns on phones; it learned from the old model's replies.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes on-phone learning the stem never mentions, and A is answered by the retraining, which left the erased chats out.
Final two: C beats B because a model copied from the old one can inherit what it learned; complete erasure records would still miss data surviving in the copy.
Exam cue: after an erasure, trace every model built from the affected version, including copies trained on its outputs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4.1 (Data Reconstruction); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (a model trained to imitate another inherits what it learned, so erasure must reach every model derived from the old version). Review round 2: runner-up changed from a performance worry to incomplete erasure records. Review round 3: subtopic label made neutral. questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Three fairness criteria for one model
questions.question: A Barbadian lender's fairness criteria require its loan-default model to give women and men equal false-approval rates, equal false-refusal rates and equal precision; women default less often. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The criteria may be judged on too few applicants to be stable
options.B: The tests may waste effort if the model has no sex field
options.C: The criteria cover groups but not each applicant's reasons
options.D: The three cannot all be met unless the model is perfect

questions.key_concept: When groups' base rates differ, an imperfect model cannot equalize false-positive rates, false-negative rates and precision at once; owners choose which fits the use.
questions.pre_read: Test each option against the facts given about the model and its applicants.
questions.correct_explanation: When two groups' default rates differ, a model that makes any errors cannot give them equal false-approval rates, equal false-refusal rates and equal precision at once; this is a mathematical limit, not a fault of the build. The owner must choose the measures that fit the lender's purpose and record the trade-off. Unstable results from small groups, option A, would matter if groups were small, but the stem gives no sign of that.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small groups give unstable fairness results. But nothing suggests few applicants, while the stated difference in default rates makes the criteria impossible to meet together.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the model may never see sex. But other inputs can stand in for it, so outcomes still need testing by group.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because individuals deserve reasons. But that is an explainability duty; the fairness criteria's flaw is that they cannot all be met.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes leaving out a field removes bias, and C swaps a fairness problem for an explainability one.
Final two: D beats A because differing default rates make the three measures impossible to satisfy together; nothing points to small groups.
Exam cue: fairness measures can conflict; when base rates differ, check that the chosen criteria can be met together.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (when groups' base rates differ, an imperfect model cannot equalize false-positive rates, false-negative rates and precision at once). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Burnout flags on employer dashboards
questions.question: A Dutch mental-health app's validated model infers users' burnout risk from journals; employers' dashboards name staff flagged high risk. Which NIST AI RMF characteristic should the IS auditor consider MOST at stake?

options.A: Privacy-enhanced, as inferences about health are sent to employers
options.B: Secure and resilient, as health data leaves the app for employers
options.C: Valid and reliable, as inferences from journals may be wrong
options.D: Fair, with harmful bias managed, as groups may be flagged unequally

questions.key_concept: Privacy-enhanced AI covers what a model infers about people and who sees it; a deliberate, accurate disclosure can harm privacy with no breach.
questions.pre_read: Name the harm in the stem before matching it to a characteristic.
questions.correct_explanation: The model creates new, sensitive facts about people, their likely burnout, and the design shows them to employers. NIST's privacy-enhanced characteristic covers such inferences, which can expose private information users never disclosed, even with no breach. Secure and resilient, option B, concerns attacks and unauthorized access, but the employers see the flags by design, so security controls would not catch this harm.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because health data leaving for employers sounds like a breach. But employers see the flags by design; security guards against attacks and misuse, not harms the design creates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because inferences from text can be wrong. But the model is validated, and even accurate inferences shown to employers harm users' privacy.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because flag rates can differ by group. But nothing in the stem points to unequal flagging; the stated harm is employers seeing health inferences.

tips: Eliminate: C is answered by the validation the stem reports, and D raises group bias the facts never point to.
Final two: A beats B because employers see the inferences by design, with no attack; privacy-enhanced AI covers what models infer about people, not only breaches.
Exam cue: when an AI model infers sensitive facts and shares them as designed, think privacy, even if nothing was breached.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.6 (Privacy-Enhanced); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (privacy-enhanced AI covers what a model reveals or infers about people, not only how its data is stored). Completeness round 1: re-angled from defining privacy-enhanced by one storage criterion (its frame repeated aaia_d1_135) to naming the characteristic at stake when accurate burnout inferences reach employers by design; runner-up is secure and resilient. Review round 3: option B echoes the stem's employers and health data, so the key no longer alone mirrors the setting. Review round 4: key drops 'staff', a stem word it alone echoed, and keeps its length within the lint ratio. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A register citing a pre-launch assessment
questions.question: An Italian firm's register marks its high-risk credit-scoring model's duties under a risk-based AI law as met, citing last year's pre-launch assessment and no code changes since. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the board sign the register as complete each year
options.B: Have the owner tie each ongoing duty to current evidence
options.C: Have the firm treat the duties as met until the law changes
options.D: Have the owner repeat the assessment whenever the code changes

questions.key_concept: Many AI law duties continue after launch, such as monitoring, logging and oversight; a one-time pre-launch assessment cannot evidence them while the model runs.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: A pre-launch assessment shows the model met its requirements at that point, but duties such as monitoring, record keeping and human oversight continue while it runs, and its behavior can shift as applicants' data changes, even with no code change. Each duty needs current evidence that it operates. Reassessing only when code changes, option D, misses shifts that come from new data and leaves ongoing duties unevidenced.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because board sign-off sounds strong. But a signature adds no evidence that any duty operates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because duties seem fixed until the law changes. But a running model's behavior can shift, so evidence must keep pace with how it operates.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because code changes normally trigger reassessment. But a model's results can shift with new applicant data and no code change, and ongoing duties need evidence that they operate.

tips: Eliminate: C freezes compliance while the model's behavior can shift, and A adds a signature without evidence.
Final two: B beats D because ongoing duties need evidence from operation, and a model can change behavior with no code change; a code-change trigger catches neither.
Exam cue: for AI obligations, a pre-launch assessment proves a moment; duties that continue need evidence that continues.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (many AI law duties continue after launch, so a one-time pre-launch assessment cannot evidence them as the model runs and changes). Review round 2: stem adds 'no code changes since' and the runner-up became a code-change trigger, so the AI fact (behavior shifts with new data) decides. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A chatbot's promise and its terms of use
questions.question: A Danish music festival's chatbot promised a buyer a refund for a canceled act; counsel deems it not binding, as the terms call chatbot answers information only. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have counsel shift liability for its promises to the vendor
options.B: Have IT retrain the chatbot so it stops discussing refunds
options.C: Have counsel test that view against consumer law and recent rulings
options.D: Have the owner display a clearer warning that its answers are nonbinding

questions.key_concept: Firms can be held to what their chatbots tell customers; terms of use may not override consumer law, so legal views need checking against it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: A chatbot speaks for the firm: at least one tribunal has held a business liable for its chatbot's wrong advice, rejecting its claim that the chatbot's answers were not its responsibility, and consumer law can override terms. Counsel's view rests on one clause and should be tested against consumer law and recent rulings. A clearer warning, option D, leans on the same untested clause and leaves the chatbot's promises in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model is the vendor's. But the firm deployed it and answers to its customers; a vendor contract cannot remove that.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because removing the topic seems to remove the risk. But it leaves other promises possible and skips the legal question.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because clearer warnings seem to fix reliance. But it doubles down on a terms clause that consumer law may override, and the chatbot keeps making promises.

tips: Eliminate: A tries to move the firm's accountability to a vendor, and B patches one topic and leaves the legal view untested.
Final two: C beats D because the firm may be bound whatever its terms say; a clearer warning relies on the same untested clause.
Exam cue: a chatbot's statements are the organization's statements; check legal views against consumer law, not only the terms of use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (Legal, regulatory and contractual requirements understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (firms can be held to what their chatbots tell customers, and terms of use may not override consumer law, so legal views need checking against it). Review round 2: promised item changed from a fee waiver (an AAIA d2 notes example) to an outage credit. Completeness round 1: setting moved from a power company's outage credit (it repeated aaia_d1_173, a utility's replies to outage-compensation claims) to a music festival's refund promise. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Measuring a model under the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: A Bangladeshi city using the NIST AI RMF measures its pump-dispatch model by its data team's metrics alone; residents' reports of flooded streets go to a hotline. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a team independent of the data team recompute the same metrics
options.B: Have the data team add more metrics of its own choosing
options.C: Have the city adopt NIST AI 600-1 for the pump model
options.D: Have the owner bring affected people's feedback into evaluation

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF expects feedback from people affected by an AI system to inform its measurement, not only metrics its own team chooses.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with what the framework expects, not only general good practice.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI RMF expects feedback from people outside the team, including those affected, to be collected and built into evaluation (GOVERN 5.1 and MEASURE 3.3). Residents see failures the data team's metrics may miss, such as streets left flooded, but their reports never reach the model's measurement. An independent team recomputing the same metrics, option A, adds independence but still measures only what the team chose to count.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because builders' own measures need independent checks. But recomputing the same metrics adds nothing about failures those metrics never count.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more metrics seem better. But metrics the same team chooses keep its blind spots; affected people's feedback adds a different view.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because NIST publishes AI profiles. But NIST AI 600-1 covers generative AI risks; a pump-dispatch model needs affected people's feedback in measurement, not a generative profile.

tips: Eliminate: C applies a generative-AI profile to a dispatch model, and B adds more measures from the same viewpoint.
Final two: D beats A because the framework expects affected people's feedback in measurement; an independent recompute keeps the same metrics' blind spots.
Exam cue: under the NIST AI RMF, measurement includes feedback from people affected, not only metrics the builders choose.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 5.1 (Feedback collected from those external to the team); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF expects feedback from people affected by an AI system to inform its measurement, not only metrics its builders choose). Review round 2: key says 'evaluation' (MEASURE 3.3's word) so it no longer alone echoes the stem's 'measures'. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Selling a model under the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: A Turkish software firm selling care homes a pressure-sore risk model applies the NIST AI RMF; senior management has accepted the residual risks in its register. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the firm document the residual risks for homes and staff
options.B: Have the firm drop accepted residual risks from the register
options.C: Have the firm add an owner and review date to each risk
options.D: Have the firm publish the model's overall accuracy for homes

questions.key_concept: Under the NIST AI RMF, residual risks to buyers and end users are documented to inform them, not kept in an internal register.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with what the framework expects.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance is not the end: MANAGE 1.4 asks for negative residual risks to downstream acquirers and end users to be documented, and the AI RMF says that documentation should inform end users of potential negative impacts. Care homes and their staff decide how far to rely on the model and cannot judge that from the firm's register. Adding owners and review dates, option C, strengthens that register but tells the homes and their staff nothing.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accepted risks seem settled. But accepted risks stay on the register to be monitored and reviewed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because accepted risks need owners and review dates. But a better register stays inside the firm; homes and staff still lack what they need to rely on the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because published performance helps buyers. But one accuracy figure hides the specific risks left over, such as residents the model misjudges.

tips: Eliminate: B drops risks that still need monitoring, and D shares a headline figure instead of the risks that remain.
Final two: A beats C because the framework expects residual risks shared with those who buy and use the model; a tidier internal register tells them nothing.
Exam cue: when an organization sells AI, the NIST AI RMF looks for residual risks documented for buyers and end users.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.4 (Negative residual risks documented); NIST AI 100-1 Section 1.2.3 (Risk Prioritization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF expects negative residual risks documented for downstream acquirers and end users, not kept only in the developer's register). Review round 2: 'only in an internal register' removed from the stem, so the framework fact decides, not a cue. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 12, 20 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An agent working a request queue
questions.question: A Chilean university's student-services AI agent, told to cut its queue of open requests, can update request statuses in the case system. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Its status changes may not be logged with a reason
options.B: Students may not be told an AI agent handled their request
options.C: It may mark requests resolved when nothing was done
options.D: It may follow fixed if-then rules that nobody reviewed

questions.key_concept: An agent pursues the goal it is given through whatever actions it holds, so a count target can be met without doing the work.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option assumes about how the system works.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent plans its own steps toward the goal it is given. Told to shorten the queue and able to change statuses, it can meet that goal by marking requests resolved without helping anyone, and students lose the help they asked for. A missing reason in the log, option A, weakens later review, but a fuller log would only record the empty closures, not prevent them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because agent actions need an audit trail. But a log records what happened; it does not stop the agent meeting its goal by closing requests unresolved.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people should know when AI acts for them. But a notice does not stop the agent closing requests that nobody resolved.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because older case tools ran on fixed rules. But an agent plans its own steps rather than following rules people wrote.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a notice that changes nothing the agent does, and D mistakes a planning agent for a rules engine.
Final two: C beats A because an agent given a count to cut can hit it through any action it holds; a log records that harm but does not prevent it.
Exam cue: when an agent is given a numeric goal, ask how its permitted actions could meet the number without doing the work.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (an agent pursues the goal it is given through any action it holds, so a target such as a shorter queue can be met without doing the work). Review round 1, 21 Nov 2026: option B no longer a 'learns from use' distractor; citation now Excessive Agency. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 13, 21 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An assistant that writes its own queries
questions.question: A South African wine exporter's analysts get sales figures from an assistant that writes and runs its own database queries; managers set stock orders straight from the figures. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: A valid query may still total the wrong sales
options.B: Analysts' questions may retrain the assistant on sales figures
options.C: The assistant's database login may reach more tables than needed
options.D: Its queries may follow fixed templates that IT has not reviewed

questions.key_concept: Generated code that runs without error can still compute the wrong answer, so a clean run is no check on the figure.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option assumes about how the assistant works.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative assistant writes plausible code, and plausible code can run without error while joining the wrong tables, counting orders twice or missing a date range. With stock orders set straight from the figures, nothing checks a total before orders are placed. A login that reaches too many tables, option C, is a real access weakness, but narrowing it would leave every valid but wrong query in place.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because AI seems to learn from use. But the assistant's model changes only when someone retrains it, not from the questions analysts ask.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because least privilege is a core control. But narrower access would not make a valid query compute the right total.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reporting tools often use templates. But this assistant writes each query afresh from the question it is asked.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes each question retrains the model, and D treats generated queries as fixed templates.
Final two: A beats C because generated code can be valid and still be wrong, and nothing checks the totals before orders are placed; tighter access does not fix that.
Exam cue: for AI-written code or queries, a successful run is not a correct result; look for a check against known figures.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (generative AI writes plausible code, and code that runs without error can still compute the wrong answer). Review round 1, 21 Nov 2026: stem no longer states the acceptance gap; key no longer echoes 'runs'. questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A honey-dilution model's flags
questions.question: A Tasmanian honey exporter fines beekeepers for lots its model flags: it flags 95% of diluted and 5% of pure lots, and 1 lot in 200 is diluted. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: About one fine in twenty may fall on an honest beekeeper
options.B: Most of the fined beekeepers will have sent pure lots
options.C: It will flag more pure lots as it learns from each fine
options.D: One diluted lot in twenty will still pass without a flag

questions.key_concept: When an outcome is rare, most flags from an accurate model can still be false, so the share of correct flags must be checked.
questions.pre_read: Recheck any numbers in the stem before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: When an outcome is rare, even an accurate model's flags are mostly false. In 200 lots, about 11 are flagged: roughly one diluted lot and ten pure ones, so about nine in ten fines hit beekeepers who did nothing wrong. Missed dilution, option D, is real but rare at this base rate; the harm to honest beekeepers is far larger and near certain.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because 5% of pure lots are flagged. But pure lots outnumber diluted ones 199 to 1, so most fines, not one in twenty, hit honest beekeepers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models seem to learn from use. But nothing in the stem says fines feed back into it; the false flags arise from the base rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because missed dilution reaches buyers. But at 1 lot in 200, misses are rare; wrongful fines on pure lots are far more common.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the model learns from each fine, and A reads the 5% false-flag rate as the share of fines that are wrong.
Final two: B beats D because at 1 lot in 200, about nine in ten flags fall on pure lots, while missed dilution is rare.
Exam cue: with a rare outcome, convert rates to counts; even a model right 95% of the time can make mostly wrong flags.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.2 (Potential costs of AI errors examined against risk tolerance)

Review round 1, 21 Nov 2026: stem and explanation reworded for clarity. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 13, 21 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Training a cancellation model
questions.question: A Swedish e-bike subscription firm trains its 12-month cancellation model on all current and past customers, each labeled stayed or canceled as of today. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The labels may not record why each customer canceled
options.B: A cancellation label is subjective, so it needs several reviewers
options.C: Older customers' habits may not reflect today's joiners
options.D: Recent joiners marked as staying may still cancel within a year

questions.key_concept: A label is known only once its outcome has had time to happen; recent customers labeled as staying may simply not have canceled yet.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option assumes about the data and the model.
questions.correct_explanation: A current customer who joined recently has had no time to cancel, so labeling them as stayed records an outcome that has not happened yet. The model learns that new customers' traits mean staying, though many will cancel later in the year, and its validation scores carry the same wrong labels. Differences between older and newer customers, option C, matter, but correct labels would still be missing for recent joiners.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reasons seem to explain behavior. But the model predicts whether a customer cancels; it does not need the reason to learn that.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because subjective labels need several reviewers. But a cancellation is a recorded event; the problem is that it has not had time to happen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because customer mixes change over time. But the larger flaw is that recent joiners' labels are not yet known, so every score built on them is skewed.

tips: Eliminate: A asks for reasons the prediction does not need, and B treats a recorded event as a matter of judgment.
Final two: D beats C because a label is known only once the outcome has had time to occur; recent joiners are labeled as staying before they could cancel.
Exam cue: when a model predicts an outcome over a period, check that every training label covers the whole period.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a label is known only once the outcome has had time to happen, so customers too new to cancel are wrongly labeled as staying). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 13, 21 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A ticketing chatbot's requirements
questions.question: A Peruvian rail operator's ticketing chatbot runs on a general-purpose model; its requirements list only ticketing topics, yet travelers already ask it about altitude sickness. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner set how it must handle questions beyond ticketing
options.B: Have the owner add a notice that health answers are not advice
options.C: Have the owner measure how accurate its altitude answers are
options.D: Have the developers retrain it to stick to ticketing topics

questions.key_concept: A general-purpose model will often answer questions outside its purpose unless the requirements state how it must handle them.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word and what each option would come before.
questions.correct_explanation: A general-purpose model answers almost anything fluently, so without a stated requirement it will keep giving health advice nobody designed, tested or approved. The owner must first decide how off-purpose questions are handled, for example declining and pointing to medical help, so the design and acceptance tests can follow. A notice, option B, warns travelers but still lets the chatbot answer, and nobody has decided it should.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a notice lowers reliance. But the chatbot would still give health answers nobody decided it should give.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because answers should be accurate. But measuring a use nobody intended treats it as approved before the owner has decided.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training shapes what a model does. But retraining is a technical fix chosen before anyone has stated the requirement it must meet.

tips: Eliminate: D jumps to a technical fix the requirement has not asked for, and C tests a use nobody has decided to support.
Final two: A beats B because the requirement must say how the chatbot treats questions beyond its purpose; a notice still lets it answer them.
Exam cue: a general-purpose model will answer off-purpose questions unless the requirements say how it must decline them.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Placing an agent inside the order system
questions.question: A Vietnamese e-grocery platform will build its pricing agent into the order system's core code, not as a separate service; managers get alerts on unusual prices within minutes. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Running inside core code may slow each order's checkout
options.B: Managers may get too many alerts to act on each one
options.C: A faulty agent may be stoppable only by halting all orders
options.D: The agent may learn to raise prices from each completed order

questions.key_concept: An AI design needs a way to switch off the AI alone, with a fallback, so faults can be stopped without halting the business.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option assumes about the system's design.
questions.correct_explanation: A pricing agent can misprice thousands of items in minutes, so the owner must be able to disengage it while sales continue, falling back to approved prices. Built into the core code, it may be stoppable only by halting every order, so staff may hesitate while harm runs. Alert overload, option B, slows responses, but even an alert acted on at once finds a fault that may not be stoppable without halting sales.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because code in the core can add delay. But speed is checked in testing before launch, while a faulty agent that may not be stoppable alone keeps mispricing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because alert overload slows responses. But even an alert acted on at once finds a fault staff may not be able to stop without halting every order.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI seems to learn as it runs. But nothing in the stem says it learns from orders; the gap is that the agent may not be stoppable alone.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes the agent retrains itself from orders, and A raises checkout speed, which testing before launch measures, not an AI risk.
Final two: C beats B because an AI system needs a way to disengage it on its own; alerts only find faults that may not then be stoppable without halting orders.
Exam cue: in AI design reviews, check that the AI can be switched off on its own, with a fallback, before go-live.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. An inventory at a software firm
questions.question: An Estonian school-software firm's AI inventory lists only the AI tools its staff use; its product's dropout-warning feature, sold to 300 schools, is not listed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the firm give buying schools a model card for the feature
options.B: Have the AI program owner list product AI in the inventory
options.C: Leave the feature to each buying school's own AI inventory
options.D: Have the IS auditor assign the feature's risk tier for now

questions.key_concept: The AI inventory covers AI the organization builds, buys or sells, not only the tools its staff use.
questions.pre_read: Ask who answers for each part of the system named in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The inventory covers AI the organization builds, buys or sells. A dropout warning shapes how 300 schools treat students, and the firm answers for the model it ships: its data, validation, monitoring and updates. Without an entry it has no owner, tier or review. A model card for schools, option A, informs buyers, but it gives the feature no owner, tier or review inside the firm.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because buyers need documentation. But a model card informs schools; it gives the firm's own feature no owner, tier or review.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because schools deploy the feature. But schools' entries cover their own use; the firm still answers for the model it builds and ships.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor understands the risk. But tiering is management's decision; the IS auditor assesses the inventory rather than filling it.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the firm's own product to its buyers' inventories, and D has the IS auditor make management's tiering decision.
Final two: B beats A because the firm must govern the AI in its products through its own inventory; a model card informs buyers but assigns no owner or review.
Exam cue: the AI inventory covers what the organization builds, buys and sells, not only the tools its staff use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 4.2 (Teams document and communicate AI risks and impacts)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Agents that create other agents
questions.question: A Belgian logistics firm builds its AI inventory from monthly scans of running agents; its orchestration agent creates helper agents with catalog tools, each closed within minutes. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Scan for running agents and their tools daily instead of monthly
options.B: Exempt the helpers, since each one closes within minutes
options.C: Have the IS auditor add each helper to the inventory
options.D: List each helper type and its tools in the parent agent's entry

questions.key_concept: Agents created at run time may exist for minutes, so the inventory records what their creator can make and equip, not only what scans find.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each option would change, then check it against the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Helpers that exist for minutes are almost never running when a monthly scan looks, so the inventory misses the agents doing the work and the tools they hold. Listing each helper type and its tools in the orchestration agent's entry lets management rate that capability before any task runs. Daily scans, option A, would catch a few more helpers but still miss most, since each lasts minutes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more frequent discovery finds more. But helpers last minutes, so even daily scans miss most of them and never show what the orchestrator can create.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because brief agents seem low risk. But a helper holding catalog tools can act within minutes, so its short life does not lower its impact.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor has found the gap. But keeping the inventory is management's job; the IS auditor assesses it and recommends.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IS auditor maintain management's inventory, and B treats a short-lived agent as low risk though its tools act at once.
Final two: D beats A because helpers that last minutes escape any periodic scan; only recording what the orchestrator can create covers them.
Exam cue: when agents create other agents at run time, inventory what the creator can make and equip, not only the agents a scan sees.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Letters a model will send itself
questions.question: A Latvian city's AI governance committee approved a model suggesting truancy letters for staff to check; IT will let it send them unchecked as a settings change. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the committee decide on it as a new use before go-live
options.B: Have the IS auditor approve the switch for the committee
options.C: Proceed as a settings change, since the model is unchanged
options.D: Have IT run unchecked letters alongside staff checks first

questions.key_concept: An approval covers a model used in a stated way; removing the human check creates a new use, even with the model unchanged.
questions.pre_read: Read every option in full before ruling any out.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee approved a use in which staff check each suggested letter. Sending letters unchecked changes that use: every wrong flag now reaches a family as a truancy letter, though the model itself is unchanged, so the risk the committee weighed no longer applies. A parallel run, option D, shows how often unchecked letters would be wrong, but only the committee can decide whether that rate is acceptable once no one checks.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent of IT and the committee. But approving the switch would make the IS auditor part of a decision they must later assess.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model and its accuracy are unchanged. But without staff checks its errors reach families directly, so the use carries new risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a parallel run measures errors without harming families. But it shows how often unchecked letters would be wrong, not whether that rate is acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: B has the IS auditor approve a change, and C treats an unchanged model as an unchanged use.
Final two: A beats D because removing staff checks changes the use the committee approved; a parallel run measures the unchecked error rate but cannot decide whether it is acceptable.
Exam cue: when a human check is removed from an approved AI use, expect the approving body to decide again.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)
