questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A committee approval and a tolerance
questions.question: An Indian state's AI governance committee will approve a ration-card fraud model flagging 3% of honest households, over senior management's 1% tolerance, expecting a fix from retraining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team set a 3% tolerance for this model
options.B: Have the IS auditor accept the 3% rate on senior management's behalf
options.C: Have the committee refer the decision to senior management
options.D: Have the committee approve it, tracking the retrain monthly

questions.key_concept: A use that breaches senior management's tolerance needs senior management's decision; an AI governance committee cannot accept the breach itself.
questions.pre_read: Note who holds each role named in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Senior management set the 1% tolerance, so only it, or the board above it, can decide to run a model that breaches it. A retrain is a change whose results are unknown until tested, so an expected fix does not cure today's breach, and honest households would be flagged at three times the accepted rate. The committee should refer the decision. Approval with monthly tracking, option D, still accepts a breach the committee cannot accept.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because builders know what the model can achieve. But tolerances express how much harm is accepted, which senior management sets, not the data team.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IS auditor knows the test results. But accepting risk would make the IS auditor own a decision they must assess.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tracking keeps the fix on schedule. But a retrain's results are unknown until tested, and approval would still accept a breach the committee cannot accept.

tips: Eliminate: A lets builders set the limit their model must meet, and B has the IS auditor accept risk.
Final two: C beats D because a use that breaches senior management's tolerance needs senior management's decision; conditions on approval do not give the committee that authority.
Exam cue: when an AI use would run outside a tolerance, look for escalation to whoever set the tolerance.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.3 (Executive leadership takes responsibility for AI risk decisions); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.5 (Organizational risk tolerances determined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Structural calculations moved to a model
questions.question: A Jordanian engineering firm's model does the structural calculations its graduates once did, so it hires none; the senior engineers checking each one retire within five years. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model validated independently before the seniors retire
options.B: Have new staff trained to do and check the calculations
options.C: Have the model check its own calculations after they retire
options.D: Have IS audit check a sample of calculations every quarter

questions.key_concept: People who check AI output need skills built by doing the work, so workforce plans keep training people in tasks AI takes over.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Checking a model's calculations takes the judgment engineers build by doing the work. With no graduates doing it, no one will be ready to check once the seniors retire, and the human check becomes a formality. Training new staff to do and check the calculations keeps that skill growing. Independent validation, option A, tests the model once on chosen cases; each later calculation still needs a checker who can spot a plausible wrong result.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because independent validation is strong evidence about a model. But it tests the model once; each future calculation still needs an engineer skilled enough to check it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models can flag results they are unsure of. But a model checking itself can repeat its own errors, leaving no independent human check.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because sampling finds errors. But IS audit would be performing a control it must assess, and the skill gap would remain.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a model to check itself, and D has IS audit run a control.
Final two: B beats A because validation tests the model once, while each future calculation still needs an engineer whose judgment comes from doing the work.
Exam cue: when AI takes over junior work, ask who will be skilled enough to check its output in future.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.4 (Operator and practitioner proficiency defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.2 (AI risk management training for personnel and partners)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A staffing plan built on a model's accuracy
questions.question: An Indonesian halal certifier's model, 99% accurate, decides applications it is sure of and passes the rest to reviewers; management will halve reviewer posts so it decides more. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner shift cases from reviewers in steps, checking accuracy
options.B: Have an independent team recompute the 99% on the model's cases
options.C: Have the owner report the 99% with the model's average confidence
options.D: Have the owner test the model on cases reviewers now handle

questions.key_concept: A model deciding only cases it is sure of reports accuracy on those alone, which says nothing about the cases it passes on.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word and what each option would come before.
questions.correct_explanation: The 99% covers only the applications the model was sure of, usually the easier ones. Halving reviewers moves harder cases to the model, whose accuracy on them nobody has measured. Past cases reviewers decided, with known outcomes, can show how it would do before staff go. Shifting cases in steps, option A, still learns its accuracy on hard cases from live decisions, after applicants are affected.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a staged change limits exposure. But each step still tests the model on live applicants, when past reviewer cases could show its accuracy first.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because independent checks improve evidence. But recomputing the 99% confirms a figure that still covers only the cases the model chose to decide.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because confidence seems to show quality. But a model's confidence is not its accuracy, and it says nothing about the cases reviewers handle.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the model's confidence as accuracy, and B rechecks a figure that covers only the cases the model kept.
Final two: D beats A because the 99% says nothing about the harder cases reviewers now decide; past ones can be tested before staff go, while steps learn on live applicants.
Exam cue: when a model decides only cases it is sure of, its accuracy covers only those; test it on the rest before widening its role.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.5 (Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process)

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Releasing a model's weights
questions.question: A Czech cybersecurity firm will publish the weights of its model that explains malware code, rating misuse unlikely because its web service filters requests to write new malware. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Copies run from the weights would skip those filters
options.B: Rivals could build competing products from the published weights
options.C: Published weights could let anyone change the firm's web service
options.D: The service's filters may block some honest researchers' requests

questions.key_concept: A risk rating that credits controls in the organization's own service no longer holds once the model's weights are published and run elsewhere.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The misuse rating rests on a control in the firm's own service, but published weights can be downloaded and run anywhere, outside that service and its filters, and cannot be recalled. Anyone could then ask a copy to write malware, so the rating's basis falls away and harm could reach many organizations. Rivals copying the model, option B, is a business loss, but it leaves the understated misuse risk untouched.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because published weights give away the firm's work. But that is a commercial loss; the misuse rating rests on filters that copies will not have.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because weights sound like system access. But weights are the model itself; holding them gives no access to the firm's web service.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because filters can over-block. But over-blocking is a minor cost next to copies that have no filters at all.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses holding a model with access to the firm's systems, and D worries about the filters working too well.
Final two: A beats B because the rating relies on filters in the firm's service, which downloaded copies run without; a commercial loss does not change the misuse risk.
Exam cue: when a risk rating credits a control, check that the control still applies wherever the AI will run.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.9 (Information Security)

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Renewal prices set by a model
questions.question: A Latvian electricity retailer's renewal model, rarely wrong in validation, flags customers unlikely to switch for higher renewal prices; its risk assessment names no risks to customers. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Its predictions may have been validated on last year's renewals
options.B: Correct predictions may make customers pay more for staying
options.C: Wrong predictions may raise prices for customers about to switch
options.D: Outages may stop customers from renewing their contracts online

questions.key_concept: AI risk identification covers harm from a model working as designed, not only harm from its errors.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: This model can harm people when it works exactly as designed: customers it correctly predicts will stay pay more simply because they are unlikely to leave. Risk identification must cover harm from intended use, not only from errors. Wrong predictions, option C, are rare in validation and touch only the customers the model misjudges; correct predictions raise prices for every customer the model flags rightly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because stale validation can overstate accuracy. But better validation sharpens the very predictions that raise prices for customers unlikely to leave.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because prediction errors are the usual model risk. But this model is rarely wrong, and errors touch only misjudged customers; correct predictions raise prices for every customer flagged rightly.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outages hurt renewals. But outages are an availability matter; they say nothing about whom the model's prices harm.

tips: Eliminate: D names an availability risk that says nothing about pricing harm, and A would only sharpen the predictions that cause the harm.
Final two: B beats C because accurate predictions used as designed raise prices for every customer flagged rightly; errors touch only the few the model misjudges.
Exam cue: AI risk identification asks who is harmed when the model works as designed, not only when it is wrong.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed)

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. One model serving two uses
questions.question: An Austrian social-insurance agency's letter classifier routes incoming mail and also flags letters as possible fraud; senior management set one 5% misclassification tolerance for the model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner track the 5% using the model's average confidence
options.B: Have the owner set one tolerance per error type from tests
options.C: Have senior management set a tolerance for each of its two uses
options.D: Have senior management tighten the single tolerance to 1%

questions.key_concept: Tolerances follow harm, so a model whose uses cause different harms needs a tolerance for each; owners set use-level criteria within them.
questions.pre_read: Read each option for who it gives the decision to.
questions.correct_explanation: One classifier serves two uses with different impact: a misrouted letter is delayed, but a wrong fraud flag can put a claimant under investigation. Tolerances express how much harm is acceptable, so each kind of harm needs its own, and the fraud use needs a limit on wrongful flags that its owner's criteria sit within. Tightening the single limit, option D, still mixes routing errors with fraud errors, so wrongful flags could rise unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because confidence is easy to track. But confidence is not an error rate and can stay high while errors rise.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because owners turn tolerances into criteria. But tolerances express accepted harm, which senior management sets for each use; error types still mix the two uses.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a stricter limit sounds safer. But one combined rate still mixes routing errors with fraud flags, so wrongful flags can rise unseen.

tips: Eliminate: B has the owner set tolerances that senior management sets, and A treats the model's confidence as an error measure.
Final two: C beats D because tolerances follow the harm of each use, not the model; one rate, however strict, lets fraud-flag errors hide among routing errors.
Exam cue: when one model serves uses with different impact, look for a tolerance per use.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. An appetite stated as zero
questions.question: A Norwegian housing-benefit agency's board states zero appetite for wrongful denials by its eligibility model, whose denials are final, and asks senior management to set tolerances within it. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The board should set the model's tolerance itself instead
options.B: Validating the model to 100% accuracy will meet the appetite
options.C: The statement suits a use deciding claimants' housing benefit payments
options.D: Such an appetite leaves no tolerance any model could meet

questions.key_concept: Every model makes some errors, so a zero AI risk appetite leaves no workable tolerance that can sit within it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each conclusion against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Model outputs are estimates, so any eligibility model will wrongly deny some people; even a well-validated one errs above zero. The NIST AI RMF warns that trying to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive. A zero appetite leaves senior management no tolerance to set within it, and any model it uses would breach it. Option C tempts because high-impact uses call for low appetite, but zero is not low; it is unmeetable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the board owns appetite. But tolerances are set by senior management within the appetite, not by the board.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because validation shows accuracy. But no validation brings a model to 100% on future cases; models give estimates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because low appetite fits high-impact decisions. But a zero limit is not low; no model can meet it, so it cannot guide tolerances.

tips: Eliminate: A moves tolerance setting to the board, and B expects validation to make a model error-free.
Final two: D beats C because models give estimates and every model errs, so a zero appetite leaves no tolerance any model could meet; an unmeetable limit protects no one.
Exam cue: AI risk appetite must allow for some error, because models are probabilistic; a zero limit leaves no room for a workable tolerance.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. An exit plan for a search index
questions.question: A Zambian geological survey's assistant searches decades of borehole reports via a vendor's embedding index; its exit plan relies on an open-format export, complete in a trial. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Reports added since the trial may be missing from the export
options.B: The vectors may be unusable without the vendor's model
options.C: The vendor may keep copies of the reports after the exit
options.D: The vendor may stay accountable for search results until exit

questions.key_concept: Embeddings work only with the model that made them, so an exit plan needs the source documents and re-embedding, not just the exported index.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option assumes about leaving a vendor.
questions.correct_explanation: Each stored vector is a list of numbers made by the vendor's embedding model, and it matches only queries encoded by that same model. After exit, a new model would encode queries differently, so searches of the exported index would quietly fail. The plan needs the source reports and a re-embedding step. The trial shows the file arrives complete, not that another system can search it; newer reports, option A, can be exported again.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an export goes stale as reports are added. But a fresh export at exit would still hold vectors that only the vendor's model can match.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because exit terms should cover retained data. But a copy left with the vendor would not stop the survey searching its reports; unusable vectors would.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor runs the index. But accountability for the assistant's results stays with the survey, before and after exit.

tips: Eliminate: D moves accountability to the vendor, and C is a data-retention term that leaves search working.
Final two: B beats A because vectors are tied to the model that made them; even a fresh, complete export leaves an index no new model can search.
Exam cue: when an exit plan moves an embedding index, check that the source documents and a re-embedding step come too.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A hosted chatbot's contract
questions.question: An Omani money-exchange firm's contract forbids probing its vendor-hosted customer chatbot, set up with its transfer guides, for harmful answers; the vendor shares a red-team summary. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the firm secure the right to run its own adversarial tests
options.B: Have the IS auditor probe the chatbot despite the contract
options.C: Have the firm obtain an independent red-team report on the vendor's model
options.D: Have the firm accept the summary, as vendors know their models

questions.key_concept: How a hosted chatbot fails depends on the buyer's own setup, so the buyer needs the right to test the system as deployed.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each option would let the firm know.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm answers for what its chatbot tells customers, and how a hosted chatbot fails depends on the firm's own setup: its transfer guides, customers and likely misuse, which the vendor's summary may not reflect. Only the firm's own adversarial testing, which the contract now forbids, shows how this deployment fails. An independent report on the vendor's model, option C, removes the vendor's bias but still tests the model, not the firm's deployment.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IS auditor gathers direct evidence. But testing in breach of the contract is not the IS auditor's call; the gap is the firm's missing testing right.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because independent testing beats the vendor's own. But a test of the vendor's model still misses the firm's own setup, transfer guides and customers' likely misuse.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors know their models best. But the vendor's tests reflect its own choices, not the misuse the firm's own customers might attempt.

tips: Eliminate: D takes the vendor's view as assurance, and B has the IS auditor test in breach of the contract.
Final two: A beats C because how a hosted chatbot fails depends on the firm's own setup; even independent tests of the vendor's model do not show that.
Exam cue: for hosted AI, look for the buyer's right to test the system as deployed, not just the vendor's reports.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Loans from two lending arms
questions.question: A Bolivian fintech will train one repayment model on loans from its two lending arms, which mark a loan defaulted after 30 and 90 days late respectively. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the data team drop loans that appear in both arms' records
options.B: Have the data team add each loan's lending arm as an input
options.C: Have the data owners set one default definition for training
options.D: Have the owner train on the larger arm's loans and defaults

questions.key_concept: A training label must mean the same thing across every source, so data owners settle its definition before data is merged.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word and what each option would settle.
questions.correct_explanation: Here a loan 30 days late counts as defaulted in one arm and as performing in the other, so the model learns a blend, and its scores and accuracy mean different things for each arm's borrowers. The data owners must first agree the definition the model will predict. Adding the arm as an input, option B, lets the model learn each arm's rule, but one score would still carry two meanings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because duplicate records distort training. But removing duplicates leaves the two arms labeling the same lateness differently.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a model input can capture group differences. But the model would then predict two different events under one score, which no input can reconcile.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one arm's labels are consistent. But dropping the other arm's loans narrows the data and leaves no agreed definition for the combined use.

tips: Eliminate: A removes duplicates when the labels disagree, and D narrows the data instead of settling what the label means.
Final two: C beats B because the owners must decide what 'default' means before training; an input that learns each arm's rule still leaves one score meaning two things.
Exam cue: when training data comes from several sources, check that each label means the same thing in all of them.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Answers drawn from the web
questions.question: A Mongolian road authority's winter-travel chatbot answers from its own road advisories and, where they are silent, from live web search results. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Each web search may retrain the model on what it finds
options.B: Travelers may not know their questions reach the search provider
options.C: Answers may differ in wording for the same question
options.D: Web pages that nobody owns or checks may steer its advice

questions.key_concept: Retrieved content needs an owner answering for its quality and currency; live web results have none, yet they can shape the answers.
questions.pre_read: Consider each source the chatbot draws on.
questions.correct_explanation: The authority's own advisories have an owner answering for their accuracy and currency; web results have none. Whatever page a search returns, outdated or plain wrong, can become the basis of advice on whether a road is safe to drive, and the chatbot passes it on as fluently as an official advisory. That questions reach the search provider, option B, is a privacy point to manage, but it does not make the advice reliable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI seems to learn from what it reads. But search results feed one answer; they do not retrain the model.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because queries leave the organization unseen. But that is a privacy matter; the bigger risk is unvetted pages shaping safety advice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because consistent answers seem safer. But generative answers vary in wording by design; the risk is unvetted content shaping their substance.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes searches retrain the model, and C treats normal variation in wording as the risk.
Final two: D beats B because retrieved content needs an owner answering for its quality; web results have none, and they shape safety advice.
Exam cue: when an assistant adds web results, ask who owns and checks what it retrieves.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A call-recording notice and model training
questions.question: A Trinidadian gas utility plans to fine-tune a reply model on recorded customer calls; callers were told calls are recorded 'for quality and training purposes'. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt the call recordings before training begins
options.B: Have the privacy officer assess whether the notice covers AI training
options.C: Proceed, since callers agreed to model training by staying on
options.D: Have the owner test the tuned model for repeating callers' details

questions.key_concept: A call notice that mentions training usually means staff training, so whether calls may train a model is settled before tuning or testing.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Training in a call notice is usually read as training staff, not building an AI model, so callers may never have been told their words would train one. Whether the notice covers this new purpose, and on what lawful basis, is the first question, and the privacy officer should answer it. Testing the tuned model for memorized details, option D, is sound, but it does not decide whether the calls may be used at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recordings need protection. But encryption does not decide whether the planned use is permitted.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the notice mentions training. But it most likely meant staff training; callers did not knowingly agree to model training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tuned models can memorize what callers said. But leak tests make safer a use that may not be allowed; whether the calls may train a model comes first.

tips: Eliminate: C reads a staff-training notice as consent to model training, and A answers a permission question with encryption.
Final two: B beats D because whether the calls may train a model comes first; memorization tests protect a use that may not be permitted.
Exam cue: check that the notice people saw covers AI training before weighing how the data or the model is protected.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Totals from an HR assistant
questions.question: A Mexican brewery's HR analytics assistant answers managers' questions about staff, such as sick days by team, showing only totals and never names. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Narrow questions can reveal one employee's details in a total
options.B: Managers may type staff names into their questions
options.C: Stored totals may be encrypted too weakly for staff sick-day data
options.D: Managers may see totals for teams they do not manage

questions.key_concept: Totals are anonymous only when they cover enough people; narrow or overlapping questions to an AI assistant can single out one person.
questions.pre_read: Consider how the assistant's answers could be used.
questions.correct_explanation: A total is anonymous only when it covers enough people. Managers can ask an assistant narrow questions it answers instantly, such as sick days in a team of two last March, or compare two overlapping totals, and so learn one person's health absences without seeing a name. Access by team, option D, matters, but even a manager's own team can be sliced until a total describes one employee.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because prompts can carry personal data. But managers already know their staff's names; the exposure is totals that reveal one person's absences.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because sick-day data is sensitive. But encryption protects stored data; it cannot stop a total from describing one person.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because access should follow management lines. But even within their own teams, managers can narrow totals until one person stands out.

tips: Eliminate: B worries about names managers already know, and C applies encryption to a disclosure made through answers.
Final two: A beats D because small or overlapping totals can single out one person; limiting managers to their teams still leaves that open.
Exam cue: removing names from AI answers is not anonymity; ask whether narrow questions can isolate one person.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A lawsuit and monthly retraining
questions.question: Borrowers are suing a Nigerian digital lender over its credit-limit model, whose versions are deleted after each monthly retrain; counsel's legal hold covers emails and documents. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have counsel describe how the current model sets credit limits
options.B: Have the IS auditor take custody of the model versions
options.C: Have counsel extend the hold to model versions and their data
options.D: Have IT pause retraining until the hold is lifted

questions.key_concept: When AI decisions are disputed, a legal hold must cover model versions, training data and decision logs, not only emails and documents.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The borrowers' claims turn on what the model that set their limits actually did, and each monthly retrain deletes an earlier version, the very evidence in dispute. A legal hold must cover model versions, their training data, settings and decision logs, not only emails and documents, so counsel should extend it now. Pausing retraining, option D, saves today's version but protects none of the training data or decision logs the claims also turn on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the current model is easy to explain. But it is not the version that set the disputed limits, and earlier versions are being deleted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because custody protects evidence. But preserving records is management's and counsel's job; the IS auditor recommends it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining replaces evidence. But pausing it keeps only today's version; the hold must also preserve training data and decision logs.

tips: Eliminate: A offers a description of today's model as evidence of past decisions, and B has the IS auditor take over management's records.
Final two: C beats D because the hold must keep every version that sets disputed limits, with its training data and decision logs; pausing retraining saves only today's version.
Exam cue: when AI decisions are disputed, legal holds must cover model versions, training data and decision logs.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure and a fixed test set
questions.question: A Danish furniture shop's model owner will not remove erased customers' records from its recommender's fixed release test set, as changing it would break comparisons between releases. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the records, since test copies sit outside erasure duties
options.B: Have the privacy officer weigh comparability against each request
options.C: Have the owner remove them at next year's test-set refresh
options.D: Have the owner delete them and retest the previous version

questions.key_concept: Test sets follow deletion rules; retesting the previous version on the revised set keeps release comparisons valid.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Deletion rules reach every copy, test sets included, and comparability is not a reason to keep data erased everywhere else. The comparison problem has a technical fix: retest the previous version on the revised set, so the new release is still judged against a like-for-like baseline. Weighing each request, option B, turns a settled duty into a case-by-case exception that a retest makes unnecessary.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because test sets feel internal. But erasure duties reach every copy of the data, whatever the copy is used for.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the privacy officer judges exceptions. But comparability is no ground for keeping erased data, and a retest removes the need.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a planned refresh keeps comparisons clean. But erasure cannot wait a year for a test schedule, and a retest keeps comparisons valid now.

tips: Eliminate: A exempts test copies from erasure, and C delays erasure for a year to suit a test schedule.
Final two: D beats B because retesting the previous version on the revised set keeps comparisons valid, leaving nothing for a case-by-case exception to protect.
Exam cue: when a fixed test set must change, retest the earlier version on the new set rather than keep data that must go.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A safety criterion for a wellbeing chatbot
questions.question: An Irish university's student-wellbeing chatbot, written to sound warm and personal, met its only safety criterion: no unsafe replies in 20,000 test messages. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Students may come to rely on it in place of people
options.B: 20,000 tests are too few to rule out rare unsafe replies
options.C: Students may teach it unsafe replies over many chats
options.D: The IS auditor may not have signed off the safety criterion

questions.key_concept: Chatbots built to sound personal can draw people into relying on them; safety criteria on reply content alone miss that harm.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: A chatbot written to sound warm and personal invites students to treat it as a confidant, and some may lean on it instead of counselors or friends, a risk NIST's Generative AI Profile calls emotional entanglement. A criterion counting unsafe replies never measures it, so students could come to harm while every reply passes. A larger test sample, option B, would tighten the estimate of unsafe replies but still measure nothing about reliance.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because zero failures in a sample is not proof. But more test messages still measure only what replies say, not whether students rely on the chatbot.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because chats seem to shape the bot. But the stem gives no sign it learns from use; separate chats do not change its model unless its owner retrains it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor reviews criteria. But the chatbot's owner sets safety criteria; the IS auditor assesses whether they suit the use and never signs them off.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes chats retrain the model, which the stem never says, and D expects the IS auditor to sign off a criterion the chatbot's owner sets.
Final two: A beats B because a chatbot built to sound personal invites reliance, which no count of unsafe replies measures; a bigger sample cannot show it.
Exam cue: for chatbots people confide in, check that safety criteria cover reliance on the chatbot, not only what each reply says.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A wording-overlap quality criterion
questions.question: A Finnish research-ethics board's protocol-summary model meets its quality criterion: each summary shares at least half its wording with a board reviewer's summary of the same protocol. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Half of each summary's wording may differ, so half may be wrong
options.B: A summary can share most wording yet get one key fact wrong
options.C: Half the wording may be too low a bar for protocol summaries
options.D: Shared wording may not show that summaries are explainable

questions.key_concept: A wording-overlap score measures shared words, not correct meaning, so it cannot show that a summary's facts are right.
questions.pre_read: Consider what the criterion is meant to show.
questions.correct_explanation: A wording-overlap score rewards shared words, not correct meaning: a summary that copies most of a reviewer's phrasing but turns 'no children enrolled' into 'children enrolled', or misstates a dose, can still pass. The criterion never tests the facts the board decides on. Raising the bar, option C, makes the same measure stricter, but a summary can match more wording and still carry the one error that matters.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because half the wording differs. But different words can state the same facts correctly; overlap does not count errors either way.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a higher bar sounds stricter. But it tightens a measure of shared words; a summary can match more and still misstate a key fact.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because explainability is a trustworthy-AI characteristic. But a protocol summary's job is to be accurate; explaining a model's decisions is a different criterion.

tips: Eliminate: A reads differing wording as errors, and D applies a characteristic the summary's purpose does not call for.
Final two: B beats C because an overlap score does not test meaning, so raising it still lets a fluent summary carry a wrong fact.
Exam cue: check that a criterion's metric measures the quality that matters, not something easier that resembles it.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. AI-made images in fundraising ads
questions.question: An AI law requires a Belgian charity to tell viewers its appeal ads' realistic flood-survivor photos are AI-made; it relies on the generator's provenance tag in each image. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Viewers on social platforms may get copies with the tag stripped
options.B: The law may bar the charity from using generated photos
options.C: The tag may not record which prompt produced each photo
options.D: People viewing the photos may never see a tag inside the file

questions.key_concept: A duty to disclose AI-made content to people is met by a label they can see, not by a machine-readable tag inside the file.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option's risk would leave undone if it occurred.
questions.correct_explanation: A disclosure duty is met when the people who see the content are told it is artificial. A provenance tag is machine-readable data inside the file, written for software, so a viewer looking at the ad sees nothing unless a platform chooses to show it. Stripping by platforms, option A, is a real weakness, but even a tag that survives every upload leaves the disclosure to platforms; the charity needs a label people can see.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because many platforms remove file data on upload. But even a surviving tag sits inside the file, so viewers are told only if a platform chooses to show it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because realistic images of disaster victims can mislead. But a disclosure duty assumes the photos may be used once people are told.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because records help show how content was made. But prompt records serve the charity's own trail; they tell no viewer the photos are artificial.

tips: Eliminate: B reads a disclosure duty as a ban, and C gives the charity a record rather than telling viewers.
Final two: D beats A because a provenance tag is machine-readable data inside the file; even if no platform strips it, viewers are told only if a platform chooses to display it.
Exam cue: a duty to tell people content is AI-made needs a label they see; machine-readable marks serve detection tools.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.8 (Information Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (a duty to disclose AI-made content to people is met by a label they can see, not by a machine-readable tag). questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Mapping an incident-reporting duty
questions.question: A Slovenian firm's high-risk emergency-call triage model serves ambulance services; the firm maps an AI law's serious-incident reporting duty to a process started only by model-monitoring alerts. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Reporting incidents may expose the triage model's design
options.B: The duty may rest with the ambulance services, not the firm
options.C: Harm seen only by ambulance services may never start the process
options.D: The process may not meet the law's reporting deadline

questions.key_concept: Monitoring of a model's scores rarely reveals one harmful output, so AI incident reporting needs reports from the users who see the harm.
questions.pre_read: Consider how the mapped process would work in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring alerts watch the model's inputs and score patterns, so one call wrongly triaged as routine, with a patient harmed, can look entirely normal to them. That harm is seen by the ambulance services using the model, and nothing feeds their reports into the firm's process, so serious incidents may never be reported. Meeting the deadline, option D, matters only for incidents the process ever learns of.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reports can reveal design details. But a legal reporting duty is not set aside to protect commercial secrets.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the services make the triage decisions. But the provider of a high-risk system holds its own reporting duty.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reporting duties have deadlines. But a deadline matters only once the process learns of an incident; harm seen by users never reaches it.

tips: Eliminate: A weighs commercial secrecy against a legal duty, and B assumes only the users hold the duty.
Final two: C beats D because model monitoring cannot see one harmful output among normal-looking scores; without reports from the services that see the harm, deadlines never start.
Exam cue: when an AI reporting duty is mapped to a process, check it hears from the people who see the harm.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.3 (Incidents and errors communicated and tracked); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 3.3 (Feedback and appeal processes for end users and affected communities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (AI incidents are often harm from wrong outputs while systems run normally, so a reporting duty mapped to outage-triggered processes is never triggered). Review round 1, 21 Nov 2026: setting moved from Austria; deciding fact now who sees the harm (outage-trigger frame was aaia_d1_121's). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 13, 21 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Risk responses in an AI procedure
questions.question: A Ghanaian student-loan agency's risk procedure, based on the NIST AI RMF, lets owners only mitigate or accept risks; a model's risk to borrowers is rated unacceptable. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner mitigate the risk while the model stays in use
options.B: Have management add ceasing use to the allowed responses
options.C: Drop the framework, since NIST guidance is voluntary
options.D: Transfer the risk by insuring against borrowers' claims

questions.key_concept: Under the NIST AI RMF, an AI system presenting unacceptable negative risk should cease safely until the risk can be managed.
questions.pre_read: Compare the procedure with what the framework expects.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF says that when an AI system presents unacceptable negative risk, development and deployment should cease in a safe manner until the risk can be sufficiently managed. A procedure offering only mitigate or accept leaves no way to stop. Mitigating while the model stays in use, option A, is what the procedure allows, but it leaves borrowers exposed to a risk already rated unacceptable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the procedure allows mitigation and the work can start now. But a risk rated unacceptable calls for stopping until it is managed, not fixing it in use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the framework is voluntary. But voluntary does not mean unhelpful; the gap is in the procedure, not in choosing a framework.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because transfer is a valid response. But insurance pays claims; it does not stop the harm to borrowers.

tips: Eliminate: D transfers a harm that insurance cannot prevent, and C treats voluntary guidance as unusable when the gap is in the procedure.
Final two: B beats A because the AI RMF expects a system with unacceptable risk to stop until the risk is managed; mitigating while it stays in use leaves borrowers exposed.
Exam cue: under the NIST AI RMF, unacceptable AI risk means stop safely until managed, not keep running while mitigating or accepting it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 1.2.3 (Risk Prioritization); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.3 (Responses to high-priority risks planned: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF says a system presenting unacceptable negative risk should cease safely until the risk can be managed, so a procedure must allow halting it). Review round 1, 21 Nov 2026: key names its actor. Review round 2, 21 Nov 2026: key no longer echoes 'procedure'. Review round 3, 21 Nov 2026: option A changed from accepting the risk to mitigating it while the model stays in use, so the runner-up needs the AI RMF fact to defeat; key reworded to a missing response type in the procedure rather than a halt mechanism. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 13, 21 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A measurement plan under the AI RMF
questions.question: A Guatemalan cash-transfer program using the NIST AI RMF will measure its targeting model's overall error rate this year, and its errors for Indigenous households next year. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner measure errors for Indigenous households first
options.B: Have the owner wait for complaints from Indigenous households instead
options.C: Keep the plan, since the overall error rate covers every household
options.D: Have the owner give every risk equal effort in one cycle

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF selects measurement approaches starting with the most significant risks, not the easiest metrics.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with what the framework expects.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF expects measurement to start with the most significant risks. An overall error rate can look low while errors fall mostly on Indigenous households, and wrongly leaving them out of cash transfers is the harm that matters most; a year's wait leaves it unmeasured while decisions continue. Keeping the plan, option C, seems enough because every household is counted, but a pooled rate cannot show who bears the errors.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complaints show harm. But excluded households may never complain, and waiting leaves the main risk unmeasured.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the overall rate counts every household. But a pooled rate can look low while errors fall mostly on Indigenous households, the most significant risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because complete coverage sounds thorough. But the framework asks for priority by significance, not equal effort on every risk.

tips: Eliminate: D spreads effort evenly instead of by significance, and B waits for complaints from people who may never be heard.
Final two: A beats C because an overall error rate can hide errors that fall on one group; the framework starts with the most significant risk.
Exam cue: when a plan measures overall errors now and a group's errors later, look for the group most at risk of harm to be measured first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.1 (Methods and metrics selected starting with the most significant risks); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF selects measurement approaches starting with the most significant risks, not the easiest metrics). Review round 1, 21 Nov 2026: setting moved from Mexico; runner-up now an overall error rate. Review round 2, 21 Nov 2026: plan now measures the overall error rate first (not speed and uptime), so the runner-up 'keep the plan' falls only to the fact that a pooled rate hides group errors. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 13, 21 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Photos prepared by an AI tool
questions.question: A Kittitian building-control office runs blurry drone photos of roofs through an AI tool that sharpens them before inspectors judge whether hurricane straps are fitted. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The vendor may update the tool without telling the office
options.B: The tool may learn from each inspector's pass or fail decision
options.C: Detail in photos may be invented rather than captured by the camera
options.D: Inspectors may not know which photos the tool has changed

questions.key_concept: AI image enhancement generates plausible detail, so a sharpened photo can show features the camera never captured.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option assumes about how the tool works.
questions.correct_explanation: AI sharpening is generative: it fills in detail that looks plausible, so a blurred strap can appear fitted, or a fitted one missing, and inspectors would pass or fail roofs on detail nobody photographed. Unannounced vendor updates, option A, are a real change risk, but every version, updated or not, can invent the detail inspectors judge.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors change AI tools without notice. But even an unchanged version invents detail; notice of updates would not stop it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because AI seems to learn as it is used. But the tool does not retrain from inspectors' decisions as it runs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI-altered photos should be marked. But a mark shows a photo was sharpened, not which detail in it was invented.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes the tool retrains from inspectors' decisions, and D marks changed photos without showing which detail was invented.
Final two: C beats A because any version of a generative sharpener can invent the detail inspectors judge; notice of updates cannot prevent that.
Exam cue: when AI 'enhances' images, audio or text later used as evidence, ask whether it adds content that was never captured.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (AI image enhancement is generative, so a sharpened photo can show detail the camera never captured). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An agent that keeps notes between tasks
questions.question: A Guyanese freight firm's AI agent initiates supplier payments and saves 'lessons' from each staff chat to a memory it reads before every later task. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: A one-off instruction may become a rule for later payments
options.B: Each saved lesson may retrain the agent's underlying model
options.C: Saved lessons may keep details of payments longer than allowed
options.D: Its memory may fill up and drop the oldest lessons

questions.key_concept: An agent's memory carries content from one task into others, so a one-off instruction can become a standing rule nobody approved.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option assumes about how the agent works.
questions.correct_explanation: The agent reads its saved memory before every task, so a lesson drawn from one chat, such as 'pay this supplier early' or 'skip the second check this once', can steer every later payment, quickly and with no one approving it as a rule. Keeping payment details too long, option C, is a real retention gap, but it exposes data rather than changing how money is paid.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the agent seems to learn from chats. But saving notes to a memory does not retrain the model; it adds text the agent reads.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a memory can hold payment and personal details. But over-retention exposes data; a standing lesson changes how many payments are made.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because memory limits are real. But losing an old lesson costs some efficiency; a one-off instruction kept as a rule can misdirect many payments.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses a memory store with retraining, and D worries about losing lessons rather than keeping a wrong one.
Final two: A beats C because a memory read before every task can turn one chat's instruction into a standing payment rule; over-retention exposes data but moves no money.
Exam cue: when an agent keeps memory across tasks, ask what one wrong entry could make it do next time.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.5 (Security of Agents)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.1 Kinds of AI Systems (an agent's memory carries content from one task into others, so a one-off instruction can become a standing rule nobody approved). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A general model ranking written statements
questions.question: A Botswanan volunteer-abroad charity ranks applicants' personal statements with a hosted general-purpose model, never trained on its past selections, so staff say it cannot carry their past bias. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Applicants may not be told a model ranks their statements
options.B: It may reflect biases learned from its broad training text
options.C: It may train on the bias in each ranking staff accept
options.D: Its rankings may change when a statement is scored again

questions.key_concept: A general-purpose model learns from vast amounts of text, so it can bring that text's biases into rankings it was never trained to make.
questions.pre_read: Consider where each option says the model's behavior comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: A hosted general-purpose model learned from huge amounts of public text, which carries associations about names, dialects and writing styles, so it can rank some applicants' statements lower without ever seeing the charity's history. The staff's reasoning rules out only their own bias. Rankings that shift when a statement is rescored, option D, are a real consistency problem, but steady rankings could still be steadily biased.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people should know AI is used. But disclosure does not stop a model ranking some applicants lower for learned associations.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models seem to learn from use. But a hosted model does not retrain on the rankings staff accept.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generative output varies from run to run. But consistency is not fairness: a stable ranking can still carry learned bias.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the model trains on each ranking staff accept, and A fixes disclosure while the ranking stays biased.
Final two: B beats D because a model's behavior comes from all its training text, not only the user's records; consistent rankings can still be biased.
Exam cue: 'never trained on our data' does not mean unbiased; ask what the model did learn from.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.6 (Harmful Bias and Homogenization); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a general-purpose model learns from vast amounts of text, so it can bring that text's biases into rankings it was never trained to make). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A learned cooling controller
questions.question: An Irish data-center operator's cooling controller learned by trial and error in a simulator, where it cut energy use by 30%; it has not yet run real chillers. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: It could not learn without labeled examples of good settings
options.B: It may follow cooling rules that engineers wrote into it
options.C: The 30% saving in the simulator was measured by its builders
options.D: It may rely on behavior that works only in the simulator

questions.key_concept: A model that learns by trial and error exploits whatever its training environment rewards, including quirks a simulator has and the real plant lacks.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option says about how the controller learned.
questions.correct_explanation: Learning by trial and error rewards any action that scores well in the training environment, including gaps or quirks in the simulator, such as cooling physics modeled too simply. The 30% may therefore come from moves that fail, or overheat servers, on real chillers. Builders measuring their own result, option C, weakens independence, but an independent rerun in the same simulator would repeat the same flaw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because many models learn from labeled examples. But trial-and-error learning uses rewards from outcomes, not labels.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because control systems often run engineers' rules. But this controller learned its behavior; no one wrote its rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because builders' own results lack independence. But an independent rerun in the same simulator would still miss quirks absent from real chillers.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes all learning needs labels, and B mistakes a learned controller for engineers' rules.
Final two: D beats C because trial-and-error learning can exploit simulator quirks; independence does not help when the test environment itself is the flaw.
Exam cue: for a model trained or tested only in a simulation, ask what the simulation leaves out of the real world.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a model that learns by trial and error exploits whatever its training environment rewards, including simulator quirks the real plant lacks). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Reaching staff from a chatbot
questions.question: A Ugandan pay-TV firm requires that any customer asking for a person can reach staff; its support chatbot's model judges whether each message asks for one. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner test the model on sample requests for staff
options.B: Have staff review a monthly sample of chats for misses
options.C: Have the owner add a path to staff that bypasses the model
options.D: Have the owner retrain the model on each missed request

questions.key_concept: A requirement left to a model's judgment holds only as often as the model reads intent correctly, so enforce it outside the model.
questions.pre_read: Read the requirement and the design separately before the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A model judging intent is right most of the time, not always, so some customers who ask for a person, perhaps in slang or another language, would stay stuck with the chatbot, breaking a requirement meant to hold every time. A route that does not depend on the model, such as a fixed menu option, meets it. Testing sample requests, option A, measures the miss rate but leaves the misses in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because testing shows how often the model misreads requests. But a measured miss rate still leaves some customers unable to reach staff.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sampling detects problems. But it finds misses weeks later, after customers were already stuck.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining reduces known errors. But a probabilistic model will still misread some new phrasings, so the requirement still fails sometimes.

tips: Eliminate: D expects retraining to make a probabilistic model perfect, and B finds failures only after customers were stuck.
Final two: C beats A because a requirement that must always hold cannot rest on a model's judgment; testing measures the gap but does not close it.
Exam cue: when a 'must always' requirement depends on an AI judgment, look for a control that does not depend on the AI.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.6 (System requirements elicited from relevant AI actors); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (a requirement that must always hold cannot rest on a model's judgment, which is right only most of the time). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An approval step in a design
questions.question: A Romanian retailer requires supervisors to approve each model-recommended warning to warehouse pickers; the planned screen offers only 'approve' or 'rescore', which reruns the model with their note. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner let supervisors reject a warning outright
options.B: Have the owner let supervisors approve a sample of warnings
options.C: Have the owner require a second supervisor to approve each warning
options.D: Have the owner raise the accuracy target the model must meet

questions.key_concept: A person can oversee a model's recommendation only if the design lets them decide against it, not just approve or rerun it.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option adds to the approval step.
questions.correct_explanation: With only 'approve' or 'rescore', a supervisor who thinks a warning is wrong can only ask the model again, note or not, and the rerun may repeat it, so the model still decides and approval becomes a formality. The design must let supervisors reject a warning outright. A second approver, option C, doubles the sign-off, but neither supervisor can overrule the model either.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sampling saves time. But it removes the check the requirements demand for every warning.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because dual approval is a classic check. But two supervisors who can only approve or rescore still leave the model deciding.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because better accuracy means fewer wrong warnings. But accuracy does not let supervisors stop the errors that remain.

tips: Eliminate: D substitutes model accuracy for the human check, and B drops the per-case approval the requirements set.
Final two: A beats C because oversight needs the power to decide against the model; a rescore, note or not, just asks the model again, and a second approver adds a signature, not a choice.
Exam cue: when a design puts a person in the loop, check that they can actually decide against the AI.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.3 Business Requirements and Architecture Fit (a person can oversee a model's recommendation only if the design lets them decide against it, not just approve or rerun it). Completeness review: moved from a council withdrawing disabled parking badges, which mirrored the 2D.1 notes example of officers confirming license suspensions, to a retailer's warnings to warehouse pickers. Blind review: rescore now carries the supervisors' note, so it looks like an override to audit sense; all options now start alike.
