questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Risk tiers from a governance platform
questions.question: A Bruneian energy group's governance platform tiers each model's risk from its code and data types, scanning every account that holds models; the AI policy adopts the tiers. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The platform's tiering rules may not have been validated
options.B: Tiers may ignore what each model decides about people
options.C: Tiers may change whenever a model's code is updated
options.D: Tiers may not reflect each model's accuracy

questions.key_concept: AI risk tiers depend on each use's impact on people and the business, which code and data types alone cannot show.
questions.pre_read: Ask what information each option says the tier should rest on.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI policy tiers uses by impact: the same code and data types can drive a canteen forecast or decisions cutting off customers' gas. A scan sees technical features, not the decisions a model makes, so high-impact uses can be tiered low and escape review. Validating the tiering rules, option A, would confirm they work as designed, but the design itself is blind to impact.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tools that set risk tiers should be validated. But validation confirms the rules run as designed; rules built on code and data types still cannot see impact.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because stable tiers seem reliable. But re-tiering when a model changes is expected, not a weakness.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because accuracy seems to measure risk. But tiers follow each use's impact on people and the business, not accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: C treats re-tiering on change as a flaw, and D ties tiers to accuracy instead of impact.
Final two: B beats A because a tier must reflect what a model decides and for whom; validating rules that read only code and data cannot supply that.
Exam cue: when a tool assigns AI risk tiers, ask whether it can see the use and the people affected.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.3 (Level of risk management activity set by risk tolerance); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (AI risk tiers depend on each use's impact on people and the business, which code and data types alone cannot show). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Requests for new AI uses
questions.question: An Ecuadorian law firm's AI strategy sets drafting goals; partners keep asking IT whether the firm's general-purpose assistant may profile witnesses or opposing parties from social media. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT decide each request as partners raise it
options.B: Have IT set the assistant to refuse profiling requests
options.C: Have management bar AI tools from litigation matters
options.D: Have management state which AI uses are ruled out

questions.key_concept: An AI strategy states the uses the organization will not pursue, so contested uses are settled once, not request by request.
questions.pre_read: Identify who acts in each option before comparing them.
questions.correct_explanation: Profiling witnesses or opposing parties from social media raises legal and ethical questions, and a general-purpose assistant makes such uses easy to try, so requests keep arising. Stating which uses are ruled out gives every partner one answer, set by those accountable, while the drafting the strategy aims for goes on. Barring AI tools from litigation, option C, also stops that drafting and may push lawyers to personal tools where profiling is unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because IT knows the tools. But whether a use is acceptable is a business and ethical decision, not IT's.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a refusal setting is a firm control. But it enforces a choice management has not made, reworded requests can get past it, and other contested uses stay open.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a ban removes the risk at once. But it also stops drafting the strategy aims for, and may push use to personal AI tools the firm cannot see.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves an ethical decision with IT, and B has IT enforce a choice no one accountable has made, which a reworded request can slip past.
Final two: D beats C because ruling out the contested use keeps the drafting the strategy wants; a blanket ban stops that value and may drive use to unseen personal tools.
Exam cue: when the same contested AI use keeps coming up, look for management to rule on the use, not a tool setting or a blanket ban.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.3 (Mission and goals for the AI technology documented); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.2 (Trustworthy AI characteristics built into policies and processes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.1 AI Strategy, Policy and Inventory (an AI strategy states the uses the organization will not pursue, so contested uses are settled once, not request by request). Cross-domain review: re-angled from a purchase-triggered policy (the frame of aaia_d1_027, in a setting shared with CISA d4_209) to uses the strategy rules out. Review round 4: setting moved from jurors (Ecuador has no jury trials) to witnesses and opposing parties; stem names the firm's general-purpose assistant, and runner-up B is now a refusal setting on it. Review round 5: option C now a management ban on AI in litigation, so the key is not the only management option and the shadow-AI and lost-value facts decide; neutral pre_read; principle tag removed (low confidence). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Accountability for an agent's approvals
questions.question: A Mauritanian miner's AI agent approves expense claims with approval rights each site manager delegated to it; the AI inventory names a finance systems lead its owner. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the agent's named owner answer for every approval
options.B: Have the finance team that pays claims answer for them
options.C: Have each manager answer for approvals in their name
options.D: Have the AI governance committee answer for the approvals

questions.key_concept: An agent acting under a person's delegated authority does not take on accountability; the person whose authority it uses still answers for its decisions.
questions.pre_read: Consider each party's role in the approvals.
questions.correct_explanation: Each site manager delegated their own approval rights to the agent, so every approval is that manager's decision, and the manager answers for it as if they had approved it themselves. Delegating to an agent changes who acts, not who answers. Making the agent's named owner answer for every approval, option A, confuses owning the agent's setup, limits and monitoring with owning the decisions made under managers' delegated rights.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because every AI system needs a named owner. But that owner answers for how the agent runs, not for approvals made with rights the managers delegated.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the finance team pays the claims. But paying relies on the approval; it does not own the approval decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the committee oversees AI use. But a committee sets standards and approves uses; it does not answer for each claim approved.

tips: Eliminate: D gives single decisions to a committee, and B gives them to the finance team, which only pays.
Final two: C beats A because each manager delegated their own rights to the agent; owning the agent covers its setup and limits, not the approvals made in managers' names.
Exam cue: when an AI agent acts under someone's authority, that person still answers for what it does.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (an agent acting under a person's delegated authority does not take on accountability; the person whose authority it uses still answers). Completeness review: restated from a 'who holds accountability' stem (as aaia_d1_005, 030) to a recommendation, with the agent's named owner as runner-up instead of its builders. Blind review: the stem now says the managers delegated their rights, the fact that decides C over A. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Switching a chatbot off after hours
questions.question: Only its owner may switch off a Namibian city's drought-rules chatbot; one Saturday it told residents watering was allowed, and IT spent 14 hours reaching the owner. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner let on-call staff disable it on set criteria
options.B: Have internal audit approve any shutdown made after hours
options.C: Have the chatbot learn from residents' complaints about errors
options.D: Have the owner get the vendor to block advice on watering

questions.key_concept: AI harm continues while people wait to approve a shutdown, so owners pre-authorize who may disengage a system, and on what criteria.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option changes the next time something goes wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Because only the owner could switch the chatbot off, it stayed live for the 14 hours IT spent reaching them, while residents could act on the wrong advice. Pre-authorizing on-call staff to disable it when set criteria are met lets harm be stopped within minutes, while the owner stays accountable. Having the vendor block watering advice, option D, fixes this one error but leaves the next harmful answer live just as long.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit is independent. But internal audit assesses controls; it never approves operating decisions such as switching AI off.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complaints reveal errors. But a deployed chatbot does not learn from complaints, and the harm continues meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes the harmful answer. But it fixes one error; the next harmful answer would stay live just as long.

tips: Eliminate: B gives internal audit an operating decision, and C assumes the chatbot learns from complaints.
Final two: A beats D because the gap is who may stop the AI and when; a filter for one error leaves that gap open.
Exam cue: for live AI harm, look for pre-agreed authority to disengage quickly, with the owner still accountable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.4 (Mechanisms and responsibilities to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.2 Ownership, Roles and the AI Governance Committee (AI harm continues while people wait to approve a shutdown, so owners pre-authorize who may disengage a system and on what criteria). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A value figure for a detection model
questions.question: A Jamaican shipping line's AI program reports 'spoilage avoided' as the cargo value of each refrigerated container its failure model flags; the board tracks this as program value. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The figure needs checking by finance outside the AI program
options.B: Wrong flags on sound containers still inflate the figure
options.C: The figure is reliable once flagged container counts hold steady
options.D: The figure must rise as the model grows more accurate

questions.key_concept: A model's flags are predictions, some wrong, so a value metric counting every flag as savings reports activity, not results.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each conclusion against the facts given.
questions.correct_explanation: Every flag is a prediction, and some flagged containers would never have failed, so counting all their cargo as spoilage avoided reports the model's activity, not losses actually prevented, and can grow as wrong flags grow. A results metric counts faults confirmed when flagged units are serviced. Checking by finance, option A, adds independence, but an independent check of a wrongly defined figure still confirms the wrong measure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because independent checking improves reliability. But checking a metric that counts every flag still confirms the wrong measure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because stability seems to show reliability. But a steady count of flagged containers says nothing about how many flags were right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because better models seem to avoid more spoilage. But the figure grows with flags, including wrong ones, not with accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes the total tracks accuracy, and C treats a steady flag count as proof of value.
Final two: B beats A because the metric's definition counts predictions as results; independent checking cannot fix a wrong definition.
Exam cue: an AI value metric built from the model's own flags measures activity; look for confirmed outcomes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.2 (Mechanisms sustain the value of deployed AI)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (a model's flags are predictions, some wrong, so a value metric counting every flag reports activity, not results). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. What an awareness course teaches
questions.question: A Bangladeshi garment maker's AI awareness course calls approved tools, including a general-purpose assistant, safe for any task; staff now use it to rank workers for layoffs. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Replace the course with the firm's general security training
options.B: Have the policy owner update the course whenever tools gain approval
options.C: Have IT block every unlisted tool until its impact is rated
options.D: Have the policy owner teach which uses need review, with examples

questions.key_concept: AI risk depends on the use, not only the tool, so training must teach staff which uses need review, even with approved tools.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option changes for staff.
questions.correct_explanation: A general-purpose assistant takes on a new use with each new prompt, so approving the tool cannot approve its uses: ranking workers for layoffs needs a review that drafting a memo may not. A course calling approved tools safe for any task teaches staff that approval covers every use, so such uses never reach review. Keeping the tool list current, option B, fixes a smaller gap and leaves use-based review untaught.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because security training is well established. But it does not teach which AI uses need review.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because an out-of-date list misleads staff. But the larger gap is that the course never teaches which uses need review.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because blocking stops unapproved tools. But it does not stop high-impact uses of approved tools, and it can push use out of sight.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on blocking, which misses risky uses of approved tools, and A assumes security training covers AI duties.
Final two: D beats B because a general-purpose tool's risk depends on each use; a current tool list cannot teach which uses need review.
Exam cue: awareness content must teach what the AI policy actually requires, which is often about uses, not tools.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.2 (AI risk management training for personnel and partners); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-01 (Personnel given awareness and training)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B.3 Program Metrics, Awareness and Workforce Impact (AI risk depends on the use, not only the tool, so training must teach which uses need review, even with approved tools). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A model that refers some cases
questions.question: A Samoan disaster-relief fund's model decides high-confidence claims within a day and refers others to staff, who take six weeks; its risk assessment counts only wrong decisions. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Wrong decisions on confident claims may go unappealed
options.B: Referred cases may teach the model to grow less confident
options.C: Claimants rare in its training data may face most of the delays
options.D: Referring cases to staff may itself count as automated decision-making

questions.key_concept: Which cases a model refers depends partly on what its training data covered, so referral delays can fall unevenly on groups it saw less of.
questions.pre_read: Consider which concern the facts in the stem support.
questions.correct_explanation: Which claims a model is unsure about is not random: it depends partly on what its training data covered, so referrals, and their six-week wait, can cluster among claimants the data held few of, such as those from outer islands. An assessment counting only wrong decisions misses that harm. Unappealed wrong decisions, option A, would matter, but wrong decisions are already counted and nothing suggests appeals are missing; the delays go uncounted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because automated decisions need an appeal route. But the assessment already counts wrong decisions, and nothing suggests appeals are missing; the uncounted harm is the six-week delay.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models seem to learn from feedback. But the model does not retrain itself from referred cases.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because automated-decision rules worry organizations. But a case a person decides is not a solely automated decision.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes the model learns from referrals by itself, and D treats a staff decision as automated.
Final two: C beats A because referral itself causes harm, and which cases get referred depends partly on what the training data covered; the assessment counts only wrong decisions.
Exam cue: when a model routes some people to a slower path, ask who lands there and what the wait costs them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (which cases a model refers depends partly on what its training data covered, so referral delays can fall unevenly on groups it saw less of). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A risk assessment for a bought model
questions.question: A Finnish town uses a vendor's risk assessment unchanged for its model, trained on another country's data, flagging households at risk of energy debt for support visits. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner assess the risks of its own use
options.B: Accept the assessment, since the vendor knows the model best
options.C: Have the owner get the vendor's bias and accuracy test results
options.D: Have the vendor update its assessment whenever it retrains

questions.key_concept: AI risk depends on the deployer's use, data and the people affected, so a vendor's generic assessment cannot stand in for the owner's own.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would change about the assessment.
questions.correct_explanation: The same model carries different risks in each deployment: which households the town serves, how visits follow flags, and what a missed or wrong flag means locally; a model trained on another country's data may also err differently here. The vendor's assessment reflects its own assumptions, so the town's model owner must assess its own use. The vendor's test results, option C, describe the model, not this town's households and visits.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor built the model. But the vendor cannot know the town's households, process or appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because test results are evidence about the model. But they reflect the vendor's test data, not which households this town flags or what a wrong visit means here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining should trigger reassessment. But a current vendor assessment is still not the town's assessment of its own use.

tips: Eliminate: B hands the risk judgment to the vendor, and D keeps the generic assessment, just fresher.
Final two: A beats C because AI risk depends on the deployer's context; the vendor's test results describe the model, not this use.
Exam cue: a bought model still needs the buyer's own risk assessment for its own use and people.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.1 (Third-party AI risks monitored and controls applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (AI risk depends on the deployer's use, data and the people affected, so a vendor's generic assessment cannot stand in for the owner's own). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. An indicator for an agent's bookings
questions.question: A Montenegrin film studio's AI travel agent books flights and has a staff email login for hotel queries; a daily KRI counts booking-system entries above its spending limit. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The KRI tracks bookings rather than crew satisfaction
options.B: Commitments made through other tools may never be counted
options.C: The spending limit may be set by the owner, not the board
options.D: A daily count may miss a burst of bookings within the day

questions.key_concept: An agent can act through any tool its login reaches, so a KRI reading one system misses commitments made through the others.
questions.pre_read: Consider how each concern would affect the indicator.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent pursues its goal through any tool its login reaches, so it may confirm a hotel room by email when that seems quickest; such bookings never become booking-system entries, so spending above the limit escapes the KRI. The indicator needs sources covering every channel the agent can act through. A daily count, option D, reacts late, but counting the booking system more often still misses email.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because crew satisfaction matters. But that is a performance measure; this indicator watches risk against a spending limit.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because limits sound like risk appetite. But the board approves appetite; an owner setting a use-level limit inside tolerances is expected.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because timing matters for indicators. But counting the booking system more often still misses bookings made by email.

tips: Eliminate: C expects the board to set a use-level limit, and A swaps a risk indicator for a performance measure.
Final two: B beats D because the agent can commit spending through a tool the KRI never reads; counting more often cannot see it.
Exam cue: a KRI on an AI agent's actions must cover every tool the agent can act through.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (an agent can act through any tool its login reaches, so a KRI reading one system misses commitments made through the others). Review round 3: moved to a film studio's travel agent (the property maintenance agent repeated aaia_d2_086); the email login has a stated harmless purpose. Final round: stem now states the KRI is daily, which option D and the explanation assume. Re-audit: stem names the spending limit that the explanations and tip 2 assume. Last pass: option C says spending limit, the limit the stem names. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. An indicator scored by a checker
questions.question: A Tongan national library caps wrong chatbot answers at 2%; its KRI uses a checker that scores answers against the FAQ, skipping those it cannot match. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner drop the KRI until the checker matches every answer
options.B: Have the chatbot report its own confidence as the KRI
options.C: Have senior management tighten the cap on wrong answers to 1%
options.D: Have the owner sample unmatched answers into the error rate

questions.key_concept: A KRI must cover the outputs most likely to be wrong; excluding unscorable answers removes exactly the risky ones.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option changes about the indicator.
questions.correct_explanation: Answers the checker cannot match to the FAQ are the ones the chatbot generated beyond its approved content, where errors are most likely, yet the KRI leaves them out, so it can stay under 2% while wrong answers grow. Sampling them into the rate restores coverage. Tightening the cap, option C, sets a stricter limit on a measure that still misses the riskiest answers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an incomplete indicator misleads. But dropping it leaves no measure meanwhile; fixing its coverage keeps the warning.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confidence is easy to collect. But a model can be confidently wrong, so its own confidence is no error measure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a stricter cap seems safer. But a tighter limit on an incomplete measure still misses the answers most likely to be wrong.

tips: Eliminate: A removes the only indicator instead of fixing its coverage, and B trusts the model's own confidence as an error measure.
Final two: D beats C because the KRI leaves out the riskiest answers; a tighter cap on the same partial count does not see them.
Exam cue: when an indicator skips what its checker cannot score, the skipped items are often where the risk is.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (a KRI must cover the outputs most likely to be wrong; leaving out answers a checker cannot score removes exactly the risky ones). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Buying a company for its model
questions.question: A Uruguayan road-construction group, which holds many photos of its own roads, will buy a start-up for its pavement-crack model, trained on photos former partner councils supplied. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the group fine-tune it on its own road photos
options.B: Have the start-up's source code placed in escrow
options.C: Have counsel confirm rights to the photos behind the model
options.D: Rely on the start-up's warranty that its model is lawful

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning on clean data keeps what a model learned from earlier data, so rights to that data decide whether a bought model is usable.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would leave unresolved.
questions.correct_explanation: The deal's value rests on a model trained on the councils' photos; if the start-up lacked rights to train on them, or those rights ended with the partnerships, the group could be forced to stop using the model and lose the asset it paid for. Fine-tuning on the group's own road photos, option A, adds learning on top, but the weights still carry what the councils' photos taught.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the group's many photos seem to dilute the partners' share. But fine-tuning starts from the existing weights, which keep what the partners' photos taught.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because escrow protects continuity. But source code cannot rebuild a trained model or fix its data rights.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because warranties shift some liability. But a warranty cannot keep a model in use if the data owners or a regulator force its withdrawal.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on the seller's promise, and B escrows code that cannot rebuild a trained model.
Final two: C beats A because fine-tuning builds on weights shaped by the partners' photos; however many photos the group adds, only confirmed rights settle whether the model can be used.
Exam cue: when buying an AI asset, confirm rights to the data it learned from; more training on clean data does not remove what it learned.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (a model built on data without rights to use it can be ordered withdrawn, so data rights decide whether a bought model is worth anything). Review round 3: stem states the group holds many photos of its own, so fine-tuning is the runner-up the AI fact defeats; explanations no longer call the photos disputed. Final round: moved from a mining group's ore-grading model (setting of aaia_d2_058) to a road-construction group's pavement-crack model (a telecom tower-defect model was rejected as near aaia_d2_140); key names the photos behind the model, not the group's own photos. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A vendor speech model for a charity
questions.question: A Ghanaian literacy charity will license a speech model to score children reading aloud; its vendor says children's voices were in training and cites 95% test accuracy. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner measure its accuracy for a sample of children
options.B: Have the vendor's contract promise accuracy for young readers
options.C: Have the vendor say how many child recordings it trained on
options.D: Rely on it, since children were in its training data

questions.key_concept: Data in training is not evidence of performance; only testing on the people a model will serve shows how well it works for them.
questions.pre_read: Consider what evidence each option would produce.
questions.correct_explanation: Including children's voices in training does not show the model scores children accurately, and the vendor's 95% does not say whose reading it measured; only results on children, the people it will judge, can show that. The owner should test it with children before relying on it. Asking how many child recordings were used, option C, describes the inputs but still gives no measured accuracy for children.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because contracts shift some liability. But a promise is not a test result, and children would be scored wrongly before any claim succeeded.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the amount of child data seems relevant. But knowing how much was used still gives no measured accuracy for children.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training on children sounds sufficient. But being in the training data is not a test result.

tips: Eliminate: D treats training data as proof of performance, and B relies on a contractual promise instead of measured results.
Final two: A beats C because only results the owner can check on children show performance; more detail from the vendor is still not a test.
Exam cue: 'it was trained on X' is not 'it works on X'; ask for results on the people it will serve.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Cataloging an assistant's log
questions.question: A Paraguayan freight broker's IT team will catalog its in-house generative assistant's log of prompts and answers as an ordinary system log, rated internal. Which basis for its classification should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: The rating of the broker's other system logs
options.B: The most sensitive data staff may type into it
options.C: The classification of the model's training data
options.D: The rating its hosting provider gives the service

questions.key_concept: A generative assistant's prompt log holds whatever users type, so it takes the classification of the most sensitive data they may enter.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option bases the rating on.
questions.correct_explanation: Unlike a log of system events, a generative assistant's log keeps the full text staff type and the answers built from it, which can include client, contract or personal details. Because it holds whatever staff enter, it must be classified at the most sensitive level they are allowed to enter and protected to match. Rating it like the broker's other system logs, option A, judges it by the tool, not by its contents.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs usually record events, not content. But this log keeps the full text staff type, so its contents set its rating.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because training data shapes the model's answers. But the log holds what staff type, not the data the model learned from.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider runs the service. But classification is the data owner's decision, based on what the log holds.

tips: Eliminate: D hands the rating to the provider instead of the data owner, and C rates the log by the model's training data, not by what it stores.
Final two: B beats A because a prompt log stores the full text staff enter, not just events; its rating must follow the most sensitive data allowed in.
Exam cue: when AI creates a new store of data, classify it by what users can put into it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)

Completeness review: replaced a frame on who decides a new use of a model trained on shared data (as aaia_d1_040, 074) with the classification of a prompt log. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. An assistant over internal documents
questions.question: A Vietnamese software reseller's new staff assistant answers from all 12,000 documents rated 'internal', which every employee may already open; IT rates the assistant internal too. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT log each question and answer for later review
options.B: Have data owners recheck each document's 'internal' rating
options.C: Have staff check each answer against its source documents
options.D: Have data owners rate what the documents reveal together

questions.key_concept: An assistant that draws on many documents can reveal in combination what no single document states, so its sensitivity is judged on the combination.
questions.pre_read: Consider which risk each option addresses.
questions.correct_explanation: Each document may rightly be rated internal, yet an assistant that searches all 12,000 and summarizes across them can assemble conclusions none states alone, such as a plan pieced together from scattered notes. Rating the assistant like its parts ignores that, so data owners should rate what the documents reveal together and set access to match. Rechecking each document's rating, option B, cannot find exposure that exists only in combination.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs help investigate misuse. But logging records answers after they are given; it does not judge how sensitive they are.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because ratings drive access. But each document can be rated correctly while answers drawn from many reveal more than any one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because answers should match their sources. But an accurate answer can still reveal what only the combination exposes.

tips: Eliminate: C checks accuracy, not exposure, and A records answers without judging what they reveal.
Final two: D beats B because an assistant can join scattered facts into new conclusions; ratings that are right for each document miss what they reveal together.
Exam cue: when AI draws on many sources at once, judge sensitivity by what the combination reveals.

Completeness review: replaced incentive-biased labels (as aaia_d2_305) with what documents reveal in combination. Blind review: key shortened so it is no longer the longest option. questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Releasing a model trained on case records
questions.question: A South African domestic-violence support network will publish the weights of a model trained on its clients' case records; its privacy assessment found the records well de-identified. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner re-test the records for re-identification risk
options.B: Rely on the assessment, since the records are well de-identified
options.C: Have the owner test what the model reveals about individuals
options.D: Have the owner add noise to the answers the model returns

questions.key_concept: Membership inference starts from a known person and tests whether their record trained a model, so de-identification cannot protect membership.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would examine.
questions.correct_explanation: Membership inference starts from a known person and tests whether their record trained the model; as every record belongs to someone who sought help for domestic violence, a match reveals it, and published weights allow unlimited probing. De-identification cannot stop this, because the attacker supplies the person. Relying on the assessment, option B, trusts a review of the records, not of what the released model reveals.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because de-identified records can later be re-identified. But the assessment already covered the records; the exposure is what the released model reveals.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a privacy assessment found the records well de-identified. But an attacker who already knows a person can test whether that person's record trained the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because noise on outputs can blunt inference. But anyone running the published weights gets answers the owner never touches.

tips: Eliminate: A re-tests records the assessment already covered, and D adds noise the owner cannot apply to copies run from published weights.
Final two: C beats B because membership inference probes the model with a known person; however well the records are de-identified, they cannot show what the released weights reveal.
Exam cue: when a model trained on sensitive records is released, assess what the model reveals, not only the records.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4.2 (Membership Inference); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (membership inference uses a model to learn whether a person's record trained it, and when every record shares a sensitive trait, membership reveals it). Review round 3: moved from HIV patients (near aaia_d2_044) to a domestic-violence support network; stem states the records passed a de-identification review, so relying on it is the runner-up. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. An agent that profiles applicants
questions.question: A Canadian babysitting app's AI agent searches the web about each sitter applicant and writes a profile for parents from whatever it finds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner limit collection to what vetting needs
options.B: Allow it, since anything published online is free to use
options.C: Have IT encrypt the profiles stored for parents
options.D: Have staff check each profile's facts before parents see it

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design limits what an AI agent collects to the purpose; an agent searching freely can gather details nobody needed or should hold.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would change about the profiles.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent told to use whatever it finds can gather health posts, family details, religion or old disputes unrelated to whether someone can safely mind children, and hand them to parents who may then discriminate. Collection must be limited, by design, to what vetting needs. Fact-checking each profile, option D, makes the details more accurate, but accurate details that should never have been collected still harm applicants.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the information is public. But being online does not make collecting and using it lawful or fair.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption protects stored data. But it does not limit what was collected or how parents use it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because profiles may contain errors. But checking accuracy does not stop the agent collecting details vetting never needed.

tips: Eliminate: B treats public data as free to use, and C protects storage without limiting collection.
Final two: A beats D because the harm is collecting what vetting never needed; accurate profiles can still be excessive.
Exam cue: for agents that gather personal data on their own, look for limits on what they may collect, set by purpose.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (privacy by design limits what an AI agent collects to the purpose; an agent searching freely can gather details nobody needed). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure and a provider's base model
questions.question: A Slovak news site's chatbot, calling a provider's base model through an API, keeps stating a resident's home address from its training data; the resident seeks erasure. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner retrain the chatbot's model without the address
options.B: Have the owner filter the address out of the chatbot's replies
options.C: Delete the chat logs that mention the resident's address
options.D: Tell the resident that erasure is the provider's duty alone

questions.key_concept: A deployer cannot retrain a provider's base model, but can filter outputs and raise the request with the provider, which can act on the model.
questions.pre_read: Consider each option's effect on what readers see.
questions.correct_explanation: The address sits in the provider's base model, which the news site reaches only through an API and cannot retrain, yet the site answers for what its chatbot tells readers. Filtering the address out of replies stops the harm now; the owner should also alert the provider, which can act on the model. Retraining, option A, would be the thorough fix in principle, but the site has no means to retrain a provider's base model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining removes learned data. But a site calling the provider's base model through an API cannot retrain it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the logs hold the address. But deleting logs leaves the model repeating it to the next reader.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider trained the model. But the site deploys the chatbot and answers for what it tells readers.

tips: Eliminate: D passes the duty to the provider, and C deletes records while the model keeps repeating the address.
Final two: B beats A because the site cannot retrain a provider's base model; filtering its own outputs is the control it holds, with the provider alerted.
Exam cue: when erased data lives in a model you cannot retrain, filter outputs and involve whoever controls the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-15 (Information Output Filtering)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (a deployer cannot retrain a provider's base model, but can filter outputs and raise the request with the provider, which controls the model). Last pass: stem says the chatbot calls the base model through an API, the fact behind 'cannot retrain'. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Tuning on patient emails
questions.question: A Croatian fertility clinic will fine-tune its reply model on patient emails, full of names and treatment details, to learn its writing style, retraining per erasure request. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Hold erasure requests until the next scheduled retrain
options.B: Tune on emails from patients who have consented
options.C: Tune on the emails, as tuning keeps patterns, not text
options.D: Remove personal data from the emails before tuning

questions.key_concept: Removing personal data before training is privacy by design; it keeps most erasure requests from reaching the model.
questions.pre_read: Consider each option's effect on the model and on the patients.
questions.correct_explanation: The model needs only the writing style, so removing names, treatment details and other personal data before tuning keeps most of it out of the model, and later erasure requests rarely reach it; because removal from free text misses some details, the owner still checks what slips through. Consent-only tuning, option B, gives a lawful basis, but patients can later withdraw or seek erasure, with their details already in the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because batching cuts retraining cost. But the model may keep repeating the patient's details until then, and erasure should not wait on a schedule.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consent gives a lawful basis. But patients can withdraw consent or ask for erasure later, and their details would already sit in the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tuning for style seems to learn general patterns. But tuned models can memorize rare details, such as names and treatments, and repeat them.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes tuning keeps no text, and A leaves patients' details in the model until a scheduled retrain.
Final two: D beats B because consent can be withdrawn, and details already learned need a retrain to remove; keeping them out of training avoids that.
Exam cue: for erasure and AI, prefer designs that keep personal data out of the model in the first place.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (removing personal data before training keeps most erasure requests from reaching the model). Review round 3: stem states the model is tuned to learn writing style, so the personal details are not needed. questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Fairness criteria in a new market
questions.question: A Singaporean lender's fairness criteria for its loan-limit model compare outcomes by sex and age, set for its home market; the model will now serve borrowers in India. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner revalidate accuracy on Indian borrowers' loan records
options.B: Keep the criteria, since sex and age apply in every market
options.C: Have the owner revise which groups the criteria protect in India
options.D: Drop the criteria until Indian outcome data builds up

questions.key_concept: Which groups fairness criteria must protect depends on context; perceptions of fairness and patterns of discrimination differ across cultures and markets.
questions.pre_read: Consider which step the others depend on.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness criteria are set for a context: groups at risk of discrimination in India, such as by caste, religion or region, are not covered by sex and age alone, so testing against the old criteria could pass a model that harms them. The owner should revise the criteria first. Revalidating accuracy, option A, is needed too, but without suitable criteria no test can show the model treats those groups fairly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a new market needs fresh validation. But tests should follow criteria that fit the new market's groups, so the criteria come first.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sex and age are common protected groups. But which groups face discrimination differs between markets.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fairness testing needs data. But dropping the criteria leaves the model with no fairness test at all.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes fairness groups are universal, and D drops the criteria instead of adapting them.
Final two: C beats A because criteria must fit the context before tests against them mean anything; accuracy checks cannot show fairness to groups nobody named.
Exam cue: when an AI system moves to a new market or population, revisit its fairness criteria before retesting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (which groups fairness criteria must protect depends on context, so criteria are revisited before a model moves to a new market). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Fairness figures for a subsidy model
questions.question: A Moldovan heating-subsidy fund's model, used only through its smartphone app, has equal approval and error rates across applicants' ethnic groups. Under the NIST AI RMF, what is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Fairness also depends on who never gets to apply
options.B: Equal approval and error rates show the model is fair
options.C: Some applicants' recorded ethnicity may be wrong
options.D: Ethnicity data should be left out of any fairness test

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF notes that balanced predictions across groups do not make a system fair if some people cannot access it.
questions.pre_read: Consider what the reported rates can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: The rates describe only people who applied through the app; households without smartphones or digital skills never reach the model, so balanced results among applicants cannot show the subsidy reaches people fairly. The NIST AI RMF notes that balanced predictions can coexist with inaccessibility and the digital divide. Wrong ethnicity records, option C, would weaken the comparison, but even perfect records describe only applicants already counted.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because equal rates are a common fairness test. But they cover only applicants, not those the app excludes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fairness tests depend on accurate group labels. But even perfect labels describe only people who applied through the app.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ethnicity data is sensitive. But fairness testing can use such data lawfully; avoiding it hides bias.

tips: Eliminate: B treats balanced rates as proof of fairness, and D rules out the data fairness testing needs.
Final two: A beats C because the NIST AI RMF says balanced predictions do not make a system fair if some people cannot access it; better ethnicity records still cover only app users.
Exam cue: before trusting fairness figures, ask who never reached the AI system at all.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (balanced predictions across groups do not make a system fair if some people cannot access it, as with the digital divide). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. An impact assessment a law requires
questions.question: An AI law requires public bodies using high-risk AI to assess fundamental-rights impacts; a Luxembourg housing agency cites its data protection impact assessment for its high-risk tenant-priority model. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The vendor may not have done its own rights impact assessments
options.B: Non-privacy rights, such as non-discrimination, may be missed
options.C: The duty may start once the model has caused harm
options.D: The data protection assessment may be out of date for the model

questions.key_concept: A data protection impact assessment covers personal data; a fundamental-rights assessment also covers harms such as discrimination and loss of access to services.
questions.pre_read: Read the duty's wording before the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The law asks for an assessment of impact on fundamental rights, which reach beyond data protection to non-discrimination, access to housing and effective remedy. A data protection impact assessment examines personal data handling, so it may support the duty but can leave unassessed whether the model disadvantages some tenants. An outdated data protection assessment, option D, is a weakness, but even a current one would cover only data protection.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors document their models. But the duty falls on the body using the AI, for its own use, whatever the vendor did.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some legal duties follow incidents. But an impact assessment is done before use, to find harms before they happen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because assessments must be current. But a fully current data protection assessment still covers only data protection, not the wider rights the law names.

tips: Eliminate: C treats an up-front assessment as triggered by harm, and A looks to the vendor for a duty that falls on the agency.
Final two: B beats D because a data protection assessment, however current, does not cover rights such as non-discrimination that the law names.
Exam cue: map each legal duty to evidence that covers its full scope; a related assessment is not automatically the required one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.1 (Intended purposes, context and laws documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (a privacy impact assessment covers personal data; a fundamental-rights assessment also covers harms such as discrimination). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Crawling websites for training
questions.question: A Portuguese travel-guide publisher crawls tourism websites to train its guide-writing model, relying on a text and data mining copyright exception; its crawler never reads sites' machine-readable signals. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Opt-out signals may keep useful tourism pages out of training
options.B: Crawled copies may be kept longer than the exception allows
options.C: Training may be unlawful for pages whose owners opted out
options.D: The crawled pages may hold personal data about the travelers

questions.key_concept: Where copyright law allows text and data mining unless rights holders opt out, ignoring their machine-readable opt-outs can put training outside the exception.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each concern would put at stake for the publisher.
questions.correct_explanation: Some copyright laws, including in the EU, allow text and data mining for commercial purposes only where rights holders have not reserved their rights, for example through machine-readable opt-outs. A crawler that ignores those signals can take the training outside the exception the publisher relies on. Personal data on the pages, option D, needs assessing too, but it does not decide whether the copying is lawful at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because opted-out pages shrink the training set. But honoring opt-outs is a condition of the exception; how much data remains is a design question, not the main exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the exception can limit how long copies are kept. But copies made against an opt-out fall outside it from the start, however briefly they are kept.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because web pages can hold personal data. But the publisher's legal basis for copying depends on honoring opt-outs, which the crawler never reads.

tips: Eliminate: A treats opt-outs as lost training data rather than a legal condition, and B worries about retention when the copying itself falls outside the exception.
Final two: C beats D because ignoring opt-outs can remove the legal basis for all the copying; personal data is a separate check.
Exam cue: when training relies on a legal exception, check that its conditions are actually met.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (where copyright law allows text and data mining unless rights holders opt out, ignoring machine-readable opt-outs can take training outside the exception). Review round 3: option B now claims deleting copies cures ignored opt-outs (the paywall wording was a subset of the key). Final round: options A and B rewritten as concerns, parallel with C and D; neutral pre_read. Re-audit: key reworded so 'site' is not echoed only in it. Last pass: stem says the crawler never reads machine-readable signals, so knowing these carry opt-outs decides. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 14, 25 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A certificate offered as evidence
questions.question: An ISO/IEC 42001:2023-certified Emirati courier's statement of applicability excludes data controls for its vendor-trained parcel-damage model, which it tunes monthly on its own photos. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The certifying body may not itself be accredited
options.B: The courier's certificate omits the vendor's own photos
options.C: Clients may read the certificate as covering data controls
options.D: The courier's own photos may have no data controls

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning is training, so a deployer that tunes a bought model on its own data needs data controls for that data.
questions.pre_read: Read each fact in the stem before the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Excluding data controls might suit a model only a vendor trains, but the courier tunes this one every month on its own photos, so its own data shapes how damage is judged, possibly with no controls over quality, labeling or rights. That clients may read the certificate as covering data controls, option C, is a weaker concern: the controls themselves may be missing for data the courier trains on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a certificate's value depends on the certifier. But even an accredited certificate covers nothing the courier excluded.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor trained the model. But no buyer's certificate covers a vendor's own processes; that is due diligence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because certificates are often read as covering more than their scope. But that matters less than whether the data the courier now trains on has any controls.

tips: Eliminate: A questions the certifier, which cannot add excluded controls, and B expects the courier's certificate to cover the vendor's own data.
Final two: D beats C because fine-tuning makes the courier a trainer; how others read the certificate matters less than training data with no controls.
Exam cue: fine-tuning a bought model is training; check that the deployer's data controls cover the data it tunes on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.4 (Risk management process established through transparent policies and controls); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped)

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A bias review under the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: A Czech mining authority's NIST AI RMF bias review of its quarry dust-check model checked data balance and regional error rates; inspectors choose which flagged quarries to visit. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The review shows no bias, as data and error rates balance
options.B: Balance may not hold after the model's next retraining
options.C: The review omits bias in how inspectors act on outputs
options.D: The framework needs zero bias before inspectors use any model

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF names three bias categories: systemic, computational and statistical, and human-cognitive, which includes how people act on AI outputs.
questions.pre_read: Read what the review checked before the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Data balance and error rates address computational and statistical bias, one of the three categories the NIST AI RMF names. Human-cognitive bias, such as inspectors visiting flagged quarries in some areas more readily, sits outside the review, as does systemic bias in which sites get inspected, so biased outcomes can arise around a balanced model. A later retrain, option B, could undo the balance found, but the review already misses those categories now.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because balance and equal errors are standard tests. But they cover only computational and statistical bias.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining can change a model's errors. But that is a later risk to the checks done; the review already misses how inspectors act on flags.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the framework stresses managing bias. But it seeks harmful bias managed, not zero bias, and it is voluntary.

tips: Eliminate: D misstates the framework as demanding zero bias, and A treats statistical checks as covering all bias.
Final two: C beats B because the review misses whole categories of bias now, including how people act on outputs; a future retrain is a separate, later risk.
Exam cue: the NIST AI RMF's bias categories are systemic, computational and statistical, and human-cognitive; check a review covers all three.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An agent that works through web portals
questions.question: A Liberian aid charity's AI agent works out its own steps to file monthly grant reports in each donor's web portal; donors redesign their portals often. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: A changed page may lead it to submit wrong entries unnoticed
options.B: A changed page may stop it and leave reports late
options.C: Each page it reads may retrain its underlying model
options.D: Its report wording may vary from one month to the next

questions.key_concept: A scripted bot usually stops when a page changes; an agent plans its steps, so it can adapt and file wrong entries that look complete.
questions.pre_read: Picture the first month after a donor redesigns its portal.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent plans its own steps, so when a portal changes it adapts instead of stopping: it may put figures in the wrong fields or skip a section and still submit, with nothing showing the report is wrong. A halt, option B, is how scripted bots usually fail; a late report is visible and can be fixed, while a wrong one filed with a donor looks complete.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scripted bots break when pages change. But an agent adapts and carries on, so its failures are quiet wrong entries, not visible stops.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the agent seems to learn as it works. But reading pages does not retrain its model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because generated text varies from run to run. But varied wording is harmless if the entries are right; wrong entries are the risk.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the agent retrains as it reads pages, and D worries about wording, not whether the entries are right.
Final two: A beats B because an agent adapts around a change and can file wrong work that looks complete; a halt is visible and fixable.
Exam cue: when an agent works through screens that change, ask how it fails, not only whether it stops.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An audit program reused for a new kind of AI
questions.question: An IS auditor's work program for a Gibraltar marine insurer's new generative assistant, which drafts claim-decision letters, reuses the program for its fraud model: accuracy on a labeled holdout set. Which addition is MOST important?

options.A: Checks that each draft follows the insurer's letter template
options.B: Tests of accuracy on recent claims rather than older ones
options.C: Checks that adjusters' edits retrain the assistant weekly
options.D: Checks that each draft's statements match the claim file

questions.key_concept: The kind of AI decides the evidence: generated letters need checking against source records, which label accuracy on a holdout set cannot show.
questions.pre_read: Consider what evidence each option would add to the program.
questions.correct_explanation: A predictive model is tested by comparing its labels with known answers, but a generative assistant writes new text, which can state reasons, dates or amounts that no claim file supports. No holdout label measures that, so the program needs checks of drafts against the file. Testing on recent claims, option B, refines the predictive test, yet recent labels still cannot show what a letter invents.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because letters must look consistent. But layout checks cannot show whether a letter's statements match the claim file.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recent data shows current performance. But it still measures labels, not whether a letter's statements match the file.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tools seem to learn from corrections. But edits retrain nothing unless a retrain is run, and that would still not test what letters state.

tips: Eliminate: A checks layout rather than content, and C assumes edits retrain the assistant.
Final two: D beats B because generated letters must be checked against source records; label accuracy, recent or not, cannot show invented content.
Exam cue: when an audit moves from a predictive model to a generative one, add checks of output against source records.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A model that ranks late filers
questions.question: An Antiguan tax office's model ranks businesses by risk of filing late; officers phone top-ranked businesses before each deadline, and it retrains on which businesses later filed late. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Firms' filing records may hold tax data needing protection
options.B: It may learn the traits of firms officers called as safe
options.C: It may update its ranking from officers' daily call notes
options.D: Each retrain may change rankings without the owner's review

questions.key_concept: Acting on a model's predictions changes the outcomes it later learns from, so retraining can teach it that the risks it prevented were safe.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option assumes about how the model learns.
questions.correct_explanation: If officers' calls prompt firms to file on time, retraining sees risky firms labeled 'filed on time' and can learn their traits as safe. Rankings would then drop similar firms nobody has called, which may then miss deadlines. Reviewing each retrain, option D, rightly treats retraining as a change, but nothing says review is missing, and a reviewed retrain still learns from labels the officers' calls rewrote.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because filing records are confidential tax data. But protecting them does not stop the ranking learning the wrong lesson.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models seem to learn as they are used. But it learns only when retrained, not from daily call notes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a retrain is a change that needs review. But nothing given says review is missing, and a reviewed retrain still learns from labels the calls altered.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the model learns from daily use, and A raises data protection rather than how the model learns.
Final two: B beats D because acting on predictions changes the outcomes the model retrains on; reviewing each retrain would not reveal labels the calls altered.
Exam cue: when people act on a model's flags, ask what those actions do to the labels it learns from next.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A pension fund's withdrawal screen
questions.question: A Palauan pension fund holds for fraud review any withdrawal request its anomaly-detection model scores as unusual; it was trained on past requests. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Honest members making rare requests may be held most often
options.B: Staff may be unable to explain holds to the members affected
options.C: The model may retrain itself on each request it scores
options.D: Members' records may hold personal data needing protection

questions.key_concept: An anomaly model learns what is common, so it flags what is rare, whether honest or wrong.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option assumes about the model.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that learns only what past requests usually look like flags what is rare, not what is false. Honest members whose requests are uncommon, such as a hardship withdrawal or a first payment after retirement, may be held again and again, and each hold delays their money. Unexplained holds, option B, are a real gap, but the larger harm is honest members held simply for being unusual.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people whose requests are held deserve reasons. But the deeper flaw is what the model flags: rarity, not fraud, so honest uncommon members bear the holds.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some models update as they run. But nothing in the stem says this one does, and it would still flag what is rare.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pension records hold personal data. But protecting the records does not change whom the model holds.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the model learns from each request, and D raises data protection rather than whom the model flags.
Final two: A beats B because a model trained on past requests flags what is rare, not what is false, so honest uncommon members are held; explaining holds would not change who is held.
Exam cue: when a model flags what is unusual, ask who is honest but uncommon.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A photo tool for property listings
questions.question: A Sardinian holiday-rental agency will let staff stage empty rooms in listing photos with a generative editing tool, prompting each edit in plain words. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner mark every edited photo as changed by AI
options.B: Have the owner rely on the vendor's terms on allowed edits
options.C: Have the owner set which photo changes are allowed
options.D: Have staff review each edited photo before the listing goes live

questions.key_concept: A generative editing tool can make far more changes than planned, so the owner first sets allowed edits; reviewers need those limits to check against.
questions.pre_read: Consider which step the others depend on.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative editing tool can do far more than stage a room: a plain-words prompt can as easily erase stains or brighten a view, hiding defects guests would care about. The owner must first state the tool's intended purpose and the edits it must never make. Staff review, option D, adds a check, but without stated limits each reviewer decides alone what a fair edit is.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disclosure is a common answer to AI content. But a label tells guests a photo changed, not that a defect was erased.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors set usage terms. But the agency answers for its listings, so it sets the limits for its own use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a person checks every photo. But with no stated limits, reviewers have nothing consistent to check edits against.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a label as making any edit acceptable, and B hands the agency's limits to the vendor.
Final two: C beats D because reviewers need stated limits to check against; without them, each decides alone what a fair edit is.
Exam cue: when a generative tool can do more than the planned task, look for stated limits before labels or reviews.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Other parties' AI tools in meetings
questions.question: An Isle of Man financial regulator's AI policy covers staff's own tools; licensees now join confidential video meetings with AI note-takers that send transcripts to outside providers. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Leave the note-takers to licensees, since the tools are theirs
options.B: Have management set rules for guests' note-takers on its calls
options.C: Have IT switch off note-taking in the regulator's own video app
options.D: Have each licensee's provider delete transcripts after every meeting

questions.key_concept: A policy written for staff's own tools misses AI that outside parties bring, such as note-takers that join meetings and send transcripts to their providers.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would reach in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: Guests' AI note-takers join as participants and send transcripts to outside providers the licensees chose, so switching off the regulator's own note-taking feature does not stop them. Its policy must say when staff refuse, remove or allow them, especially in confidential sessions. Switching off note-taking in its own app, option C, controls the regulator's tool, not the bots licensees bring to the call.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tools belong to licensees. But the confidential content is the regulator's, so it must set the rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a technical switch looks decisive. But it turns off only the regulator's own note-taking feature, not the note-takers guests bring.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because deletion limits exposure. But the providers serve licensees, so the regulator may have no way to make them delete anything.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on providers the regulator has no hold over, and A leaves its confidential content to others' tools.
Final two: B beats C because guests' note-takers are not the regulator's feature; a rule on when to admit or remove them reaches those bots, while the switch reaches only its own app.
Exam cue: when AI arrives through someone else's tool, look for a rule on its use, not a setting on your own systems.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.4 (Risk management process established through transparent policies and controls); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property)
