questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A policy on what staff paste into chatbots
questions.question: A Comorian ylang-ylang distiller's AI policy only bars pasting buyer data into public chatbots; sales staff use one to draft buyer emails quoting oil purity and certifications. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the provider confirm it does not train on staff's prompts
options.B: Have IT monitor prompts for buyer data sent to the chatbot
options.C: Leave email content to each sales manager's judgment
options.D: Have management set rules for checking claims the chatbot writes

questions.key_concept: A generative tool can invent facts in what it writes, so an AI policy that covers only what staff paste in leaves its output unchecked.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option changes about how staff work.
questions.correct_explanation: A chatbot writes fluent text that can state purity figures or certifications the distiller never had, and buyers may rely on them. A policy that only bars pasting buyer data controls what goes in, not what goes out under the distiller's name, so it needs rules for checking claims before emails are sent. Monitoring prompts, option B, enforces the existing rule, yet leaves invented claims in sent emails unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because training on prompts is a real input risk. But it concerns what goes in, not claims the chatbot invents in drafts.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because monitoring shows whether the rule is kept. But the rule covers only inputs; invented claims in drafts would still go out.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because managers know their buyers. But it sets no rule for checking what the chatbot states.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves claims to each manager with no rule, and A secures inputs while the larger risk lies in what is written.
Final two: D beats B because the chatbot can invent purity figures and certifications; monitoring prompts enforces an input rule but checks nothing the drafts state.
Exam cue: when an AI policy covers only what goes into a generative tool, look for rules on what comes out.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.2 (Trustworthy AI characteristics built into policies and processes); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A second approver for payments
questions.question: An Armenian dried-fruit exporter's payments over $50,000 need two approvers; after a clerk approves, an AI agent reading the same invoice and emails gives the second. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a named person sign the second approval on each payment
options.B: Have a second agent on another provider's model check this one
options.C: Have the agent tested on invoices carrying planted instructions
options.D: Have the agent's vendor answer for any wrong payment approvals

questions.key_concept: A second approval needs a person who answers for it; an AI agent cannot be held to account and may share the first approver's inputs.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option changes about the approval step.
questions.correct_explanation: Dual approval exists so a second accountable person checks the payment. An agent cannot be held to account, and because it reads the same invoice and emails as the clerk, a planted instruction or bad record that misled the clerk can pass both. A named person restores the control. Testing the agent on planted instructions, option C, measures one threat, but a well-tested agent is still nobody who answers for a payment.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because different models make different mistakes. But another agent is still not an accountable approver.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because planted instructions are the agent's main threat. But a well-tested agent is still nobody who answers for a payment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors supply the agent. But accountability for payments cannot pass to a vendor.

tips: Eliminate: B treats more models as more independence, and D hands accountability to a vendor.
Final two: A beats C because dual control needs a person who answers for the approval; testing measures the agent but does not make it accountable.
Exam cue: when AI fills a role in a two-person control, ask who answers for the decision.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 3.2 (Roles defined for human-AI configurations and oversight)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Wrong answers from a rules assistant
questions.question: A Greenlandic hunting-permit office's assistant answers from rules its policy team owns; after wrong answers, the team says it owns only the documents, IT only the platform. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT own the answers, as it runs the platform
options.B: Have senior management name an owner for the answers
options.C: Have the platform's vendor answer for wrong replies
options.D: Have IT show the source rule beside every answer

questions.key_concept: Owning the documents an assistant draws on is not owning its answers, which can misstate correct documents; someone must answer for the answers.
questions.pre_read: List each party in the stem and what it controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant writes its own answers, which can misstate or merge correct rules. The policy team is the data owner of the documents and IT the custodian of the platform, but neither role covers what people are told. Senior management must name an owner accountable for the answers. Showing each answer's source rule, option D, helps people check, yet an answer can misstate the rule beside it, and still no one is accountable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because IT runs the system. But running a platform does not make IT the owner of business answers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor supplies the platform. But accountability for the answers stays with the office.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because citing sources supports checking. But a generated answer can misstate the rule it cites, and a link leaves no one accountable for the answer.

tips: Eliminate: C hands accountability to a vendor, and A makes IT the owner by default.
Final two: B beats D because generated answers can misstate the rules they cite; a source link aids checking but leaves the answers without an owner.
Exam cue: for an assistant over documents, look for an owner of its answers, not only of its sources.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Renewals split between a model and staff
questions.question: A Bahamian passport office's model approves the 70% of renewals it is surest of; staff settle the rest, still measured by the 40-a-day target set before launch. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Approved applicants may not be told a model decided
options.B: The model may retrain itself on the cases staff settle
options.C: Staff may rush the hardest cases to keep their daily pace
options.D: Staff may lose skills once built on routine renewals

questions.key_concept: A model that decides the cases it is surest of leaves staff the hardest ones, so targets set on the old case mix stop fitting.
questions.pre_read: Consider which concern the facts in the stem support.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that approves the cases it is surest of leaves staff the unusual and hardest renewals, so a target set on the old mix now demands more hard cases per day, inviting rushed or wrong decisions. Lost skills on routine renewals, option D, are a real risk over years; the unchanged target bears on every hard case staff settle from now on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because people should know when AI decides. But these are approvals in their favor; the harder cases staff now decide carry the risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models seem to learn from use. But it learns only when retrained, not from each case staff settle.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because routine work builds skill. But that loss builds over years, while the old target bears on every hard case now.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes the model learns from each case, and A worries about notice on favorable approvals.
Final two: C beats D because the model leaves staff the hardest cases, so an old pace target harms decisions now; skill loss builds more slowly.
Exam cue: when AI takes the easy cases, check that staff targets and training fit the harder work left.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A voice-cloning feature for learners
questions.question: A Laotian language app will let learners clone any voice from a short clip for dialogue practice; its risk review covers learners' data and clone quality. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner encrypt learners' uploaded clips while they are stored
options.B: Have the owner add a notice that clones are for practice use
options.C: Have the owner get learners' consent before storing their voice clips
options.D: Have the owner assess harm to people whose voices could be cloned

questions.key_concept: Generative AI that imitates a person can harm people who never use the system, so risk identification covers them too.
questions.pre_read: Consider which step the others depend on.
questions.correct_explanation: Cloning any voice from a short clip lets a learner copy someone who never used the app, such as a relative or a public figure, and the copy can be used to impersonate them in calls. A review covering only learners misses that harm to non-users. Learners' consent, option C, protects people already assessed, not those whose voices are copied.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because uploaded clips are personal data. But encryption protects stored clips, not people whose voices a clone can imitate.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because notices set expected use. But a notice does not stop a clone being used to impersonate someone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because learners' own clips need consent. But it covers people already assessed, not those whose voices are copied without their knowledge.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the risk as a storage-security issue, and B treats a notice as a control.
Final two: D beats C because cloning reaches people who never use the app; learners' consent protects only those already assessed.
Exam cue: when generative AI can imitate a person, ask who is harmed besides the users.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. An AI aid in gymnastics judging
questions.question: A Fijian gymnastics federation's two judges score each routine independently; both now see the same AI tool's suggested deductions before scoring. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The second judge's score may now add little to the first
options.B: The judges' scores may now differ from each other more often
options.C: The tool may be untested on the federation's own athletes
options.D: The tool may learn from each judge's final score

questions.key_concept: Two independent human checks lose their value when both people first see the same AI output, since its misses and emphasis shape both.
questions.pre_read: Read what changed in the scoring process before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Two judges score independently so that one judge's misses are caught by the other. If both first see the same AI deductions, they tend to look where the tool looks, so a fault it misses can be missed twice and their agreement stops confirming anything. Testing the tool on the federation's athletes, option C, matters, but even a well-tested tool would leave both scores leaning on one view.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a new tool changes how judges work. But a shared suggestion pulls both judges toward it, so agreement rises, not falls.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a tool needs testing on its real use. But a well-tested tool still makes both judges look where it looks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tools seem to learn from use. But it learns only if someone retrains it on the scores.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes the tool learns from each score, and B expects more disagreement when a shared suggestion pulls both judges together.
Final two: A beats C because one shared AI view removes the independence the second judge exists for; testing the tool does not restore it.
Exam cue: when every reviewer sees the same AI output first, ask whether the reviews are still independent.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A KRI for an ID-check model
questions.question: A Gabonese betting site's KRI for its ID-check model is the share of sampled rejections staff overturn on screens showing the model's reasons; it stays below tolerance. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner double the sample of rejections staff review
options.B: Have staff judge each case before seeing the model's output
options.C: Have the data team retrain the model on the overturned cases
options.D: Have the data team set the tolerance the KRI reports against

questions.key_concept: People who see a model's output before judging tend to agree with it, so a KRI built on their reviews understates the model's errors.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would let the KRI show.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff who see a model's reasons tend to agree with it, a pattern called automation bias, so wrongful rejections they should overturn can stand and the KRI reads low. Judging each sampled case before seeing the model's output gives an error count independent of the model. Doubling the sample, option A, adds cases but repeats the same lean in every one.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a larger sample gives a more reliable rate. But every added case is judged with the model's reasons in view, so the rate stays biased low.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because overturned cases are useful training data. But a retrain changes the model, not how the KRI is measured.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data teams know the model. But tolerances are set by senior management within appetite; the data team supports measurement.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a retrain as fixing how the KRI is measured, and D gives a tolerance decision to the data team.
Final two: B beats A because reviewers shown a model's reasons lean toward agreeing with it, so a bigger sample repeats the lean; only judging before seeing the output measures errors independently.
Exam cue: when people check an AI's decisions to measure its errors, ask whether they saw its answer first.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A model tuned through a provider's service
questions.question: In 2024 a Bermudian reinsurance broker fine-tuned a provider's model on its treaty files through the provider's service; corrected versions of that base model have since been released. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Corrected versions may retrain the copy without testing
options.B: The provider may change the base model without notice
options.C: The copy may keep weaknesses later versions corrected
options.D: The provider's controls report may omit its tuning service

questions.key_concept: A fine-tuned copy stays on the base model version it was tuned from, so fixes the provider releases later do not reach it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each concern assumes about how the copy works.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning creates a separate copy built on the base model as it stood in 2024; the provider's later fixed versions do not flow into it, so weaknesses corrected since may remain in the copy the broker uses. Unannounced changes, option B, matter for live hosted models, but this copy stays on its 2024 base until the broker fine-tunes again on a newer one.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fixes seem to spread automatically. But a tuned copy is separate; base fixes need a new tuning run.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because providers do update hosted models silently. But a tuned copy stays on its original base, so the gap is fixes it never gets.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor evidence. But such reports cover the provider's environment, not which model version the copy is built on.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes base fixes flow into a tuned copy, and D looks to a controls report for model-version facts.
Final two: C beats B because a tuned copy stays on the base version it was built from; provider fixes reach it only through retuning.
Exam cue: for a fine-tuned model, ask which base version it sits on and how provider fixes will reach it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 3.2 (Pre-trained models monitored as part of regular maintenance); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.12 (Value Chain and Component Integration)

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 15, 26 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A hosted model for a sensitive service
questions.question: A Scottish harm-reduction charity plans a chatbot on a general-purpose provider's hosted model to coach people who use drugs on safer dosing. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner confirm the provider's terms permit this service
options.B: Have the owner add a notice that answers are not medical advice
options.C: Have the owner rely on the provider's filters to keep advice safe
options.D: Have the owner test which dosing answers the filters block

questions.key_concept: Hosted providers commonly enforce usage policies with automated checks and may suspend accounts, so a sensitive use is first confirmed as permitted.
questions.pre_read: List what each option depends on before ranking them.
questions.correct_explanation: Hosted providers commonly enforce usage policies with automated checks and can suspend accounts, and a general-purpose provider's policy may restrict drug content, so a chatbot discussing dosing could be cut off if flagged, leaving people who rely on it with nothing. Whether the policy permits this use comes before other design work. Testing which answers filters block, option D, matters, but a permitted use is the precondition for running the service at all.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because disclaimers are common. But a notice neither keeps the service running nor makes its advice safe.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because providers build safety filters. But they target general harms, not safe dosing advice for this use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because blocked answers would hurt the service. But if the use breaches the usage policy, the whole account can be suspended.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts general filters for a specialist use, and B treats a disclaimer as a control.
Final two: A beats D because the provider's terms, including its usage policy, decide whether the service can run at all; filter testing comes after.
Exam cue: before building a sensitive service on a hosted model, check the provider's usage policy and its power to suspend.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.2 (Contingency processes for failures in high-risk third-party data or AI); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-06 (Due diligence before entering supplier relationships)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.3 Third-Party and Supply-Chain AI Risk (a hosted provider enforces its usage policy with automated checks and can suspend an account, so a sensitive use must be confirmed as permitted first). Round 1 review: the stem no longer states the provider's power to suspend. Round 2 review: the key no longer echoes 'chatbot', the stem says the provider is general-purpose, and the key concept is hedged. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 15, 26 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Printed codes converted for an assistant
questions.question: A Surinamese mining regulator's assistant answers inspectors from printed mine-safety codes, converted to text by character recognition and indexed as converted. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Inspectors may ask about hazards the codes do not cover
options.B: Answers may word the codes' rules differently from the print
options.C: Some printed codes may have been replaced by newer ones
options.D: Misread limits or figures may be stated as the rules

questions.key_concept: Text converted by character recognition can misread figures, and an assistant answering from it states them fluently, so converted text is checked before indexing.
questions.pre_read: Consider who could be harmed under each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Character recognition can misread characters, especially digits, so a 2-meter limit can become 7 meters. An index built from unchecked text holds each misreading as the rule, and the assistant then states it fluently, with nothing showing the error. The data owner should check converted text against the printed codes. Replaced codes, option C, are a currency question worth confirming, but nothing given suggests the codes are out of date.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because no source covers everything. But nothing given suggests coverage gaps, while unchecked conversion points to wrong figures.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because answers should match their sources. But rewording is normal; a wrong figure, not different wording, misleads inspectors.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because printed codes age. But nothing given suggests these are out of date, while unchecked conversion is a known source of wrong figures.

tips: Eliminate: B worries about wording rather than meaning, and A raises coverage gaps the facts never point to.
Final two: D beats C because unchecked character recognition puts misread figures into the index as rules; whether codes are current is unconfirmed here.
Exam cue: when documents are converted for an AI system, ask whether the converted text was checked against the originals.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Voice assistants beside hospital beds
questions.question: A Seychellois hospital puts voice assistants beside its ward beds; each answers patients' requests and remembers past requests to personalize later answers. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Patients' voice recordings may be sent to the vendor abroad
options.B: Next patients may hear what earlier patients asked or shared
options.C: The assistants may mishear patients' requests in some accents
options.D: Each patient's requests may retrain the vendor's base model

questions.key_concept: An assistant that remembers past requests carries one user's personal details to the next person who uses the same device.
questions.pre_read: Follow one request from the moment it is spoken.
questions.correct_explanation: A memory that personalizes answers carries one patient's requests into the next stay unless it is cleared, so a new patient asking for a reminder may hear an earlier patient's name, medicines or appointments. Clearing memory at discharge is a privacy-by-design default. Recordings sent abroad, option A, need a transfer and contract review, but the memory exposes each patient's details to whoever uses the bed next.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because cross-border transfers need review. But the memory reveals details to strangers at the bedside, a more direct exposure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because speech models err more on some accents. But a misheard request is usually noticed and repeated, while remembered details reach a stranger unseen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because assistants seem to learn from use. But remembering requests stores them; it does not retrain the base model.

tips: Eliminate: D confuses a memory with retraining, and C raises a misheard request, which people notice, rather than a hidden exposure.
Final two: B beats A because memory on a shared device passes one person's details to the next user; a transfer abroad needs review but reaches no stranger.
Exam cue: when an AI remembers past requests, ask who else uses the same device or account.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A public calculator trained on clinic records
questions.question: An Eswatini sexual-health clinic network's planned web calculator, trained on patients' records, shows visitors exact risk scores; its privacy review covered only what visitors enter. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner give results as broad bands, not figures
options.B: Have the owner ask visitors not to enter others' details
options.C: Have the owner delete visitors' entries once each score is shown
options.D: Have the owner retrain it monthly on the details visitors enter

questions.key_concept: Exact outputs from a model trained on a sensitive group can reveal whose records trained it; coarser outputs reduce that signal.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would leave exposed.
questions.correct_explanation: A model can score people it was trained on differently from strangers, so exact scores let anyone holding a person's details test whether that person's record trained it, which here reveals they were a clinic patient. Coarse bands reduce that signal. Deleting entries, option C, limits what the site keeps, but the exposure comes from the model's outputs, which the review never covered.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because others' details should not be entered. But a request stops no one, and the exposure comes from what scores reveal.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because entries are personal data to minimize. But the risk lies in scores revealing who trained the model, not in stored entries.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more data can improve a model. But it adds visitors' data to training and does nothing about what scores reveal.

tips: Eliminate: D adds visitors' data to training rather than protecting anyone, and B relies on a request that stops no one.
Final two: A beats C because exact scores can reveal whose records trained the model; deleting entries protects only the inputs the review already covered.
Exam cue: when a model trained on a sensitive group is public, ask what its outputs reveal about who was in that group.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4.2 (Membership Inference); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. An assistant after an erasure request
questions.question: A Guinean telecom's staff assistant has semantic caching switched on; after an erasure request, staff deleted the customer's records and index entries. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Backups may still hold the customer's deleted records
options.B: The model may have learned the details from staff questions
options.C: Saved replies may still carry the customer's details
options.D: The erasure may need the provider to retrain its base model

questions.key_concept: An assistant's store of reused answers holds personal data outside the records and index, so deletion procedures must reach it.
questions.pre_read: List every place the customer's details could now sit.
questions.correct_explanation: A semantic cache stores the assistant's answers and serves them again for similar questions, so any answer written about this customer, with names or account details, sits outside the records and index staff cleared and can be served to other staff. Answer caches must follow deletion rules. Backups, option A, are usually restricted and restored only for recovery; the cache is live and keeps serving the data.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because backups often outlive deletions. But backups are rarely served to users; the cache is live and reused.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because assistants seem to learn from use. But questions do not retrain the model; cached answers keep the details.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because models can memorize data. But the details sit in the telecom's records and cached answers; nothing suggests the provider trained its base model on them.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes staff questions retrain the model, and D places the customer's data in the provider's base model.
Final two: C beats A because cached answers are reused live after deletion; backups are restricted copies kept for recovery.
Exam cue: when erasing data an assistant used, include its stored answers and other caches, not only sources and indexes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.10 (Privacy risk examined and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Licensing a tuned model to a partner
questions.question: A Gambian online grocer retrains its reply model, tuned on shoppers' complaint emails, after each erasure request; it will license a copy to a partner bakery chain. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the grocer delete the emails once the copy is licensed
options.B: Have the license let the grocer replace or recall the copy
options.C: Have the license limit the chain's use of the copy to replies
options.D: Have the chain encrypt its copy of the model once received

questions.key_concept: Erasure by retraining reaches only copies the organization controls, so a licensed copy of a tuned model needs terms to replace or recall it.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option changes, and for whom.
questions.correct_explanation: The grocer honors erasure by retraining, but a licensed copy may still carry the details of any shopper who later asks to be erased, beyond the grocer's reach. The license must let it replace the chain's copy with each retrained version, or recall it. Limiting use to replies, option C, narrows the chain's purpose, yet the copy still holds data the grocer must erase.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deleting the source seems to end the exposure. But the copy may still carry what it learned, and the grocer could no longer retrain for erasures.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because use limits are standard data-sharing terms. But they leave erased shoppers' details in a copy the grocer cannot update.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects files. But it protects the copy from outsiders, not erased shoppers from what it holds.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes deleting the emails clears the model, and D treats encryption as removing the privacy risk.
Final two: B beats C because erasure here works by retraining, which never reaches a licensed copy unless the copy can be replaced; a use limit leaves erased data in it.
Exam cue: when a model trained on personal data is copied out, ask how erasures will reach the copy.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Mapping a legal duty to a chatbot control
questions.question: New Zealand reserves most immigration advice to licensed advisers; a dairy-labor agency there maps that duty for its overseas-worker chatbot to a system-prompt line forbidding such advice. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner add a notice that replies are not advice
options.B: Have counsel confirm the prompt's wording covers the duty
options.C: Have the owner put changes to the prompt under change control
options.D: Have the owner test replies to visa questions for advice

questions.key_concept: A prompt instruction is not evidence a legal duty is met, since users can word questions around it; tested replies are the evidence.
questions.pre_read: Consider what evidence each option would produce.
questions.correct_explanation: A prompt instruction shapes what a model tends to say, but workers can word visa questions so the model gives advice anyway, so the system-prompt line is not evidence the duty is met. The mapped control needs evidence from replies, such as tests with realistic and reworded visa questions. Change control over the prompt, option C, keeps the line stable, yet a stable instruction still does not stop the advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because notices are common. But a notice does not stop the chatbot giving advice the law reserves.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because counsel interprets the law. But well-worded instructions are still not reliably followed by the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because prompt edits are changes that need control. But a well-controlled instruction can still be talked around.

tips: Eliminate: B treats instruction wording as the control, and A treats a notice as meeting the duty.
Final two: D beats C because only tested replies show the duty is met; change control keeps the prompt stable but cannot make the model obey it.
Exam cue: when an obligation maps to a prompt instruction, ask for evidence from the outputs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.2 Risk-Based AI Regulation and Mapping Obligations (a prompt instruction is not evidence that a legal duty is met, because users can word questions so the model breaks it; evidence comes from tested replies). questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A general-purpose assistant put to a new use
questions.question: A Bulgarian health insurer's underwriters price individual applicants' cover with a general-purpose assistant set up only through prompts; its AI inventory records the insurer as deployer. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have counsel assess whether this use carries a provider's duties
options.B: Have the owner rely on the provider's compliance for every use
options.C: Have IT confirm the provider holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification
options.D: Have the owner tell applicants when AI has priced their cover

questions.key_concept: Putting a general-purpose AI system to a high-risk use, even through prompts alone, can make the deployer its provider under risk-based laws.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would leave unexamined.
questions.correct_explanation: The EU AI Act, which applies in Bulgaria, lists risk assessment and pricing of people for health insurance as high-risk, and an organization that puts a general-purpose system to such a use, even through prompts, can take on a provider's duties: risk management, documentation, testing and conformity assessment. The deployer label may be wrong. Telling applicants, option D, is a deployer-level duty, but it leaves the larger provider duties unexamined.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the provider built the assistant. But the provider's compliance covers its intended uses, not this one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because certification sounds like assurance. But it covers the provider's management system, not this use's legal duties.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because transparency to applicants is a real duty. But it leaves unexamined the larger duties a provider carries.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes the provider's compliance covers any use, and C treats a management-system certificate as legal compliance.
Final two: A beats D because repurposing a general system into a high-risk use can shift provider duties to the insurer; a notice is a smaller deployer duty.
Exam cue: when an organization gives AI a new, higher-risk purpose, ask whether its legal role changed.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A live comparison of chatbot versions
questions.question: An Estonian stop-smoking app's developer, applying the NIST AI RMF, will compare two versions of its coaching chatbot by giving each, unannounced, to half its live users. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner run the comparison on recorded past chats instead
options.B: Have the owner add human-subject protections, such as consent
options.C: Have the owner judge versions by which one keeps users longest
options.D: Have the owner stop the trial, as the framework bans live tests

questions.key_concept: Under the NIST AI RMF, testing AI on live users is an evaluation involving human subjects, expected to meet applicable human-subject protections.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would change for users.
questions.correct_explanation: A live comparison on unaware users is an evaluation involving human subjects, and the AI RMF's MEASURE 2.2 expects such evaluations to meet applicable requirements, including human-subject protection such as informed consent, and to represent the people affected. Replaying recorded chats, option A, avoids live risk but cannot show how users respond to each version, so it gives up the evidence the comparison is for.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it removes risk to users. But recorded chats cannot show how people respond to a new version.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because engagement is easy to measure. But keeping users longest is not the same as helping them quit safely.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the framework stresses safety. But it is voluntary and expects protections for live tests, not a ban.

tips: Eliminate: D invents a ban in a voluntary framework, and C judges a health tool by engagement.
Final two: B beats A because the RMF expects live trials on people to meet human-subject protections; replaying old chats cannot test how users respond.
Exam cue: when AI is tested on real people, look for human-subject protections such as consent.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.2 (Evaluations involving human subjects meet requirements); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.6 (Evaluated regularly for safety risks, fails safely)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (under the NIST AI RMF, testing AI on live users is an evaluation involving human subjects, expected to meet applicable human-subject protections). questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Bought AI under a framework-based procedure
questions.question: A Bolivian city applies the NIST AI RMF only to AI its staff build, as a developers' framework; bought AI gets vendor checks of finances and security. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have management drop the framework for bought AI, as vendors own it
options.B: Have procurement cover bought AI through its vendor procedure
options.C: Have management apply the framework to bought AI too
options.D: Have internal audit map each bought system's risks

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF covers AI an organization acquires as well as builds, with outcomes for third-party AI risk.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would leave unresolved.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF is written for AI actors across the lifecycle, including those who acquire and deploy AI: its Govern function expects policies for third-party AI risks, and Map and Manage expect bought components' risks mapped and monitored. Bought systems affect residents as much as in-house models do. Vendor checks of finances and security, option B, say nothing about model changes, data use or behavior in the city's own setting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors build the systems. But the city answers for AI it uses, and the framework covers third-party AI.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendor management covers suppliers. But checks of finances and security do not map model changes, data use or behavior in the city's setting.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because internal audit knows risk. But mapping risks is management's work; internal audit assesses it, and doing it would impair its independence.

tips: Eliminate: D gives management's mapping work to internal audit, and A hands accountability for bought AI to vendors.
Final two: C beats B because the RMF expects acquired AI managed like built AI; checks of finances and security miss model-specific risks.
Exam cue: a framework-based AI procedure that skips bought AI misses most of many organizations' AI.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Measuring a declaration-check model
questions.question: Applying the NIST AI RMF, a Jamaican health agency measures its model, set to replace officers' checks of ships' health declarations, only against management's 3% error target. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner track the model's error rate monthly after launch
options.B: Have the owner adopt the framework's error tolerance for such checks
options.C: Have the IS auditor set the error target the model must meet
options.D: Have the owner record today's manual error rate for comparison

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF notes that AI meant to replace human work needs a human baseline to compare against, not only a target.
questions.pre_read: Consider what evidence each option would produce.
questions.correct_explanation: When AI is meant to replace people's work, the AI RMF notes that risk management needs a human baseline: without the officers' current error rate, by error type, a 3% target cannot show whether the switch makes declaration checks better or worse. Monthly tracking after launch, option A, watches the model over time but still compares it with a target, and once the officers stop checking, their error rate can no longer be recorded.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because production monitoring is sound practice. But it still compares the model only with the 3% target, and once officers stop checking, their error rate cannot be measured.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because frameworks guide risk work. But the AI RMF sets no error tolerances; senior management sets them within appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors assess targets. But setting the target is management's decision; the auditor assesses it.

tips: Eliminate: B credits the framework with a tolerance it does not set, and C has the auditor make management's decision.
Final two: D beats A because replacing people's work needs a human baseline taken before the switch; monthly tracking still tests only against a target.
